What more can be said about Portal 2 that already hasnt been said? The game takes a simple concept, and reshapes it into a challenging puzzler that will sure to make your brain cramp. You are a tester at Aperature Sciences. You have awoken from a deep sleep, and immediatley find yourself solving puzzles in order to escape the evil computer, GLADOS, who wants to make your life a living hell. You are also joined by a little robot friend with hilarious dialogue who assists you on your journey. The dialogue within  this game is what makes it a sheer masterpiece. You are constantly called fat, ungly, and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, in the literal sense, on a hourly basis, perhaps, forcing you to question whether you are what the game paints you as. I mean, the dialogue is top notch, better than GTA in my opinion. Anyway, I digress. What puts the icing on the nonexistent cake are the NUMEROUS puzzles. The learning curve is perfect, and you dont feel codled and taken care of. All in all, this game is a masterpiece, one I would put above GTA and TLOU any day.
A little late to the party, but wow! Just as fun as the original!

In my opinion this is the greatest franchise Valve has ever come out with.
This game in its entirety is genius to me; the whole concept is just amazing. It has mind boggling puzzles that are extremely creative (which now you can make your own with steamworks), and an amazing plotline with a real cinematic feeling to it when it comes to the cut scenes. There’s one scene that gives me a chill every time, and that in itself is amazing.
For a puzzle game it sure does feel like there is a lot of action in this game. It can be very fast paced at times, and slow paced at others. Which I like, it’s nice to be stood there for ages thinking so hard at one point and running around franticly trying not to die at another.
There’s an amazing set of characters which are so perfectly done in terms of voice acting. I really couldn’t think of any better match for the characters they came up with. It has awesome little secrets and things to find that really expand your curiosity even further and make you really want to know more about the goings on at Aperture Science Laboratories.
The humour in this game is wonderful, and there was more than a few times I had a real chuckle to myself, I was pretty impressed with how well it was done.
There is a lot to this game, and it really is one of the best gaming experiences I have ever had.
You are a test subject, and you are once again trying to find your way out. But a lot stands in your way.
I was pretty sad when I finished this game, as I’m not sure there’s anything to go on to turn into a future game. If there is, bring it on. I would love to once again be thrown into this world, but sadly I doubt there will be. It’s an amazing franchise, definitely one I can see myself playing again in future.
There is also a comic online on the Portal website for anyone that would like to see a beautifully constructed comic with some wonderful art that fills in some gaps and shows you how Aperture Science got to be how it is today.

I bought Portal 2 with completely reversed expectations, given my feelings regarding the first one I thought I wouldn't care about the single-player aspect and would soley focus on the coop. How wrong was I. Portal 2 in my opinion completely trumps the previous one in terms of gameplay, humor and appearance as well as story. The addition of the Wheatley character, Cave Johnson's mad ramblings and insight of GL@DoS' origins learned while cooperating with her makes for a far more gripping story than "do crap, get cake". While I was rather dissapointed with the coop mode for it's repetitive and tiring nature it doesn't mean that it's completely overshadowed by the single player portion, while it lacks a certain appeal it's simplisticly lovable and somewhat childish characters and plot bring something different to the table that's worth a taste. In summary, I loved Portal 2 so much more than Portal, even if it completely overshoots the modest charm that Portal has.

Portal 2 is a worthy sequel to the first game. Although it does a poorer job of mixing story with gameplay, both the former and the latter are better than they were in the first game; Portal 2 sports more characters, although our old friend GLaDOS makes a return as a main character and is still the most likable in the game. There's a host of new gameplay mechanics, such as propulsion, repulsion, and conversion gel, all substances that either propel the player into the air, speed up the player's movements, or makes a surface portal-a-ble. This game also provides to us what I consider to be one of the best endings in gaming history, at least for the single player campaign, which leads me to my next point: there's more than one campaign! Portal 2's cooperative campaign thrusts you and another player into the position of Atlas and P-Body, GLaDOS' personal testing androids. You'll solve very complex test chambers with a friend, and it proves to be a true meeting of the minds as you combine your intellect to complete these puzzles and achieve a strong sense of satisfaction afterwards. Aside from this, it is also worth noting that thanks to the Perpetual Testing Initiative, a free map editor fully equipped with workshop support, this game's replay ability is now as infinite as its community's imagination.
TL;DR
Better than the original, definitely worth your money.

It starts out in similar fashion to the original, with test subject Chell forced into a battle of wits against malevolent, cold calculating GLaDOS, but grows so much more. It's difficult to explain without spoiling it but it features a number of characters with famous voice actors whilst maintaining the lonely atmosphere of a rat trapped in a cage. It's funnier than the original too. GLaDOS remains the star but characters such as Wheatley and Cave Johnson will leave a lasting impression.
The puzzles are great, leaving you completely stumped one moment and feeling like a genius the next. There's few highs in video games and this won my heart and placed it as my top game of 2011.

Portal 2 is a fascinating puzzle game with a complete unique gameplay and setting. From the first second I loved it, a perfect game that should be in every steam library and thanks to the workshop you have infinitely and different content.
Like in
you play as Chell. She wakes in a stasis chamber where a voice guides her through a test before she get back to sleep. When she wakes again, the Enrichtment Center is completely overgrown and destroyed. Wheatley, a personality core, helps her to escape but they accidentally reactivate GLaDOS who separates Chell from Wheatley and rebuilds the laboratory. And because GLaDOS likes it to let Chell do some tests, you have to do that, just like old times...
GLaDOS and Wheatley are both very important parts of the story. If you know GLaDOS from the first Portal, than you know that she is very sarcastic and uses every opportunity to humiliate Chell. It's fantastic, they voice acting is perfect. Wheatley is a funny and stupid individial but don't underestimate him.
Like the original Portal, which is very short, you have a Portal Gun which allows you to create two portals [blue and orange]. If you step through one you will directly come out of the other without a loss of time. With these you have to complete the level but it’s sometimes very hard, because you have many other elements to use. These aspects include lasers which destroy obstacles or energize power outlets in order to help you progress, gels which can be used to coat surfaces and allow you to either speed run, super jump, or portal your way to otherwise unreachable platforms.
The gameplay sounds simple and it is, but the levels can be very difficult. It’s a unique gameplay that I have never seen in any other game.
This game is created with Valve's Source Engine so the graphic is nice but nothing special. It has better visuals than the prequel but you see that's the same engine. Valve did a great job, because the textures, the lightning and the physics in Portal 2 are very beautiful and fits the game perfectly. It was releases in 2011 but still looks amazing.
The performance is also nice and stable, like all Source games you can minimize the game without the fear that you can't maximize it back. I have more than 100 hour and this game never crashed and became never boring.
The sounds are the same as in every Source game, nothing more to say about it. But the soundtrack is amazing, also the voice act especially GLaDOS sounds so good and insane, it's a true masterpiece.
You are alone and without friends in an unbelievable big complex under the earth in many test chambers with a crazy artificial intelligence which let you test just because it amuses her. With the nice visual effects thanks to the Source Engine and the great soundtrack Portal 2 has a really bizarre atmosphere.
Next to the campaign Portal 2 has a coop mode with different levels. That's the best coop game I've ever played and you can only solve the test chambers if you work together. It is so much fun that I played it multiple times with different friends and it was every time a new experience.
In Addition to that Portal 2 includes a level editor and the workshop from steam, where you can upload your created levels or download test chambers from other players. This means that you have infinitely content and thats a very big argument to buy this amazing game.

Though it's hard to fill the shoes of the original, Portal 2 does a pretty great job. Tons of new story and content to play through, though GLaDOS is a bit different from what you may remember. The Co-Op mode in particular however brings back much of her original bile, as well as introduces the opportunity to play with a friend. It's been hours of fun every time so far. My only regret is that there's only so many maps to play through. Even though the game is gigantic, I still want to solve more puzzles, explore new environments and dunk loved ones in acid. Fret not, for there is an online community and although good maps with no glitches can be hard to find, they are out there. Also, if you feel up to it, as always with Source games, you get the SDK, so you can create your own environments. So get crackin' peeps. Get portalin'! For science!
P.S.: The soundtrack is fantastic!

My experiences with the Portal series are really worth remembering.
This game is what introduced me to Steam, my friend told me about Portal, and he told me it was on steam.
The hype of Portal 2 is really huge, due to it being a sequel to the original Portal, part of the Orange Box. Portal really hyped up the community with its portal mechanics (inspired by Narbacular Drop), sad to say it was really short, so the community demanded a sequel, which originates Portal 2.
First gameplay through Portal 2, puzzles are really confusing, requiring you to think outside the box. Luckily, either GLaDOS, Wheatly or Cave are there to hint the players to go through the puzzles. There are lots of new mechanics too, especially the paint mechanics (inspired by Tag: The Power of Paint). The story is good and its comedy won't bore you. The game has a well made narration, showing the good and bad sides of each character.
The other thing that hyped it up was the Coop mode. Portals alone are confusing enough, now we have two sets of portals waiting to solve tons of other puzzles provided. This mode requires lots of cooperation and teamwork, and also a keen eye on possible solutions. Portal 2 also provided lots of utilities for coop plays, like gestures to express emotions, ping to show stuff, or even timers to sync in movement.
Once singleplayer and coop was done, nothing else is able to be done besides repeating the stories or doing challenges. Until, Valve released the workshop. Portal 2 was associated with the Steam Workshop, giving players a chance to create their own maps with ingame tools and playing endless amount of maps created by other players. This revived the Portal 2 hype, having players back on the game, creating maps and playing maps. Some maps are insanely hard, some maps are for casual players who love to stroll and play around.
Puzzle SP/Co-op FPS game, challenging your mind to think outside the box while refreshing you with comedy and silly stuff. In-game Co-op features are well made. The workshop implementation also gives it a big boost, for players to come back and play new maps created everyday.

Jumping off of the success of Portal 1, Portal 2 here actually prides it self on what amounts to an absolutely FANTASTIC story. As goes with 1, pretty much 70% of it is tutorial, although it isn't as seamless as it was and you can actually feel it more this time around since the first tests each seem short at first and not really a new test to be solved, but actually trying to get you to learn the new mechanic. Where you had a free and open area to try out different ways to solve a challenge, now you have a certain number of pieces to a puzzle that you try and find the right order they go in. If you want straight puzzles and lots of 'em, they're in the multiplayer, which is also AMAZING, and with its own separate storyline. The new elements all add so much more to the game and ways any test can be completed. I would have gladly paid double for this game with how immersive the story is and of course the absolute flawlessness of the gameplay, not to mention it is purely fun.

Portal 2 is a game that puts you in a room with various puzzles to solve, using portals.
If you're playing the single player, you will be faced with quite an ominious story line with very expansive and eerie environments. Along with this, there is some good humor to go along with this game. One part will have you chuckling while another will have you wanting to leave immediately.
If you're playing the multiplayer, you are given an entirely different story line with different puzzles meant for cooperative team work, and trust that your partner will not try to kill you.
This game has Steam Workshop support, as you can create levels for other people to play through and try to solve your puzzle, or you can download other people's levels to try and solve them yourself!
Lastly, my favorite thing about this game is the soundtrack. It can be ominous, it can be epic, and it can be uplifting.
If for some reason you don't already own this game, you need to buy it. There is just too much fun to be had from this game that you're severely missing out.

I was very skeptical of Portal 2, how could anyone hope to really build on the simplistic wonder that was Portal? Well I forgot we were dealing with Valve because Portal 2 is a textbook example at a perfect sequel. It's everything Portal 1 was but more, yet at the same time without going overboard or overstaying its welcome. The story is even more involving and a terribly fun romp from beginning to end, the dialogue is even funnier than before, the graphics are more varied and detailed,  even more great tunes to test to, and even the puzzles don't stop where the original ended, instead it starts completely fresh with more crazy designs you would've never even though of! The co-op isn't a tacked on feature at all nor is it an overdone feature as both the singleplayer and co-op campaigns are superbly written and designed. Minus a draggy plot developing part in the middle of the game, Portal 2 is one of the best sequels I have ever played.

It's been a long time since i Played the first game, and it made me wonder what this installment could possibly bring to the table.However once the game started I was hooked. Portal 2 is a fantastic game. And I would highly recommend this to any gamer as well as the first one as it ties the story together.
Pros:
-The story is engrossing raising the bar and filling in the gaps left by it's predecessor
-The characters and voice acting is top notch
-There are better looking games out there, but few come close to presenting the story both visually in the environment and audiotrack with such perfect execution.
-coop multiplayer
-Painting the levels with gel is just plain fun(you know what I mean once you play it)
Rating: 10/10

Local coop (splitscreen) possible with a keyboard and a controller!
- Enable your controller, start Portal 2 and open the console in game (default by pressing the ` key in the menu).
- Load a map with the following command ("ss_map mp_coop_start" for the calibration course or "ss_map mp_coop_lobby_3" for the main lobby).
- Enable cheats on your local server ("sv_cheats 1") *
- Switch keyboard controls to second player ("in_forceuser 1")
- Enjoy Portal 2 in coop! =)
* Because you need to enable cheats to switch controls, you can't unlock achievements.
More technical information (and another workaround to enable coop) in this thread:

Extremely well put together, visionary title! Portal 2 reclaims the original splendor of its predecessor while synthesizing Portal's legendary gameplay mechanics into its own unique, well-defined experience, transcending the common pitfalls of producing a mere reiteration. While it seems unnecessary to point out, given Valve's integrity and approach to game development, it is not always guaranteed that a remarkable original translates to a respectable sequel. However, in this instance, the visionary qualities of Portal are easily detectable throughout Portal 2. No resting on laurels here. I strongly recommend giving this a shot, even if you're not particularly keen on most puzzlers.

As the people at Valve said, "Portal was a test bed. Portal 2 is a game." I cannot agree more.
Portal 2 brings the player back to mysterious Aperture Laboratories, many years after the first Portal happened.
The game is at least twice as long Portal 1 with plenty of callbacks to it. The visuals are stunning and offer a wonderful sense of time, with the original 19 chambers completely overgrown and partially destroyed. With a glimpse into the beginning of Aperture the visuals deliver again, showing just how old the place really is, and how massive.
Aside from the vast storyline, the writing is extremely humorous. Characters such as Wheatley and Cave Johnson steal the show with their witty dialogue, while GLaDOS offers the same dry humor she did in the first game, only now with more well-written insults and a surprising backstory.
The Cooperative Testing Initiative gives you a whole new storyline with a two-person style of gameplay. With four portals, the tests get more challenging.

Local coop (splitscreen) possible with a keyboard and a controller!
- Enable your controller, start Portal 2 and open the console in game (default by pressing the ` key in the menu).
- Load a map with the following command ("ss_map mp_coop_start" for the calibration course or "ss_map mp_coop_lobby_3" for the main lobby).
- Enable cheats on your local server ("sv_cheats 1") *
- Switch keyboard controls to second player ("in_forceuser 1")
- Enjoy Portal 2 in coop! =)
* Because you need to enable cheats to switch controls, you can't unlock achievements.

Extremely well put together, visionary title! Portal 2 reclaims the original splendor of its predecessor while synthesizing Portal's legendary gameplay mechanics into its own unique, well-defined experience, transcending the common pitfalls of producing a mere reiteration. Everyone knows this game is good. It has received dozens of accolades and since its release, still has a strong fanbase as attested to by the influx of community made maps. So instead of further praising this masterpiece, I'd prefer to explain some of its drawbacks.
Expect a lot of loading times. That is by far, my biggest gripe. After every few puzzles, you will be greeted with a loading screen. In some instances where the puzzles are extremely easy, you'll begin to feel as if you've spent more times on loading screens than actually playing.
Unfortunately (or fortunately), that is the only negative thing I have to say about this game. Face it: the puzzles are cleverly crafted, the dialogue is witty and hilarious. The campaigns, both single player and cooperative are decent in length. There really is nothing to dislike... well maybe hats. If you don't like hats, then you won't be too happy to see them online.
Grade: A

I would not call myself a gamer.
I doubt many others would call me a gamer either.
I really like games--lots of games. I play lots of board games, a couple card games.
I have played a variety of games throughout my life, but not many at a time, and certainly not many at all currently.
All that to say, I am not an expert on these matters. I will not waste your time reviewing and analyzing matters of technicality of which I am woefully ignorant, nor pretend to be otherwise. Let us leave it that I thoroughly enjoyed (and enjoy) Portal 2. Perhaps not through the perspective that a gamer or video game critic may experience, but I loved it all the same.
Ahem.
----
The overall experience was one of intense thinking, frequent (but always temporary) frustration at the cleverness and complexity of the puzzles, and laughter at the varying levels of wit and humor scattered throughout the game.
Portal 2 was undoubtedly the product of genius and layman, brute tech and vision, and a great deal of propaganda, I might add. It is likely my favorite video game to date. High praise or not, it is truth.
The graphics of Portal 2 were impressive, relatively smooth, and fitting to the style of the game. The landscape and interface was easy to understand and work with. Simplicity and style were interwoven with grace and compotence.
The puzzles that Portal 2 is infamous for were tantalizing at times, quite often seemingly impossible, but always satisfyingly challenging in the end. *Spoiler alert* For CoD fans, this isn't probably your first pick. Thinking caps required at all times during Portal 2, no exceptions. The ingenuity behind each map is obvious from the get-go, and I was surprised to see the consistency of strategy throughout the game. (For those of you who replay games: no worries--you won't breeze through the second time, remembering every single puzzle and how to solve it--trust me)
The story behind Portal 2 is entertaining, fascinating, and secondary, in my opinion. There are numerous secrets behind the scenes, which I would love to go into, if I were not afraid of spending any more time writing up this review. Certainly it is a game with a campaign easily played multiple times. I assure you it will take you several tries before you memorize ALL those witty quotes.
The game was amazing. I'm out of praise. I can't think of any criticisms at the moment, and I'd rather not anyway, so there you go. Buy it, it's well worth your money. Savor it and enjoy the ride!

Thinking caps required at all times during Portal 2, no exceptions. The ingenuity behind each map is obvious from the get-go, and I was surprised to see the consistency of strategy throughout the game. (For those of you who replay games: no worries--you won't breeze through the second time, remembering every single puzzle and how to solve it--trust me)
The story behind Portal 2 is entertaining, fascinating, and secondary, in my opinion. There are numerous secrets behind the scenes, which I would love to go into, if I were not afraid of spending any more time writing up this review. Certainly it is a game with a campaign easily played multiple times. I assure you it will take you several tries before you memorize ALL those witty quotes.
The game was amazing. I'm out of praise. I can't think of any criticisms at the moment, and I'd rather not anyway, so there you go. Buy it, it's well worth your money. Savor it and enjoy the ride!

Expect a lot of loading times. That is by far, my biggest gripe. After every few puzzles, you will be greeted with a loading screen. In some instances where the puzzles are extremely easy, you'll begin to feel as if you've spent more times on loading screens than actually playing.

If Portal was a tech demo of an amazing concept, Portal 2 is the full, golden release of it.  A tour de force of alternative first-gameplay, Portal 2 clocks in at 6-8 hours of awesome single player puzzles and another 4-6 hours of multiplayer.  More content is planned by Valve, and the modding community has made some stunning levels on their own.  Definitely worth picking up, especially if you have a friend who has it already. If you liked the first Portal, you won't be too disappointed.  Portal 2 is definitely more polished and refined, both visually and gameplay-wise.  The new mechanics involving things like gels and excursion tunnels work well in the Portal environment, and even better when manipulated with the handheld portal device (portal gun).  I'll admit that I expected more of a challenge like in the first Portal, but was surprised when I passed everything without a problem.  The single player campaign is also more linear with the puzzles; I couldn't find alternative solutions to solve chambers like in the first game.  The single player portion seems to primarily exist to expand on the Portal world.  It does so wonderfully.
The two-player campaign is where the real challenges are.  These puzzles were a blast to play.  Unfortunately, this portion is short and has little replay value.  Hopefully this will be changed in the future, because these were the puzzles I expected of the single player mode.

The cooperative multiplayer mode is a completely different game from the single player game... but is equally awesome!
Chronologically, the single player game takes place after Portal 1, and  the multiplayer game takes place after the ending of the Portal 2 single player game.

First person puzzle game.  Awesome!  One of the best games I've played in a while.  There aren't many games that I want to play again right after finishing it, but this is one of them.  You really have to think outside of the box to solve these puzzles.  Most of the puzzles are actually very simple once you understand them... but solving them with portals can make that simple solution very difficult to see at first.  The cooperative multiplayer mode is a completely different game from the single player game... but is equally awesome!
Chronologically, the single player game takes place after Portal 1, and  the multiplayer game takes place after the ending of the Portal 2 single player game.
I highly recommend this title to anyone who liked Portal 1.  Portal 1 was good, but Portal 2 takes the concept of Portal 1 and makes a bigger, better, and much more involved game with a much more interesting story.  And the sense of humor in the character dialog is fantastic!

Portal 2 was good fun.  The single-player story is rock solid and the world is amazingly detailed.  I caught myself looking around at things instead of playing the game a bunch of times because the world is just so inviting.  The single-player story by itself is worth the price of admission.
But then there's co-op.  There isn't much that can be said about co-op Portal.  It's something you just have to experience for yourself.  I played with a few different people and each experience was different.  It was a good time watching some of them try to figure out how to solve the puzzles while I mostly got them killed and gave up figuring the puzzles out for myself.
All around fun here and something that should be in your Steam collection.

Portal 2 is essentially every bit as good as the first game in the series, and yet that seems to leave it somehow a little short of the original in terms of resonance and overall impact.
While Portal 2 as a whole is an excellent and rather unforgettable experience, it doesn't deviate far from the original at all. The gels definitely add a new dimension to the gameplay, but not a great deal and only to about 1/3 of the whole game. As a collection of puzzles, Portal 2 feels significantly easier than Portal. Many times I found that the goal of a puzzle was not necessarily to find a clever solution, but simply to understand what the very simple but slightly obtuse solution was.
Co-op is another story. It changes the game almost entirely and is very fun to play. However, it, almost moreso than the single player campaign, lacks replay value. This is because playing with a partner whose skill level doesn't match yours can be frustrating, regardless of which side of the equation you're on.
If you don't enjoy Portal 2, chances are that I don't care for you as a human.

Portal 2 is probably one of my favorite games of all time. The writing of the game is phenomenal, not just in the hilarious writing, but in the environment as well. As the levels change themes throughout the game, going from dilapidated and plant filled, to clean and shiny, to a 60''s abandoned feel, the world is full of character.
The storyline of the game truly shocked me. I did not expect to feel any remorse or guilt for my actions. While the main character may be mute, in no way is she characterless. The actions you undertake have a permanent mark on the facility. By the end of the game, there is no room for a Portal 3.
And the puzzles. They are paced fantastically. With the exception of one chamber, I never felt like I needed a guide to solve them. While on the other side, even early on, I had to think through what I had to do quite often.
If you liked Portal 1 in the slightest amount, then get this game. You will not regret it.

I was so excited about Portal 2 I was sure it wouldn't meet up to my expectations unless the game literally sucked me into my monitor.
Portal 2 does not disappoint, but it is not what I expected ether. Now that Valve gave the game a load of cash the developers had the freedom to give the game a complexity the original lacked. More characters, a larger story, and far more complex puzzles just to name a few things. For you Portal 1 fans, Portal 2 gives you a back story as well as quite a few scenes that will make you laugh and cry.
At the end of the single player I didn't feel cheated as much as I was disappointed it was over. Then I moved on to COOP and it was like playing Portal 3. Its an entirely new story. However, I would strongly recommend playing with a friend who has a mic. The COOP saves your progress (I believe) and took us about 6-7 hours to complete if your not rushing through it.

Where Portal was too short, Portal 2 is twice to three times as long. Where Portal was too easy, Portal 2 ramps the difficulty up significantly; especially toward the end. Where Portal had a mediocre soundtrack, Portal 2 makes you want to pause the game and bump the jams.
Portal 2 is the perfect example of what a sequel should be. It addresses all of the issues it had as well as improve on everything that made it great. The great dialogue is here in spades (this is the funniest game ever made, by far) and the wonderful art style is vastly improved and solidified with help from the simply gorgeous graphics. Now throw in some co-op missions and you've just multiplied everything that made Portal great by two. Some of the later co-op levels will leave you crying in frusteration. TAKE SOME ♥♥♥♥ING NOTES FOR DRAGON AGE III, BIOWARE!

The story, characters, and writing are all just as good as the original; funny and clever.
The graphics are even better.
The puzzles, however, are not. Rather than the portals being the puzzle, the puzzles tend to focus more on all the various other tools they've added to the game, while any actual "portal" based puzzle is relegated to a "where's Waldo" hunt-and-seek.
For me, the most "difficult" of puzzles were actually just me not realizing that I had reached the end of a puzzle, and had to find that one tiny little blotch of pixels hidden either at a great distance or behind several chunks of scenery to advance. (I once spent ten minutes exploring a vast space because I had completely solved a puzzle, but had no idea where to go next).
Worse, portals increased "suction" mechanic can prevent you from solving a puzzle in a unique way.
Absolutely worth buying, just don't expect a more difficult game.

After months of hype, Portal 2 is here and having just completed the single player and co-op campaigns, I can say that it delivers. The graphics look polished, with high-res textures that look pretty impressive considering this game was made on a 7-year old game engine. The voice acting, a strong point of the original Portal, shines. Stephen Merchant is a welcome addition to the cast, and his neurotic Wheatley provides an excellent foil to the calculating and sarcastic GLaDOS. There have been rumors that the single player mode of this game can be completed in 4 hours, which couldn't be farther from the truth. I've personally gotten 20 hours of gameplay combined from both modes, and so far... it's been a blast. The game mechanics have been significantly re-tooled with plenty of new devices making for considerably more complicated puzzles than its predecessor would allow. I hope to see Valve release more content for co-op, but if not, there's always a mod community that will provide.

If you've played Portal, you'll walk into Portal 2 expecting a twist here or a turn there, but somehow Valve managed to make their follow-up game keep you guessing. The sequel replaces the original's creepiness with intensity; if the first game was fearing what might be under the bed, the second is making eye contact with it & running for your life. This is balanced with plenty of humor, lightening the mood often enough to stave off the need for numerous breaks, but thankfully not overdoing it & allowing the gravity of situations to be maintained. For those concerned about the game's length, it's easily two to three times longer than the first in single player.
The addition of co-op will surely add hours to the game's replay value & there's even some aesthetic-only downloadable content for the co-op section; for those TF2 fans whose main question is "...but will there be hats?" the answer is a resounding "Yes, there are several."
In conclusion, money well spent; a great game.

Valve expanded upon the short-burst, cinematic experience of the first Portal, and the result is a full-fledged, amazingly detailed adventure, that provides both an entertaining atmosphere and answers to a few crucial questions from the first game.
Portal 2 boasts a quality singleplayer playtime that puts many contemporary AAA-titles to shame, interesting puzzles that can literally twist your mind upside-down and a multiplayer co-op mode, all wrapped in a detailed graphical engine, and grade A+ voice acting.
Also, a starting price of ~35e is really nice for a game of this caliber.

Portal 2 is the long awaited sequel to Portal and is Valve's last game ever made in house (Dota 2 and CS:GO being handled by other devs while Valve slaps their names on them).
You know how YMS says that "Everything Pixar made after Wall-E was an after thought"? Thinking about it, it really does seem like The Orange box was pretty much Valve's Equivalent of Wall-E, the hyped up "Greatest deal of all time" (it's debatable, but for the time it was a pretty great deal) put Valve and their steam client on the map, but it also meant they were making more money off of merch and other games than Half Life could ever hope to make them. In 2008, we get Left 4 Dead, an original Valve game that was pretty cool and introduced some neat mechanics and an AI director. Then we get Left 4 Dead 2 in 2009, a sequel no one wanted, but got anyways despite valve promising to still support L4D1, however, despite this, Valve ended up porting every L4D1 campaign to L4D2 and, what do you know, ended up stopping support for L4D1, not even giving the first game a linux version for whatever reason. Then we got Alien storm, which was an awkward top-down version of Left 4 Dead, but in space, it was free but still rather awkward and not memorable. And then, we finally get Portal 2 in early 2011, a game we actually all wanted.
Portal 2 is a pretty nice step up from the first game as it's actually longer and has more features than the first game, along with more environmental variety, instead of just white test chambers and abandoned utility rooms. There's stuff like gravitational pullers and pushers, light bridges, and of course, the three varieties of gel that do interesting things. All of these really do add a lot to the game, and makes it better than the predecessor.
Unfortunately, Portal 2 would later just fade into irrelevancy to valve when they learned that they were making more money off of other people's games, esports and virtual items than any singleplayer game can bring them. While I can't exactly say Valve completely fits what the "What if valve were 100% honest with us" video has to say, it really does seem like they don't really want to make games as much as they used to anymore when they could just make a virtual hat for less and sell it to make more.

Great soundtrack full of chiptunes, but unfortunately little else about this game is good. This game could and should be so much better but instead it feels like so much wasted potential.
The controls are terrible: You'll be sliding dramatically left and right even with the slightest press of the controls, as if the entire game is covered in a thick sheet of ice. In a game where obstacles are often placed in rapid succession, this makes it almost impossible to actually avoid everything. If you're lucky, you'll grind off the side of something and get bonus points. If you're not, you'll bounce off of the very same thing and fly off the track, immediately ending the level.
The levels are procedurally generated in such a way that you can get a different track even when playing the same stage at a different time, so while this adds some variety it also makes the game feel even more inconsistent. It feels like the the music should be synced to the gameplay but it never is. This might be in part because the start-of-level animation also starts the music, meaning you can skip up to 15 seconds of the song just by letting that play out.
There are plenty of smaller quirks that make the game feel unsatisfying and frustrating. If it detects a controller, you can't interact with the game using keyboard and mouse at all; it will refuse to cooperate. When using keyboard and mouse, you have to use the keyboard in the game but the mouse to navigate everything else: you can't use mouse controls like in Audiosurf and there is no way to quickly replay a level or advance to the next without using the mouse. Smaller issues, such as an in-game timer that always shows 0 tenths of a second, pale in comparison to the greater problems with this title.

I try not to review games unless I feel like I've really experienced them but this one doesn't seem to deserve that kind of time investment.  Plot and atmosphere will often drag me into a game and this one isn't very strong in either.  Sure it's creepy, but 'house in the middle of nowhere at night' isn't exactly unique or inspired and as far as I can tell the plot is 'you're a burglar, there's a haunted house, burgle the haunted house'.
I'm unsure why, but it ran terribly on my machine which is pretty decent.  So my guess is it's poorly optimized or something like that.  I had to lower the resolution to about 1280 and turn down the graphics to get it to move without chugging.  That complaint out of the way, we'll get on to the meat of my complaints.
Tracking the sole ghost I experience in the game seems to consist of listening to it stomping around this house and trying to not get it's attention.  Problem is, the ghost is so heavy-footed that half the time it feels like it could be anywhere in the immediate vicintiy and the house feels so small that you're never very far from it.  And (again maybe it just hated my machine) when it would get me all I saw was a static square blip in front of me armed with a scream.
Speaking of screaming, that cough function was just a terrible idea.  Your professional burglar of a character seems to have a nasty cold or some of the most sensitive lungs around, and that minor and randomized QTE to not cough only distracts from anything else going on.  A purely obnoxious function thrown in to try to add more gameplay depth and challenge and I hated every second of it.
That's it, that's my experience.  Didn't manage to nab any items, didn't manage to survive for more than a moment or two in the house.  I get it a 2/10 for a spoopy atmosphere.  That was the sole high point.

Dream Catcher Chronicles is an old-school pure hidden object game. Its English translation is a bit rough and it also almost serves as a botanical vocabulary, but it is undeniable a fun little game.
Dream Catcher Chronicles: Manitou is from 2013, but its game mechanics are much older, as they consist of nothing but hidden object scenes and the occasional minigame interludes. (One of them is a match-3 type and the other is… something I still do not quite understand how it works.)
Since it lacks the modern point ‘n’ click elements, it is also short, despite reusing each of its scenes at least once. Do not underestimate it though, because the item list can be tricky. Each scene focuses on searching for potion ingredients, which mostly means animal and plant names that may require even some native speakers to look them up.
Said potions are used by our protagonist, the daughter of an Indian tribe’s shaman, who is looking for her missing husband with the help of the local spirits. Although the entire story uses a simple comic format, it has a great flow that suits this game style well enough.
It's not a bad game, but it's not a good game either. Namsayin?

Here's hoping someone else tries to do something with Native American lore - Great Idea, but it really really doesn't work in this game.  Pity.

What a disappointing game. I finished it in less than 2 hours, it has WAY less content and challenge than most other hidden object games. Every HO scene is visited twice, and they're very easy to complete -- this isn't really a drawback to me but some of the scenes took less than a minute to finish, and that's even without spamming clicks!
The mini-games are terrible:
- The 'mandatory' match-3 is boring and uninspired (the first couple of them are of the endless type, you'll just have to match mindlessly until you get the Skip button to show up), and it's even buggy -- sometimes it'll just stop dropping the stuff you need permanently. Use the Skip button.
- The potion-making thing is only seen twice, and doesn't make sense at all (by the time the Skip button shows up, you'll only be halfway through *planning* the right path to generate the final potion color). Again, use the Skip button.
- The Fire Manitu mini-game is interesting but is only used once (and once again, the Skip button shows up way too quickly). Don't use the Skip button, or only if you can't get it right after a few tries. There's only one solution that works, I'm afraid.
- And in the final chapters you get to do some offensive match-3 against adversaries, except they get 3 times your HP and way more luck, and of course there's no undo button to prevent that terrible move that just cost you your victory. And talk about lackluster combat: you can ALSO skip them, even the final boss... After beating the first opponent I didn't want to bother with that stupid boss. Clicked the Skip button. Then they showed me the end credits. Fantastic.
Other than that, the writing is mediocre, with terrible English (I'm gonna try and assume this is the Indians' way of talking), and worst of all, it's all shown in Comic Sans MS. Yes, I'm not kidding you, Comic Sans MS. What is this, a game straight from 1998?!
I'm still going to give a positive review because I enjoyed the game art, the music wasn't too irritating, and the setting is quite unusual for a video game. I didn't feel like I wasted too much time. Sometimes, you play a game that's just objectively terrible, and you'll still enjoy it, mostly because it doesn't overstay its welcome. Well, that was the case for me here. 100 minutes is just right. Just don't forget to spam that Skip button because only the HO scenes are worth it.

IN A NUTSHELL:
I'm told that Super Mutant Alien Assault is a lot like Super Crate Box, but since I haven't played SCB (and maybe you haven't either), I'll give you a quick rundown on the idea of Super Mutant Alien Assault:
The game is broken down into 3 zones (each comprised of 3 regular levels followed by a boss fight).  Every level randomly presents you with one of a handful objectives ranging from surviving until a timer runs out, to shutting off devices before they catastrophically overheat, to retrieving fuel rods from one part of the map and depositing them in another location.  Along the way, you're beset by a variety of enemies (the titular aliens) and, true to form, "game over" is a single death away.
Fortunately, you'll have access to a generous array of unlockable weapons and items scattered throughout the game--and this, in my opinion, is where the game shines.  The sheer variety of weapons and items may be impressive, but the fact that they're generally well-balanced is shocking--particularly when you consider how diverse they are.  There's the shotgun with its typical buckshot spread, the sniper rifle that pierces multiple targets, a laser that becomes more powerful as it fires, and...an electric pogo stick?
Yet you'll discover combinations and quirks that aren't immediately obvious.  Orbs ordinarily prevent you from firing your weapons while you carry them, but if you're using that electric pogo stick, you're still able to kill enemies...because the pogo works by dropping down on their heads (plus it lets you move faster!)  The explosive boomerang will injure you if it's still armed when it returns...but if you're nimble, you can kite it around indefinitely, letting it chew up enemies as you run around with your sidearm.  The "Mega Chakra" is a sloppy and temperamental thing, yet even after being abandoned for another weapon, it'll violently react to enemy contact.
And that's to say nothing of all the sidearms, explosives, defensive items, special abilities, and perks the game has to offer.  Hacking modules, a transforming blaster for a sidearm, remote satchel charges, a radioactive unit that passively accumulates the resource used for special abilities, teleporters, forcefields, etc.  The point is that there's a great variety of tools at your disposal, and many complement each other in unexpected ways.  Since each player can hold a primary weapon, sidearm, explosive, special ability, defensive ability, and perk at any given time, the combinations and strategies are surprisingly vast.  Perhaps not quite "Binding of Isaac" levels, but great nonetheless.
There's a commendable ecology of enemies, as well, bolstered by the game's mutation mechanic:  Smaller, weaker alien variations will grow into monstrous versions if exposed to too much radiation (the result of leaving them alive for too long while radioactive beacons are spilling green light everywhere) or if they pick up the green radiation pellets that drop as ammo for special abilities.  In other words, if an enemy beats the player to the pellet, not only do they begin mutating into a more powerful version of themselves, but the player is denied a valuable resource.   It's a refreshing dynamic and forces a balance between hoovering up pellets despite your tank being full, and leaving them until you need them (but risking the chance that they benefit an enemy instead).
At the lowest difficulty, the game is appropriately easy; on the hardest, the average player won't be able to sleepwalk through a run (sleeprun?).  And despite getting killed a lot at higher difficulties, I can't recall any moments where I felt like the game cheated me.
Of course, if you're still having trouble, the couch co-op allows two players to tackle all 12 levels together on one screen.  Combined with the aforementioned abundance of strange and novel items, this feature makes for some intense and hilarious moments that really amplify the game's crazier side.
PROS
+ Fantastic diversity and balance among weapons, items, and enemies
+ Mechanically solid:  Easy to pick up, but harder to master.
+ Solid pixel-art style
+ Couch co-op
+ Very responsive developer
CONS
- Strange technical issues in conjunction with Nvidia Optimus
- Limited assortment of game modes
- Level design and aesthetics can get too "samey" after a while

The players' struggle for perfection might also be hampered by the sometimes unfair obstacle placement which, while it is avoidable, requires a sort of hair-trigger reaction time that not even the most seasoned Counter Strike players have. It's when your ship is going downward on a track and then in suddenly tilts up, and it's very likely that there will be a block in the way causing you to lose a certain number of points. This can be increasingly frustrating when you've built up a lot of points up until this section and you end up losing them all to a randomly placed block. That's the issue with procedurally generated levels: you're never quite sure on what you'll get and there will be times that it does seem that the game is stacking the deck against you. While it does test your mettle, it can be frustrating and cause quite a few outbursts of profanities.

If you’ve played Super Crate Box but wished there was more to it chances are this game could fill that void.
The story in the game is pretty barebones and while I feel like it is there for the sake of it, it’s a nice addition nonetheless. Basically a fleet of alien ships found Earth and completely annihilated the entire planet except for 3 fleets of spaceships which managed to escape while carrying humans in cryostasis.
Despite Humanity’s best efforts in order to preserve our species the aliens still manage to track down the fleets and are now attempting to destroy our last hope of survival. You play as one of several robots which were tasked of safeguarding these last humans and you’re the only thing able to prevent Humankind extinction.
As for the game itself, it features 3 different difficulty settings which you can unlock by beating the game in the hardest difficulty available. You can play either the endless mode, once you unlock it, or the “story mode” which is divided into 3 different galaxies, each corresponding to one of the 3 different fleets and each galaxy consists of 4 levels with the last level having a boss. If you beat all the 3 bosses it’s game over and you win, simple as that. The game does offer local co-op but I’ve not been able to test it out, it’s a shame there is no online or some sort of leaderboard system though.
As far as I can tell the levels are not procedural generated, the game just picks one from a pool of handcrafted maps. However, each level can be played in a different way, sometimes you have to eliminate all enemies while other times you have to carry fuel tanks from one side of the map to the other in order to power the hyper drive to complete the mission. Each level can also have some machines that after a certain period of time can give you either a new weapon, a new type of explosives or HP. There are also crates that can spawn at the beginning of a level which can contain certain perks such as, double jump, dash, dodge, increased fire rate, etc. Overall the weapon variety is enough to keep a satisfying experience by having weapons such as a RPG, a lightsaber, shotgun, among others but I do wish the game had some unique and silly weapons that could potentially make things a lot more fun. As for the enemy variety, I think there’s plenty of it in order to keep the game a challenge, especially when there’s this certain machine which boost the enemies making them bigger and more powerful.
Now, in theory each level is pretty short and one playthrough could easily be accomplished in under half an hour but the more you play the more things get interesting because you’ll unlock new enemy types, new items and weapons that you can choose as starting gear as well as new robots to play as. That said, due to the fact that a single run is rather short, especially if you die in the first levels, the game has that “one more” feel to it. The game does start slow but as you progress through the levels the speed of the game ramps up and the game goes from this slow paced shooting platformer to a very fast paced and hectic one, and I guess that’s one of the things I really like about it.
All in all, Super Mutant Alien Assault is a very solid Super Crate Box clone that brings some new mechanics to the formula which can either appeal you or not, depending on how you like these kinds of games. Despite having a fair good amount of time with the game, I do wish there were more galaxies, unlockables and map layouts or even a little more focus on the story side of the game to keep me coming back to it every now and then, I also think a level editor and Steam Workshop would benefit this game greatly. And, while I do like the pixel art style I can’t really say the same for the soundtrack, even though it seems to be praised by others it just isn’t my thing.

I would call this a sleeper, great gameplay, good storyline, and mostly definitely a Hidden Object game.  It is fast paced with smooth transitions, so fast and smooth in fact one is at the end (hours later) before one realizes it.  It is not a short game though and about the average length for an HO game (around 4 or so hours).
Storyline:  Singing Star's husband White Wolf is missing, and she sets off to find him.  She goes to the Manitu (element or nature spirits) for help.  Her journey involves finding various plants and objects in different locations to use in spells.  As the journey unfolds the player meets the Manitu and learns their intentions are not always what they seem.
Gameplay:  98% of this game is HO scenes, no point and click elements or any puzzles.  Even the map is only used to move between HO scenes in any order the player choses.  There are several HO scenes for each chapter while looking for ingredients and objects needed to make a potion or later at the request of the Manitu.  The HO scenes are colorful and detailed.  (Even the chapter transition "black and white" ink drawings are quite amazing.)
A few things to note about the HO scene find clues.  1) They are unusual clues, mostly plants and animals most people have not heard about.  Since there are no hint penalties I suggest using them.  I had to hint and look up some myself.  I had no idea an ewer was a pot-like jug with a handle.  Some other examples are cane (which means cane sugar plants which look like cattails in fact), puddle (Really? A puddle of water? - How unique!), algae (and not the normal pond scum variety, but the long Sagrasso type that grow like monsterous wide bladed grass under the sea), and of course I can not forget the flying cow.  (Totally serious the clue is cow and it is flying and the player has to click on it when it zooms by.)  I have not had this much fun playing HO scenes for a while.  Such unique and unusual clues.   2) None of the find clues are unfairly hidden either.  But in every scene there are one or two that are especially cleverly hidden.  Oh the player can see them quite plainly after finding them but they blend so well, one either needs to know where they are there or really has to look for them.  3) The find clues are more and less appropriate to the settings.  Or at least to the game theme of Native American indigenous cultures (both North and South America) all jumbled together and throughout time.  Basically what I mean is there are no used tires or hammers or bicycles.  Very nature oriented with an entire education on plants, animals and birds if one is so inclined.  4) I only found one clue misspelling: broken bow should be broken bowl.  It happens (shrugs).  Can not complain otherwise about the text.
Remember I said this game is 98% Hidden Object, the other 2% is a mini-game the gamer plays twice and a Match 3 game which has various uses.  First the mini-game, it is potion making (in a cauldron).  The point of the mini-game is to change the color of the potion to a different color using the plants or things gathered from the HO scenes using a recipe chart and quite literally drawing a magic symbol over the brew.  Sounds easy, but it is not.  This is a real brain teaser of a puzzle, and if one goofs up one has to start from the beginning again. Fortunately there are only 4 things that can be put in the brew.  The gamer only plays the mini-game twice but gathers stuff to make potions often.
Second is the Match 3 game.  This Match 3 game is used as a Hidden Object scene, gathering mana orbs to make potions and boss battles.  Yes, you read that correctly BOSS BATTLES.  Boss battles in a Hidden Object game, my oh my.  Then again the player is dealing with nature spirits.  I have run into this type of boss battle scenerio before in a game called Cave Quest.  But comparing those battles to these, these will kick your butt if not careful.  Think Gems of War maybe.  Good luck with the battles.  They are tough since your opponent starts out with 2-3 times higher hit points then you do.  (No skip option either.)  My only suggestion is take your time, there is no time limit.
Beautiful artwork, great gameplay, fast moving storyline and 98% Hidden Object.  Who can could ask for anything more from an HO game? (That's rhetorical by the way, so do not answer.)
Highly recommend.

This is a decent hidden object game, if you take a few things into consideration.
First of all, although the game has a Native American setting, it has no real resemblance to any real tribe.  If you're a stickler for historical accuracy, you may want to skip this.  The game is riddled with cliches and downright silliness at times, but if you're not too serious about realism, you'll be fine.
That said, the music and graphics are quite pretty.  The game is almost exclusively hidden object scenes with an occasional minigame tossed in for variety.  There is no inventory management or item-based puzzles as in most modern games of this genre.  This doesn't make it bad, but if you're looking for a more complex game, this isn't it.
The hidden object scenes themselves are nicely done and aren't too easy.  There are some naming conventions that might be bothersome to some people, such as using more formal names for animals and plants (I'm well aware of what a Calla lily looks like, but I might be a minority there).  However, there is a handy hint button or the ever-present power of Google if anything is too weird.  I feel that the quality of the scenes outweighs the sometimes-odd naming.
Lenth of the game is pretty comparable to others of this type, maybe slightly shorter.  At the time of this review I believe I'm over halfway through at a little over an hour.
With these things in mind, and with there being no frills, extra content, achievements, or trading cards at this time, I would recommend this game on a half-price sale.  Although the game is decent aside from its quirks, it's not $9.99 worth of decent.  But I would still recommend it to genre fans, especially people like myself that tend to run out of titles to play!

The other issue that is making the game unenjoyable for me is what I can only determine to be translation issues. In one hidden object scene, a vulture was labled as a "griffin." TL;DR : There is a reason mixing first person and platforming is generally considered a bad idea. You're too concentrated on what's in front of you to both be aware of your environment and see where you're jumping. It can work when it's a secondary aspect of the game or when every little detail has been balanced and polished to perfection. This is not the case here. After an hour, the game was uninstalled. I don't doubt new game mechanics are introduced later on, but I couln't put up with it any more. It just isn't fun.
Visually, while passable, it looks pretty bland. In a game where all the action takes place in the sky, the least you'd expect is a beautifully rendered skybox. Instead you get a static one, cheap medium-res clouds in-between, and no fancy light effects.
Looking at the screenshots, you could think this has some light elements from Magrunner, The Turing Test or Portal in it, but really this is a parkour game. As such, making every element of the environnment easy to "read" should have been a top priority. Yet, it felt esthetically uninspired and artificial to me, but more importantly, hard to read as everything looks so similar and dark.
Let's talk about physics a bit. See that moving platform or that giant rolling cylinder ? Well, you can jump on them, sure, but you'll stay in place while they slide or rotate beneath your feet, leaving you to fall to your death. In this world, friction and Newton's laws are seemingly optional.
The worst part though is performance. For a game like this, you'd expect, and really, NEED silky smooth framerate. Instead you get constant micro-stuttering, no matter which resolution or graphical setting you choose. Even at 60FPS, this feels like a 20FPS experience. After a few minutes, I was starting to get a light migraine.
Have a look at the discussions if you think this is just a case of bad luck on my part. This has nothing to do with bad drivers, and better hardware won't solve anything. That the devs themselves can't see and won't fix this is mind boggling. To add insult to injury, some random guy found a partial fix :
I say partial because while this makes the game playable, I still found that the game felt smoother when forcing 30FPS+Vsync in the options, which says a lot.
Maybe buy Deadcore on a sale if you're really into the speedrun aspect, otherwise I don't see the point.

Lets preface. I dont expect this review to stay up. I see how the devs have handled criticism. I am going to be fair in this review. I doubt it will matter.
Its built on the Unity engine. There have been some really nice games built in Unity. Right now, this isnt one of them. Let's discuss why.
Graphics: Offers multiple options to alter your graphics settings. There is a slight visual difference from the lowest to highest setting. HOwever, it doesnt really matter. The graphics are pretty bad. Stills from this game are its best case scenario. The minute you move, you have flickering textures, massive pop-in, muddy colors, and the whole thing just looks outdated. There is mention of a day night cycle, which yes, is functional and included. Multiple problems here though. Its very short. At night, the game basically becomes unplayable, as its TOO dark. Flashlight mind as well be a candle. Cant see a thing. And yet you still get massive sun flare, as the devs hide the sun, flare included, behind the mountains at night. Awesome.
Gameplay: No. You have soldiers shooting you with pinpoint accuracy the minute you turn the corner. Thats fine, I like a challenge. However, heres where the gfx screw you over. You cant find them. Occasionally you will see a muzzle flash, but it doesnt matter. Since everything is muddy and streaky, you cant find anyone. Funny thing is, as the soldiers close in on you, they seem to get less accurate. I spawned once with a soldier right on top of me. Kept shooting me, and I barely got hit. Took out the sniper rifle, scoped his head, and fired. 4 shots to the head later, he died. Realism kids. Realism.
Sound: Some of the guns do sound pretty good. Grenandes need help, as the explosions are pretty bad. The rain sound cuts out at least 30 seconds before the rain stops. Other than that, its.. fine? I mean you will be noticing alot more before you worry about the sound.
Performance: This is where it gets ugly. I get it. Its early access. But guys. Come on. I have 2 GTX 980s, an i7, and 32gb of DDR4 ram. I averaged 15 fps. some spots gave me 20-25, other it became a slide show. I tried the graphics on max, then on min. Nothing. No change. Unity games I have played in the past have had zero issues on my system. I am not expecting things to work from day one flawlessly. But to release a game in this condition is a travesty.

Usually, if I learn that a game originally started off as a browser title, I enter cautiously. Mainly because there is a huge difference between being a free browser game that you go on just to kill some time and charging money for it on a professional storefront and have to download it. However, despite my original concerns, Wheely turned out to be a really enjoyable time for me and has gotten almost 6 hours of play time out of me and maybe a game I'll return to again in the future to continue playing.
Wheely is a game split up into 8 different stories, each consisting of varying amounts of stages between 12 and 15. In these stages, you're met with the challenge of getting your little red car over to the flag at the end of the stage. In the stages, you can also try finding the two hidden items, one wheel, and one miniature toy car. Completing the stage, finding the car and finding the wheel each contributes you one star for your overall performance on the stage.
As stated earlier, you navigate your car from one end of the stage to the next, however, it isn't as simple as that, this is a puzzle game after all. You have to use your environment to create a pathway and clear off any obstructions that may stand in your way. The majority of the stages are pretty easy, but there is the odd level that was a pain to try and figure out how to complete as it sometimes required timing and precision with how you used your environment. I'll give the game praise on the variation in how you actually get to the end of each stage as with each stage you're presented with different challenges so the game doesn't necessarily turn into something that's too tedious to play through. The game still has this sort of obsessive grab of you that keeps you wanting to play more of the game and leading your car to the end of each of the stories.
The stories themselves aren't really anything too good or even necessarily all that clear most of the time. They're mainly just used as a type of background or an "explanation" of why everything that's happening is happening. Some of the stories like the medieval one does offer a new theme to the levels, similar to how the Angry Birds series works, which does also show off some levels of creativity at times.
If I could name one complaint though is that I feel like the last two stories have less overall polish than the previous six. There seemed to be at times frequent glitches with actually pulling off some of the puzzles such as Wheely falling through platforms and getting stuck between two different platforms, which may also fall under bad level design for the final two stories. It may not matter all that much but I came across these issues quite a few times in the last two chapters.
The graphics in the game are bright, colorful and a joy to look at. The music department though is somewhat of a mixed bag. For maybe the first 30 minutes, the music is pretty upbeat, joyous and overall of good quality, the same music repeats for the whole game, and can later on down the play time become repetitive and maybe even annoying at times, as I ended up having to mute the music around 2 hours in.
As of writing this review, I have 5.9 hours recorded into the game, and I have completed the game and gotten its collectibles, and I did this in two run-throughs. You can probably complete the game fully in one run though if you take your time and analyse the stages to find the collectables, but by doing so this may make you not enjoy the game as much because you may spend more time just looking around the screen for a collectable, which may take up more of your time than completing the stage it's self.
Overall, Wheely was a really enjoyable, at times relaxing at times frustrating experience that offered some good challenges that will be good for both kids and adults.
Pros
+ Simple yet enjoyable gameplay
+ Bright colorful graphics
+ Challenging at times
+ Variety in challenges
+ Long play time and possibly replayability for some
Cons
- Repetitive music
- Last two stages seem less polished than the rest
Final verdict: 8/10

Spectra is a flashy cyber punk score attack game that features simple mechanics, but challenging gameplay.
The game's premise is pretty simple. Keep your ship on the track, steer it away from danger, and collect points. Hit an obstacle and you lose your current score chain. The game focuses more on the score attack aspect than actually completing the track, though for obvious reasons, completing a track gives the player more opportunity to build his or her score. There's 10 tracks total, and a hardcore version of them as well, offering the player a decent amount of gameplay.
Visually the game looks great, with a cyberpunk, almost Tron aesthetic. The music and audio are great as well, with fantastic upbeat chiptunes that fit right into the game's atmosphere. Presentation wise, I have no complaints.
Though the game is simple, yet challenging, it does suffer a little from monotony. Though each progressing track get harder and harder, it's really more of the same, but with more obstacles, or an extra turn. As far as variety is concerned, the game lacks in the department.
Overall, Spectra is a very easy to learn, yet hard to master game. It has a nice polished presentation, and ideal for the who like score attack games, or as a distraction from your more main staple games.

Polterheist is an indie horror game where you are tasked with robbing a haunted house. I was interested by the concept of pulling off a heist in a haunted house, but this is a poor attempt at a horror game.
Story:
This game is light on story. The introductory cutscene shows your van pulling up to a house, and then you are then thrown into the game itself. However, the store page for Polterheist tells you a bit more. You play as a robber with a preference for houses in very remote locations. The house you end up picking out turns out to be haunted, but that doesn’t stop you.
Graphics:
In terms of graphics, Polterheist is as basic as most of these indie horror games get. It looks like a bunch of assets were thrown into a game map and then the developer called that a game. Most of the stuff you have to steal are detailed models while the rest of the house seems to be a sloppily put together mess.
Most of the game has to be played in the dark because the ghost is alerted by the light. At times, it’s hard to see around you and at some points it seems like it was intentional so people wouldn’t notice how lazy the developers were when they were creating this game.
Audio:
The sound effects are going to be the worst enemy of yours when playing the game. The game heavily revolves around audio to be able to tell where the ghost is exactly in the house, but let me tell you this doesn’t work. At all. When you are hiding away in a room and waiting for the ghost to pass, you hear foot stomping, but his foot stomping sounds like he is on the other floor of the house while in actuality he is right outside the room you’re hiding in. This becomes tedious when you swear you hear him on the other floor, but it isn’t the case.
When you do certain things like close a door, the ghost is alerted and starts screaming and sprinting towards your location, which is an indicator for you to get out ASAP. However, this mechanic is rather useless due to the unreliable nature of the cues.
Polterheist is light on other sound effects. As for the music, it sounds like the generic stock horror songs that you can get on royalty free music sites.
Gameplay:
Polterheist is a pretty simple game to pick up, but as soon as you start playing, you notice how flawed everything is. First of all, the game revolves around stealth and almost all the time you are hiding from the ghost, trying to be as silent as possible, but this proves problematic. One of the things you have to do is not cough. Your character coughs at random and you have to press either RMB or LMB to be silent. If you click the wrong button or not click anything, the ghost is alerted. This becomes annoying because there’s no indication this is going to happen, so you have to be paying attention all the time.
The ghost is invisible, but sometimes he flashes to give you indication where he is. This happens at random and sometimes the ghost doesn’t flash at all which makes tracking him incredibly difficult.
Stealing the stuff out of the house is also incredibly difficult as you slow down while carrying objects. This includes things which shouldn’t slow you down, like a gun or a laptop. Also, it’s incredibly hard to pick up the items because the button you press doesn’t seem to work half of the time you use it.
Verdict:
Polterheist is a really bad game. Even on a sale, I think this game should be avoided because of its issues. At times, these problems make it seem like the game is impossible to finish. For the same price, you can find way better horror game worth both your time and money.
Final Rating:
1/10

After giving poor ratings this morning to a couple of other games in the "Pretty Girls" series (Mahjong Solitaire and Poker Battle), I was very pleasantly surprised by this one. Japanese (Riichi) mahjong is very different from the solitaire tile game, and it's even harder to find a good digital version. This one is actually decent, with a few caveats. First, don't attempt this complex game if you don't know the rules, because you won't learn them here. There is no tutorial, and the only available help is in a few sentences of poorly translated text. In the How to Play section, for example, you'll read this: "It lifts when hand tile is done in the click once. When the same tile is done in the click again, it throws it away to the place." And in the actual Rules section (which really just outlines the options available in this version), you'll find this example: "East round, leader is changed When leader is no ready hand."
If you're already familiar with Riichi mahjong, then you'll find the action here to be pretty fast, and the controls are intuitive. All special moves (such as chi, pon, and kan) and the dora are completely automated. There are a couple of features I'd like to see implemented. For example, you cannot arrange the tiles in your hand (that's also automated), and there is no confirmation for normal moves. More than once I've accidentally got rid of the wrong tile by clicking too fast, but these are really minor complaints. A bigger complaint is that the game itself is not configurable. You can't, for example, alter the number of hands in each round, so you're stuck with the standard 4-hand-2-round game, which will take you a while. (Saving mid-game doesn't seem to be an option, either. EDIT: The game supposedly autosaves on exit, but it hasn't worked for me.) Sounds and music are well done, and there are even video resolutions available, which is a rarity in this series. Unfortunately, it lacks multiplayer, but you can find that on several browser-based versions if that's your thing. Because of the solo-only play and lack of game configuration options, the current price point of US $15 is about $5 too high, but it's frequently on sale and has been bundled twice already. Wait for a sale, and then pick it up. Recommended.

I've been following this game since I first saw it pop up on Steam Early Access. I'm a fan of Super Crate Box. It reminded me of gems from a bygone era like the NES Mario Bros (not Super) that was a simple arcade platformer with an endless array of levels. Super Crate Box was an iteration of that same arcade formula, and this game in turn, is an iteration of the Super Crate Box formula.
There's not so much procedural generation as there a randomization of game modes and the creatures and weapons that spawn in each level. There are bosses, and they appear at appropriate intervals. There's also an endless mode which is more reminiscent of the aforementioned titles.
In its simplicity, there is a lot of fun to be had here. I haven't put in a ton of hours due to only experimenting with new patches during early access, but I intend to play it for a long time yet to come. Super Mutant Alien Assault is a mechanically excellent title that yearns to be experienced, and you'll be particularly aware of this if you are from older generations who still visited local arcades. Super Mutant Alien Assault is the unofficial Super Crate Box sequel that all of us have been waiting for.
Super Mutant Alien Assault as stated before is a very similar game to Super Crate Box which is a one screen platformer where the main goal is to survive long enough to see the other level, but this game has a ton of different objectives. A few of the things that levels have you accomplishing are surviving, bringing fuel, boosting thrusters and cool down pillars which will blow up and of course at the end of every galaxy there's a boss fight waiting for you.
Super Mutant Alien Assault takes place in the future where Earth has blown up and Alien ships are chasing human ships to destroy them and you play as a little droid who has to save humanity.
While the story wasn't needed it was certainly a very nice addition to an already pretty good game.
The graphics are great. The pixel art style is beyond awesome with the environments and the enemy designs being really cool.
The soundtrack is also really sweet, with techno and dubstep music accompanying the fast and tense gameplay. It might not be everyone's cup of tea, but I personally loved it and I think you will too.
The game has three galaxies to go through and each one of them is 4 levels long. All levels are randomly generated and when you die the levels will reset into something new which is a very welcome addition.  To unlock the higher difficulties you will have to play through the game without dying once (which I wasn't able to do) so people who want replay value will have a lot to go through.
But people who don't like that big of a challenge don't worry, because after you unlock a galaxy you can start the game from whatever galaxy you want.
The game took me 1 hour to complete the three galaxies, but there's a lot of stuff to do. As mentioned before you can go and play through it without dying and there's also endless mode where you can put your skills to the test and try to survive as long as possible.
I didn't encounter any problems with the game whatsoever. It ran smoothly from beginning to end, so I doubt any of you will encounter any problems.
Super Mutant Alien Assault is incredibly fun and is definitely a game I will come back to in the future. It's incredibly fun and without a doubt the best Super Crate Box type of game I've played to date.
Pros:
+ Insanely Fun
+ Great Soundtrack
+ Awesome pixel art style
Cons:
-  Only Three galaxies
