I really liked this game. It nicely combines elements from other popular horror games, most notably Outlast (immersive exploration of dark + disturbing environments), Amnesia (you're chased by a mostly unseen danger, and encounters with enemies are intentionally short, meant to keep building tension) and Slender (you go around collecting "pages" in order to advance, and the more pages you have, the more dangerous it gets)
To aid you in the finding of these pages you get glowsticks, which highlight containers where the pages _might_ be hiding.
Also, you do not have access to weapons per-se, but instead are given flares to make enemies "disappear" for a little while.
Those are the only items you get, and can carry a maximum of 4 (each) so yo can't go around spamming them
Problem is, once you get the hang of it, it becomes quite easy to move around and never really be in any danger. By "getting the hang of it" i simply mean explore before collecting pages, learn the basic layout of the level, don't spam glowsticks/flares and that's it.
Worst thing that can happen is you hit a dead end with an enemy behind you, but even then you might be able to just run past it without dying (and you auto-heal pretty quick so the damage taken isn't really an issue)
Also, the protagonist never runs out of stamina, so you can basically run like hell for the whole playthrough and effectively reduce enemy threat to zero
The game takes you through a total of 4 environments: Hospital, Prison, Sewers and Forest. Personally I found the Hospital and the Prison to be the scariest (mostly because they're very closed spaces with long dark hallways and it's really easy to imagine the suffering the residents must've endured), the other two are just not that creepy and are too illuminated for my taste
The story is fine, enough to hold the game together. You learn most of it from the "pages" you collect (which can be newspaper excerpts, diary notes, institutional documents, etc.). Keep in mind that you do not necessarily find them in order, and there's also a lot of them so you probably won't be collecting all in the first few playthroughs.
Graphically it's amazing. I do not have a powerful computer and it still looks great. The environments are very well done and seem quite realistic (which just adds to the immersion aspect of the game)
The ambient sounds are pretty neat too, they really help in building up the terror atmosphere
Controls are OK, i just had this issue where sometimes i was standing in front of an object and tried to use it but couldn't, and had to step back and move around a little before the game actually showed the "Use" prompt (which is kind of annoying when you're in a dangerous situation trying to run away)
TL;DR this is an excellent scary experience, packed inside an average game

I have not played this game for long, just over 10 hours I think. I even had to restart my game due to the early plant spawning bug. I understand that some people will get very frustrated and leave negative reviews and bombard the discussion forums with rants, but I think a lot of people have forgotten what early access means. There are now so many Early Access games that they have become the norm and people are "demanding" higher and higher quality on day 1.
When you buy an Early Access game, you:
- Pay for a vision of a game, not a final product. You need to help shape the game
- Must be prepared to see and experience lots of bugs...potentially scratch around in your pc settings and folders for fine tuning
- Be a tester and provide feedback.
- Restart the game, from scratch, multiple times!
If you develop an Early access game, then you make use of a lot of placeholders...things that might seem strange when people first see them, i.e. weird crafting recipes, strange AI behavior, weird resource containers, empty spaces, non conventional FPS mechanics...and I can go on. The reason for this refers to my point #1 above; you need to tell them how you would like the placeholder to function in the final product. Why will the developer spend days and days on a feature and then get negative feedback upon EA release? Rather put something in place that works relatively well, so that people can see your intention and provide feedback.
All the things mentioned above are applicable to Hold Your Own but with one big difference...the Developers are very, very active. I mean they have made over 10 updates since launch! They are always in the forums answering questions. Yes there will always be bugs, but compared to other EA titles, the game is running quite smooth for its launch month.
The developers recently also shared their ideas on what might come next for community feedback, which is something really great to see!
So, after reading my babble on how you should look at early access games AND you are still up for some grinding to test your patience then buy this game! There are a lot of content to keep you busy for hours and hours and you will get more than your money's worth!

Ok so after loggin 27 hours into the game here's what I have to say!
The game itself is absolutely fantastic, easily will have over 1000 hours into this one, the devs themselves put out updates at least once a day and actually listen to community feedback.
The game itself already on launch has TONS for you to do, granted yes there is some balance concerns that need to be taken care of but I'm not worried about it one bit, they will get it taken care of.
Now onto the gameplay and whether or not this game is for you.
If you are looking for a game that just hands everything to you, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!
This game requires quite a bit of farming but it is VERY rewarding when you get a solid foundation and survival becomes much easier once you have a "solid foundation" to support yourself with.
The hardest part of this game is getting your foundation setup in the beginning, once you have your forge, workbench, and mill, this game becomes very fun very quick. The early parts of the game are rough and difficult for sure, hunters and wildlife walk over you as you are not prepared for them, once you have your foundation, got some ammo crafted and possibly your rifle/shotgun equipped, the table turns.
This game has TONS of content already and it is going to keep you busy for some time though, especially when the devs are releasing patches every single day.
Only complaint, and I'm sure it will be fixed soon is mechanical parts, you need them to craft the forge and in the beginning it is pure RNG, your either lucky and get it early, or your luck sucks and you get it later on, however the forge is needed very early and having to wander for 3-4 in game days to find them can be a hassle, I personally dont think the forge should require mechanical parts at all tbh.
Other than that, I consistently find myself on my toes and the edge of my seat quite frequently as I scout through these large islands looking for ores and loot just wondering when a bear/wolf/hunter will hapily show up and blast through me, once I hear that howl/growl/hunter speech I found myself constantly being paranoid (especially at night) wondering where the are at and who is going to throw the first shot out.
Game is pretty much balanced for the most part, some tweeking is needed but it isn't terrible at all. You can definintely get far in this and they even have to option to dumb down the difficulty if you wish.
All in all, a wonderful game and wondeful development team, this game will be fantastic when multiplayer comes out if they choose to do it right and make it with dedicated servers that you can host yourself.
Do I recommend? ABSOLUTELY!

Disclaimer: I was generously given a free copy of Labyronia RPG with the understanding that I was expected to review the title after spending some time with it.
Before I even began playing, I already had a gripe: Labyronia was not built for HD. Yes, I know that the art style mimics that of old SNES RPGs but that is no excuse for looking absolutely janky when in fullscreen. Following up the poor initial presentation was a story that was... cheesy? I find it difficult to accurately describe it. There are Gods who have a super power ancient artifact, non-gods are at war with them, non-gods lose and the world is fractured into X number of factions/regions, etc. It’s not quite “cookie-cutter” but very generic for these types of games.
Speaking of broad stereotyping of RPG maker games, the opening scene-as if following the cliche template bullet for bullet-begins with you waking up in your bedroom. At least others give some quasi-convincing exposition for why you of all the inhabitants of the world are going to begin a journey to defeat the prior specified evil. Labyronia opens with “Time to fight this evil, which I am qualified to do because I have magic and skills. Let me get my sword out of the chest.” I don’t think a game has ever motivated me less.
So what was my gameplay experience like? I wandered around the room and clicked on things (like you do) bringing me to the first straw: the default key binding for interacting with anything is O (B for 360 pads). Yes this is a almost pointless gripe, but I was curled up and comfy in bed with no desire to get up to the keyboard to remap it. I sucked it up and headed out side, using the button ubiquitously responsible for cancel/escape to talk to people. In the process I managed to open my inventory, a critical RPG feature which I have no idea how to access since the only button pressed thus far has been O/B. This led to the acquisition of straw number two. I got out of bed determined to figure out all the buttons once and for all via the F1 menu. This was the most horrendous mapping interface I have ever seen; gamepad buttons were mapped to random letters with no explanation as to what they actually did. I couldn’t be bothered to decrypt this menu so I returned to the game for the final straw. I COULD NOT leave the inventory screen. For those who are thinking “Oh, you just don’t have the button mapped to the controller correctly”, you’re right. Do you know where else it wasn’t mapped? ANYWHERE. I pushed every-and I do mean every- button on the keyboard and mouse and nothing did more than give me a rude buzzer.
RPG Maker shovel-ware is a dime a dozen (often literally) and unless you offer something mindblowing out of the gate, any small flaw or defect can become a dealbreaker. I have a key for Labyronia RPG 2 which is next on my roster; here’s hoping they have polished it up considerably.

Labyronia RPG is a classic turn-based RPG in the style of Chrono Trigger and the earlier Final Fantasy titles. As an RPG fan, there is little not to like in this title. There is world-adventuring, dungeon-crawling and puzzle-solving. There are small villages and larger towns, each with their own style and feel. There is lore to the game, revealed in books and scraps of paper throughout the game. Hidden in caves and dungeons all over the map are rare items and secrets, and players should take note of anything unusual they see to come back to.
A fundamental aspect of the combat are Auras, derived from Cues found around the game world. An example of this might be an angry chef, who gives you the Cue for a flame attack. These Cues are scattered all over the place and serve as a fun and lasting impetus for players to really explore every nook and cranny of the world.
The story is sparse and anodyne at first - stay with it. It really picks up, especially towards the end. I feel like the developers really caught the atmosphere of world-changing events well. The climactic boss battle felt grounded in the game world's events - not only difficult, but meaningful. It felt as if the outcome mattered, and the sense of reward when beating something which makes you feel that way is exactly what I play videogames for.
The music was great, even the omnipresent world music I never tired of. The enemies are varied and interesting, a far cry from the re-coloured skins of Final Fantasy eg., and helped give the dungeons they inhabit their own distinct atmospheres.
My only negatives with this game were as follows: the lack of direction - often I was very unsure where I was going and what to, and I could see how this might put a more casual gamer off; the confusing maps (looking at you, frozen field, forest and desert) that take far longer to traverse than should be necessary, and SPOILER
And then MEGA SPOILER
Some players may also have trouble with the game's difficulty, particularly at the start. All I can say is to stick with it. Longtime RPGers should have no problem, and more casual gamers will certainly find that grinding for a level or two or finding a new Cue will make once-impossible foes much more beatable.
If you take the time to look past the admittedly minor problems, you will be rewarded with an entertaining, nostalgic game based around a solid combat mechanic and set in a colourful, vibrant world. I finished the game in one 12 hour playthrough and there is still more to do. For its price, Labyronia RPG is a steal and I would highly recommend you buy it.

You can also find good gear that you dont know what it is, Lore skill lets you inspect them so you can equip/sell them.
Then threre is persuasion and quite a few others that give you different advantages and perks. The trick is whether or not to use your level up points towards combat or other skills.
Combat is rather tough as well. From early on its clear things can kick your♥♥♥♥♥ Ive found taking things slow in appoarching enemies works well. Good party placment can mean alot so if you get the 1st move you have a good start.
I ussualy get my tank to run out all "hey guys look at me" and the enemies ussualy focus on him. Which leaves my other guys to dmg them up and heal. So yea the combat system might not be that complicated but dont underestimate party placment. also food is life lol.
Overall im enjoying the game alot.
A few cons when it comes to the interface but i guess it adds to the hardcorness a bit. Like when you level up and allocate points, theres no fooling with them or backtracking before you commit them, once you hit that + button they are there to stay. The mini map/big map could be more useful but i suppose that adds to the challenge as well.
Will come back and add more once i get further into the game and see how the story> mid game> end game play.

Classic RPG with modern sensibilities.

This game seems to take inspiration in equal parts from Ultima VII and Elder Scrolls: Daggerfall, both for good reason--heavier on Ultima for the mechanics.
The atmosphere is great and really fun.  The big publishing houses just don't make them like this anymore, and this is yet another example of us getting what we want via Kickstarter.  I really look forward to playing this game more, to seeing how the community reacts and what enhancements get made, and whether there will be expansion packs, DLC or sequels.  Orphic has a very good thing going here.

This game is great, I initially played the concept demo and loved that and when it came out I torrented it but soon decided to buy it if not for the achievments then at least to support the makers of such a cool game.
This game shows what can be done when a simple concept (first person platformer about climbing a tower with a focus on speed) is done well. The controls are tight working around the limitations of platforming in first person (as any half life player will be aware of) and using its strengths (shooting mechanics and air dashes). This combigned with great level design which encorages exploration and the taking of alternate routes reinforcing the ideas of speed all helped along with the scattering of collectables cleverly placed so that finding them is a fun and rewarding challange.
The music and visuals come together to give a great vibe and the first time you see the tower in all it's glory you will stop and stare. It looks like the cover of some wierd prog-rock album cover (looking at you Dream Theater) but a game.
Games like this truly showcase what the unity engine is capable of.
If your a fan of games where "iteration for perfection" is key and you like fast paced puzzeling where quick thinking can often save you after you make a mistake, I you like CS surf maps and climbing a tower this game is for you.
Mandatory cons section:
This is a FPS platformer, you have to be resonably compitent with first person games to get the most out of this without getting frustrated.
The story is a bit weak but it's such a small part of the game that you can ignore it (Mario's story ain't much to write home about either you know)
Performance wise I don't know how well optamized it is. I have a pretty stong PC and it runs smooth wiht one excetpion. My I recommend doing some research if you PC is below average, might be nothing.
Overall though, great fun!

At it's core, this is a speed running game before it is a platformer. With sharp visuals, clean controls and a fitting sound track it's an easy game to lose time to trying to shave that short second, but beware, on your first playthrough be prepared to die ALOT.
The game relies on precision movement and quick reflexes and will punish you off you're off the mark. Look for checkpoints as you play through as they will save you a lot of time, and hence comes the risk when trying to cut corners; skip a checkpoint, and be punished if you screw up. This also plays into the routes, some are harder than others, some have fewer checkpoints, but if you plan to go for it, you can shave off minutes if you're successful. Due to this, it would be nice if they introduced a way to revert your checkpoint furthur, say, previous or 3 checkpoints before. It would make the overall game more casual friendly as some of these alternate routes, once you start on them, you're not going back... In this sense, the game pulls no punches. Shaving off minutes becomes really satisfying given how punishing trying to do so can be. Practice and memorise if you want to feel any real satisfaction, otherwise, this game is probably not for you.

I played Trails in the Sky FC and SC extensively on PSP before going onto here for the 3rd. Of course FC and SC are NEEDED to be played before this.
Overall the series has the best world building I have seen in video games as a whole, and the characters are top notch as well. Combat is strategic and fun throughout the series and the stroylines are consistantly good. 3rd keeps up this trend while also creating excitement for what is to come. This is now my favorite trilogy in gaming and I cant wait to play the other stories taking place within Zemuria.

Here we are at the end of the sky trilogy. Set 6 months after the conclusion of second chapter, we follow the adventures of mysterious priest Kevin Graham and his new partner as well as childhood friend Ries Argent. A routine mission for the septian church quickly evolves into an unexpected adventure where the past of the sky cast is laid out for all to see. Alright now, the 3rd is a tad different from the Trails games that came before it. Trading out the sprawling npc filled world of Liberl for dungeon crawling Phantasma. As first I wasn't sure about this change in design, but where the 3rd shines is character & gameplay. The entire sky cast returns along with some new faces for one last adventure, featuring a whopping 16 playable characters. The 3rd's narrative is very focused on Kevin, Ries and their connection to the main conflict, but everyone has their moment in the sun. Scattered throughout Phantasma are various doors which flesh out the characters, world, and foreshadow events in future Trails games. Every character has at least one door dedicated to them and they also provide in game rewards should you decide to pursue them, they are completely optional. Now it goes without saying that as a 3rd entry, that you should play the other 2 games before touching this one. As the characters are the heart of Sky as well as this game. While the events of this game lead into the Crossbell arc, you do not need to touch this game to understand cold steel. Aside from a reference or two. Still I recommend the heck out of this game. Trails in the Sky is a great trilogy and I'm grateful for the memories it has given me and many others. I say if it suits your tastes check it out.

+ The Moon/Star doors. I'm reluctant to even call them Side quests. DO NOT MISS THESE! Some of them are incredibly important to the overall plot, while others do a great job of fleshing out events from the first two games.
- Majority of the game is made up of reused areas from the first two games. Several of them end up feeling lifeless due to the lack of NPC's.
- Being forced to only use 4 characters at once. It's torture!
- I could have done without the mini games (The Sun Doors). Would have preferred more Plot in the form of Moon/Star Doors. The arena mini game was nice though.
Trails TC is an epilogue to the first two games, wraps everything up very nicely, and sets up for the "Crossbell Arc". It's an absolute must play if you liked the first two.
Final Score - ★★★★☆

I had to spend some time thinking about whether I would hit "Yes" or "No" for "Do you recommend this game?".  The game started out pretty awesome.  It was obvious fairly fast that this would be a crawl through one dungeon, but the first floor was really fun and I was enjoying the combat and the pacing.  The game stopped proceeding at an enjoyable clip, however, as I accumulated more characters and unlocked more side stories, many of which suffered from dragging on, forcing me to explore areas and dungeons that I had already done in both the first and second games, or had me build up characters who were only in that particular side story.  Also, unlike the first floor, many areas of the overarching dungeon were just areas from the first 2 games, which I had already explored twice.
There were many times when I couldn't wait to just be done with this game, but when it's good, it's really good, like the other games from the series.  Building up parties from the huge cast of characters, with plenty of high-level gems available and plenty of skills already unlocked, is really fun when exploring new areas with new content.  If the whole game had been like that, this game would be easy to recommend.  Also, this game had a considerable amount of buildup that I'm sure is relevant to the next 2 games in series, which are currently not available in English or even licensed at all.  I would have felt more excited for all the foreshadowing and buildup that occurs in this game if I had a reason to believe I would ever be able to play the next 2 games.
One last thing that really helped me decide to recommend this game is the music.  The Falcom sound team was in top form for this game...the tracks that are new are amazing and possibly the best of the whole series.  I always enjoyed listening to this game, even when the parts I was playing weren't that interesting.

At first I felt apprehensive playing Daylight, feeling it did a pretty good job of building up an oppressive atmosphere; however so little happens (and what does  is incredibly predictable), that my mood quickly changed to frustrated, and soon after; boredom. For example the random closing of doors had me spooked at first, wondering what I was going to see when I opened it... Nothing ever appeared. Things get knocked over or gently pushed across the floor, but they're completely unconnected actions; it's not to lure you in a particular direction or deter you, it’s just a random event that the developers thought would be spooky. Any fear I experienced came from my own expectations of what a horror game would involve.
The game boasts procedural content; however on the two occasions that I died (once because a ghost spawned right next to me, the other because I fell into water and couldn’t find a way out, exciting ways to go) I didn’t see much to support this. The layout of the area seemed to stay exactly the same, only the letters that you’re tasked with finding seemed to move. If there is more to it I certainly didn’t see it, and if you’re going to claim that each playthrough is going to be different, the game either needs to be good enough to warrant that second time or offer some incentive to. The game fulfils neither of those. The rooms and corridors are generally devoid of content and all look practically the same for a given level, to the extent where it feels like there are two sets of corridors and two room types. Procedural content is pointless if you only experience it once.
There's a few different areas to experience, with you being blocked off from the previous one each time you progress, so while there are no loading screens after the initial one, these serve as obvious barriers to save them having to keep too much geometry in memory. That may sound like trying to delve too much under the hood, but the knock on effect of the game play is that the game areas feel incredibly small, and not confined in the “good” claustrophobic way you'd want from a horror game.
Glowsticks are provided that highlight objects you can interact with when used; however not only is it not really necessary, it’s usually pretty obvious what you can click on, but it bathes the world in a garish shade of green. The only weapon you have against the shadows is a flare (no idea why), but it takes so long for the lighting animation to finish that if they’re close you may as well just run. Also, as per the silent hill radio, if a shadow is nearby the phone screen flickers, meaning; the moment you notice that, light a flare and spin around, since all shadows are killed instantly by it there is no danger at all in the game. The game provides a “threat” meter on screen, which gradually fills up as you find remnants, which I assume is supposed to be tied to shadow spawn frequency, however I've had shadows constantly spawning every few seconds with only a sliver of the threat meter filled in.
As such the game becomes a tedious chore of looking around the current environment for letters that are marked with a red seal, though the game doesn’t provide any context as to why these letters are littered around. Finding all the ones in the level spawns a sigil in the maze room, no indication as to why there are maze rooms in each level, which you then take to some aura… thing, which blocks the exit to open up the next level. Again, no explanation as to what the mysterious power that blocks your way is.
Something that really brought me out of the experience was Sarah's insistence on calling out "is someone there?" and the like, while I'm trying everything in my power to remain inconspicuous. While I understand it sells that Sarah is her own character and is affected by the situation, everytime I'd assume it was provoked by something and start spinning round trying to work out what it was, unfortunately there never seemed to be any specific trigger, which got really tiresome after the first few times. The other use of audio isn’t particularly noteworthy, you’ll hear the assortment of effects you’d expect from a horror game, but they never appeared to be tied to anything in game.
It took around two hours to finish the game, which, considering how little fun it is to play, may be some small solace, but even at the reduced preorder price I paid, I felt ripped off. Regardless of how long it took to beat though, the gameplay is essentially 15 minutes long; once you've been through the first environment you’ve essentially experienced all you’re going to with the game. The “puzzles” (if you get stumped moving a box into position or finding a switch to flip you can remove the quotes) are completely unnecessary and offer nothing to distract you from the tedium at hand.
The story itself is competent enough, and put into a more tailored experience where the environments you go through actually mean something rather than being a conduit for letters, it’d be fine. It really is a shame that the gimmick of the game is what ultimately fails it. I’m not going to say the game is absent of horror, I’ve been to plenty of movies where the rest of the audience has been in shock and disbelief at something I’ve shrugged at, but for me, Daylight was one of the mildest horror experiences I’ve had in a long time.

Uniball is one of the few games that I've played that is entirely skill based.  The basic mechanics are simple and the ships perform identically, which allows individual skill and team play to dictate the outcome of games.  Good players and teams will seldom lose to opponents with less skill, but really this is how it should be and is no different than any other sport played on a field or court.
But this shouldn't discourage newer players.  The game is a blast to play at any level of skill and the staff and player base are eager to help new players find their way.
In addition, it's possible to create private games where new players can play against their equally newbish friends and be terrible together, which is actually a lot of fun.

Outside of the occasional RPG or party game, I don't play too many video games anymore, but Uniball is the type of game that I never feel "too busy" to play.  The game is very strategic and should appeal to sports fans all over the world.  There is always the opportunity to get better and the people around you push you to do so.  The chat room feature also encourages connections past just the game play, which helps strengthen the community.  I would recommend this game to anybody looking for a game that challenges them mentally and discourages going through the motions.

Ok.  So I'm enjoying this game so far.  The visuals are great, it seems to perform well, and there's a decent amount of basic tasks you can complete.  This game IS Early Access (as is being mentioned alot) so remember that.
I find there are many frustrations that I can only attribute it to being Early Access.
For a first-person survival game (of which there are MANY in the genre) it is probably one worth looking at, though it doesn't really offer anything super unique you can't find in other games implemented better.
Some of my worst frustrations are as follows:
A)  Everyone and everything is either scared of you or wants you DEAD.  I find that once a hunter targets you, it's either kill or be killed.  You can NOT run away from a hunter.  They will shoot at you and hit (guaranteed) whether it's day time or the thick of night.  So avoid them, or kill them.  (running out of ammo is suicide)
B) Combat is frustrating at this time.  If you start running from a wolf or hunter, you can't bead your weapon on him while you are running. You have to stop running, aim your weapon, then start running backwards again.  More of an annoyance, but it has cost me my life several times.
C)  A hunter will kill you in 2 or 3 unerring shots.  They will NEVER miss, and they will always shoot at you.  Avoid them unless you are full health because even if you kill them, they will get at least one hit on you.  You can NOT pick up their shotgun (which is mind blowingly frustrating) but you can get their shotgun shells.  WHEN you die, you lose 5 from your overall health, and there seems to be NO way to get it back.
D)  Night time is a frustratingly useless half of the game.  The only thing you can do is gather enough resources in the day so you can just craft craft craft at night.  I find I can wander a bit, but my torch gives me about 5 feet of visibility, and if you happen to run into another hunter, or a wolf, you are dead.  Stay near your base foundation, as it seems to be a safe spot for you.  My frustration of it is compounded by the fact that even though you BUILT a bed, you can't sleep on it to bring the day quicker.
E)  Nails are frustratingly hard to come by.  You can earn enough in the very early game by doing the sanctioned quests, but later on they are impossible to find.  I haven't yet built a crafting table, so I don't know if you can built them.  I assume so.
F)  Do NOT try to swim across to the next island.  You will reach an invisible wall about 3/4 of the way across.  However, if you find a ferry, there is some mysterious 'requirement' that I haven't been able to meet yet that will let you cross.
Anyway, I will play for a bit longer, as I enjoy discovering some of the goals (Trying to build a crafting table, but you need a forge and at least 100 iron to do it.)
Certainly some potential.

* Gathering/Crafting/Farming system is good. Typical of most survivor game. There's a little RNG involved to craft some items and find some resources. Crafting starts off with basics like camp fires and expands to making stoves. I also like the ability to raise animals via the husbandry system.
* Traders - Sometimes they will be your main source for certain supplies.
* Helicopter - I mean it's a helicopter. Not everyone likes this but I think it adds to the exploration.
* The world - The world consists of islands to explore. You can reach islands using the ferry once it's unlocked. Later on you can craft a helicopter to fly to other locations. You can also swim to some of the islands. I think this will allow for future content as new islands and locations can be added.
*Developer - They've been very active. They are listening and making changes based on community feedback. They are also reponding to bug reports and pushing out patches on almost a daily basis.
There are things that need to be worked on. The combat system needs to be improved. The hit boxes are weird and you will miss enemies a lot. Weapon damage also needs to be adjusted to justify the expense of later weapons. Some structual changes to base building need to be made.  If you set a platform at its highest height you can't walk under it even though it's open underneath. Also need more variety of base parts. As I mentioned before this is early access so expect bugs. I've had to start over because fixes are not always retroactive. I also expect a lot of the issues or shortcomings will be addressed in future updates.
I'd recommend this game to any survival game fan. I think it's definitely worth $14.99.

Labyronia RPG is a classic RPG adventure game made from the RPG Maker. As the main protagonist, your main objective is to retrieve the pendant of Labyronia in order to save and reunite the realm of Labyronia. The game gives a very nostalgic vibe to avid RPG gamers especially to those who have played the classic Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest series. The game features the traditional turn-based battle system and also the classic on-field puzzles that you need to finish in order to progress the main story. The game also features a mix of different monster encounter designs throughout the game. You encounter actual monsters roaming on the dungeon maps while you also encounter random monster battles on the world map.
Labyronia RPG is a decent and good RPG game but the only problem I see is the merciless AI of the monsters. There will be times that you'll encounter and battle a set of monsters that will take you down with a series of attacks without giving you a chance to at least make a move. I don't know if the developers did it on purpose but there will be times that it can be a bit frustrating to players especially in cases when you're trying to strengthen your character and you accidentally bump into that annoying set of monsters.
Still, I recommend this game to big fans of classic Adventure RPG games. The game would even be worth more if you can get it during a sale although it's already cheap.

For costing just a few bucks, this game was pretty good. An ambitious setting, solid combat, and unique mechanics kept me playing even when the puzzles had me flustered.
You can tell the creators spent a lot of time dreaming up the world of Labyronia, with a history of war, magic, gods, and monsters to discover as you play. Some details seem superfluous, while you may want to keep others in mind if you want to progress. Talk to every NPC, read every book, and examine everything that looks even slightly out of place. You'll find that rewards await the diligent investigator in the form of quest items, spells and abilities, and treasure.
The combat is simple enough, with most enemies sporting elemental weaknesses that you find by setting them on fire and such. There is a difficulty curve that can be quite steep if you don't take some time to grind a level here and there. The acquisition of the second and third party members is relatively close together fairly late in the game, which trivialized several battles but made up for it near the end of the game, when combining abilities is almost essential to prevail.
Cues are in-game locations and objects that serve as skill books, with each cue teaching a spell or ability to a certain party member. Keep each cue you find in mind, as you may not be able to use it the first time you run across it. Some are for abilities you might never use, but others are pretty much required to beat the game. With a wealth of items and several tiers of gear, you'll upgrade at a nice pace. Since the best gear is found in the world and money isn't really ever an issue past the beginning, it's easy enough to dilute the difficulty by buying stacks of health potions and revives and whittling away at stronger enemies while chugging healing drinks.
The puzzles ranged in difficulty from "that was a puzzle?" to "there is no way this is a puzzle, the game must be broken," and I had to look up the solution once or twice because I'm bad and I should feel bad. But you shouldn't feel bad if you have to. As you may have guessed from the name, there are several labyrinths involved in this game. Another, less obvious theme is that of fractals. These two concepts serve as the foundation for the design and aesthetic of the world, for better or worse. You'll wind your way through a labyrinth, spot that chest sitting just out of reach on another spur of land, and wonder where you had to turn three intersections back to get to it. Likewise, you'll wonder what lay in the center of this strange pattern of terrain and go back and forth to find an entrance and wriggle your way through, usually to a prize.
A few of my gripes were that some areas were just too big, with a lot of empty space you have to run through, usually while you're backtracking from a dead end. All of the quest items are only used once to get past a specific obstacle, which was a bummer for me at first. After getting these shoes that let me walk on lily pads, you think I would be able to walk across all the lily pads, and not just the one floating in front of the door of a shrine I need to burglarize. Many puzzles could have easiliy incorporated elements that would put these items to use so that when you find one it doesn't just get used once and lay forgotten in the key items tab of your inventory. Even some of the usable items were literally useless, except to provide flavor. I thought that maybe this drakna cigar or whatever might have a use somewhere down the line, perhaps to trade with an NPC, but apparently it's just for when the hero gets to jonesing for a smoke. Sure, it probably restores some (of what replaces) mana, but I never noticed. It's the same sort of thing with several other items. At the end of the day, all you need are the potions that fullly restore health, the ones for mana, and the revive items once you get party members.
Labyronia is a great game, especially considering the price. If you can get it on sale, even better. It's several hours of puzzling, fighting, and storytelling on par with a more expensive game, with just a few drawbacks to test your patience.

DeadCore is a very back and forth experience, and not just because you'll be making baby-step progress while relentlessly respawning at checkpoints that are just a bit too far away. Many of the features and mechanics in DeadCore are rather self-defeating: it's a platformer that relies on extreme awareness of environmental hazards and body positioning, but at the same time, is a first-person viewed game where you can't see your feet. It's a game that is so conscious of the impending need for repetitious retrying and respawning that it mapped a quickspawn button next to 'use,' but it spreads checkpoints thin for the sake of exploration. Movement is typical WASD, allowing for a straight vector of movement at 45° angles relative to the camera’s center, but will frequently require you to run a straight line while aiming at targets outside such a range.
Point is, DeadCore's biggest enemy is itself. But getting beyond that, if you can get used to the quirks and have a high tolerance for the inevitable friction, all while surviving a skill-based game that takes no prisoners, DeadCore offers an engrossing aesthetic that is well-implemented and even more well-polished; thankfully, the game seeks to capitalize on a more zen-like experience, rather than the standard (and played out) frantic cyber-savvy motif. A simple, quiet package, DeadCore may very well frustrate you, but it will reward you greater.

Don't let the looks of the game fool you, it's actually really good.
The game starts off similar to quite a few RPGs of old, you're prisoners that by blind luck get a second break at life. The village you were in has been mysteriously wiped out and the guards that left you to go battle never returned, and in their haste left the prison door open.
After you make it out, you're confronted by a strange individual and your journey begins.
The RPG mechanics live up the the games claim of being old-school. It's very D&D like at the character creation, which like Icewind Dale allows you to create your party when you start the game, and since those games even current large RPGs don't have as defined racial bonuses to stats are as many sub stats and specs; and you can even put points into Luck to try and help you. There are several races to pick from, a few portraits for each and craft a team of 4 characters before you set out.
Let me just say, the game is hard. It punishes silly mistakes even on normal difficulty. I actually like it, you need to think ahead, make smart choices and have some luck on your end. Good thing you can put points into luck.
The start of the game is rather slow, but the game really encourages you to explore and talk to people. The first major quest you get in the area involves a Butcher that's gone insane and set up shop in the sewers. A humble little nod to Diablo one in a way.
You simply can't rush through the quest, or any quest. You get mangled, bbq'd and ripped apart if you try. Even simple rats and cockroaches are deadly enemies that can wipe out your small team of would be adventurers.
The mechanics are simple, everything is turn based. Even outside of combat, but then during that time you simple hold in the mouse button and walk about. The turns here execute rapidly for you and NPCs so as to give the feel of normal motion. Stand still though and so does everyone else.
Let me just say that a healer is essential, if your starting party doesn't have a White Mage you're in for trouble. Potions are rare, and the only other way to heal and recoup mana is through sleeping. Which is only possible through food. Each hour you sleep requires one piece of food. The quality doesn't seem to affect it, as a grilled Steak and Apple seem to do the same thing.
The music is good, nothing amazing or mind blowing; and the ambience is alright. One very nice touch is weather. Fog and rain make it hard to see, and lower your characters visibility. Making it easy to get caught off guard by enemies. The same for dungeoneering or being in caves. Torches are essential for avoiding stumbling into groups of enemies unprepared.
The dialogue options in game are nice, although don't expect sprawling conversations and lots of political depth. The game is a bit lacking there, but even then offers more than 2-3 on occasion.
It's a strange little RPG, and I actually enjoy it. It might look shallow in the screenshots, and I was rather skeptical but the game is expanding before my eyes as I play, and more and more depth is piled on as I progress.
I'm several hours in and I've barely touched anything related to the main story because the other quests, and exploration is simply fun.
I would easily recommend the game to folks that like some proper old-school RPG fun, and enjoy a good turn based challenge.

After about 7 hours and a half in this game I think I can write a proper review for it. It has both bad and good things but it's not unplayable, despite it's flaws.
At first it was really fun, but as you play more and more you start to observe the problems with this game. And they are annoying:
1°) Lack of a save feature (last puzzle has 350 pieces and it took me about an hour to complete). If you are not patient enough, this game is not for you. You could Alt+Tab the game and do something else as a break from the puzzle, but I wouldn't do that to much (in the past I had some problems with some games on steam where I couldn't Alt+Tab because that would break the game).
2°) The music is kind of nice, but it becames repetitive quite fast. You could try to mute it, but that would mute all sounds of the game and there is a little click sound when you place a piece in the right place which I found quite useful.
3°) The images are nice, but have too many similar colors and aren't in HiRes. As the puzzles had more and more pieces it became quite hard to find the exact place where one piece would fit. It's even harder if you have a small screen (I played mine on a laptop and it was very painful and it placed a lot of strain on my eyes). The fact that it doesn't show you a big picture of what the puzzle should look like it doesn't help at all. It does have a little "hint" thing where it shows you the picture for a few seconds, but it puts the pieces over the actual picture and when you have many correct pieces it became even harder to find where you should put the other pieces (you can move the pieces normal when this "hint" it's activated). The "hint" button is charged at random when you place pieces correctly; you need 8 charges and you can get them all in a row or you can place 20 pieces and won't gain a single charge.
4°) Picking the piece that you want from the pond can be really hard. Due to a glitch (or bad programming), if yhere are 2 consecutive pieces overlapped, it will ALWAYS give you the first piece (the left one) regardless of which is on top. This can actually help you to solve the puzzles (it is explained in guides how to do it), but it aomewhat kills the fun of doing a puzzle.
It has some good parts too:
1°) It has a decent variety of piece shapes, but sometimes this can be annoying.
2°) The pieces are always oriented the right way (you can't rotate the pieces). It the beginning it may seem boring, but later on you will be grateful that you don't need to rotate the pieces.
3°) You won't lose any of the pieces like you would with a classic jigsaw puzzle if you are not careful.
4°) Achievements are not hard. 24 of the you will get just by finishing all puzzles. You also have to catch the fish which is moving around in the water (you will probably do this by mistake) and you must the fish in the Shishi-odoshi (I think that's what it's called that water thingy at the bottom left corner).
Overall it's not a very bad game, but it's not worth 7 €/$. If you can get it in a bundle or on a sale (at least 66%) then you should give it a try (if you like jigsaw puzzles of course).

Probably the most well-balanced and easy to pick up RTS you'll find. Superweapons are powerful, but not overly so, and every faction has something different and interesting to try out, without being too overpowered or ridiculous.
The micromanagement hell present in other RTS does not exist here. Three production queues at most (infantry/tanks/air), all in the same panel, with increased rate of production being the benefit of more factories/barracks. Resources (only one type - oil money!) go fairly quickly, which forces people to break out of their base and actually fight for the remaining stuff in the middle. Matches are usually no longer than 30 minutes, so no rage inducing 2 hr loss nonsense.
The faction mixups are interesting, too! Only in this game you'll see Warcraft, Starcraft, and Command and Conquer, married up and actually being well balanced. Every faction feels different - and seeing UFOs fight Dragons is incredible.
The netcode is solid, with few disconnections, and the AI is really good early game (albeit bad at late game). Picking up this game for $8 is a steal - but even at $15, you'll still find hours of enjoyment here. It's so good, and so cheap (at $8), that I was able to get all my gamer friends to play it - and they're genuinely enjoying it. We have daily matches, and I'm always surprised by new strategies that I see.
I've played nearly every RTS that has ever existed, from the original Command and Conquer to Company of Heroes, and all sorts of games in between. The critic rating of 69 is way too low. This is a solid 85 or 90, for what you get in price and value.

UniBall is one of the longest-standing games on the internet.
It has been in beta, for several years, and seen many periods of isolation from its players, though, presently, a lot of the old players are coming back. It expresses a great learning curve, though it may seem built for the elites, this game teaches things about movement, intuition, teamplaying, and how to work with another person on the internet.
In fact, I believe if you become skilled at playing UB, your intuition, and natural abilities IRL will improve since it is such a profoundly unique game to natural physics; employing "gravity" and ship movements based perhaps on actual laws of this world.
If you were to play UniBall tonight, you would likely see a large number of faces to whom were once players of this game well over ten, to even fifteen years ago, however, you will also find a great degree of respect toward the new player, since this is by far one of the most challenging games to learn in a day.
I myself have played UB for over 16 years, which began in late 1999.
In spite of UniBall's learning curve, however, I have noticed a great and rather profound degree of skill in the new player recently. The fact that it took me (myself) over three months to master dribbling, I have somewhat found myself very impressed with some of the skill in the new players of UB.
Tutorials, articles, and etc. will be written to advance the first few days of the new player, if not by myself, then by other players, and hopefully all of the vets, and new players, alike, can get along in this terribly unique game.
Please log in with hope, and don't disregard the fact that this is a very different game from most games on the internet. It is, in my opinion, the "best" game on the internet. I have held true to this opinion for the entirety of my career there, and I have even played with its original creator, to whom I once interviewed, a very skilled programmer. The resident programmers of UB have great skill, and also the administration of UB has proven very effective over the past few years.
One last mention is a man named "Zoop" who you may see in the chatroom. If you see him, don't be afraid to ask for help. He will give you guidance, because he truly cares about the game of UniBall.
This game is worth playing. It deserves attention. And it needs new players.
-Brendan

The 3rd and final game of the Sky Trilogy provides a wonderful conclusion and sendoff of the entire cast of characters throughout the Liberl arc.  For a gaiden-esque game that focuses on Kevin and Ries, these two main leads really grew on me just as much as Estelle and Joshua did in the previous two games.  Aside from having the best gameplay/battles out of all 3 games, the memory doors scattered throughout provide amazing backstories; some heartwarming, some with expanded lore of Zemuria, and some heartwrenching.  The final Star Door of the game was especially soul-crushing and brilliantly done in its method of conveying an important character's past, especially with the psychological factors involved.  The music for this game is truly amazing, and definitely my favorite ost out of all 3 games.  Falcom really outdid themselves with all these memorable pieces!
This 3rd game's structure does differ in structure quite a bit compared to the previous two games, so it may not be everyone's cup of tea for having followed Estelle and Joshua's journey up to this point.  But hey, having finished both FC and SC, you might as well go all the way to play the trilogy towards its emotional conclusion!  I can safely say this final game delivers on many fronts and definitely won't dissapoint!  I thank Falcom for creating this series and XSeed Games for their unparalleled localization work in making this JRPG journey my all-time favorite and unforgettable one!

I am writing this review as someone who has gone through the stories of all three Trails in the Sky games, as well as 90% through the two currently released Trails of Cold Steel games.  This is an important point, as it is part of why this game had such a signifigant impact for me.
Trials in the Sky 3rd, while not as strong by itself as SC (Which is now my favorite game, hands down, no exceptions), is a great connecting piece for what is to come in the series, and a fantastic look into the inner workings of some of the old AND new characters that show up within the game.  Kevin Graham and his squire Ries Argent are the biggest examples of this, as these two go from relatively unknown characters to VERY fleshed out people throughout the course of the game as their past is laid bare for all to see.  The world of 3rd is a large dungeon-like area, which threw me off for a good while, but did not necessarily take away from the bigger picture.  It made the stakes feel a bit higher in fact, as you explore the illusionary world of Phantasma to find out what is going on.
The big draw for me though was the Memory Doors.  For those who haven't played, the Memory Doors are doors scattered throughout the game (25 total, though a few have multiple events) that contain mini stories about that certain characters' lives.  For an example, there is one particular door showing how Scherazard became a senior bracer, and her final job before this happens - while also showing a bit of Aina's - the guild receptionist from Rolent - past.
Others, like Prince Olivert's final moments in Liberl, show events that took place between SC and 3rd.  This one I just mentioned in particular, as well as several other plot points and doors, set up for what is going to happen in Trails of Cold Steel, and some of the plot points are first revealed within this game.  This fact REALLY helped me appreciate 3rd and its story, even if I feel that it is overshadowed by SC in almost every other aspect.
So, with that, I recommend this game to any who have played the first two, or the Trails of Cold Steel.  Many of the things that happen in that subseries are introduced here, and this helps shed some light on what brought them about.  I would highly recommend though, if you haven't already, play through the first two of the Trails in the Sky games first, as they are fantastic games!

A true nostalgia trip for early 90's pixely point&click adventure game fans. An ordinary, somewhat shy guy gets whisked away to a fantasy land and tasked with a quest that he neither understands much of or feels up to - but nevertheless sets out on this unexpected journey of discovery and growth. Along the way he'll make friends and enemies. He'll meet some crazies and non-human forms of inteligent life. As you'd expect from a fantasy tale, there's swords, magical creatures - and love. But all of that has its own unique flavor, specific to the creators -- a wife and a husband -- and the flerd between Paul and Lily feels all the more personal and adorkable for that. The game itself leans to the comedic side, and the puzzles especially require some unorthodox, out-of-the-box thinking -- but while the solutions might not be evident at once, they're fair and require only that you mind your surroundings and inventory. I enjoyed it thoroughly, and while I've never played King's Quest or Simon the Sorcerer (which, I think, might've been major inspirations), as a LucasArts adventure fan I some of my favorite things out of it, too.
Pros:
- the old-school graphics! Today's mainstream where games seem to revel in being hi-res festivals of murkiness -- and I love me some pixels and saturated, juicy colors
- the comedy - I've always preferred the funny point&clicks with odd-ball characters, and this one has plenty
- the heart - the game's a passion project that was made on and off for 10 years! You have to admire this kind of devotion!
Cons:
- there's one Click Time Event that I found annoying (but the creators say there's an option to skip it if you've failed twice)
- one puzzle leads to a dead end after much effort taken, which seems a bit unfair (but the actual solution isn't far away, actually)
Had a lot of fun playing this -- took around 4 hours (Steam isn't showing the playtime correctly for some reason).   Thanks for the adventure!

I just finished Deadcore for the first time last night and I've already started a second playthrough to see if I can find all of the collectibles, get the second ending and earn some more achievements.  I'll probably mess with the speedrun mode for a bit as well.  So, my verdict?  Deadcore is a blast.  The game is a sci-fi styled puzzle/platformer/shooter where you're stuck in a sort of computer glitch/alternate dimension where you must scale a huge tower using quick reflexes and every ability in your arsenal.  If you mix Mirror's Edge, Portal, the movie Cube, Megaman and some other similarly themed games and movies, you will have Deadcore.  This is not a game for those looking to relax or have an easy go of things.  Your patience will be tested but there was certainly a sense of accomplishment whenever you'd complete a very difficult section and finally reach that elusive next checkpoint.
The meat of the gameplay sees you jumping from block to block/platform to platform while dodging moving laser fields, robotic foes hellbent on knocking you into the abyss and every other oddity you can imagine.  There are disorienting anti-gravity sections that will turn you on your head, jump pads, gravity tunnels that send you hurtling towards danger that you must avoid and much, much, much more.  You get a few abilities like a dash to help you out as well as the Switch Gun that does everything from activating objects in the enviroment that you need to use in order to progress to stopping your robo-foes dead in their tracks.  There is a story and it's told passably enough through numerous data logs that you can collect as you climb this digital Tower of Babel.  Speaking of collectibles, there's plenty to find.  In addition to the logs there are also music tracks, Switch Gun upgrades and Sparks (that open up new pathways of travel) to find.
Deadcore takes place in a pretty unusual setting that is brought to life thanks to some excellent graphics.  You'll truly feel the awe and scope of the situation you're in as you look up and see how far you literally have to climb to get to the next area.  Particle effects dazzle, threats are well-animated, dizzying gravity changes look awesome as the scenery flips every which way and the overall atmosphere is a slice of sci-fi goodness that looks simultaneously grand and opaque, all in the same breath.  It's not THE most beautiful game ever created as some of the enviroments can get a bit samey, but 90% of the time Deadcore is a pleasure to the eye.  The sound is pretty strong as well, if not quite as crystalline as the graphics are.  Robotic foes make c3po noises, your Switch Gun shots pack a fair punch and everything is perfunctory in terms of special audio FX.  Where the sound really shines is with the techno/industrial soundtrack that pumps adrenaline in the background; complimented by numerous dips into trip-hop ambience.
Even if Deadcore packed a simply average presentation it wouldn't matter much because in a game as challenging as this one, the controls are the most important aspect.  MOSTLY, they are competently well done and accurate enough for you to do the job but let's face it...you're going to DIE and die you will as you struggle with all of your might to pass the 5 main levels in story mode.  Jumping, dashing, shooting the Switch Gun and avoiding threats works most of the time and pulling off a series of daring saves and escapes is satisfying and breathtaking to chain together.  The real big BUT here is that sometimes things just don't work as they should.  Movement is a bit floaty and even if your leaps and dives are dead on the money, you are bound to go sliding off your perch.  The game has its own physics to master. Sometimes the game requires lining up perfectly between several moving lasers and these segments are rarely passable on the first attempt.  In addition to the "float" controls, there are instances where your button presses won't register AT ALL.  My keyboard is new, clean as a whistle and generally in top-notch condition, but that didn't stop the f*cking Space Bar from not accepting my double jumps many, many times even if I waited a moment on a platform to make sure that the double jump ability reset itself.  Checkpoints are oftentimes pretty fairly located but there are several portions of the game where you'll need to cover a darn good chunk of distance to reach one and in these cases the ill-response of the controls will have you repeating these portions over and over and over again.  What makes it fun is the fact there is a Steam Achievement that can only be unlocked by dying a hilarious # of times.  I laughed to myself seeing this, saying, "Ha, even if this game is tough as nails, I'll never die THAT much."  I'm not sure what's scarier...the fact that I scoffed at the idea of dying so frequently or the fact that I reached the achievement before I totally completed level 3.  Good God...I died fast and hard!   But I kept trying and playing...
In terms of replay value, masochists like myself will find more than enough of it in Deadcore.  I'm already starting a second playthrough to see if I can grab all of the collectables at the very least and there is also a speed-run mode available where you can stack yourself up against the competition all over the world and try to best the developer's times.  This is one of those games  that I'll probably lose interest before getting every single achievement (I won't be good enough to get a few either I'm sure), but it's going to keep me playing long after a single completion.  In fact, I hope to get some more out of it in after writing this review.  There's not much else to say here.  This game was pretty darn great and worth the money I spent on it.  Though I hit on the controls fairly hard, I do want to enforce the notion that you will get better and come to get a grip on the movement in this game the more that you play.  I kind of disagree with the folks that say you can't get better at it.  I did.  It has its quirks, but I see them as masterable quirks.
Let me break down as always into what I liked and what I didn't in a more quick reference style!
Pros:
-Excellent graphics and visual effects
-Great lighting and particle explosions
-A small but useful selection of abilities and Switch Gun modes
-Fun level design with alot of different challenges packed into each one
-Decent sound design with exceptional music
-Lots to see and do (collectibles, alternate modes, different paths, etc.)
-Controls are a pain but somehow become adaptable if you stick with the game
-Interesting story premise
Cons:
-Controls are NOT for the casual gamer (I'm pretty hardcore...not the best, not the worst, so I had fun learning to get better at them)
-While the graphical sights are impressive, they do get samey as the game goes on
-Though the music was excellent, sound was rather humdrum
-Story itself becomes passe as the game progresses (perhaps ending #2 will shed more light)
-Enemies feel like an annoying afterthought.  They aren't particularly challenging as the platforming is the real challenge and they feel more like an annoyance than necessary to the gameplay.
-For a game focused on speed, there are certain segments where you must sit and assess the situation even if you already know the level.
-Sometimes the controls flat out don't respond
Overall, I had a blast with Deadcore.  I got more enjoyment out of it than Portal...just my humble opinion.  It's going to tick you off sometimes but every time I wanted to put the game down I found out that I simply couldn't for long.  It was fun more often than it was annoying.  The sci-fi setting was cool and when the controls were hitting their stride, there was plenty of satisfaction in pulling off several quick movements in succession.  Hopefully, a few of the games issues will be addressed and upgraded, or fixed in a sequel.
Rating:  8/10

why you cant colonate said houses,
why there is random AI scattered throughout a island set up as your only enemy aside from a few animals,

How the oceans are completely empty,
how you float like your wearing a safety harness in the water therefore making underwater exploration unattainable,
Ferrys that literally teleport you from one side of a 1000 foot island LOL. Like you would travel there faster on foot rather than waiting for the long loading screen and potential bug that would ultimately crash or prevent travel all together.
How am i supposed to feel like im "surviving" if every time i die i dont lose ANY hp stam or anything else past 50.I feel as if they made it this way because of how OP their Ai is.. which is backwards in my opinion. When sprinting with 50 stamina the character literally runs for about 3.5 seconds then goes to a complete standstill for a good 2 seconds.. that makes no sense to me. Even worse though; they set their system up so that you get repeatidily killed in the beggining with absolutely no ammo or weapon. The only way to craft anything is to mindlessly mine iron ore as its basically the only valuable resource that applies to literally everyone building structure that is important.
ONE THING THAT I COULD SEE GOING SOMEWHERE is the animals.
At this point this game would be more enjoyable if it was implemented into some type of farming/harvest moon game with killing. The animals and the barn set up is awesome. You can set up your own crops and barns with animals and have your own little space but without any comunicative AI. I have 8GB so i dont know how that would apply. Also can play this game on max settings. So the publisher really does not care about its customers. 1) I would add a moon or at least stars to the sky at night.  If you look up and see nothing at all, it takes a little away

can tell there is a sound loop kinda thing going on

4)  The hunters need a purpose.  Maybe have them near some type of camp protecting it or near the ferrys stopping you from using it or patrolling between houses. Let's set things straight: the game itself is a fine, simple, jigsaw puzzle game with a terrible, horribly frustrating addition. I'm unsure wether this is a regional tradition, or just a cruel joke on people who just want to get things done such as myself, but apparently the damn puzzle pieces flow in a river stream. A. River. Stream.
So, whenever you set your eyes on the damn piece you've been looking for since the beginning of the puzzle, it WILL end up being either submerged, or dragged in a larger clump of pieces. Is this bad for everyone? Not sure. Is it making me wish i could drown myself in the rriver for the sake of never ever being forced to fish up pieces ever again? You bet.
"C'mon man, it can't be all this bad" you might say... Of course you never tried to get ahold of THAT single goddamn piece of puzzle for 2 minutes straight, as your mouse pointer hovers over it giggling at your feeble attempts. Because, of course, even if you're pointing the piece you want as if you were an italian pointer dog, it WILL fail. Repeatedly.
If the whole point of the game is supposed to be relaxation and patience, may I say it fails kind of hard in both regards. Even the music, which is kind of interesting to listen to at first gets kind of unnerving after a few rounds of "catch the ducking piece" enchancing the whole "i hope this damn stream explodes and just leaves the damn pieces lying around the board" sensation.
Ah, and "dulcis in fundu", you don't even get a damn clue on what the final image will look like ingame, so have fun trying to figure out where each piece belongs based purely on INSTINCT and, idk, supernatural powers of farseeing.
I won't say anything about the puzzle selection menu, which is a game per se, in which the sole objective is to START THE GAME because I can't muster enough strength to bash it as well.

Pretty simple, but still quite fun RPG. The game uses some basic RPGMaker assets, such as the mountains and trees, but the art is much better than a lot of the custom assets in other RPGMaker games I have played. And I really appreciate that it doesn't spend the first half hour of the game on exposition.
You start the game, you grab your sword, and you go out into the world.
This is a very good way to make a game IMO.
The combat is punishing and attacks have decent animations.
Minor annoyances are that the games seems to have no option screen to rebind keys or change resolution outside of the typical RPGMaker F1 keybind. Resolution is limited to fullscreen or a small window. On my 360 pad the action key was on X by default rather than A, which took longer to figure out than it should have as I assumed my controller was just being stupid instead of trying all the buttons like a sane human being. I would've preferred to change the keybindings in game, but I can deal with the RPGMaker menu.
Overall I'd say it's worth your time if you don't like handholding and are a fan of RPGMaker titles. Solid game and pretty darn cheap even without a sale.

On October 26th, 2014, I was stumbling around Steam, looking for some RPG to spend some time on. A game by the name of Trails in the Sky caught my eye, so I decided to try it out. I wasn’t prepared for this series to completely blow me out of the water and change my outlook and give me so many new possibilities of the awesome world of Falcom. After the ending of FC, I scoured the internet to figure out when the sequel of this great game I just played would come. Sadly, it seemed that it would never come, through a series of events that could only be described as Murphy’s Law. About a year later, Trails in the Sky Second Chapter came out in English. This game again blew me out of the waters due to its amazing characterization and world building. I played Trails of Cold Steel I+II on the PS3 in the meantime. Then finally, around a year and a half after SC was launched, Trails in the Sky the Third, the final game in the ‘Sky’ arc of the Trails series, and I have to say, it is definitely the best.

Firstly, this is the Third game of the Sky series, and not much will make sense if you start here.
is the place to start. The Third is pretty different from the average JRPG, and certainly different to the normal Trails game. It could best be described as “dungeon crawler” but that doesn’t do it justice. The Third mostly takes place in one giant area called Phantasma, and it includes doors that when opened with the right character or situation, will grant a memory fragment. These memory fragments are essentially huge amounts of development for characters and the world around them, and it wraps up well on how everyone is doing after the events of SC. There is so much more that gets explored in Phantasma, but it’s hard to include what they are without spoilers. The only negative here is that there are much fewer chances to talk to NPCs, but inter party interactions rise up. Battles are in the same grid system as the first two, and plays similarly to SC, but with a few new arts added in. It’s nice, fun, and difficult at the higher difficulties. The Third's difficulty is
. SC had some pretty bad difficulty spikes, especially in the beginning of the game, but the Third hits the spot of being difficult, but not too difficult in certain areas, and is generally a much more internally balanced game than FC or SC between characters.

With the end of SC, it is also the end of Estelle and Joshua’s main story, but they do appear as side characters in the Third as well. Instead we have Kevin Graham, the somewhat mysterious Gralsritter Dominion of the Septian Church. It’s hard to go into explaining him without spoiling anything, but he has quite a few secrets up his sleeve. Also with him is the newly appointed Knight, Ries Argent, a childhood friend of Kevin’s. She’s probably one of the few characters I could complain about, but that was mainly due to her being one of the few new characters and without the development of previous games. Luckily, by the end she is definitely a very dear character. Kevin and Reis gain much of their development through the main story, where the rest of the original cast is farther looked upon in the doors.

Speaking of the doors, they also offer insight on the continent of Zemuria as a whole, and bring up some plot points that come up in later Trails games.

The Third has much darker tones than the other Trails games. Chapter 7 as a whole and star door 15 were absolutely beautiful, in a horrifying and depressing way.

The music is up to Falcom’s high standards, and I’d argue it has the best soundtrack out of all the Sky games. I mean, who wouldn’t want to overdose on that heavenly bliss?

XSEED’s translations are amazing as always, and they didn’t even censor a scene that could've been. Thumbs up here.

All the things I love about the Trails series is here; lovable characters, excellent and detailed storytelling/worldbuilding/writing, awesome soundtrack. I could gush on about how some random NPC mentions a jewelry store in a city in Erebonia, in which game was made 6 years in the future, or that the literature of the game has some surprising backstory to them, or the cynical, sarcastic, 4th wall breaking, or reference creating empty chest quotes. Thank you Falcom and XSEED for this fun ride of a series.

I hope Trails to Zero and Azure can be localized, but that will require these games to get good sales. Please at least try out Trails in the Sky First Chapter, or Trails of Cold Steel, coming soon to Steam. I’d appreciate it.

RpgMaker game that has a somewhat classical JRPG setting but does things differently by having a world that is literally a labyrinth. For me this is a hard game to review as i must confess classical JRPG games with all their clichés dont have a chance in my eyes with their worn out mechanics and this game comes close to this category. So is it different enough? Yes, so it seems after some hours of gameplay.
The most defining feature of the game is the Map of the world that is literaly a labyrinth. Lots of back tracking and figuring out routes.  Combat is hard and there is lots of it once you start to explore the world map and lots of grinding for experience. Game has a tendency to show you that you just took a wrong turn by sending unbeatable monsters in your way.  Many monsters will hit you with status attacks and kill you. It also goes the other way around and this makes combat one of the better designed feature in the game. Abilities are learned with 'cues' that are scattered around the map. Books can be found during the travels that explain the story. Pretty straightforward actually.
I am really on the fence with this game. It is a new kind of blast from the past with a hardcore heart built on a old game engine.
Buyer beware. Look closely to what you are about to buy before getting this. There is nothing casual about this title so prepare for a tough adventure where no one holds your hand and tells what to do.

If you like old school RPGs this is a well-designed one for a RPGMaker game.  The story is reminiscent of when we had to defeat elemental lords of water, fire, earth and air to beat the earlier Final Fantasy games, although it is a bit simpler than any of the classic RPGs.  That's okay, though, if you're just playing this game to kill some time.  It does a good job of that - expect to spend at least 20 hours in finishing this game.
Game progression can also be pretty non-linear, meaning I had to figure out how I would like to proceed - and there were enough options to make the game more interesting than most of your cookie-cutter RPGs out there.  It was easy to miss something important and a lot of backtracking might have to be made.  If you're very thorough with exploring, it will pay off, though.  And if you miss something, you might come back much stronger, making backtracking that much easier to do.  I was especially satisfied with how I came back to one particular area - the Deep Grotto - and was able to handily beat a mob that I couldn't the first time I went through it.
The story itself is linear, though - your actions won't change how the game ultimately plays out.  The puzzles are somewhat challenging but not overly frustrating if you have a good memory and pay attention to what you're doing.  There are some key items you absolutely need to make any progress at all, however.  The pickaxe is especially important and you will always have occasion to look for a way to use it.  The labyrinths are only frustrating if you keep forgetting the way to go.  The enemies have vulnerabilities you have to learn how to exploit.  You also have to learn new abilities from finding "cues" which can be anything from a statue to an animal, as well, so keeping an eye out for anything unusual is important.  Learning what gear can be best for specific battles is also useful in many different situations.
Dialogue was pretty well done, although I had to chuckle at some of the text in the books that you read in the game - one called a historical decision "ret..arded" for example, not exactly what you'd expect in the lore of a fantasy game.  A blossoming romance in the game also felt unnecessarily forced.  Forming an actual party actually doesn't happen until much later in the game which I felt like was something that could have been done sooner.  That being said, the game is very fun to play for old school RPGers and I recommend it if you like that type of game.
