This game is quite good and fun. It's Mega Man with a splash of Gradius. The spritework and music are both quite good. The story is vapid but ignorable. The difficulty ramps way up in the final stages.
There's a few annoying little problems with it. Don't let this discourage you from buying the game, I'm just very adept at finding flaws.
First, the fact that it has camera options reeks of bad game design. Especially when designing a 2D game, you should pick camera settings that work, and design the game around them. And, surprise surprise, none of the camera options quite work perfectly. After some effort, I found the least bad ones.
Put "camera position" on the highest setting, which pushes your character far to the back of the screen. You won't be able to see much of what's behind you, but this won't matter for most of the game, as there's only a handful of places in the game where enemies respawn. You will find the ability to see and shoot enemies far ahead of you to be extremely useful.
Put "camera speed" to its lowest setting, which counterintuitively makes it the fastest possible speed. This setting doesn't actually change how fast the camera scrolls—this is slow as molasses regardless. What it does do is cut out the delay before the camera starts scrolling, which makes the process as fast as possible.
There are other places where the camera work is sloppy too. Whenever you have to go downwards in a stage, such as down a cliff or staircase, you either have to do the jump blind or stop and hold down to reveal what's below you. This isn't a BIG deal, but a smart game designer would program the camera to scroll downwards to reveal these places automatically.
Playing as the second character, Riva, is awful. She's simply inferior to Zizou. She requires more effort to learn how to use her, and then when you do, she's STILL worse. Sword Rain and Extra are completely useless. Dash seems cool but it's almost impossible to control properly unless you're a superhuman.
I would like the ability to configure what upgrades the semi-automatic mode installs. I sometimes miss the opportunity to install the upgrade I want during a tense moment, but the default loadout is undesirable.
The PC port is a little sloppy too. There's unremovable black bars on the left and right because this is a 3DS port and the 3DS screen isn't quite 16:9. You can't configure which monitor it outputs to. The only way to quit the game is to hit Alt-F4... or attempt to Alt-Tab out of it. You can only remap the face buttons, not the directional buttons, or even the quick weapon change buttons. You may have to use JoyToKey to get a reasonable control setup in this game; I simply decided not to bother with the quick weapon change buttons.
All in all, it's a good game, and I do recommend it. The flaws are dwarfed by the quality of the game. Just don't bother playing as Riva unless you want a challenge and Lunatic Mode as Zizou doesn't scratch it.

Visuals just fits the average pixelart anime style you might've seen in many other games from the genre. You'll find many significant and original enemies through your gameplay, for example (my favourite) is the snow giant with Santa's hat who breathes fire.

-

This is not the best game, but it is not a bad game either. It seems to more or less be a port from the 3DS, which is significantly better than a mobile port that tries to translate taps and swipes into mouse movements. It is similar to Megaman with some RPG elements thrown in for flavor. Kill a boss, steal its weapon, another boss is weak to your new toy, rinse repeat.
The game starts out... odd. It opens in a tiny window that you can change when you hit the options, I turned full screen on and never had that issue again. It also starts by dropping you into a black screen that tells the controls, stays on that for a few seconds then goes to the title screen, no screens to tell who made the game or anything.
There are 3 difficulties, Hard is unlocked by beating the game on Normal first. There is an unlockable character, which I don't have yet, although I hear they play differently. And various goodies by beating levels/the game certain ways. The options menu has a few interesting things on it besides the normal stuff. Screen scrolling time (up and down, left and right) and  jumping options (either always the same height or varies by how long you hold the button). Nothing really special to mention, it's an option menu.
The story is sparse, very sparse. If you are looking for a deep story this is so not the game for you. The mcguffins have disappeared, you are trying to find the mcguffins. Hunt down bosses, ask about mcguffin, fight. That is about it.
The music is decent, nothing bad but in all honestly I can't remember a single song I've heard. There is some minor voice acting, but it is only before a boss fight, and unless you speak Japanese you're not going to know what was said as there's no subtitles for the lines.
The game looks nice! All the sprites are nicely designed, although some are used multiple times (I have seen at least 3 variations of the "pitchfork man", palette swap and different attack pattern). The levels all look different and are fitting of the theme of the area. At the beginning of each level it is like you're in a VR world/hologram until you hit a white line then everything switches over to the area's design... which has not been explained. The game also runs at a smooth 60FPS on my system, and I so do not have a good system, so it should run very nicely for most people.
And now the most important part! The controls and how it plays! The controls are obviously a port over from the 3DS. If you've ever played a flash game the keyboard controls should be easy enough to pick up. ZXCV are your attack, jump, install(upgrade), and attack menu. AS let you quick swap to the previous/next attack type. Arrows are movement. The spacebar of all bloody things is the pause button, which makes absolutely zero sense to me. In every other game pause is either escape or P, why is it the spacebar here? The controls can NOT be changed. Ok, I take that back, they can... you can change which of the ZXCV keys does what, you can not change the movement keys, pause, or the next/previous weapon keys. The game also has controller support, which I did not try out, but I imagine work just fine seeing as the original game was designed for a system that has a controller. Any prompts given in game are taken straight from the 3DS version, so expect it to say "hit the A/B/X/Y key to do this".
You can autofire by holding the attack button, and that will clear the way through most of any given level. That is actually a little disappointing. There are hazards to dodge, and some enemies that you can't hit without either a weapon upgrade/change or waiting for their shield to drop, but autofiring will get you through a majority of any given level. I've gotten hurt more on hazards that were hard to dodge than any non-boss enemy. Autofiring will not work on the bosses, they get invincibility frames and their attacks are harder to dodge than the trashmobs in the levels. There is also a blocking mechanic that is poorly explained in game. Pretty much you perfect guard by tapping left or right (doesn't matter which) right as a projectile would hit you. Get it right and you get a small amount of XP and don't get hit, get it wrong and you lose a chunk of XP and lose some HP. You're better off dodging the attacks in my opinion.
There are also plenty of instant kill pits around, and you get knocked back when hit, so you can see where that goes.
DO NOT Alt+Tab out of the game or it closes the game entirely! Shift+Tab works just fine, but Alt+Tab closes out the window for some reason. Oh, and to exit the game it tells you to Alt+F4... which I find cute.
The leveling system is interesting. You gain XP (tres) from killing enemies and it fills the bar at the bottom of the screen, and if you want the upgrade that is highlighted in red you hit the install key to use up all the XP to get it. You can't get previous ones if a higher level one is highlighted. The install upgrades are temporary and are gone if you die/finish a level. Also any XP not used you can use outside of levels for permanent upgrades which include more lives, get more XP from enemies, more HP, upgrades to weapons, etc. Your special weapons, the ones you steal from bosses, use XP as their ammo, so fire them wisely if you're trying to get an upgrade. Oh, and since I mentioned HP, there are no health items. If you get hit that HP is gone until you die or finish the level.
Overall I like the game, it's fun and challenging and the bosses are great fun to fight. I find the life system arbitrary, especially since I lose all my temporary upgrades and most of the XP bar upon death. But that aside I'll be finishing this game. And remember, don't Alt+Tab!

I wanted to like this game, but I can't.
By now you already know that the game is like a hybrid between the mechanics of Gradius and Mega Man. Sounds good, but it is a terrible idea in practice. The game feels like its own mechanics constantly go against fun - remember having a separate energy bar for every new weapon in Mega Man so you could experiment freely without hassle? Well, too bad, because this game actually uses the exact same Gradius-like energy for those weapons. You are basically given a choice of: Do you want to upgrade your basic weapon into a supercannon or just use up that energy to fire weapons that may or may not be effective, and sometimes absolutely useless because of their godawful range?
You might as well be told to choose between getting a gun and getting shot.
I won't say this is a problem for someone who feels really hardcore defeating bosses with minimal effort, even without essentials like speed boosting (Gradius-style upgrade), but when you die in a boss or any enemy in a stage, you are set back to zero. Even worse, this game has no way for you to get your health back. This is made even further frustrating when you notice that the screen scrolls
when you turn around. I cannot emphasize the slowness of this enough, you basically have to stand still and wait for the screen to scroll if you happen to zig zag around a maze or just want to explore carefully.
Speaking of exploration, remember how much fun in Mega Man it was to see a power up and figuring out how to get to it? Well here they went for something completely unfun; The power ups are invisible and hidden in a specific spot on each map, and you have to just blindly jump around looking for them, at which point the slow scrolling gets even more annoying when you get blindsided by enemies that suddenly respawn as you carefully hit every empty air space you can.
Then when you get knocked around a few times in a level or boss, your last resort is to basically grind respawning enemies until you level up your basic attack - and I am genuinely asking right now for someone out there to explain to me what's the point of having to choose between the two attacks, Line and Meteor, when there is no discernible difference that would make one better over the other? It just makes you scream when you switch your attack to the other accidentally, wasting your power meter for something you didn't want.
Still with me? Alright, now, when you finish the game first time around, you're given another character to play as, and she is even more frustrating to play with - that's the theme here. It's frustrating and it's not fun to play as these characters. But the second character is even worse because her basic attack's reach is spitting distance, and its reach is leveled through the Gradius-style system. She can charge her attack like in Mega Man, but its reach remains the same, dependent on the attack's level. You have to be as close as possible to enemies and bosses to hit them, and at this point I just wanted to go play Mega Man and Gradius instead.
As a big bonus "up yours" the second character's last and most expensive upgrade is something that lets you fire charged up attacks with just a push of a button, but only for a short time. You know what the problem is with this? It's that the bosses have momentary invulnerability between attacks, so this skill is entirely pointless - none of the little enemies are so badass that you would need to shoot multiple charged attacks at them, and just tapping the button is already good enough. You are doing the exact same damage to bosses without this skill if you just charge, shoot, wait for the invulnerability to wear off, and attack with a ready charged shot again.
The design decisions make no sense, the levels feel lifeless, the music is pretty nice, the bosses are dull and made frustrating with the needless power downgrade that comes with death, and the fusion of Mega Man and Gradius just makes it feel like taking the
parts of both games.
If you like a game that demands perfection with your moves, like I know some people do, then you might enjoy this game. If you are looking for something that feels like Mega Man or Gradius and is fun and rewarding to play, then this will just make you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off.
Let's finish this wordy rant of a review with one more thing: The final boss in the game with the first character is terrible. It's a gauntlet of enemies that you just defeat as they spawn, while the boss itself hovers overhead, spewing slow projectiles. The boss's health slowly drains while you just wait and kill the enemies from memory. There is no tension or a feel of a big battle, you are just standing in place and killing regular enemies. I could've recommended this game based on boss battles alone, but seeing how most of them are just completely immobile cannons, it just clinches this game as a missed opportunity.
I hope that the developers don't give up just yet, though. There is a good chance these folks could make a good Mega Man-like if they dump the Gradius part and make a simple platformer instead. Mega Man and Gradius do not mix.

Based on a mobile game, Risky Rescue is an action game where you fly your helicopter and try to rescue as many survivors as possible.
The concept of the gameplay is simple. Click left to make your helicopter go left and up. Click right to make it go right and up. And yep, you can't make it fly straight fly. The basic reaction of someone would be to think this game plays poorly, especially with the fact it's a port of a mobile game.
Actually, the gameplay is done incredibly well! Heck, it's very playable! Easily one of the best mobile ports on Steam, Risky Rescue doesn't disapoint.

Wow, what a huge suprise. I bought this game during the Steam Summer Sale and thought it might be worth a few hours of fun, but I sure didn't expect it to be THAT good.
At first, DeadCore appears to borrow a lot from the Portal franchise: the silent protagonist in first person who has only one gun that is actually a sciencey contraption, the vast, dehumanized and very dangerous environments, the fact that you can fall from any distance without hurting yourself, no health bar, most of the sound effects are very similar, the clean techno-futuristic æsthetics... it even has got the cute little robots that casually try to kill you while doing silly voices.
But the comparison stops right there. Far from being a Portal knockoff, DeadCore seems rather like an homage, with its own distinctive personality and game mechanics. Here, the emphasis is really not on puzzles and reflection — most puzzles are solved at a glance and necessitate about mere seconds of thought; even if it gets mind-bending with the introduction of the G-Mod, it still doesn't really require you to think — but on pure skill. Mad skills, I would say.
This game seems like the embodiment of the popular gaming expression "Git gud or git REKT". It really requires you to concentrate to a point you're not used to, even if you're a core gamer, and I apologize to my keyboard and mouse for the liters of sweat I've been pouring on them because of it. You hear you roommate sneeze in the distance, it breaks your concentration for a handful of nanoseconds, and BAM you don't know it yet but you are already dead. This game tolerates no approximation, and even less attention deficit. Which quickly becomes a great thing because you really feel yourself get better, and better. It's like a simulation of the process of honing your skills. Which feels AWESOME. And yeah, you won't ragequit and storm off the room. You will get better. Because the game is very addictive.
The most beautiful part of it is that it is never frustrating. The game keeps punishing you, but you always feel like it's well deserved and that it's your fault if you just respawned on the checkpoint. Even the checkpoint system itself, which I am not a fan of, isn't as punishing as it could be, as there are plenty of said checkpoints — the only problem with it is when you accidentally freefall from a high place right onto a checkpoint that is located at a much earlier point in the level: that is worth a few screams.
Wait, have I mentioned how æsthetically pleasing it is? It looks really beautiful. Gorgeous lighting, very fine textures, particle effects up the♥♥♥♥♥.. and it seems crazy how well it is optimized. On my old entry-level rig (Core i5-2400S / GT 730 / 8GB DDR3) the game gets an average of 45 FPS, in 1080p, with the graphical settings on Ultra. On the lowest settings I blasted through the 300 FPS barrier. This seems insane for a game released in 2014. How did they accomplish this magic? Maybe the fact that most elements are cube-shaped lowers drastically the general polycount? Anyway, it looks very good; and the music is very good too. Its blend of ambient and drum'n'bass just goes perfectly with the levels, which is actually quite rare in a game. It is really well done.
Now, a bit of criticism, because this game isn't perfect either. My biggest enemy in the game? Keyboard lag. In a game like this, it is particularly deadly and frustrating. I don't know why it happened so much, but damn, it did. There were also quite a few bugs along the way. Some were harmless, some were helpful, some got you killed instantly. And, in my humble opinion, making this game a FPS was a mistake. Sure, it looks cool, and helps a lot with the immersion. But in an environment where any literal misstep can cost your your life, it would actually be great to be able to see your damn feet! How often did I get touched by one of the laser barriers and wonder which part of my body actually triggered the death! Did I get hit on the left? Right? Head? Legs? Actually seeing your character would have made a lot of deaths way less puzzling. Sometimes the game feels like playing a manic shooter where you can't see your hitbox. It makes the experience less enjoyable.
But globally, DeadCore is enticing, very pretty, tons of fun, and never boring. It is a puzzle-platformer-FPS but often feels more like a racing game and procures sensations similar to the likes of games such as F-Zero or WipeOut. This, despite the fact that nothing about it is actually new, makes it feel innovative and very very refreshing.
Obviously, I would recommend it in a heartbeat. This is videogaming as I love it and most gamers — from the Tetris hardcore player to the Super Mario Galaxy fan — should love it and enjoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it.

First of all, the visuals are great and the sound is appropriately minimalistic.  However, I have two main gripes with the game that prevent me from even caring to continue playing it.
1) The "Story" mode just...isn't.  Perhaps it is only because I never even completed the first level (more on that in point #2), but upon starting the game, you're thrust into the gameplay. No explanation of where you are or why.  No indication that there is any goal to the game other than just jumping to the next platform.  Now, I'm not saying every game needs to have a fantastic story in order to be enjoyable, but if there's an option for a "Story" mode, there really ought to be a story.
2) This is the deal-breaker for me.  It's been talked about over and over again: platforming from a 1st-person perspective is a horrible, horrible idea.  Since it is impossible to see your feet, prepare to die.  Again. And again. And again.  Why?  Not because you made a grave mistake, but because it is IMPOSSIBLE to tell exactly where you are going to land.  Every jump is an estimate (unless you look straight down whilst jumping, thus making the shooting mid-jump impossible).
So do I recommend this?  No.  I did not even complete the very first level because I was first completely bored with the gameplay and lack of story, and then because I just kept dying over and over again due to the design of the game (not due to its difficulty).
If I'm bored within seconds of starting a game, that's probably a bad sign.
Now, I'm sure some will love the competetive nature of the game and the leaderboards and to them I say "Wonderful!"  This isn't the type of game I can get behind, however, because unless you're willing to devote hours to trial and error just to get your name at the top of a silly, pointless list, this is just a waste of time.

Obviously, making a "full review" on a game like this one is quite hard. But, i'll give it a try. I haven't played many visual novels in the past, but after Carpe Diem I'm seriously considering them. Quoting Wikipedia "Carpe diem is a Latin aphorism, usually translated "seize the day", taken from book 1 of the Roman poet Horace's work Odes". And it means that you have to live for the present, to make the most of your time. At least that's what i got from googling.
It took me exactly 12 minutes to finish the game. I guess I'm a fast reader, because most people say it took them more than 20 minutes. There is no interaction besides pressing [space], [enter] or left-clicking to progress through the dialogue. Oh, actually there is one point, near the start of the game, where you get to choose where you wish to go. From that point, the story unfolds in three different ways, each and one of them being slightly different from the others. The simplicity of that brings lots of haters who complain that these kind of games aren't even games. I disagree, because they are meant to be like that. A different movie-like experience. Moving on, the game also has a save system. I really appreciate the fact that the devs included it, even though i didn't use it a single time (like most of us). Apart from those, there aren't many noteworthy mechanics.
So, the game is mainly focusing on the two main characters, the boy and the girl. The boy, who remains unnamed and the girl named Ai meet at the park. The dialogue seems fluid between them and you can easily get attached to the characters. On that matter, it's more likely that you'll start attaching yourself to Ai, because she's the only one whose face is shown in the game. It gives the feel that you're participating in the events through the eyes of the male character, because Ai is always facing the player. The visuals are great, i personally love the arwork. Aside all that, what really matters are the characters themselves. The development is great, but if were given more time to understand the characters it would be awesome. Within the range of 15 minutes, it's hard to make something really good. But, by giving us a taste of what the characters seem to be and then, twisting the reality that we were slowly getting into is... awesome! I loved the twist at the end and i believe it's one of the main reasons that people loved this game.
- Nice visuals

- Awesome plot and character development
- Value for price (free!)
- Too short
- Not much interaction compared to other similar games

This game is amazing. I generrally don't like rpgs, sidequesting, or grinding. This game, however, makes it enjoyable. THe main stryline is pretty simple: kill the members of the evil organization that is influening the king, but the world is so rich and vibrant, the story feels a lot stronger than most games that meerely use their setting as a backdrop instead of following through. Egypt is beautiful and lush. There is so much to do in an area and the sidequests are incredibbly intresting. Normally I skip quests unless I need the XP to level up, but AC origins has made the quests so interesting that I sometimes neglect the campaign to figure explore the area. A prime example is Letopolis, If you only complete the story quest then the total time spent would be about 15 mins, but one of the sidequests tells you the lore of the city which is way more interesting then the predictable plot twist in the scarab arc.
Story wise, its a generic revenge story. It definetly feels a lot more in depth then Unity or even AC 2. Bayek's son is killed and he wants to kill all those involved. The villans are fleshed out and interesting and add a lot to the story. Bayek is an interesting character. He is a man, unlike the proteagonists in most AC games who are boys. There is a clear difference in the way Bayek carries himself compared to Ezio, Arno, or even Conner. His personalty is far more mature and centered. This makes the conflicts less emotional and more cerebral. Bayek already understands that the world can't be changed by the flick of the blade, but he doesn't care. He isn't a naive child, he has seen evil and he wants to protect the innocent from it, not change the world.
Overall this game is an easy 8/10 there is tons of content and an immersive world. The quests are sometimes stupid, but the pay offs are more than worth it.

8-Bit Armies
Released
Petroglyph
Petroglyph
Real Time Strategy
22nd of April, 2016
Singleplayer & Multiplayer
Irony would have it that I’m now writing the third review relating to the 8-Bit series, but Armies is in fact the first one to be released by Petroglyph and that can be clearly seen as soon as you start playing it. Not because of any blatant lack of polish since this developer certainly has experience on their side but for the lack of better words, 8-Bit Armies simply doesn't have the spark and the soul of its successors, Hordes and Invaders!
I have a lot of respect for Petroglyph. They developed Star Wars: Empire at War which remains one of the best 3D real time strategies for the SciFi genre and it’s definitely among my Top 10 favorite games of all time. What’s important to understand about this dev team, is that they strive to stand out from the dozens of RTS’ which litter the Steam Store. Even in 8-Bit Armies, the weakest of the three games from this particular series, you can still notice their efforts and attention to details. From the unit animations and down to level design, this isn’t a developer that simply rearranges game assets and calls it “another level/mission is done”. I was certainly disheartened by the Petroglyph’s decision to lock one of the two faction campaigns under the sorry excuse, most gamers refer to in disgust as, “DLC”. A three-letter acronym which forever changed gaming for the worse.
Unless you fork over 4 euros/dollars (outside of Steam Sale, of course), you won’t be able to play the Guardians campaign, with only the Renegades being unlocked from the start along with 25 singleplayer missions detailing their struggle. At least the dev team had the decency to offer the locked faction for skirmishes and unit voice pack (which are still missing from Hordes, for example) through free DLC. Was it the negative feedback they received upon the Armies’ launch date, that compelled them of those wise decisions? It’s not really relevant any longer, since the Guardians are free to try out in the game’s Skirmish mode.
So you essentially get half a game, for the price tags of 8-Bit Hordes and 8-Bit Invaders. Titles that are far superior from the perspectives of both unit diversity,  originality and obvious replay value from having two full fledged SP campaigns in each, free of further charge. Why should you purchase Armies, then? Well for start if you’re a collector, that’s a fairly easy choice to make. But even if you’re simply an RTS fan looking for something different from the “regular” kind of 3D graphics, 8-Bit Armies might strike your fancy. The story is generic to say the least so I won’t bother you with any details. The bread and butter comes from the large pixel visual style and the highly-competitive potential, should you play in either co-op or the good ol’ skirmish against the AI.
The gameplay mechanics are as old school as they come. C&C type of strategy which focuses on a reliable base of operations from which you build and maintain a veritable army consisting of land and air forces. Some units have certain weaknesses and strengths just enough to take into consideration, their type and quality far more than sheer quantity. Nothing new on the horizon but fully functional and beautifully presented in missions of gradually scaling difficulty, as far as the single player campaign is concerned. Command & Conquer literally wrote the book on this genre, but that is by no means the case to cease trying to improve it.
Cards and plenty of Achievements do provide the much needed bonuses that many gamers on Steam look forward to. I’m grateful that I was given the chance to review the entire 8-Bit trilogy and I can only hope that Petroglyph has learned a valuable lesson from selling DLC instead of including the content in the base game. Steam could certainly benefit from more strategy titles that bring a speck of color to an otherwise murky genre that many devs try to implement but few actually succeed in doing so.
+ Pleasant graphics and sounds.
+ Plenty of replay value for both SP and MP modes.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
- Slightly overpriced considering the inclusion of just one unlocked faction and payed DLC for the other.
- No units really stand out since the game’s theme is rather ubiquitous.

Isometric stealth action game that plays *somewhat* like a casual Metal Gear Solid. While lovely hand-drawn animation tells an interesting story about tribal politics between chapters, your main task is to bypass or takedown each enemy using any means necessary. Progress further and levels also introduce some basic puzzle elements.
Almost immediately your character is given the ability to freeze time and take control of enemies, which works in a small radius and runs on a cooldown timer. Recharge time could be lowered by mashing the space bar. Throughout levels you discover 'patches' that are effectively magic which can be used after controlling enemies. Some of these abilities included instant execute, swap positions and health tap. Ultimately I found the game a little on the easy side but still had fun playing. Levels left plenty of room for experimentation, though backtracking in later stages could be refined as some of it felt like extra padding.
No in-game options were available other then sliders for sound. Gamepad didn't detect and controls could not be remapped, I personally had no issues with the default keyboard/mouse setup. Screen resolutions of 4k+ were supported using the unity launcher. Currently includes 15 chapters (minus training), most were split into 2-3 areas taking 5-15min each depending on your playstyle. Tidal Affair feels content complete and it's another respectable early access game that's worth keeping your eye on. First part of a series but does play as a standalone. Cheers folks.

Zombie Studios tried its best to bring hype to their horror game Daylight. They went as far as enabling Twitch commands in the game to have viewers attempt to influence the game with spooky soundbites and occurances (definitely inspired by the Twitch Plays Pokemon frenzy that gripped the internet a number of weeks ago). They delayed the game for a few weeks in attempt to make it scarier (given what is in the game now, they must have forgotten to put the monster into the game and had to buy time). It was all for naught.
The game starts with a young woman name Sarah waking up in an abandoned hospital to the strange voice of a man who spouts in riddles. The goal of the game is rather basic and unfortunately repetitive: collect a number of 'remnants' (items that glow in a weird yet cool fashion under the light of a glowstick), find a big magic circle and then move to the next level. There are four levels in all and not much changes outside of the level design. The more time you waste or the further you progress in your quest, you will run into the witch, the only monster and threat in the game. The witch's method of killing you is flying around, popping up in front of you as you do a quick turn and then shove you into a tunnel of red and weird rune shapes until you die or pull a flare out in time to banish them. Fortunately in my playthrough she did this only a few times and gave me some frights when she appeared. Unfortunately she's the only unit in the game and basically a creepy one trick pony. Outside of the witch, the only kind of scares that the game tries to use are feint scares. Items suddenly fly out towards you but do no harm. Screams come down the hall but there is no actual creature wandering around and making that noise. Besides the witch, the game felt like walking through a cheap haunted house that the neighborhood put together for one Halloween night to spook the kids. More silly than scary and no actual harm is done.
Daylight is apparently the first game released to the public that uses the Unreal 4 engine. But given the potentials of the tech demos of the engine, it felt like they didn't even try to create an immersive world and used it more for the sake of marketing. They bought expensive paint but went and fingerpainted what appears to be a red house, a green tree and a happy stick figure family. But hey, they bought that expensive paint! You should consider that!
Sarah's character was very hard to immerse with. She fills the atmosphere with her gasps and her occassional strange lines, which are very frequent. I kid you not, I was investigating a desk when Sarah yelled out "Is anyone in there?". Maybe she was afraid that the witch would pop out of the drawers and get papers all over the place. The problem with Sarah is how little she contributes to the story. She collects remnants, questions Mystery Phone Man of what's going on and then goes on her merry way to collect more remnants without any hint of defiance or free will whatsoever. It was very strange to see her panic and question every thump in the dark, real or not, and remain silent to the witch that constantly screams at her face.
Daylight was written by Jessica Chobot, who is best known as that woman who achieved internet fame for having a photo of herself licking a PSP. She worked for IGN and did a voice role as Diana Allers in Mass Effect 3 (although it's clear that she slept through her voice acting classes). Her writing comes in the forms of Mystery Phone Man's riddlespeak and the dozens of documents lying around about patients being crazy and workers suspecting something isn't right in the hospital. The concept of incredible amounts of notes in games started with Resident Evil and was recently enforced in Amnesia. But those kinds of documents either clued to upcoming puzzles, environmental obstacles and monsters or provided a piece of a story of things slowly going to hell.  The problem with Daylight's notes is that they provide nothing but fluff and make the very short game feel much longer. There are no traps to be warned about ahead of time. There are no upcoming characters that you must help or fight off. Besides vaguely explaining what is actually going on, the notes do nothing to change how the game should be played.
I reached the disappointing conclusion to the game in just two hours. For $15 dollars and no significant replay value besides achievements, I feel cheated. Outlast had the atmosphere, Dear Esther had the writing and Amnesia had both. Daylight had neither. It's tradition under my household that a horror game is to be played at night. Daylight, amusingly enough from the title alone, should be just played in daylight. Or shouldn't be played at all.

I thought that Super Galaxy Squadron was a pretty decent little 2D shooter, but this edition is flat-out superb.
First off, apologies to the individuals responsible for this game's storyline. Everytime I played, I skipped all of the cut-scenes. All I know is that the bad guys have to be destroyed, and there's something involving a core. I'll be real here, I tend to prefer STG storylines that are badly-translated, don't make a lot of sense, or are just flat-out insane. Anyway, there are six stages and several ships to choose from, have at it.
The level of difficulty can "best" be described as bullethell...but not really. There are more tiny orbs of deadly danger than average, but rarely will you ever navigate a sea of bullets. Why? Because if the situation comes to that, then you did something very wrong, and you'll probably die soon. Enemy ships tend to stay on-screen a long time. This gives them more than a couple opportunities to unleash their payload. While it certainly benefits your livelihood to destroy enemies as quickly as possible, you might want to hold off occasionally...
The scoring system is based around a multiplier guage. Almost every type of ship is worth a +.1, and these add up very quickly. Sometimes you'll want to keep enemies alive for an extra half-second or so to help manage your guage. Upon hitting the maximum of x10(!), then you'll want to use your hyper weapon. This will trigger overdrive aka FEVER mode, and all pick-ups are worth ten times their value.
When it comes to making a good STG, dodging and shooting are the most important aspects. This is where the game really shines. Everything has a natural feel to it. When you're avoiding bullets, you acquire this 6th sense, and sink into a sense of sublimity. To put it another way, I like this game because I
notice anything that stands out. To me, 2D shooters should be business as usual. Things that stand out tend to be bad, like erratically-moving bullets, weird/poor hit-boxes, and so on. There's none of that nonsense in this game.
The overdrive/fever system is really neat, but unfortunately it doesn't come into play very often. I suppose this should be blamed on my lack of skill, but I can only catch the FEVER maybe once or twice a play-through. At around the 7x to 9x mark, the multiplier guage can drop at an extremely fast rate, and I just can't seem to destroy enemies quickly enough. While this is going on, some potential moments for huge points are missed out on. For example, there are nearly-invisible rings at certain points in the game. If you fly your ship inside them and fire away, you'll discover a medal worth 500,000 points. Imagine grabbing that shiny behemoth while under the effects of a FEVER.
But let's consider the possibility that I'm wrong, and it's not actually my fault. The reason I and possibly others can't maximize our scoring potential is because the playable ships are a little too weak. I'm not asking for a huge buff, just 15-20% more damage for most ships, and possibly larger boosts for certain ships. I noticed that one of them uses a lot of close-range weaponry. For piloting such a high-risk piece of junk, I expect to do a ton of damage.
As good as Super Galaxy Squadron EX is, it still requires some refinements. The top-scores on the leaderboards can be attributed to the game sometimes not resetting the score when starting a new game. My 60+ million score at or near the top is the result of two play-throughs. The final boss is far more difficult than anything else in the game, and requires a lot of needle-threading. Some ships are just too fast to safely weave between everything, and other ships are too weak to destroy the boss in a reasonable amount of time. Then there are the minor issues like rumble and screen-shaking re-enabling itself everytime I start a new game.
I figure that this game is still being worked on, but even in its current state, I highly recommend it. This is one extremely solid STG.

Sokoban Land DX is a simple yet well executed puzzle game.
As titled it is a Sokoban puzzle game in which the player must push boxes to designated locations to complete the level. There is no move limit on this particular game or time limits, however if the steps taken on the later levels is done in a different way it may block you from being able to proceed to the end of the level. Due to after completion boxes can't be moved, and put back blocking your player model away from the gate.
Throughout the game there is five worlds, with 20 levels per each world consisting of a total of 100 levels to complete. As the player progresses throughout these worlds the difficulty of the levels increase, but not to anything too difficult. The game is well-built physics wise, and does well with being responsive to controls allowing direction input to be held down, and also released without a queue of commands continuing or slip forward. Alongside the game hasn't crashed or any bugs have occurred after completion of the game. The game also has a built in undo move system for undoing the last performed step the player performed, this can help out a lot if a miss movement may occur, or you take the wrong step, and push a box in a stuck spot (though this undo is only for one movement, per movement).
Alongside these the quality of assets aren't the best, but also aren't the worst, sticking to a simplistic look which is easy to follow with. The only other downsides though I would say include the music used which is repetitive, and also seems a bit generic. The sound effects though for completing a level, and menu sounds for picking options was alright with it providing a relevant small sound for these which matched nicely.
The game also does support local co-op for playing with others on the same machine. I haven't tried it myself much, but it does allow for two users to control a different character each either by both operating the keyboard, or a keyboard + controller (haven't tried controller + controller).
It's also to note that the game seems to be available on mobile for a price of £1.19 without ads, or a free version that is available for free which does contain ads within. The steam version costs £1.99, and doesn't contain ads like the mobile ads free version, just a small price increase. Even though the game is available on both devices it's done quite well for allowing support on both.
Overall the game is decently built, and functions well. It has challenging levels over time making it harder, but starts of easy giving a great sense of progression, and helps anyone who hasn't played a sokoban game before get the idea of what they need to do. It also has both keyboard, and controller support, with local co-op available for use.

The third and final part of the Sky series certainly doesn't disappoint. This game is quite different from the other ones, both in structure and in tone. This time around you play as Kevin Graham, a "priest" of the Septian Church, along with his newly arrvived partner, Ries Argent. While the game may be much ligher on main story and instead more gameplay-oriented (the game is largely a dungeon-crawler, after all), the story that's there is - as always - nothing short of brilliant. The lore of the series is also greatly expanded upon, much of which will come into play in games released almost a decade later. At times, the game takes on a darker tone than most JRPGs (especially one part, although that one is part of a side story), and the protagonists are quite different from your typical JRPG heroes (or even most protagonists in general) - which is always a plus in my book.
The gameplay is pretty good for a turn-based game; I know I've certainly enjoyed it quite a bit so far. The battle system is mostly just an expanded version of the one from the previous two entries. I would also like to point out that the OST is nothing short of amazing, certainly a major upgrade from FC & SC.
It is highly recommended that you play the previous two entries (Trails in the Sky FC & SC) before jumping into this one in order to truly appreciate all of the side stories, as well as content pertaining to the main story. These side stories flesh out many already well-developed characters even more, while also giving quite a bit of information relating to the lore and the world of the series. Playing the previous games is definitely not required though, but don't be surprised if you get confused sometimes -  it IS an epilogue after all (though loosely-related to the prequels).
I can scarcely think of any largely detrimental flaws. The only minor flaw I can think of is how loosely connected the main story and the side stories are, but that's quite understandable in this particular case, considering how the game is structured (though it still holds the game back slightly).
To conclude: Great story, great characters, great music, good gameplay, and it's a real marvel for people heavily invested in the lore and world of the series. 9.5/10.

Having recently reviewed and rubbished the over-paced Total War: Shogun 2, I move on to another game set in that extremely popular period, Sengoku Jidai, this time it is the aptly named Sengoku.
This is a much easier game to stomach. It was something of a warmup for Crusder Kings 2, I believe, and it feels thus: a lightweight, pared back real time grand strategy game with some pacific art and music working together with simple but effective gameplay.
Like Shogun 2, brinkmanship and vicious attacks are rewarded in Sengoku. Again like Shogun 2, your opponents can be cold as stone or grudingly warm. Unlike Shogun 2, none of this is shoved down your throat, and the pacing is largely in your own hands. Sure, when you get close to the borders of giant factions like the Uesugi you will have to think quick if you are going to avoid anihilation, but the pace of the game never seems subjugated by the gameplay in the same way that it is in Shogun. A bit more attention is paid to the civil affairs of the time, too, with marriages and the like a key part or the gameplay - not the mention the all important Honour currency, which is great fun to build, and even greater fun to spend.
This game is a calm, patient exercise in faction building and subtle, largely representative intrigue - you fill in the blanks with your own imagination in various instances - and it is a really nice thing to try to get your teeth into over a weekend or on a long flight.

The Legend of Dark Witch is one of the more surprising bargains on Steam. Gameplay consists of the weakness-finding run and gun platforming of Megaman paired with the powerup system of Gradius. This added a lot more depth to the game than I thought it would, as you can only power up so much and are required to choose those upgrades that will not only get you through the level, but also the boss at the end. It's a pretty tough platformer, requiring you to memorize map layout and enemy locations just like the good old days, and it also sports a series of unlockables and Easter eggs to bolster replay value. If there's any criticism to be levied against this game, it's that the boss powers seemed to be an afterthought and proved unnecessary for the most part. When all's said and done, though, The Legend of Dark Witch is a charming, challenging, and fundamentally sound platformer, and a great value for the asking price of $4.99.

At 57 minutes of playtime I feel it's time for a "I know everything about anything" review.
DeadCore set's itself apart from Valve's aforementioned puzzle-platformer within the first few minutes of gameplay when it cranks the speed dial to 9, setting a frenetic pace that thankfully is still manageable without top of the line hardware and I-frame perfect movements.  Challenges are simply designed, but punishingly brutal after the firsat dozen or so.  Thankfully respawns are instant and checkpoints are beyond plentiful.
The game's visual design at first glance might seem too basic, but I really grooved on the shiny-black-shapes-tastefully-Tronlined-floating-in-an-endless-sea-of-clouds it has going on.  HUD elements are all gathered neatly on your Switch Gun (does what it says), giving the player a clean view in a mannar similar to Dead Space.  Story is told though text logs found thoughout the game, though they can easily be ignored if the player wishes to focus solely on gameplay, a thing I found refreshing.
Controls with mouse and keyboard were tight and responsive, air control is precise and predictable, a must for this type of game.  Sound design is similarly simplistic but satisfying, with more subdued music that I enjoyed as it lends well from the experience without distracting from the gameplay.  Puzzle design is very three-dimensional,  always requireing the player to think "around" instead of "forward"
All in all an awesome Firstperson-Puzzle-platformer that get's right in the sweet spot for gamers wanting their constant adrenalin rush with zero downtime, add to that a solidly meshing theme of visuals, gameplay and music and you've got yourself a great experience.  8/10
Cons
- No Controller support as of this review, some of those jumps I really felt uncomfortable with using WASD, really missed my stick then
- Cannot keymap to extra mouse buttons, Since I'm relegated to my five button mouse I tried to map the Dash command to one of the empty ones, no luck, it's stuck at E
It was way better than I thought. Highly recommended.

Most of my favorite games are action packed shooters filled with explosions and many different guns and complex role playing games with tons of story and dialog to become immersed in. So why do I recommend this game? For one point really: it's highly relaxing.
Sometimes I want to just sit back, relax, and enjoy a game and maybe work my brain a little too. This game does just that. I got this game for free over at the IndieGala website, and when I first downloaded it, I didn't expect to like it at all, but I was completely wrong.
I load up this game after a long day at school or doing homework for hours on end. It's a great way to escape stress and just let go. Most games I play require my full attention and for me to constantly be doing something. With no timer, Pixel Puzzles: Japan lets to solve beautiful puzzles centered around famous Japanese monuments and landscapes at your own pace.
While the game is fairly simplistic, there are a few minor complaints. The first would be the higher level puzzles. As you progress, puzzle pieces become more and more strange. They're not your ordinary jigsaw pieces anymore, they're abstractly cut and hard to piece together. One way you can solve this is by starting with the sides and corners first.
Second, and it is a small minor complaint, but I don't like how the pieces float around so much. I understand that they move around to make you have to look for them more, but I wish it was just a little bit slower.
Anyways, I recommend this game to anyone looking for a relaxing and simple game to help take stress away from their lives. Sit back, grab a nice beverage and enjoy this wonderful little title, Pixel Puzzles: Japan.

Shorthand:
If you dig jigsaw puzzles and the game happens to be on sale, I totally reccommend it.
Longish-winded:
Pixel Puzzles Japan is relatively low-fuss fun. Its atmosphere is intentionally relaxing, its puzzle piece shapes vary to keep the player's eyes active and interested from puzzle to puzzle, and its lack of timer and continuous achievements allow players to feel accomplished without being rushed. While the game is far from perfect, vulnerable to minor click-and-drag inconsistencies and the occasional piece getting stuck beneath already completed sections, its theme and its ever-moving, ever-calm background make any momentary frustration just that: momentary. Likewise, the non-puzzle art isn't perfect either, but what it lacks in polish it makes up for in charm. 7/10.

After completing all the puzzles and therefore earning all the achievements, I feel competent enough to tell you about this game.
But man, it sure is hard to review it. Why is it hard, you ask? Well, if you came here to get a game that allows you to piece together jigsaw puzzles, it's exactly what it is. But still, even a simple game like this can have numerous issues that will ruin your experience with it. And this one is no exception.
The first thing and the most obvious thing is the fact that you can't piece together one small part of the puzzle and keep it somewhere to the side so you can use it later, after you make some progress on the "big picture". Every piece has its designated place on the board, and you can only put them there one at a time, after which you can't move them anymore.
The second thing is the fact that those puzzle pieces float around in the water that surrounds the board. Why is that a problem? Well, on the first few 60-piece puzzles, it isn't. You can get most of the pieces easily or with just a bit of stressful effort. But when you get to those bigger puzzles, then you'll notice this game's main flaw - the inability to properly grab a piece. Whatever could that mean? It means that the game grabs EVERY. SINGLE. PUZZLE. PIECE. AROUND. THE. ONE. THAT. YOU. WANTED. BUT. NOT. THE. ONE. THAT. YOU. WANTED. It is so frustrating that you will be tearing your eyes out after not grabbing your piece for the 20th time. I'm not even kidding, one time I counted how many tries it would take to get the piece that I wanted, and I stopped counting after I had passed twenty.
But wait, that's not all. How could it be all? It seems that the developers really wanted to make you feel the water that the pieces float in, so they tried to make this "splash" feature where, after you drop an unwanted puzzle piece into the water right above some other floating pieces, those floating pieces that were "underneath" the one you dropped will get moved to some other place in the water. And that is really annoying, because you'll always be grabbing onto unwanted pieces, and when you accidentally let go of your mouse click, the piece that you wanted will be lost within the maze of floating pieces that all look alike.
And get this - that piece-grab recognition failure occurs in every puzzle but the last one. The last puzzle is pretty smooth and it just makes me wonder why it couldn't be like that before. It's like the developer knew how to make the piece-grabbing responsive, but decided to troll you the whole time until the last puzzle.
As far as music goes, I guess it's okay if you're into that whole Japan-style culture, but I still think it could have been much better. An occasional oriental sound or two with long pauses in between doesn't make a relaxing soundtrack, it just manages to surprise you every time because you totally forget there's even a soundtrack in this game.
The puzzles mostly feature japanese architecture, so if you like that too, I think you'll be satisfied. I myself would have preferred a puzzle game featuring animals, to be honest, but that's just my misanthropy speaking. (lol)
Oh, and each puzzle has its pieces cut into different shapes, so that's pretty cool! It helps keep each puzzle fresh, in my opinion.
But ultimately, I'm supposed to tell you if you should give your money for this game, and I believe you shouldn't. Seven euros is simply too much for a game with this many flaws. I'm glad I got it for free on indiegala, so if you didn't get it there while it was still available and you simply feel the need to get it, at least buy it on a sale or in a bundle. Those seven euros can be spent on better things, whether here on Steam, or in the offline world.

lock into their precise position within the frame, which means that the player cannot connect individual pieces before he knows where they will go

*Puzzle image variety is mediocre to poor in the Japan edition and some images consist of much of the same color, which makes for boring pictures and tedious puzzle solving
*Repetitive music

7-10 hours, depending on one's skill at solving jigsaw puzzles.  I took a little over 8 hours, including some idle time.

Solving the puzzles in this game is too different from solving actual jigsaw puzzles.
Physical puzzles nearly universally come in boxes with a picture on the front, which is commonly used as a reference point.  I do not think that being able to see what one is putting together should be regarded as a hint, especially for pictures like these.  In any case, some of the fun of solving a puzzle is lost for me when I don't have the opportunity to pick up a piece and scan the image for its position.  Additionally, without any devoted space for organizing pieces or assembling different sections of the puzzle, the process is much slower.
And it should go without saying that, in a game where the player must pick up pieces and place them in specific positions, the player ought to be able to
For being frustrating, boring, and inferior in almost every way to normal jigsaw puzzles, I give this a 3 out of 10.
Note:  The same criticisms hold true of the Undead edition, with the exception of the lack of image variety.  However, the Undead edition also adds an unnecessary (and tedious, though easy) zombie defense minigame to every puzzle, so overall it is just as bad.

Beyond the Stealth Units you have a mass of 'Light' units, the Rocket Car is pretty damn fragile, the Scorch Tank is at most medium armored, their heavy armored unit is a transport that isn't all that useful frankly. For the air units the Kamikaze Drone sucks, good for scouting, but since it die to attack, and it tend to mass suicide a single unit and thus wasting a bunch of them to take done only a couple of air units, yea not great, the Heavy Drone for itself is if anything inferior to the Heavy Helicopter of the Renegades. It seem mostly this Faction is made to take out Infantry units, which would be more significant when playing 8-Bit Hordes since they have melee and much more infantry units, but against anybody else? Now for Campaigns, they are pretty grindy and boring, too many gold stars are timer based, the Renegades Campaign due to being longer but lacking content to acquire means its pretty boring, and grinding those stars for so little stuff isn't all the good either, the Guardians Campaign is even worse, its way too hard, its the only time out of the 4 Campaigns of Armies & Hordes that I failed a mission, also their are too much crate gathering missions too. Everything here sounds like the making of a great game. Imagine waking up in an old creep haunted hospital, where you can’t even see your hand in front of your face. This would be the ultimate scare. Unfortunately the only thing scary about this game is how bad of a game it is.
The game play itself feels like one of the old dungeon explorer games, where you walk through a maze of hallways to find the staircase to the next floor. Over all this game is a huge let down and not even worth the low price of $14.99. If you are looking for a game to put the tingle down your spine, keep looking.

I actually kind of enjoyed this game.
First things first though, THIS IS NOT OUTLAST. It does not pretend to be Outlast, and I highly doubt it was ever intended to be compared to Outlast (even though it is, rather frequently). Sure, it's in an asylum as well, but that's hardly an original idea on Outlast's part. As for the light source, in Outlast, the camera was useless until you held it up to your face to record and/or switch the nightvision on; in Daylight, the phone light is on all the time and does nothing other than map the area. In reality, the phone in Daylight is functionally closer to the lantern in Amnesia.
Basically, this game is NOTHING like Outlast.
If you ask me, this game plays much more similarly to that Slenderman game where you're gathering pages in the woods (right down to how you gather remnants in each area before performing a ritual and moving on). Compared to Outlast, this game is the epitome of lameness, but when compared to that Slenderman game (which I did not care for in the slightest), it is rather brilliant.
Taken as a whole on its own, the game is rather middling, but it sets out to tell a story (which it does, even if it is cliche as hell) and make you jump (which it also does). I figured out all the tricks by about the halfway point, but I still had fun in the later chapters, even if part of that was laughing at its B-movie nature.
Don't take this as a glowing endorsement, though. There are quite a few serious issues with the game. It is not very well-optimized, there are loading-induced stutters and frame drops GALORE, the times when the dialog kicks in are often nonsensical (and hilariously immersion-breaking), the story is opaque from a mile away, you rinse-repeat the same exact actions in all 5 areas, and the game is too easy (although they would have had to be smart about making it more difficult).
The reason for my last parenthetical is that, should you die, you "awaken" back at the entrance to your current area with none of the remnants you picked up, and you have to do the ENTIRE section over again. It would have been MUCH smarter if they instituted a manual save game feature like so many other horror games. Case in point, I had to attempt the 3rd area 3 times, and I was so annoyed by the 3rd try that I was beyond scaring.
The game does a few things pretty well too, though. While there are copious amounts of blur, dust, and focus issues preventing you from seeing them, the graphics are actually quite pretty. This is the first game to use the Unreal Engine 4, and if you look closely enough, you can see the subtle upgrades over UE3. Also, the menu theme is interesting, if not entirely memorable. I've tried to think of a 3rd good thing to say, but I can't.
I can't say this was my favorite horror game of all time, or even in the top 5 (maybe even 10), but if you're a horror fan and you understand it for what it is, you should get a decent amount of fun out of it.
DO NOT pay $15 for it though. The entire thing is about 2 hours long, even with having to replay some areas.
Broken as hell.  Don't buy; you are not likely to get a refund, disfunctional product or not.

This is a review for the EX version of Super Galaxy Squadron, unlike many of the reviews posted prior to Feb 18, 2016.  I have only played EX, and not the original version of the game.
I recommend this game, but with a few caveats.  First, the good:  The pixel art of the graphics is very well done.  Every ship, enemy, background, and attack looks good.  The music is amazing.  You could play this game just to listen to the music and it would probably be worth it.  There are 14 ships to choose from, and that is a huge plus.  Each has its own pilot with a couple-sentence long story that adds some flavor to the game.  I appreciated this touch.  The Endless mode is another plus for this game; it makes a fun little diversion when you are low on time but really want to just shoot stuff up.
Now, for the negative...backgrounds and enemies do get repetitive.  Many levels have the same enemies and while each level has a unique background, some have no transitions and those that do have only 1 or 2.  This can make the levels, especially the first 4 or so, kind of boring and repetitive.  If you play on Hell difficulty you may not notice the lack of variety so much, but you will definitely get used to the same enemies and attack patterns.  Speaking of attack patterns, this game bills itself as not really a bullet hell, and that is mostly true on the stages.  There are alot of patterns that aren't necessarily dense but require fast dodging, kind of like what might be seen in a Raiden game.  Then, on the bosses, there are some patterns similar to those "fast dodging" games, but also other patterns straight outta Touhou.  This game definitely treads on bullet hell territory on the bosses, which makes for a somewhat jarring experience.  Another issue I had in terms of difficulty, is the second attack pattern on the next to last boss on Veteran and Hell difficulties.  I got to the final stage and first boss pretty easily on veteran, but I cannot fathom how to dodge this pattern.  It was like all of a sudden the game jumped in difficulty tremendously.  I am fine with hard games, especially in a shmup but the very sudden spike really frustrates me (I still can't beat this boss).  I figured I would try the game on Hell for a different kind of challenge....and I still reached the boss, granted, not as quickly as on Veteran, but I didn't have any major troubles either.  Even on Hell, the difficulty spikes so high on that second attack pattern.  To make this even more frustrating, the official video on youtube for this game which demonstrates the sixth stage is actually missing this attack pattern for some reason, which really confuses me.  On novice, it can be cleared fairly easily, so I was at least able to see the ending.  And speaking of the ending...it had no cutscene, a super short conclusion, and no voiced content (whereas stage transitions did have these), so it felt very anticlimatic.  It really feels like the very end game needs a little more work.
Overall this game is worth the money, just don't be expecting a masterpiece.  Do expect a great soundtrack and good times to be had playing 14 different ships!

Bullet Hell games, So called because there's a lot of bullets and it feels like hell. It likely comes as no surprise then that these games can be pretty elitist. Searching online you'll find no end of videos of people managing to stay in the one exact pixel of safety on a screen so filled with moving things and colour that half the time you can't even tell where the ship is. What most people are after however is something more casual, or rather something that doesn't need reflexes akin to a cheetah on 10 cans of Red Bull. And along comes Super Galaxy Squadron EX.
Super Galaxy Squadron isn't actually a new game. It was released just over a year ago and EX is somewhere between a Remaster and an expansion. What's changed? Just about everything! It's a real do over. Everything has been made to look better, gauges and icons have been added to help you keep better track of your health and power levels. New enemies, better level designs and actual story!
Where Super Galaxy Squadron EX stands above other games is in two main ways; It's difficulty curve allowing  new players to be eased into a difficult genre and it's ship selection. I can't stress how important that new player experience is. If you like bullet hell games then you already know what you're after and what you're looking for. But if you don't? Then Super Galaxy Squadron EX is just what you need.
The different ships also allow for a variety of play styles. Whilst the core mechanic of 'hold down the fire button and move out of the way of all the dangerous things' stays the same the variations in the ships means you can change things up fairly dramatically. You might want a slow ship that packs a massive punch and can take a fair few hits or you might prefer a super fast, low damage ship where you do more dodging and only take down key targets. You can change your ship at the start of a mission so you can take on different missions in different ways.
The base game was pretty good. EX has made everything that much better, it could easily be Super Galaxy Squadron 2 and I don't think anyone would have been angry. But instead it's been released as a free upgrade to the original game! Whilst it's maybe not for diehard Bullet Hell fans for a first entry into a genre there isn't much of a better choice.

This Game is full of warmth and heart. It takes the trusted combat of Trails in the Sky FC & SC and turns it up a notch, to create the definite battle system for the Trails in the Sky Series. Which is of course needed, since this game revolves way more about combat and running through dungeons / labyrinths this time around. Only thing i would love to have since FC, is a way to speed up the casting animations.
Being kind of an epilogue to the Trails in the Sky Series, this game is best enjoyed after having played through Trails in the Sky FC & SC. Of course there is nothing stopping you from starting with this game, but the memory scenes will just not have the same impact if you are not familiar with the characters.
As usual for this series, the characters and their interactions are the real stars here. Kevin, who takes the mantle of main character this time around and Ries, his subordinate, make for a great and entertaining pair. Especially Ries was surprising to me, since she acts way more different than you would expect (in a good way). Both have a very loose tongue and bounce off each other really well.
Over the course of the game you will unlock many known characters from FC & SC and yes, Joshua and Estelle are also part of this game though the main focus lies squarely on Kevin.
Recommending this game is quite easy: If you played FC & SC this game is a no brainer. While it is a bit different in structure (more focused on dungeons), you just have to experience the memory fragments to get to know more about the characters you learned to love over the games.
If you have not played the other games I'd recommend checking them out first. They feature some of the best world building and character interactions in gaming and offer lenghty game time for the price.
On the technical side I didn't really run into any issues, the game runs as expected for me tho there are mentions of problems with integrated graphics cars on the forums. So if you have any problems you should check them out.

Decided to update my earlier review since I have now finished the game. To those who have followed this series through the first two "Trails" games, this is a worthy send off to the characters you've come to know and love. Since Estelle and Joshua's story concluded in the second chapter, the focus is now on Kevin Graham, the mysterious priest of the Septium Church introduced in the second game. Pretty much every major character makes an appearance, and each gets a moment to shine in side stories spread throughout the game. Make no mistake, this is a game for those who have followed the series from the first Trails in the Sky, everyone else will be absolutely left in the dark. If you haven't played the first two get them now, they are among the best JRPG's you can get on Steam.
Being the third in the series, I was afraid it would be really boring traversing Liberl for a third time. Falcom wisely decided to change up the formula of the game to make it even more narrative driven than normal, and shifting the gameplay into a more focused dungeon crawler. While there are plenty of battles, chracter customization and treasures to find, the fundamental gameplay remains nearly unchanged from the previous games. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but for me the strength in the series lies in its characters and story telling, and this game absolutely delivers. A grand total of 16 characters are available, which is a tad bit excessive in my opinion.
However I would be remiss if I didn't warn you that this game RAMPANTLY reuses assests from the previous two games including entire towns, dungeons, boss fights, even animated cutscenes are reused. I imagine this was done to reduce the development time as there's usually quite a bit of time between "Trails" games. It's normal for developers to reuse assets to reduce development time and save on the budget, but this game is agregious in how it just feels like a "greatest hits" of maps and fights we've already experienced in the other games. That being said, the writing and character development are just as strong as ever, and there were even times I was tearing up at what was going on. I came for more Trails narrative goodness and I got exactly that. I just wish the game was as mechanically strong as other games in the series.
So the TL;DR version: Fans who have played all the english language releases of the Trails games should not miss this game, despite manic reuse of old assets from the older games. A lot of plot elements are seeded here for future games in the series, including Trails of Cold Steel, which will be coming to Steam in the future for those of you who missed it on Playstation 3 and PS Vita.
It's a miracle this game exists at all in English, given the size of the scripts in these games. While I'm not actively looking for errors while playing, I noticed a grand total of one throughout my nearly 50 hours of play. Trails fans simply MUST buy this game and show XSeed the last two untranslated Trails games (Ao no Kiseki and Zero no Kiseki) have an audience here on steam. I'm used to spending 90-100 hours on these games typically, so this is on the shorter side of the series in general. Nevertheless, I enjoyed this game very much and look forward to more adventures in the continent of Zemuria, make it happen XSeed!

This allows different playstyles, such as starting out as the head of a clan and immediately going to war, or breaking free from your leige and forming your own clan and forcing your leige to commit seppuku (ritualistic suicide). The game also puts the aspect of religion, as upsetting a religious group will cause rebellions to spawn near a temple, shrine, or church of that particular group; having good relations will grant the player bonuses. Although the teminology and mechanics of the game are hard to learn at first, it's easy to understand.
The soundtrack is amazing, as well.
Would recommend Sengoku to a friend.

You know how you loved all those sections in other games where you had to first-person jump a succession of little platforms and any slip-up made you fall to the beginning of the level and/or death, and you wished there was a whole game based around this great idea?
Yeah.

This game is so much fun. Not only that, it's absolutely beautiful as well.
The best game I can think to compare this to, believe it or not is Super Meat Boy. Like SMB, Deadcore is a fast-paced trial-and-error platformer. Only this time, it's in first person.
The environment is breathtaking, and the audio only adds to an already fantastic atmosphere. Combine that with the story (here, in the form of collectable text logs) and you have a play space that truly needs no improvement.
Some might argue about that story I mentioned, pointing that it's not so much a story as it is a setting. And I'd say, they're right. BUT, in this case, that isn't a bad thing! The story ONLY exists to add to the atmosphere. This game's main focus is on the gameplay.
And hot damn is the gameplay fun. That said, it is CHALLENGING. It's not the hardest trial-and-error game I've played, but it's certainly no cakewalk. So don't go into this one expecting a casual romp through techno land.
There are, however, two big downsides for this title. The first isn't too important, but it's worth mentioning: the collectables emit a high-pitch screech that REALLY hurts my ears. I may just be sensitive to that sort of thing, and I'm sure it's just there to help you locate them. But really, it seems unnecisary.
Second, and more important, the length. This game is 5 levels long. Each level will take you around 30 minutes to beat on your first run through. Now, each level has a fork in the path, allowing you to choose one of two routes to take. This means that, including level replays to maximize content, you're going to be spending a total of 5 hours on this title. (unless you plan on dedicating time to perfecting your speedruns.)
I just can't help but feel like the game is SCREAMING for more content.
Even with it's flaws, I think this is a great game, and will fit perfectly in the library of anyone who likes fast-pased action platforming.
All in all, I give the game 8.5/10
