is a cute Japanese indie 2D platformer fusing
-style game flow and level design with
-style powerups. Originally released on the Nintendo 3DS eShop,
has now pleasantly made its way to Steam. Its port did need some tuning at first, particularly in terms of controller input and layout recognition. Now that those issues have been resolved, the game unveils itself to be satisfying and affordable enough that I can safely recommend it as a decent, enjoyable little platformer.
Zizou Olympia, the titular Dark Witch, has set out on a trek to locate and retrieve the stolen Syega crystals, which supply magical blessings to the general populace. As a goddess, and a bit of a snarky one at that, Zizou's not going to let anyone obstruct her investigation - and hence, she finds herself progressing through eight stages, each overseen by a potential culprit. The game plays out like an early-era
series entry across mostly-horizontal stages, rear-guarded by a boss who'll yield her special weapon to Zizou upon defeat. Throughout the stages, however, Zizou collects Tres power from slain foes, building up an enforcement gauge offering various
-style powerups such as increases in running speed and shot power. The game's above-average difficulty encourages the player to put these to good use rather than sit back hoarding Tres, especially since each attack Zizou survives depletes some of her accumulated Tres gauge. Fortunately, merely attacking a boss can also build some meter so that Zizou won't face the prospect of going totally without Tres at a critical moment. All acquired Tres can then be spent at the menu shop between stages to improve Zizou's base parameters and the potential utility of her newfound special attacks. Each of the opening 6 bosses can be tackled in any order, after which the penultimate and final bosses - including the Syega's thief - await. It's up to the player to learn which boss is weak to which special power inherited from defeated bosses.
The game's colorful stages definitely stand out more in HD than they did on the small 3DS screen. A few nifty stage effects reminiscent of 16-bit-era
and
games add to the flavor of the stages and gameplay. While none of the pixel art demonstrates sheer excellence, it's altogether capable and generally good-looking. Even better, the lineart assets really spring into focus in this HD polishing. Characters look sharp, eye-catching, and pleasingly adorable. Moreover, the game's decently-catchy soundtrack sounds easily clearer and beefier here than it ever could've on 3DS. Again, 16-bit-era gaming comes to mind, both in composition and presentation of the music. Few tunes really stand out as exceptional, yet similarly, few tunes prove to be headache-inducing or flat-out unlikable. There're some good songs here, listenable outside the game (without being knockout classics). On the flip side of the audio, competent Japanese voicework complements the admittedly-plain story snippets. It's not that
lacks charming ladies; it's that those charming ladies don't say or do much at all. One might draw parallels here with, for example, a danmaku/bullet-hell shoot-'em-up in the vein of
a cast of nicely-drawn gals who don't leave too much of an impression either way. Basically, the story frames the gameplay but doesn't extend beyond it. As with the older
- or
perchance? - this is fine. Not great, but fine.
As for PC conversion and compatibility,
v1.01 now natively supports 360-mode controllers. The game does play well enough on keyboard since it doesn't need a huge array of buttons to press at once, but it was wise for Inside System to better configure the initial limited controller support so as to ensure compatibility with a decent range of controllers. I'm playing it on a Logitech F310, a controller with which I've no qualms with how
recognizes it. This is a positive alteration to aid with navigating the above-average difficulty of the game, at least in regards to the Normal setting. Here's some gratitude extended to Inside System for remedying these pitfalls, as they had dampened the fun of the game for several people.
Overall,
doesn't really approach the level of a spectacular game. Rather, it's a generally *good* game throughout: good, colorful graphics; good, catchy music; good, solid gameplay. It isn't much for excelling, but it's not really horrid in any way. The story's not much, and Normal mode's no pushover. However, for what it attempts to be - a good, likable video game - it delivers.

Risky Rescue is the kind of game that kills a few minutes when you happen to have them to spare.
It does that exceedingly well, providing short levels where you must race against a bot trying to rescue the same stranded tiny people.
Pros:
+ Simple & very cute graphics

+ Easy to learn, but definitely challenging to master -- especially racing the bot to get 3 stars on all levels
+ Endless mode provides an opportunity to rank yourself with other players, and get some extra coin to unlock more 'copters.
+ Really cute graphics.  (I had to mention it again!)
Neutral:
~ Music is extremely repetitive, though in most cases, you won't play for hours at a time.
Cons:
- "Shadow" of the bot can be very distracting, especially when you are not used to it.
- Some of the faster copters put out colored "smoke" that is EXTREMELY distracting.  I don't use those copters because of it.
TLDR;
I definitely recommend this game, especially if you can get it on sale.  A fun little time-killer which provides challenge and is enjoyable to play.  (... and has really cute tiny people! ;-)

Prague is my birthplace and I've been living here for almost 27 years. Even though I don't play hidden object games, I was looking forward to playing this one hoping to see some places in my home city and hoping to read something about our legends. Unfortunately, the game consists of about 8 locations, from which only one is set in an allegedly Prague street, which in fact looks like a street in a German town.
The story is poorly written with many cringe moments, wanna-be jumpscares and flaws in logic. One of the two main antagonists is completely useless for the story, the other one, who should yield mystic powers, is a complete tool. The Golem is portrayed as a two meters tall pile of poo and if I get it correctly, he is freely roaming the streets of the city with no one noticing. One of the funniest moments in the story was when you dressed up a manequine to fool the Golem, making him think the manquine is actually the main hero. And it succeeded! Really?!
Honestly, I was hoping to see Prague and/or read either an interesting legend that I might have missed during my life, or simply play through an interesting story based on a Prague legend. I didn't get any of these.

Watch out: this game is highly addictive. Who would have thought that the simple premise of chopping wood as fast as you can while avoiding branches could make such a fantastic game?

That said, multiplayer is still a great addition to this game, and provides a welcome alternative to always playing singleplayer.
Overall, a very nice, very addictive little casual game.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.

Summary: Vertical bullet hell with lots of ships
Multiplayer: No
Completion: 1 hr
Cards: Yes
Cloud:  No
Super Galaxy Squadron is a very standard vertical bullet hell shoot 'em up.  It won't win any awards for its concept, but it does offer a surprising number of unique ships that play somewhat differently from each other. The result is a rather replayable shooter, if only to test the functions of each ship, which I found enjoyable.
Gameplay is a standard shmup. Shoot anything that moves, avoid bullets, grab items. The items dropped by enemies are mostly random; it is thus possible to have a bunch of missiles before you ever get a laser upgrade. The game lacks a "focus" mode, where you can slow down your ship to maneuver tight spaces. Thus I found faster ships, which often have less armor, work against me.
There are 14 ships to choose from in this game. Surprisingly most ships have a good balance about them, though a few stood out as being much better or much worse than the others. The majority of my time spent on this game was comparing each and every ship by fully upgrading them, and finding out which ones I liked best. Every ship possesses a unique "limit break" of sorts. As you grab points, your bar fills up and you can unleash a powerful attack or defensive ability that is based on your current ship. These occur often enough that your ship's special power is worth taking into consideration, especially on endless mode.
There's a rudimentary plot about a cold war between humans and aliens, and every ship has a bit of backstory, which is cool. Beyond that, the game largely throws story out the window, much like the entire genre does, which is a shame because it seemed like a promising story.
Unlike most bullet hells, SGS has a health system that allows you to withstand more than one hit. On top of that, enemies occasionally drop health items to replenish your life. You can even heal yourself by getting grazed by enemy bullets. Also surprising, the invulnerability period after getting hit is relatively generous. It's a refreshing system that provides some amount of tanking ability, and is thus friendlier to new players to the genre. When you get hit, your ship will drop one of its power-ups, but it's easily reacquired by simply flying over it and grabbing it again. Hardcore mode exists for those who prefer the one-hit death style of gameplay. There seems to be no additional reward for playing on hardcore.
Most of the game is easy enough. There's six stages in total, each one lasting maybe 3-5 minutes. If you die, the game generously lets you continue on the last stage you were on. The bosses are great, being hulking machines (mostly) with collapsible parts, wide bullet patterns and just as large health pools. The last boss is such a large leap in difficulty that I'm not sure I could ever beat it with certain ship designs. It's a long enough battle that it might as well be considered a stage in of itself.
Graphics are good. It's entirely pixel-art, and well-animated, particularly explosions. I like that every upgrade you acquire is a noticeable improvement, typically giving you additional shots, and sometimes even a graphical change. I have not experienced any slowdown despite the large number of moving things, even on endless, so that gets good marks. Music is chip-tunish, and somewhat upbeat but also kind of on the forgettable side.
I recommend playing the game with a gamepad, though keyboard actually works well enough. The game did not recognize my USB gamepad; if the same occurs to you I recommend Joy2Key which often solves this problem on similar games.
While I wouldn't recommend it at full price, it's not bad at a discount. All proceeds go to the Child's Play charity, so even if you don't enjoy the game, someone else may benefit. For the game to be created by largely one person, this is a pretty commenable effort. I give Super Galaxy Squadron a 7/10. It's super short, but because of that, you can replay it in short bursts with many different ships, so it works out in the end. SGS satisfies that urge to just jump into a game and start shooting stuff without rhyme or reason.

As the format of the 3rd was becoming clear to me during the first few hours of gameplay, I wasn't sure how well my interest would hold up. The strength of the series has always been within the boundaries of storytelling, characterization, and world-building. I wasn't sure how well that would translate to sectioned off zones through enumerable doors divorced from the rest of the game. While the combat and primary gameplay mechanics in the trilogy have been functional, I wasn't sure they could carry the game on their own.
Getting right to the meat of the game,The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky the 3rd( 英雄伝説 空の軌跡) is a remaster of the original PSP and Windows game. Of the things remastered, the primary thing is texture resolution, and lighting.
The textures look amazing, along with the new lighting style. This is something I think everyone can get behind, but I'm sure it will put some people off. Colors are more distinct and crisp. Playing the steam ver and PSP version side-by-side, one of the biggest differences is the lighting. Almost all of the textures are upgraded, but the lighting will really catch your eye. The game is a lot brighter than the original. I don't know if this is because of the PSP screen or not, but I tend to think it's a much better looking game because of it.
When a lot of the primary progression of the game involves trekking through dungeons that are, for the most part, fairly straightforward, having a high level of input over your team composition and strategy is fairly engaging. I often found myself swapping characters in and out of party not out of obligation, but out of interest.
Even on the normal difficulty mode, some of the battles presented in the main game involved a level of strategy that I didn't really encounter in the earlier entries; it often didn't stretch beyond utilizing elemental weaknesses and abusing S-crafts. While the 3rd could be similarly trivialized on a lower difficulty level or through copious level-grinding, I feel that it did not succumb to this weakness to the same extent.
Battles play out very similar to what players would have seen in FC and SC, except now you get to create your own dream party and use some of their awesome Crafts: if you enjoyed the battle system in the previous two games, then you’ll enjoy this one. Even though it’s just more of the same, playing the game with new characters gives a pretty fresh feeling and I never felt bored.
-The Pros-
+Additional depth/detail to every main character in the Sky Trilogy.
+Additional depth/detail to the world of West Zemuria.
+A lot of foreshadowing to future installments (Zero, Azure, Cold Steel)
+The Cons+
-Not Voice or Dub
(the difference between this and the PS VITA remaster versions, is that this one is now fully voiced on major scenarios, new visual arts, musics were fully arranged, and changes on the game balance)
-Game still have Glitch and some bugs
-Did Not Auto detect controller while starting the game(have to turn on from game settings)
Neutral
=Not The PS Vita Remaster Version
PS VITA VERSION (THE THING I WANT IT BADLY ON STEAM VERSION)
They've added more combat turn bonuses. Zero Arts and Zero Crafts allows you to use a craft or art at a cost of 0 EP or CP respectively. They also added a Rush bonus that makes your first attack give a delay of 0, which means you can get a free turn right after.
Another addition to combat they've added is the ability to hit enemies before engaging them. Like a lot of games where you have to actually run into enemies to start a random battle, you can now press O to attack them. Hitting from the front immobilizes them, and hitting them from the back stuns them, granting bonus XP at the end of the fight.
Something more hardcore players might dislike is the changes to combat, which I think will make the game overall a lot easier. I'm not far into it, but leveling will be faster cause of the 2x XP Bonus from stunned back attacks (which you can choose not to use), fights will be easier due to Zero Arts and Zero Crafts (free arts and free crafts are crazy), and Rush giving you free basic attacks.
-Conclusion-
If you haven't played the original, Trails in the Sky is a sub-series in the Legend of Heroes series, featuring its own unique world and characters. It is a classic JRPG with a large focus on story and characters and turn-based combat. The combat is more of a mix of classic JRPG random encounters with some isometric strategy game elements.
The combat is enjoyable, it allows for decent customization for all of your characters, and it offers some pretty decent challenge. Characters have their own special abilities, and they have a orbments which allow you to equip various amounts of special orbs that give special abilities based on the elements of those orbs. Lots of mix and match opportunities.
My Verdict 4/5
If you liked the first Legend Of Heroes game then this evolution is a must have addition to your collection. sadly we are not getting PS VITA remaster version which is partially voice and improve in game battle animation.

Gameplay lengh: 3 - 20 Hours if you want to practice Speedrun, even more so if you want to raise to the top of the leaderbord ranking.
Required skill level: Medium to Very High - Experience can vary considering the creativity of the player
This game is for most audiences 12 years and up
DeadCore is at its core (heh) is an interesting mix of well-known genres takes a step further. Think of it as Portal, but with an emphasis on movement physics rather than focusing on spartial problem solving. Its a rather unique mix that can be best discribed as a
game. Developer Team 5BitsGames tried hard to create a game that uses its game physics to create a very frantic game where shooting isn't the only important thing to do. The result is a unique mix of the two popular games Quake 2 and Portal.
And in my opinion it is much better than the Portal games alone.
While you still get to shoot flying robots and entities that are formed like Cubes, the gameplay is more about moving yourself in ways you wouldn't even think of in other games. More specifically the largest factor you have to consider before buying this game is the focus on movement and a calm and smooth aim rather then twitch reflexes. Furthermore memorizing each level, up of the entire game is essential for finding new ways to complete your quest in climbing the tower-themed world once again if you choose to play through it for another time.
Or in other terms, DeadCore is the perfect
game. From the beginning to end I never reached a part that was overly frustrating. The entire game really opens up once you see that this game wants you to Speedrun it instead of merely playing through it once.
As an example, the first level, which serves as a tutorial took me about 40 minutes to finish when I played through it for the first time. The second playthrough however, after a bit of foreplanning and with the small-but-useful skills you unlock during your first playthrough, took
. A
is included so you can compare the time it took to beat any level and even the entire game with your friends or everyone else if you choose to.
A Story does exist but the devs made sure that it is not rubbing you in the face. Rather then progressing with the story, you unlock bits and pieces explaining the setting by finding hidden Data Cubes through your journey, which can be accessed via a built-in journal. The Devs certainly knew that games like these focus on the gameplay. Its because of this focus on gameplay that the story itself becomes entirely a optional or even a entirely seperate factor, but it is still interesting to read through the bits and pieces you will find if you want to explore past the obvious routes. Theres also different upgrades to be found, which aren't needed if you want to beat the game, but should be gathered anyway if you try to speedrun the game. Otherwise you're up to a even greater challenge.
And that uniqueness the strongest point this game can offer to you. What may seem like a 5 hour long game that can be beaten in less then 20 minutes if you put creativity and foresight into it. Not with knowing about the route you went before, but finding a better way through the game that wasn't obvious to you during the first time. This is very similar to oldschool jump and run games, or games Speedrunners already have lots of experiences with. Or in different words, DeadCore is a modern game but with an very oldschool Heart and Soul. It takes the FPS genre, completly subverts the way people usually play these games and creates something that is

The object is simple, grab jigsaw pieces floating in a pond along the top and side edge of the screen and assemble them into a picture in the middle. No timer. No real special abilities or upgrades. No contrived storyline. Just a neat little way to pass some time and look at some pretty pictures.
Complexity is added along the way by increasing the piece count of new puzzles or by tackling a picture with fewer unique, easily identifiable features, but the most noticeable addition is the actual "cut" of the pieces with each new stage. Initially we're introduced to the more conventional shapes we'd expect to see jigsaw pieces to come in, but as you progress things are mixed up by having the interlocking segments of the pieces cut into shapes relevant to the picture for that puzzle. So, a watery picture might have pieces with interlocking segments in the shape of waves, for example, or another set might have tiny little temples or trees connecting each piece (though no Godzilla shapes are anywhere to be found, sadly). It's a really fresh take on an old formula that manages to hold your interest and keep you guessing for longer than it might have otherwise, but thankfully this really helps it to stand out.
Another factor which makes it stand out is its presentation. Everything is presented with an air of tranquillity, from the constant gentle twangs of various Japanese string instruments, to the flow and splashing of water throughout that makes you want to go to the toilet at least once every puzzle set. Visually, there's no great flare or anything flashy going on, everything is clean and simple and in keeping with the overall style and tone of the game helping it make for a sedate and pleasant experience.
During my time with the 21 puzzles (19 regular, unlockable sets, and 2 "bonus" sets that are unlocked from the beginning but don't seem to count towards overall progress, oddly), I only found myself having any difficulty with two of the sets, which was partly down to the finale's piece count, but also the lack of distinct features on their pictures, which is one of the few minor complaints I'd have with the game. I know that the colours and shapes in each picture scene has to be kept relatively similar throughout, otherwise you'd find every piece way too easily, but that doesn't mean the images have to be uninteresting. It would have been nice to assemble something that was a greater showcase of Japan and its culture, like pedestrians crossing the Shibuya intersection or some talking toilets or a schoolgirl underwear vending machine. But, instead, we have to be content with some temples or golf courses. Which are OK... I guess.
Another minor gripe I had with it was the lack of a save feature. This isn't a problem for the easier early stages, but towards the end I could see it being a real issue for some as you might want to put an hour or so aside for a couple of the later, harder sets. Another, more pressing pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ though, was actually selecting the pieces from the pond. Again, this isn't so much a concern at the start, but by the end the pond is so full of moving pieces that grabbing one out of it becomes a real problem, to the extent that more often than not the piece I clicked on wouldn't be what came out and I'd appear to have some near by random piece instead, with me having to remove all the unwanted surrounding pieces before finally being able to get the one I wanted. A really strange oversight in an otherwise well made game.
So, while it's not without its flaws, overall I really enjoyed my time with it. Full disclosure, I got the game free as part of a promotion on a bundle site, but even had I paid full price I'd still be happy with it. So if you've got a bit of spare time, a little patience, and some extra money to blow on a throwaway purchase, then I could easily point you towards this game to satisfy your crazy, insatiable jigsaw lust.

Points that made this game shallow:
- graphics are quite terrible, even setting for highest does not help much, and one can feel like beeing thrown into game from previous decade
- the plot is linear, with very few sidequests throwing very little into main action plot. Basically game is very short, possible to finish in just a few hours on normal difficuly.

Technical issues:
- graphic and character movement glitches. My char was often stuck on nothing
- game crashes randomly at start if other that default graphic settings are used. In my case it was one and the same reoccuring bug, which seems to had no countermeasures, no tech support. Even now I do not know why the game eventually run.
- combat mechanics are similar to those in Witcher 1, but done much, much worse. With many glitches and synchronization issues. E.g. often given action commands were stacked on, and I could see my character acting for several seconds with me not touching controllers. That causes playing on higher difficulty annoying rather than chalenging

Good things:
- skill tree and interesting techno-like soluions (i.e. technomancers)
- Mars location
In the end, I do not recommend this, even if given for free. It could be played just as simpler Witcher game in SF climat, but it is done so terribly.  Going though the game doesn't give anything positive. Just huge waste of time.

The RTS genre is somewhat lacking, but it's nice to see a developer trying to bring it to the masses.  I don't like the idea that it's being watered down somewhat, but you know...  Game development isn't about purity, it's about mass appeal - and if you can do that while staying true to your vision, then good for you.
I like that this game doesn't take itself too seriously and as a result, you never need a lot of time to get into this.  You can learn all of the mechanics over again everytime you play if you have to - it's that simple, but where there is surface simplicity, there's usually always some underlying depth.
The rock paper scissors aspect of the units is pushed about as far as possible, requiring you to learn whatever new Unit they're introducing on that particular level and using it.  If you've ever played an RTS you know this is how it usually goes.
Still, without departing too much from the conventions we all know and love, this game is charming enough to be whatever you need it to be now:  A temporary scratch for that RTS itch.

Nice Mahjong game with quests, minigames, items, ... (and sadly limits on how much you can play).
Cons:
- Ads for other games of the publisher on every start
- Intro plays every time (but can be skipped)
- The first-start tutorial must be played through before options menu (volume!) can be accessed
- Some resolutions (like windowed 800x600) *seem* to be supported and can be configured, but do not work. The smallest windowed resolution i was able to get is 1366x768.
- Many actions in the game cost your character energy. This essentially prevents you from playing the game at your own pace and is probably supposed to annoy the player into micropaying more energy. For a casual player, this shouldn't be an issue though; you can play "enough" games in a day and come back hours or days later without a problem. Hardcore players (or myself on a bad-weather weekend) will hit the limit in 30 minutes to an hour or two and be annoyed by it.
Neutrals:
0: The game feels a bit clumsy sometimes and you have to get used to the UI. Not all clickable things look to be clickable at first, and some clickable things don't do exactly what you expect (f.e. it isn't always clear what your next step in a quest should be, "to target" brings you to the monster you're supposed to finally fight, but you're still missing an item for that, so you have to figure out where you can get the item by yourself. The game could make that more obvious.)
0: Even when you know what a button does/is (like location buttons in the "where do i get this item?" view), you can't really tell them apart because they look so similar. This could be fixed f.e. with additional permanent text or mouseover text.
Pros:
+ Mahjong is fun, and there's a small tutorial for it. (There's a 10 minute time limit for every game, which you can only extend if you have certain items, which you don't always have.)
+ There's an elaborate tutorial for the whole game, which is well done overall. (It can't be skipped though.)
+ The chest-opening minigames are fun, too. (The time limit on them can be a bit hard, though.)

Don't let the speedrunning nature of the game discourage you, it can still be enjoyed even by old people with slower reflexes. Some patience and practice can give a very rewarding feeling everytime you hit the next checkpoint.
The game at it's core is an obstacle course, where the main goal is travelling from point A to B through lethal traps and pitfalls.
Early on the game teaches you that you can use and exploit any object in the physics-defying architecture around you, sometimes even using a trap itself to propel yourself forward. This aspect of Deadcore adds a puzzle element to the whole experience, so it's not just a twitch-based runner. Combining the puzzle aspect with the branching paths in each level the game lets you carve your own trail opting for a safer or a faster route. Even though there are no walls, no ceiling or even a floor most of the times, you can still be creative in how you progress through the labyrinthine levels, since there are multiple ways to crosss each obstacle. The player can be slow and methodical at some parts figuring out the way for himself or use timing and platforming skills at others. At first you will only be able to traverse a basic path as the developer intended, but the more tools and power-ups you unlock, the more the game itself opens up to you.
Deadcore also rewards exploration and pushes the player to search for 3 different types of collectibles. First type unlocks more bits of the story helping you to understand your environment and it's purpose. Second type unlocks more music tracks, ranging from ambient to D'n'B and jungle beats. The third type opens up completely new paths in the levels, adding even more complexity and replayability.
The main and only downside that comes to mind is the game's lengh. Takes about 10 hours for a slow casual player like myself to make 2 full cycles of the game and unlock the "secret" ending. After that point, any replayability is based on speedrunning and ranking up in the player lists, or achievement hunting if that's your thing (all of achievements easily feasible).
In summary: Deadcore is a butt-clenching adrenaline fix with a unique gameplay experience, part puzzler part speed runner.

DeadCore is a first person platforming game. It has a futuristic setting and the whole game will throw you for a trip.
I don't think there is much in the way of story, just scattered words and logs across the game. Not really a big focus.
The main gameplay has you jumping and sprinting around. It starts our very simplistic but as they give you new mechanics things can start to become very challenging. I would highly recommend you don't play this game if you have some type of motion sickness as the gravity sections might be difficult to take. That said, the gameplay is very smooth, unique, and fun. Not many platform games give you this much freedom to move around with, and very rarely do you see first person platform games at all. The game has 6 or so levels, and took me about 3 and a half hours. The game also has collectibles you can find which would greatly add to the gametime, I personally didn't go for them. The game greatly encourages speedrunning, with leaderboards and even a speedrunning mode. Hell there's a clock on the Gun at all times.  I can see how the mechanics could be creatively used by speedrunners to get through levels quickly. I'm usually pretty competent at platformers and even I had a lot of trouble in some sections so I would say this game could be pretty difficult for more casual players. It could do with more checkpoints in some sections.
The overall look and feel of the game is something to be admired. While it can be a little monotone at times, the emptiness and beauty of the levels isn't lost on me, and some of the crazy mechanics will surprise you. I feel the gravity mechanic will be either greatly loved or hated, depending on your perspective, but it is something to appreciate that you don't get to see much in a first person game.
The game also includes a weapon and enemies but this is either meant to be underutilized or just meant to give you more things to do. Enemies are just there to be shot once, to stop them for a moment, while you continue platforming. I feel it's unecessary.

Pixel Puzzles: Japan is a jigsaw puzzle simulation game. It is said to have some light gameplay elemtns mixed in with putting together jigsaw puzzles. Putting together puzzles without all the mess of getting the pieces out, making sure you get them facing up, clearing the space to put it together, and then putting it away later is nice. The actual act of putting the pieces into the puzzle is fun. Some other virtual puzzles I've done are far too forgiving on how close you need to put the pieces, but this game does a good job of making you put it in the right place before it'll stick without it being too horribly specific to make you second guess yourself constantly. Some of these puzzles were fun to put together with neat pictures as a result. Also, there were some interesting edges and piece shapes which gave the different puzzles a little life and challenge to put together. The jigsaw puzzle part is good. My issues come in when you're looking at the gameplay elements that have been included to spice the game up. Either these elements should be eliminated, or there needs to be more of the elements.
The elements that are there are mostly annoying or useless. Being able to pick up a fish and move it around isn't really challenging or fun, it's just useless. Completing puzzles to unlock more is also a bit useless, as anyone doing this for the sake of doing the puzzles is going to do them all anyway so having them all available to pick from would be nice. Plus, leveling up for completing puzzles just to unlock other puzzles is also fairly useless in the grand scheme of things if the only reason for them is to play more of the game you were most likely going to play more of anyway. The annoying part is how the puzzle pieces are stuck in a pool of water around the corner the table. So the pieces will freely float around, covering each other up and bouncing around, which makes them difficult to sift through. There's also an annoying priority going on. See, they have somewhat of an order. Pieces go from top left to top right, then down a row starting on the left again, and so on. So if you click in an area that would select multiple pieces, whichever one is highest on that priority list will be picked up, even if you clicked mostly on a different piece or didn't want that one. Also, if you drop a piece back in the water it, along with any other pieces it lands on, will sink and respawn in a spot in the water on the left. So the constant movement, piece priority, and sinking situation all make for a very frustrating puzzle experience. There's not really any penalty for these things. It just takes longer and is more frustrating. It wastes your own time and tries your patience, whch I don't think is a good reason to have the elements. The only useful element is that, once you get enough pieces in, you can click on the sun and reveal the entire picture for a few seconds to refresh your memory... even though most people would be able to look at it the while time when doing a real puzzle.
On the other hand, there could be MORE elements and it'd make the game more fun, or at least have it make more sense. For instance, maybe something with time. A time limit, or just a timer to record your time. Some type of score for using the piece you grab and taking points away for throwing a piece back. Reasons to go faster and be more precise, plus giving a point to the tedious design. Getting better ranks to unlock perks or just to unlock puzzles. Having online leaderboards to compete for scores or times with others. There are plenty of things that could be added to make the current model of the game make more sense and possibly make it more enjoyable as a video game. Even just a save feature would be nice. In real life, many people will take breaks from big puzzles. Without a save feature, you can't do that here unless you want to leave your game running the entire time, which not everyone wants to do.
A few of the puzzles were made up of similar looking things to the point of resorting to random placement to find where anything went. Maybe my eyes just suck, but they were not fun as trial and error challenges. Like the one with all the flowers... my word. Also, most of the puzzles look rather similar to each other anyway, which makes some sense with the common theme of Japan, but I still think more variety could've been had. I only found a few of the pictures interesting to look at and try to solve.
What I'm saying is that Pixel Puzzles: Japan falls just a bit short of being a good puzzle simulation, and falls very short of being a fun interactive gaming experience. There needs to be more or less features to make this work well either way, at least for my taste. I played all the way through it, aside from the bonus puzzles. I got all the achievements and did all the main puzzles. I was very worn out near the middle but kept on going to see if it got any different. It really didn't. This game was ten hours of the same thing that, despite doing more puzzles and being a decent amount of puzzles for the price, wasn't a fun experience towards the last half. Changing the elements would make it better and possibly could've made me enjoy this game as a whole. However, I just can't say I enjoyed it. The first few puzzles were fun, but it gets old fast. I got this for free and... as mean as it sounds, I still feel like it was a waste. At least the last half was a waste of my time as I didn't enjoy it, but I wanted to review it and give it a fair chance for reviewing purposes. I feel I've done that, and I honestly cannot recommend it as is, especially at the 7 dollar asking price. Pixel Puzzles: Japan gets a 3/10 for having potential to be a good puzzle simulation or puzzle video game, but failing to do much justice to either camp.

You only have right & left which make you go up-right or up-left and it automatically descends in the last direction when not going up & right/left.  You might be able to use down to decelerate down-left/right faster, but is unecessary.  (2) Your star rating seems based in time, which includes your partner, not how many guys you rescued more than the bot, but you still have to rescue more than the bot to proceed, and if the bot takes a while your rating is hurt.  Still, I ended up with 1-3 stars per level on first try, better if the bot crashed because it stops the time immediately if waiting for him.  It is partly cooperative, pertly competitive which is odd.  (3) I don't see any point to buying other helicopters.  It is so wonky as it is that I can't imagine controlling it if it were faster.  It was really ackward at first, but rather OK later.  I was happy to reach level 50 and be done, but wasn't bad by then.

This is another case where I wish Steam had an 'Eh...' option.
The one entirely positive thing I have to say is that the art is nice, but I suppose that for a point and click game that's entirely expected. There's a decent enough variety of environments and the rather large amount of FMVs look pretty alright all things considered.
Mechanically, it's fine. Items don't need pin point accuracy to register, the game doesn't freeze or lag anywhere. This is bare minimum stuff, but at least
reached that minimum, y'know?
Puzzles were also just... OK. There's a lot of matching involved and about three are sequence based. None are particularly difficult - I think the longest took me about five minutes. The bulk of the game is hidden object search.
Now, unfortunately, it's the meat of point and click games where everything goes bad. The story. Or rather, the writing and direction.
As a general idea the story is alright. The premise could have turned out fine. All of the events that take place make sense and do a good enough job of providing a motivating force for the story to move forward. It's just the writing... well the writing and the voice acting. This is a budget title and all, but good lord have the developers never heard a person speak? Our protagonist, an incredibly ditzy girl named Eva, seems to have a flair for being dramatic and idiotic at all points of the game. A skeleton just reached out to grab me? Well golly gee! Someone who I never knew apparently is dead and I don't even know how they died? It's so "SAIIYD!!!" Saiiyd is the best way to write down how the voice actress performed that line. "It's so saiiyd." Somehow the pronunciation was the same each time the line came up.
Another complaint is that while the events that take place can be logically linked together, dear old Eva seems to have lost the plot. Her lines are random and make little sense with the context of the scene. Pick up a flask for later? Yep, makes sense, flasks are useful to hold liquids. "GOLLY GEE I BET THIS FLASK WOULD BE USEFUL TO HOLD SOME ACID!" ...I mean, yes Eva, that is what it's going to be used for but why in the world is that what comes to mind? She also has a knack for picking random pieces of junk, be it broken wheels, door handles, etc.. All of this stuff does get used later on, but there's no reason for her to carry all of this. Now, you could possibly chalk this up to the story being purposefully camp, which given the content of the FMVs and general setpieces was probably the point. However, the game is never purposefully funny, it just ends up that way due to the direction.
Overall, it's like the game was written by two different teams, or people I suppose. One cared at least a bit as they wrote the overarching plot, and the other just followed that list without any attention paid to the small things. Unfortunately, this is a point and click. There's three things that hold these titles up, and that's the puzzles, art, and the story. You can't fail at any and
basically got a C, B, and a D here.
Anyway, since the game is only $1.99 and 50% coupons are everywhere - for the grand price of a $1 the game is fine. It's a single dollar, I can't really expect perfection and neither should you.

Maybe the voice acting would sound better if the lines they were delivering weren't the highest form of garbage, but it's hard to tell. 8-Bit Armies wants to be a child of the Command & Conquer series. At launch it was a very barebones game with a single faction available which made it a hard sell. Currently, it’s more fleshed out with another faction that plays much differently, Guardians, and unit voices which released on December 2nd. It had a fairly slow start in its journey of establishing an identity and added some good content, but it still lacks a complete personality.
It’s not a very difficult RTS when talking about the single player Renegades campaign (the post-launch Guardians faction is free, but its campaign costs $4). The overwhelming horde approach is usually enough to overcome most challenges on the normal difficulty. You’ll want to build your base and expand by constructing buildings as far out as you can so you can better protect those precious oil pumps. Keeping an eye out for “?” crates (money, units) is a good idea too. Plopping down the same unit producing buildings increases the production speed; for example, three Barracks means Infantry will start popping out at x3 speed. I frequently expanded with unit buildings since you can change the main one that spawns them, allowing the front line to be changed at will.
I should mention that the maps are just multiplayer maps repurposed for single player. I do like how they handle progression though because clearing maps and earning stars increases your base loadout that carries over to any map. At the end of the campaign, I had an entire base erected from the beginning with a gigantic starting army. You don’t need to have a three-star rating for everything which can take the campaign’s length down below 10 hours depending on your skill level.
8-Bit armies doesn’t have a story, just its gameplay and art style. You’ll have a hard time finding any kind of plot. There’s no over-the-top acting or cheesy dialogue to provide any chuckles. What little story there is can be found when choosing a campaign map to play. Spoilers, it’s just some text in a little box. You might notice a reference or two, but there’s nothing significant in there. The new and shiny voice acting makes the game better overall. Some of them play it straight while other units might make a dumb joke, “Ready to rocket (rock it).” It’s no story, but it’s something.
Its gameplay is competent and straightforward. There aren’t too many things to keep track of since the game isn’t very complex in its campaigns or overall structure. Units don’t even earn ranks. It comes down to who has the better army composition and positioning since every unit counters another unit type. You don’t have to worry about more than one resource type, unit abilities, or controlling hero units which makes everything easier at the cost of being less interesting to people very familiar with strategy games.
You do have typical RTS hotkeys available including control groups, Ctrl+click to queue 5 units at a time, patrolling, scattering, the ability to set fixed camera locations that cycle through, double clicking a unit to select all units of that type, and more. You can expect to control infantry, vehicles, aircraft, and one superweapon. The Guardians faction does play a bit differently since it uses two stealth units, no anti-air turrets, an airborne drone that self-destructs on other air units, and an anti-infantry theme that revolves around flames. The infantry screaming as they’re lit on fire is pretty satisfying.
The game also has multiplayer and a co-op campaign. I don’t really see people online so you’ll either want to bring a friend or family member. It doesn’t have the infrastructure for a competitive multiplayer game. What it does have is Steam Workshop which means you potentially play a different map every time and there are some old favorites from other games in there. Bay of Pigs anyone? Something I have not seen before is the “interoperability” between 8-Bit games. If you own both 8-Bit Armies and Hordes, you can mix and match factions online so that orcs fight tanks and helicopters battle dragons. That’s a pretty neat feature.
The co-op campaign is somewhat similar to the single player, but set to be much more challenging. You have limited unit types available and there’s no base loadout that’s affected by how many stars are earned. The AI has access to more stuff than you which is puts you at a big disadvantage. I might suggest both players being familiar with the game first before tackling it. “Normal” feels like single player’s hard.
It’s a decent and simple base building RTS. The lack of story makes me think of what the game could’ve been, even with some cheesy text dialogue instead of faceless and speechless enemies. Still, the gameplay should still provide a good time for a good chunk of time, but the replay value seems very low without a strong online population. I would use this RTS for therapeutic army building and commanding.

(This is a Spoiler-Free review, this review is biased to my Opinion on the game as far as I've played it.)
Oh boy, guys. Here comes Ubisoft back again with another Assassin's Creed game. And how did they do, you may ask?
Bittersweet, I guess you could say.
The game is amazing, don't get me wrong. It's like Watch Dogs 2 if it was in Egypt, not like that's bad or anything.
They improved on the Combat System since Syndicate came out and made it almost like Dark Souls.
They improved on the Story, so now there are seperate quests you can go on that'll help you upgrade yourself as you continue through the main story. And they're actually pretty fun, almost feel like main missions.
The world is so ♥♥♥♥ing big, to the point where I still don't know where I am if I'm either in the middle of ♥♥♥♥ing nowhere in the desert or discovering enemy bases or discovering new cities. It really makes you feel adventurous.
Now, this doesn't mean that this game has it's flaws, and there are a few pretty big ones.
For example, the optimization is still♥♥♥♥♥♥ basically they learned nothing from Watch Dogs 2 about how to optimize for greater performace. So you better have 400-300 ♥♥♥♥ing dollars to spend on a new Ryzen or i7 or else your FX or i5 will be bending down it's♥♥♥♥♥and leaving you at 20-30 fps, 40 if you're even lucky.
You die a lot, so get ready to rage quit a lot.
Grinding is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I hate when RPGs do this to make sure the player explores the rest of the game. If you're level 8 and want to do a main quest that is level 11. You better be ready, or else you'll have a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of instant deaths on that same enemy.
Sometimes you feel side tracked from the main story and forget some of it. And some characters aren't exactly rememberable like in the past games. That may be due to the wide expansive world and the amount of characters.
Other than that, would I recommend this game?:
You have a PC that can run this at full 60fps? Get it.
You have a PC that can't even run Crysis 3 at Max? Don't even think about it.
You enjoy Grinding? Get it.
You're a fan of the Assassin's Creed series in general? Get it.
You're a fan of Dark Souls? Give it a try, I can assure that it'll be worth every penny.
It's on sale for 55-30 dollars? Get it, except maybe 55 if you're not sure you can run it.
You have money to spend it on? Be catious and make sure you can run it, but get it.
My final verdict: It was pretty good, I enjoyed it and hated it at some parts. I would recommend this game.

This is not an assassin's creed game. At least very early in the game, this feels completely different. Where as other assassin's creed games had smooth, yet slightly buggy parkour, this game doesn't have free run implemented which is a change from past games. I personally prefer the old parkour system much better, although buggy, it was always clear what you could climb and what falls you could survive. Only two hours in, and I have died countless times because a drop was slightly too high, or I tried to jump lower down onto scaffold and I flew off a cliff.
The fighting system is more like dark souls II than I think they intended. It was more in depth than previous games, and you can't just wait from them to attack you and then counter and kill them in one hit like in the past. You are not an assassin. Your character is very much more suited to combat than sneaking around in the bushes, although the sneaking system is much better. You can upgrade some skills to be more like an assassin, and I have been told that you receive hidden blades later in the game, but many times missions will end with combat.
However, If you're a fan of the Assassin's creed series, such as myself, this game may feel disappointing to those expecting the same as last time. I personally prefer the older games in the franchise, as they are not riddle with in-game purchases, and level up systems. Assassin's creed is a game that doesn't need level up, it was fine as it was for the past 9 games. Yet I am still recommending this. So early in the game, It is hard to tell what this game would be, and I will update this if my opinion changes whilst playing through it. If you are buying this game, don't buy it as an Assassin's Creed game. If you look at it from an outside perspective without previous assassin's creed experience than it is an entertaining game. I do prefer the old system, but if you like the combat system in dark souls and level up system of far cry, than this game is perfect for you.
PS. Mounts are slightly glitchy in the way they climb cliffs like they were in skyrim.

02/18/2016 EDIT: I came to be very surprised to see the huge EX update for this game, which added 3 difficulties + normal/hardcore selection, upgraded visuals, ship tweaks, and expanded features including voice acting for the story. Another big change is the update to the multiplier system, which only decreases your chain when the active chain meter hits 0 instead of flatout losing the entire thing. You can also go above x5 multiplier and keep chains more easily as it takes longer now before chaining becomes unforgiving in timing. Since there appears to be more of a legitimate scoring system with potential to carry it across entire stages, I can safely say that I would recommend this even at full price now.
This could be best described as a guilty pleasure SHMUP.  It is more laid back than a typical shmup due to the fact that you can't "lose" or "game over" in the arcade mode as you will simply restart the stage you died on with score intact if you die.  Normal uses health for your ship, while Hardcore is a one hit then restart the stage ordeal.  The local scores saved don't differentiate Normal and Hardcore, so there's no particular reason to try Hardcore unless you want a challenge.
It is fun to take all of the ships for a spin and see what they are capable of, but there isn't too much really keeping people on here for an extended period of time after that.  Endless Normal is the most fun in the long run because you'll compete with others on the steam leaderboard there and it just becomes funny to see how ridiculously stacked the odds become against you once you live longer than 15 minutes.

Pretty much everything I loved about 90s arcade shoot'em ups is in this game... plus a tiny bit of bullet hell to top it off (which I'm also a fan of). Yes I know the trailer says "Not bullet hell", but just watch a video of the final boss and you'll get what I mean by "a tiny bit of bullet hell".
Keep in mind there's no control rebinding, so if you're someone who hates arrow keys, then you might need to take that into consideration. Personally I'd like to rebind the super to X, but it's no big deal. Arrow keys, Z, and spacebar is a sensible enough control scheme for me.
In any case, I love the music, the graphical style, and the sound design. Plus I appreciate the selection of 14 ships each with its own set of stats and weapons.
The game is a lot more forgiving than most games of its type in that when you die you just restart the stage you're on, and if you quit the game you can actually come back and pick up from the start of the stage you were on. Also, your ship can take more than one hit (on normal mode). It can actually take quite a few hits, and enemies (and their missiles) can drop health when destroyed.
When you get hit you'll drop one of your acquired firepower power ups, which after a couple of seconds will be available for you to pick up again. This actually adds an interesting dynamic, in that you probably want to pick up that power up, but you're probably going to have to weave through a shower of bullets to get to it... and if you get hit then you're just going to drop more power on top of taking more damage. Of course, none of this matters in hardcore mode because getting shot will just kill you then.
Honestly, I don't have a whole lot of cohesive thoughts to give about the game (as you can likely see above).  All I can say is that I really like it.

EDIT: Haven't played the new EX version yet, this review was based on the original.
Super Galaxy Squadron is a great little "flow" shmup: you fall into a pattern of sweeping the screen left to right and back, blowing stuff up and picking up power ups.  It's a _little_ repetitive and the enemy attack patterns/level design don't vary enough to seriously knock you out of your zone, but this serves to create a pleasant state of zen-like focus and flow while playing. (Note: I'm a long-time player of shmups, so your state of zen, boredom, or extreme panic may vary depending on your experience with the genre and taste for difficulty...)
There's a simple combo/multiplier system, but it doesn't force me play the game strategically because the level design and enemy waves don't seem distinct enough to make strategies for maintaining your combo apparent to me.
The key source of variety comes from strong collection of different kinds of ships.  I haven't had a chance to try them all yet, but each requires a slightly different play style to pilot successfully.  The ships seem to range from standard shmup tropes to more creative and unique attack types.  The different ships provide a good source of replay value, outside of leaderboard climbing.
Graphics and audio are excellent, couldn't ask for more from a retro-inspired shmup!
The game's normal mode is pretty forgiving (a shmup beginner might not think so), and hardcore is of course hardcore. (one hit you're dead)
All in all a pretty good, well executed shmup at a good price!  Veterans might not find much meat on the bone, but this would be a good start for beginners to learn the basic skills required for the genre.

Super Galaxy Squadron is not bad, but it's less than what I expected it to be.
Normal Mode is not a big challenge as it feels like the life bar lasts forever (I reached the stage 6 boss second form on the first try and cleared the game on the 2nd attempt), while in Hardcore mode from what I could tell if you get hit once you have to start the level over. I think my skill level is probably more at a middle ground between the two, but the game doesn't offer this.
The art is nice but I only noticed 1 enemy ship (pink one) which was actually animated. The music was decent but not very memorable. Only the title screen music and the stage 6 music stood out for me, although some of the music did not loop naturally.
The power up system wasn't fun for me. The power ups dropped by enemies don't fall down to you, they just kind of sit there and move a small amount before fading away. If you get hit you will also usually lose one of your powerups, which fly upwards and can't be picked up again for a couple of seconds. The tried and true hyper system is fine though and the ships do feel a bit different from each other, although I only tried a handful of them.
However, the worst part about the game is the bosses. The boss patterns are boring. Aside from the stage 5 and 6 bosses, the rest just repeat the one pattern over and over. The stage 6 boss was the best out of all, and although I did feel like I had seen the patterns before in other games, I liked it and wished the same attention had been given to the other bosses as well.
I found the most enjoyment in endless mode, since I was able to zone out and fly around shooting things and dodging bullets, without having to face any of the bosses.
In all, I would say that the game is worth a try. You may like it more than I did. But it's not something I can see myself coming back to or getting friends to play.

Seeing how many people compare this game to portal let me explain why that isnt really possible and then I talk about my opinion on deadcore itself.
Deadcore is a game about reflexes/physical challenges in general. You know what you have to do, but good luck pulling it off. Sometimes you can improve your performance by figuring out an even faster way to nmove on and sometimes finding collectibles requires some thinking but you can play through without ever just standing there for half an hour wondering what to do next.  Portal on the other hand is figuring out the solution to a puzzle. Actually performing that solution in most cases isnt that hard.
Secondly there is nigh 0 story in Deadcore. That is not a bad thing, it isnt neccesary. There are hidden collectibles that give access to texts that will give you an idea of what the story is, but you have to find those first, so there is a good chance you go through the game without any story, also there is no voiceacting. This of course also means that there is no humor, but again that is not what this game is about or needs. Meanwhile Portal has its great and funny voiceactors that carry you through the game and you always know why you are where you are etc.
third the gun. yeah you use a physics doing gun in each game. In deadcore it is used to disable enemies and activate or deactive different mechanics, you dont always need it, there is a good chance you can get through a section without using your gun once. In Portal it basically is your main mechanic
So yeah that should explain why its an apple-pears comparison.
Now deadcore itself in my opinion was great fun. Some say it is to difficult and I can agree that it can get punishingly tough, but the last checkpoint usually wasnt far away and you get right back in the action. Id say a downside is falling off stuff since you are basically waiting to slam into death or going to the menu and clicking restart from checkpoint, neither of which are as fast as dying from anything else.
The abilitys all work and except for a rocket-jump like function all work very well, though sometimes precise landing can be a problem when for example your dash shoots you farther than you wanted. The rocket-jumpish ability btw almost never comes into use (in my playstyle, which means just trying to finish the level) so it isnt a problem.
Now the mechanics of the game world itself are mostly pretty good, but the gravitation changing combined with your camera moving and often the gravitation sections being the hardest to see where to go and what to do next can be a real pain.
Also the enemies could have been done better. I kind of feel like they are more of a nuisance than anything else. THere is a swarm of tiny enemies for example that slows you down and makes you less mobile and is therefor generally your death. This of course also means that once it has you escaping gets even harder. What is even worse is that these are most commonly found in the already hard enough gravitation segments. The other 2 enemy types are less annoying but all together I think this game could have done without them.
Oh and devs you will never read this but: PLEASE DEACTIVATE PAST CHECKPOINTS THAT NO SENSIBLE PERSON WOULD USE ANYMORE IN SOME PATCH! You can easyly lose everything in some sections of the game because instead of falling to your death you fall on top of a checkpoint hat is basically where you started half an hour ago and there is no way you can undo it and that is just rage inducing and a game killer.
Thankfully it isnt possible for this to happen often and probably you just have to have my luck for it to happen at all.
Now about speedrunning: yes, this game is used for speedrunners showing off with leaderboards etc. Is it hard to speedrun through? Is it good and fun to speedrun through? No idea, if there was an opposite of a speedrunner that'd be me. Though the game often offers paths that are faster but as a price more difficult. Now if you, like me, are not a speedrunner that isnt even an issue. How fast you complete the game means nothing if you dont want to shine on some leaderboard. Oh but dont excepect the game to be slow, until you reach a platform where nothing tries to kill you you have to be fast and precise or die.
All together great fun but not very long, by on sale if you like challenges

Boulder Dash is a childhood favorite, and I've played a lot of versions of it.  The concept--grabbing diamonds before time runs out--is alive and well, but the additional layers on top of it are a bit more questionable.
There have been a lot of positive changes; unmovable rocks, new monsters with different patterns, and a consistent creativity on what levels can be created.  Mostly, that formula works.
The less favorable direction of the game is power-ups and unlockables.  Because of the decison (I could see this being the right call, but I think this added to the challenge of the original game) to allow level select, the Score -> Extra Lives mechanic were out.  Okay, instead, Score gives one to three stars afterward, with three being a 'full clear' of the level.
Where this comes apart is power-ups defeating/breaking the balance of many levels but also being required to full clear others.  There are four power ups:
Dynamite, which destroys brick walls, boulders, and foes if timed right.  Great addition to the game conceptually, but by just having a big trunk of dynamite that you can use instead of having it work per level or somehow collecting it on a level, this can really cheese a lot of problems.
Double Score, which generally cheeses three star requirements.  Most levels aren't set with this in mind, so this can full clear a lot of caves even with very subpar play.
Freeze, which actually seems like it should also be findable on a level.  This allows for things like moving falling boulders, but the major use of it is simply to survive rockfalls with too many gems included.
Spyglass, which I used only to get the steam achievement.
The overall effect of the powerups is to make the game very easy.  This is sort of a shame, because this really could have been done better (IE, you must first collect the Dynamite/Freeze/Double Score) to full clear the cave IN the cave itself.
Aside from the powerups, the other major direction of the game is unlockable worlds and unlockable characters.  The worlds are extremely easy to unlock, the characters are not going to be unlocked on my game because it will take hundreds more (top unlock is HUNDREDS of found tokens) to unlock.  And the unlockable characters never seem required or particularly critical to have.
---
So, buy or not to buy?
Anyone who played and liked former versions of the game should definitely buy this game.
Anyone else, well, it's a decent puzzler with some novel concepts.  Issues about unlockables and power ups do not stop the heart of the game from being fun, although there are some very valid criticisms of this.  It's a game I'd recommend for kids (Cartoony violence only), people who like puzzle games.
If 5/10 were average, Boulder Dash 30th gets a 6.5/10 for me, and a positive recommendation.  Probably not a game for people who don't like puzzles, but nostalagia and real puzzle fans have something for them here.

A pretty decent B grade scifi adventure.  It starts out rough, with you often feeling a bit under powered in combat.  By the end of my adventure on the red planet I felt tough as nails.  The ending feels a little rushed, but overall the game is fun and engaging for the time invested.

Bizarrely, Mars:War Logs is a lot better than its spiritual sequel The Technomancer despite being three years older. The combat seems extremely clunky at first until you get into the habit of using the tactical pause and even once you do it can be stilted due to your character getting stuck on invisible floor obstructions (unless this is just lag) or boxed in by his own allies. Control via kbd+m is terrible, not remappable, and you will likely do better with a control pad. There are also some nasty difficulty spikes that will put off many. Also the character development paths (as in Technomancer) are fairly basic with no stand-out differences when focussing in a specific direction. The crafting system is also fairly basic and quite linear.
But despite all its issues M:WL has its saving graces. The storyline is often dark and gritty to the point that situations can give rise to decidedly unpleasant trains of thought. But this emotional manipulation is deliberate and works well. The story is also well developed and the voice acting is pretty good for the most part. The combat is adequate once you become accustomed to it and if you have the patience to ignore the odd bit of glitchyness.
It isn't by any means a game you should absolutely have but is well worth picking up on one of the numerous times it pops up in sales particularly if you enjoy edgy, adult focussed, content.

I saw only negative reviews so let me bring some variation to the mix. If you have an interest in grand strategy games, and are willing to do a bit of homework (don't worry, just a YouTube search) this game will become really addictive.
The game is a strategy game, but you could also describe it as a role-playing game in the same sense as dungeons and dragons is a role-playing game. It's all about your chosen dynasty and how you develop it. So instead of a character you'll be playing a line of characters. That is if you're lucky enough to survive the onslaught going on in 15th-16th century Japan, and your family head manages to produce offspring. If you lose all your lands, or your dynasty ends it is game over.
This happens often, and that's a good thing. Not achieving the ingame goals doesn't really feel like a loss, just like the death of a character in a good book doesn't feel like a failure of the author. I just lost a game where I managed to conquer 50% of Japan (one of the in game goals) but I didn't manage to be shogun for 3 years (the other goal). So technically I lost, but I don’t remember it that way.
When early on I found out my character, the second clanleader of the Nanbu clan, had became infertile, with no male heir, I realized time had become an important factor in my strategy. Thankfully the father of the clanleader had already managed to conquer the complete northern tip of Japan by scheming with other small clans, and now the clan controlled about 20% of the map. I launched a frantic military attack on my most powerful neighbor, the Togashi, who had grown from a small region to the biggest force on the map, about 35%. With some help of another clan, the Amago, I managed to conquer most of his land, which also made his military strength weaken. There was not much the Togashi could do, being battered from the east by the Nanbu (me) and later on from the west by the Amago, who were about as powerful as I was. I started to divide my newly conquered lands under my vassals, who sadly were not my sons but other members of my court. I pressed on unrelenting, I had to achieve my goals with only little time left, as my clan leader started to grow older and older with no male heir. When the Togashi were wiped of the map and hadn't provided me with the right amount of land, I backstabbed the Amago with whom I had conspired before and took a lot of their land as well.
Because the clan leader of the Nanbu had become infertile at a young age he didn't produce any offspring. He finally became shogun at age 71. He was so close to victory he, and I, could almost taste it. And then he died at age 72, only two years short of achieving our goals.
Every playthrough becomes a short story like that. Never does the playthrough feel like you played it already, not even if you decide to pick the same clan for a second time. The thing is that you need some imagination to fill in the gaps that this simulator leaves you with. I guess that if you can't add to it with your own imagination this game is a dull list of stats. But if you can imagine the stats and the simple  portrait of your character and other characters as being real, and manage to connect the dots, this game is an endless story generator.
To summarize; this game is more like a book than a movie, where for most games it is the other way around. For me every playthrough feels like an unique interactive story. I can imagine that to others it might seem like a glorified spreadsheet.

Lost Lands: Mahjong is a F2P Mahjong puzzle game with a story that draws you in and objectives that make you keep playing.
Story: You awoken from a long sleep. All ships from different races have sailed and sunk into this mysterious island that no one can escape. There is a lot of bitterness going on with all types of races on the island. To make things worse, there are even monsters harassing inhabitants on the island. There are quests such as defeating monsters, help defend a village, gather collections, and even developing relationships. There is even a part 2 after completing all the quests! Please note that the story is the same as Lost Lands: Hidden Object.
Gameplay: Like any mahjong game, it's matching pieces and clearing the board. You get a certain amount of energy that regenerates over time. To assist that, you can fix up buildings and bridges to help. Later on, however, the energy consumption is more and you may have to rely on gem purchases to speed or progress through the game. Luckily, you get free gems for logging in daily and leveling up.
The only problem I had that stopped me for a good while was getting the Ritual Scythe from the Falger. I know they recently updated to include Sacrificial Island, which drops the scythe, but I'm not sure if the chance of getting it is still difficult or not. Otherwise, I managed to get it and progress through the story.
Graphics: The graphics are detailed like an artbook and the scenery is amazing on the playing board.
Music: The music sounds great and relaxing. However, there is only two tracks. One on the menu and one on the playing board. This can get a tad bit annoying listening to it.
Overall: Lost Lands: Mahjong is like those complimentary free-to-play games that want you to have fun and has a lot of room for not needing to purchase things with real money. Most F2P games out there have ridiculous puzzles to make you buy something to complete it. However, this is the opposite. Other than the energy system, even if the game was F2P, it would make you buy the game itself for the job-well-done on the graphics, puzzles, collections, and quests.
Pros:
-Beautiful Artwork
-Smooth Gameplay
-Great storyline and quests
???:
Getting the Ritual Scythe. With the recent update you can get it from Sacrificial Island rather than just Falgers. However, not sure if the chance is better.
Cons:
-Repetitive music.

Overall a great little shmup game.  Most games in this genre devote very little effort to storytelling, and while I wouldn't exactly call SGS a story-heavy game, I found myself getting into the world/story far more than I do with typical shmups.  My favorite touch was the couple sentences of backstory provided for each of the 14 playable ships on the ship select screen; amazing how much depth that adds to the game's world.
The soundtrack, created by Random Encounter, is fantasic, though it would've benefited from a couple more tracks. (Finish the game for an extra special version of the title theme~)
The game plays very tight and is filled with beautfiul, crisp 16-bit sprites. The difficulty curve feels just about perfect although veteran shmup players will probably be bored for the first few stages.
This is a symptom of the one real problem I had with the game: the lack of a deep scoring system. Typically shmups feature some sort of complex scoring dynamic that calls for some specific strategy to maximize your scoring (for example the spectacular "Vaunt" scoring system in Jamestown); this gives higher skill players something to go for on easier stages where survival isn't really a concern. SGS sports a very simple combo system that rewards you for killing enemies in quick succession (before your combo meter resets).  Unfortunately, the player really has very little control over maintaining a combo due to the way the enemies spawn and ultimately most players will end up ignoring the combo meter entirely. Even something as simple as being able to slow down or freeze your combo meter by letting go of the fire button would make going for high scores much more interesting.
Despite the lack of scoring depth, I'd still highly recommend this to anyone remotely interested in a good arcadey experience.  This game's difficulty makes more accessible than the average shmup a is great bridge to more difficult games like Ikaruga and Gradius.

In term of the controls, I find the gamepad the way to go rather than your keyboard. It is just my preference.

Game Details:
Boulder Dash® - 30th Anniversary™ features classic retro-style gameplay with 220 exciting levels across 11 new, gorgeous and unique worlds, and 10 playable characters. They don't make games like they used to. Just as addictive as the original.
200+ levels across 11 worlds, all themed differently that slowly introduce new items, traps and enemies. Layouts are generally well thought out and quickly become challenging to perfect with 3 stars. Game scales up to 4k+, sfx and music can be adjusted separately. Pad and keyboard were both responsive though unfortunately controls are unable to be remapped. Keyboard offered choice of movement on arrow keys or wsad so it wasn't really a problem.
With the addition of the level editor and steam workshop support, the game easily contains hours worth of digging without needing DLC. Each pack does provide 3 levels free, which you can play indefinitely without a purchase. Personally I feel the price is high and would have liked to see it at ~$10usd, apparently there is a mobile version offered in F2P form. PC uses a gold drop/item purchase system, which as another reviewer mentioned is somewhat of a grind if aiming to unlock all characters. Would suggest to the developer perhaps lower some requirements or  increase drop rates a bit.
