First off I'd like to say that Sengoku is a very good game. It focuses heavily on the internal affairs of a clan and the political relationships with the other clans in Japan. It also brings about an interesting land management system that must be used carefully. One must be careful not to promote undeserving vassals who are likely to rebel against their master. However, the combat does leave a bit to be desired as it is nothing more then really a number game. Having a general with high martial skill and a large number of troops guarantees your victory. Primarily, the game focuses on an even pacing between combat and diplomacy so as to advance your clans influence throughout the realm and not angering those within and around you by acting dishonorably or becoming too threatening. Over all, I would give the game an 8.5/10.

Surprisingly entertaining and substantially less complicated than I thought it would be, CRUSADER KINGS II: JAPAN EDITION (Sengoku) is a grand strategy game that puts you in charge of uniting the clans of Japan under your rule as Shogun. Of course, there's nearly a hundred other different clans with that very same objective, so you'll have to play your cards right using diplomacy, might and sabotage to earn the respect of the emperor and conquer the nation.
You can HIRE NINJAS to COUNTER OTHER NINJAS, assemble armies of RONIN and even stab other leaders in the back! Also, GUNS. IF you happen to be visited by western traders.
Also, since it's Ancient Japan we're talking about, HONOR is a very important currency, with a decisive hand in negociations and your internal political stability: be an honored leader and the other clans and your people will respect you and your decisions. Screw up and you might as well commit sepukku to guarantee your lineage (yes, you can do that and, yes, if your son fails to become the next ruler when you die, it's GG).
RECOMMEND. Just beware that matches can (and wil) last FOREVER (as in, more than half a dozen hours forever), so you better be patient. Also, do yourself a favor and play at maximum speed - you can pause to issue orders anyway.

Sengoku is yet another of the mods for a Paradox game turned into a full fledged retail release. This one in particular was a mod for Europa Universalis 3 intended to add dept to an otherwise neglected Japan. And it succeeded quite well, both then as a mod and now as a full game.
Where most of the other mod made retail releases from Paradox never seem to move beyond their mother game Sengoku manages to introduce several new concept and in many ways drastically change the gameplay from what was present in regular Europa Universalis 3.
The setting is Japan with all the diplomacy and politics that entails. Several concepts from the Crusader Kings series are brought over with spies, marriage and character sheets now taking up a good portion of your time. Warfare is less emphasized which is unusual for a Paradox game but for my part there is a good amount of satisfaction in finally being able to play as a political entity rather than a warmongering horde without having to handicap your advancement in the game.
Honor is introduced as an important new resource that determines many of the possibilities available to you, most notably if you can safely declare war on your neighbors. With the introduction of character sheets also comes the vassal system from Crusader Kings and all the turmoil that brings.
Perhaps one of the greatest strengths of Sengoku is also it's greatest weakness. It's location. Feudal Japan is a fascinating place full of both familiar and foreign concepts. But it is also a place few people know about and while that may be enticing to some, many others will be put off by not being able to play as a faction they know. Going into a grand strategy game is daunting enough as it is, doing it when the game is set in a world you don't fully understand with factions and people you have never heard about only makes it all that more overwhelming.
And that leads us to the flaw that all Paradox Grand Strategy games seem to suffer from. Figuring out what to do and how to do it is purely trial and error. Sengoku has little in the way of hints and tutorials and it's incredibly frustrating to have to play multiple sessions just to learn the very basics of how the game functions. In particular new players will find it a difficult game to like.
All in all Sengoku is a game with many flaws but it is also a game that manages to do what Paradox tried and failed with when they made Europa Universalis Rome.
Sengoku combines the grand leadership and empire building of the Europa Universalis series with the character development and personal politics of the Crusader kings series and once you get into it, that is one great combo.

After putting in over 800 hours into this game's predecessor, Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate, this game plays with the gameplay mechanics a bit while still retaining the good feel of victory after each hunt.
Like the other games in the series, the main gameplay focuses around your character hunting monsters, with the key focus of avoiding their attacks and attacking at opportune moments between their attacks, often times hitting their weak points for massive damage. And, like every game in the series, you can't heal and attack super quickly; you need to get out of the way of an incoming attack and heal, then continue avoiding attacks until the opportune moment to strike.
There's a smaller weapon variety in this game, but each weapon is still unique in how it plays, as how you attack with each weapon slightly differs, so I'm glad they retained that feature. Another feature that's also in this game is the limited inventory space, so you have to manage your inventory as you progress; you can't hold everything, after all.
One thing I'm sort of iffy about is the limited hunter rank; in the previous game, it was 999, but in this game it's only 20. This makes it much easier to cap your rank, and it doesn't feel as rewarding, but the grind it takes to get there is a lot quicker so I guess that's a plus.
Perhaps the best part of the entire franchise is that the main 'large monsters' get their own battle theme, and this game is no exception, providing intense battle music for the two flagship boss monsters, as well as the usual recurring map theme for regular hunts.
One mechanic that I abused greatly seemed to have been removed until the final boss, and that is the popular tactic known as sleep bombing; towards endgame, you're given the only weapon with the sleeping status effect. Nothing quite satisfies like putting the monster to sleep then destroying it with one devastating unseen strike to finish it off.
All in all, this game plays quite differently than the other Monster Hunter games, but still retains many of its core features and that's why I recommend it. It has significantly less content than the other Monster Hunter games, but it's also significantly cheaper so it balances out nicely.

JetDogs Studios have built themselves a respectable rap amongst casual gamers with the 12 Labours of Hercules series. Unfortunately, I can't say I have enjoyed any of their earlier games, which tend to have lower production values and are generally much less polished. Alchemy Mysteries is no exception.
What we have here is a run of the mill hidden object game, except for the fact that it scores below average in most aspects of its
. With graphics and animation scraping the bottom of the barrel, it at least occasionally manages to score some points in atmosphere. Things continue being standard (as in standardly not great) when it comes to the music and the voice acting, which should surprise no one.
I will not bother getting into the
, suffice to say that it is also business as usual, i.e. attempting to be spooky and ending up barely above cringeworthy. However, the designers made a decent effort to create actual reasons for sending you to look at places and solve puzzles. That would have potentially improved immersion - if only navigation was a bit less unpleasant and I didn't end up constantly using the map for quicktravelling.
But it's the
that really lets Alchemy Mysteries down.
The
feel very limited. They are relatively small and I personally didn't enjoy the way the items were drawn and incorporated into scenes. The game only displays 8 of the items you are looking for at a time, which generally means you are more likely to get stuck. There are also several HOG scenes that require you to combine items, including some from within your inventory. While this can be an interesting mechanic, it often means you have to go away from the scene to look for missing items, usually in different random places of the map and without always really knowing what to look for.
As for the
, expect to need a lot of hints, expect to be very tempted to skip many of them, and do expect a lot of pixel hunting. While most of them aren't necessarily bad, I found nothing new or memorable and nothing that I genuinely enjoyed. I don't appreciate the fact that I ended up solving many of them simply by trial and error (or dogged OCD refusal to hit the skip button).
At the end of the day, HOG players tend to have very specific likes and dislikes when it comes to wasting their time searching for random objects. :) So while I personally didn't enjoy Alchemy Mysteries, I can't say it is much worse than many other HOGs I've played. It just isn't as good as I would have hoped.

Man has colonized Mars and even introduced a breathable atmosphere, but due to a cosmic event all communications with Earth have been severed for a long time now. A couple of factions are waging war on Mars, especially for its most precious resource: water. The most notable players in the conflict are technomancers, people augmented with technology so they can generate electricity and use it as an offensive or defensive force.
You're Roy, a prisoner of war in a POW camp who has an escape plan, but he needs to recruit help and gather some resources to carry out that plan. His first recruit is a new arrival in the camp, a young POW called Innocence.
Roy shows a hint of mystery to his past but that's as far as the interesting personality traits go in this game. Innocence is naive (what's in a name, right?) to the point of being downright shallow and sometimes annoying. With barely one or two meager exceptions, all the other interactible NPCs are just vessels to get quests from and to turn in those quests to, nothing more.
The game ticks all the boxes for bad storytelling, like:
The only thing that redeems all those bad points a bit is the setting of the game. Mars! Yes, when you look at the hills and mountains in the distance they're red. And when you turn the camera up, you see an orange sky. That's nice. But during the whole game you're running through man-made trenches or you find yourself inside caves or buildings. So you don't really 'feel' like you're on Mars much. The developers didn't even bother to adjust the gravity in the game to resemble Mars': characters move exactly like they would on Earth.
The game is very combat-oriented so let's start with that. Combat consists of three elements:
In an action RPG, especially one that sometimes feels a lot like a hack & slash game (a genre often confused with action RPG's, by the way), a good loot scheme is essential. You want the player to look forward to his next reward, because it has a chance of being something great. In
you'll loot dozens of corpses and open dozens of containers, but 99% of the loot you'll find is just large amounts of the 6 crafting materials and some ammo for your nailgun. If you do loot a weapon or armor it's never anything special or better than you have equipped, so they're intended to be turned into crafting materials or sold to a merchant NPC.
Lastly, you'll also find serum as loot. Serum is the game's currency and it's completely superfluous. The only good items the merchant NPCs are selling, are the very same items you'll get from questing. So the merchant NPCs are just there for the impatient. You either buy the weapon or armor from the NPC or you'll soon get it for free as a quest reward or as fixed loot in a container nearby.
When you level up, you get some skill points and a perk point to spend. Skills are divided into three skill trees:
The perks are very limited:
also has a good/evil reputation mechanism but it's very basic. The only noticeable effect being 2 different bonuses (automatic perks) that are granted depending on your reputation.
Note that you can't change the game's key bindings. Most of the provided key bindings are very logical, though, but the freedom to change them to whatever you desire would have been nice for me and a must for others, I'm sure.
The graphics aren't top-notch like those in the games created by the major studios but they're more than okay for an indie developer. The decors look very good but the characters and especially their faces look rather basic.
During combat, you'll hear fitting up-tempo drum beats. Outside of combat, there is little music to be heard. You just hear some subtle ambient noises, which is fine and non-intrusive, really, but nothing memorable either, of course.
The sound effects are sub par and often seem absent. There's little audible feedback during combat, for example, when hitting opponents or when getting hit.
The voice actor for Roy, the protagonist, delivers a decent performance. The other voice acting ranges from slightly below average to barely above average. So yeah, very average overall. Seems like a recurring theme for this game, doesn't it?

There's a lot one can say about M:WL, and not a lot that can actually justify the experience.
The environment is certainly interesting, with a cliche'd story about water guilds fighting on in a barren dirt wasteland.
The characters are 2.5D, not quite shallow, but not quite deep, with the game having very little qualms about showing the cruel side of humanity.
The combat is difficult, especially while outnumbered. If you're facing more enemies than people in your group, you find your companions lying facedown on the ground, and you running and rolling around like you're playing Dark Souls. All of the attack animations, including your enemies, take wind up times, giving chance for counter attacks, requiring you to time your swings. The downside is, almost every enemy will start backstepping after three attacks, becoming invincible until you lure them in again and coax another swing out of them, giving the not so smart AI an advantage over the player.
The voice acting ranges from believable to funnily outlandish.
Overall, I find the game to have it's own charm, though I'd recommend you pick it up on sale.

You can't go wrong spending this little money for such a potential hidden and unpolished gem.
You start off in a dark prison complex with other inmates and fairly quickly get involved in your first dispute. I was a little underwhelmed by the visuals at first,but this cleared out rather quickly and there's some really nice scenery in the game. It's really atmospheric and there's enough occasions where you'll just want to press the screenshot button or just take a look around because you're imagining what it would be like actually being there. Don't let the very first impression turn you away.
Combat is quite simple as a whole(mechanics wise),but feels very interactive and gives you options due to several features like rolling,blocking,counter attacking and quite an array of additional skills later on once you unlocked the technomancy skill tree. Once you get the hang of it,you'll get around enemies quite a lot and know what to do.
Despite that combat and enemies (at least on hard or higher) can be quite difficult at times and you might have to retry certain fights several times. Make sure to save accordingly. It gets easier for smaller groups of enemies once you progress,build your skills and make use of the crafting system,but there's always going to be a challenge. Especially towards the very end where you'll face bigger groups of enemies that also consist of several types of enemies. There was not one part in the game where I just mindlessly ran around and got bored.
Connecting to this,you have the choice between stealthy gameplay and straight fighting,but can also mix both once you feel it's appropriate. I felt a little overwhelmed in certain fights,but blame this on my lack of knowledge at first. Looking back,you really need to make sure you make use of the rather simple crafting system given to you. Not all,but most gear will have the option to be modified with different attributes(for example physical resistance,shock resistance,more life,more damage,bleeding effects,fluid regeneration,etc). This is further increased by the option to purchase character traits that expand modifying capabilities.
Speaking of this,there's several character traits and three skill tree's to choose from and mix with each other. You can build and tailor your skills according to your playstyle.
Character progression is variable and like in other games,certain choices will divert outcomes. You can be good,bad or a mix of both. You'll also get the chance to form different relationships with several characters and choose which you want to be accompanied with. This got especially important towards the end. You can really connect to the characters presented to you and it pulls you in.
Lastly the voice acting is great. Like not even in my oppinion,but for a 3$ game it's outstanding. You'll see(or hear).
There's more to talk about,but I doubt anyone reading this cares too terribly much. Try it out,you won't regret it. The game feels like a suit that's a little too big and pinches you in the♥♥♥♥♥here and there at first,but the more you wear it,the better it fits and you'll see that spending this little amount money was well worth the experience. You'll always think fond of it when you think back.

This is my first review of a game on Steam.
When I first launched Carpe Diem, I instantly recognized that this visual novel was built on RenPy, as I already have the latest version of RenPy installed on my laptop (a HP/Compaq 8510p running 64-bit Fedora Linux).
The game starts with a meeting of Jung and Ai at a park.  Jung is a programmer by trade that is focused on his work (not unlike myself back in the 1990s when I was developing database applications for credit reporting customers).  Ai is the person whom he was dating in the story.  The name Ai is also an acronym for "artificial intelligence", as we find out at the end of the story.
The intent of the story as described in the "Background" is true to the description.  Getting priorities straight goes a long way in real life, not just in the dating scenes in this game.  For that, I would give this game an "A" for the storyline and intent.
I loved the music the developers chose for this game, though I would have chosen different pieces for each of the three choices you get at the first menu.  For example, I would have chosen for the mall scene a piece music that was commonly heard in shopping malls over the past 50 years.
Overall, I liked this game so much, it gives me an idea for a visual novel.
Overall Rating:  "A"

Diplomacy is the name of the game here in Sengoku. Sure, you can go about bashing in everyone's skulls, but going against another clan, even one that's the same size as you, is a dangerous matter that can easily lose you your territory. Better to build relations and try to make them your vassal than for it to go the other way around.
There are some things that they changed from EU3 that can be frustrating, however. Anyone can march through anyone's territory without asking, so even if you have a neutral clan between you and the enemy, they can still easily get to you. And if you take a province, it's yours automaticly. No negotiation screens or nothing, so if a large enemy army gets into your lands, best be ready to clean up after them.
A fun game when you're doing well, but a beast if you're in the hole. If you like EU3, you'll probably like this.

I've always wanted to get into a grand strategy Paradox-style game, but never had the time or will to take on the learning curve.  Then I heard about Sengoku.  Always been a fan of Japanese history and culture and something about the game (maybe also that beautiful map) just really caught my imagination.
I really appreciate the attention to detail that makes you feel like you're really in control of your clan (even when you're not, i.e., those ungrateful vassals).  The succession from father to son, ensuring the sons have good wives, sons aren't going to be at each other's throats, and all the planning that goes into ensuring a smooth transition between the generations is also one of the high points for me.  Then there's always that option to send a ninja clan to assassinate that one vassal or courtier that isn't playing by your rules.

This update to the classic Super Mario Bros. ripoff caught my attention with its shifting background conceit. You play as a duo of girls who switch back and forth mid-action, and the background switches with them. The 3D backdrops are lush, vibrant and full of activity, much like the those of the Trine series. However, the platforming action is pretty repetitive, and the Sisters Giana have a tough time nailing a landing. Also, the lush backgrounds are almost too busy, making it hard to see when important structural changes happen to the background between sister swapping.

Criminally underrated. An excellent platformer ONLY WHEN PLAYED WITH A CONTROLLER. Yet again we have a game that plays like stuttering mediocre crap when using a keyboard yet is a glorious dream with a pad in your hands, which is why you may see a mixed bag when it comes to other reviews for this title.
Being a fan of the original I found the nostalgia nods were icing on the cake, rather than a hindrance at the expense of the core experience. Chris Huelsbeck's soundtrack, just like all of his work, gives an impression of effort and passion rather than the copy/paste tunes many a low budget game offers. The visuals are great for a platformer, the two different worlds you can jump between offering two distinct themes that animate seamlessly when you switch.
Gameplay wise I would honestly say this is more of an old school 80s affair than early impressions give. The first few levels ease you in and then the game starts playing with many staples of the genre that mix well with its character switching feature. Later levels require you to really be at grips with this feature as you need to string together a combo of switches in one move (switching changes which platforms are active, which direction they move, etc.). I'd say this game has a difficulty level similar to Rayman Origins, with a little bit of Cuphead thrown in here and there (especially the boss battles, long tricky fights where you can only take 2 hits).
tl:dr - Excellent underrated 2D platformer with fun 3D visuals and pleasing audio. Gameplay wise for fans of Rayman and Cuphead, but only play it with a controller!

I'm not done with the game as of this writing; I'm almost 2.5 hrs in.  Unfortunately I don't recommend this game.  Mostly because there's a pretty bad bug where upon advancing (or turning) to another location, or using an item in an hidden object area, will cause the screen to go black.  The UI is present and the dust motes overlaying the entire game are there too, but everything else is black.  You can bring up and close the journal or map and the picture will return, but only temporarily.  And that method isn't working in an hidden object scene where I have to fix a magnifying glass; every time I pick up the lens the picture goes black.  I've read that quitting and restarting will temporarily fix this, but it shouldn't be happening in the first place.  I'd refund the game, but for $2 I guess I will manage.
The HO scenes can be very tricky on the advanced setting.  Some objects are hidden behind the UI buttons on the top, others are 90% hidden by other objects in the scene.  This leads me to clicking on every sliver of anything I cannot identify in case something I need pops out from behind something else.  The game also employs a non-traditional mechanic where you must use items in your inventory on other items in the HO scenes.  That always trips me up; I'm not sure whether this is a good thing or not.
The story is interesting enough that I don't notice how small the game world really is which I think is great.  The graphics are fairly well done although the HO scenes tend to look like Photoshop collages.  The game has a map which shows you areas you've completed, areas which have tasks to do, and has fast travel.  Unfortunately the map legend is rather complicated.
The puzzle adventures vary quite a bit in difficulty.  Some are straight forward.  Others task you with fixing game-unique objects without telling you what you'll need, so you have no idea what to do since they are not real-life objects.  Puzzles can be quite arbitrary too - at one point you have to hit a gong but neither the hammer in your inventory nor the bell clapper you find in the area will do it.
Unless you get this game at a good sale or are so lacking in other HOGs that you desperately need something to play, I'd avoid this one.
edit:  finally finished the game.  Took me about 5 hrs.  I had to restart the game several times due the black screen bug.  One puzzle (the prism puzzle discussed on the forums) was super finicky.  Getting the light to the crystal wasn't too hard but it took some unnecessary adjustments to get the solution to trigger.  The ending was a bit abrupt and out of the blue mentioned some tower (???).  While I liked parts of this game, I can't recommend it mainly due to technical issues.  Oh, the computer I'm playing on isn't great, but it is above the minimum specs on the store page.

Mars: War Logs is one of those gems that lurks behind "A" titles, just waiting to shine.  Very much like Mad Max or WoW in playability, tactics, NPC aggro proc, and utility of various game strategies, the GUI will be familiar to anyone who has played a 3rd person and the particulars are not complicated; you can also change keybinds for fine-tuning.  The detailed plot can go in at least three different major directions near the end, and choices determine results on several questlines, but the first two chapters will be very similar/same for any given playthrough.  First playthrough on"normal" difficulty was challenging to learn but not difficult, and my second on "difficult" wasn't too bad
... but "Extreme" has me stumped.  There must be a build order that I haven't identified correctly... yet.
In my 90+ hours I managed to get Roy physically stuck only once, and have not encountered fatal errors or other bugs of any sort.
Regarding achievements, they are all pretty straightforward, but achi hunters who don't want to spend time playing through twice (two separate endings with achis) or to playthrough on Extreme (game complete on Extreme difficulty achi) will not earn 100% here.
Time to complete on Normal difficulty... about 8-14 hours, depending on playstyle and choices; most people will probably be about 12-14 hours.
The layout of the first area sucks, and your interactions there tend toward the "run to this place and return" sort of mission.  Further, some things don't live in the game world, but only spawn after you've (for example) entered an area for the second time.  There is a particularly useful couple of guides for this game, one of which has to do with top armor/weapon locations in each chapter (always buff up your gear as soon as you are able to, and focus on doing damage and resisting physical damage), the other of which is about a particular achievement where you have to do all the side quests (more on that achi later***).
The one thing the game lacks is a visual skill chart progression; you can't see what future skills are, without unlocking everything before them in the tree.  That single fault aside, you can be a character who sneaks a lot and that will help you sometimes... but the non-human NPCs aren't fooled by your tiptoeing, and will require a proper threshing when they come at you 5 and 6 deep in confined quarters.  There is no functional disengagement from combat in this game; once you're aggro, you're in it until either you or they are finished; if you go down before any sidekick falls, you're dead just the same and they won't rez you.  However, you can let your sidekick fall in every fight and always get them back on their feet immediately after a fight ends (this is automatic).
Fortunately, and at least on the normal difficulty setting, you can pick just about any skills you want at the beginning, and still muddle through the game.  In my view you WILL NEED much of the combat tree, but some very useful skills are in stealth as well (bonus damage/wounding strikes from behind; throw blinding sand over a larger area; craft nailgun ammo with less resources; are all amongst the most useful skills in the game).  Conversely... I don't think you ever need a single point in the Technomancer tree, or to activate a single ability, though it will happen automagically at some cut scenes.
A note on certain character traits: most traits are bought with points earned, 1 point per level, with the traits costing varying amounts and having various pre-reqs.  I have played through as a White Knight and never done anything wrong, always helped others, and been nice to the NPCs, but I have never found out how to gain reputation on the GOOD side (first is a shopkeeper discount for good reputation, second is bonus partner HPs and damage output.  However, it's VERY easy to earn the worst reputation, and the benefit of doing so is a higher critical bonus and a chance to hurt people more effectively - and in order to earn this, all you have to do is start killing everyone you fight (you'll get a tool to extract serum from a body, which is fatal to the source).  Happy murdering; they deserve it anyway.
***Now, regarding that one guide, and the achievement "Completionist" (Finish all of the secondary quests in Mars: War Logs): First, I *suspect* the text of the achievement is misleading, and that the intention is for the player to finish the game including all of the quests
... which isn't the same thing as finding and completing all secondary quests.  As I've read at least four different accounts of popping that achi after playing through four different methods, I'm fairly confident of this theory.
there's a lot of good information in that guide (just look up the guide for the "Completionist" achi; the author did a good job of putting quest keywords in the guide as well as inserting pictures of relevance).
All in all... this is a great game, I'd say easily 8+/10, and it does go on sale periodically.

EDIT: Like some other reviewers, I'm changing my recommendation to NOT recommended. At higher levels, when the number of pieces increases, the annoyance of occasionaly grabbing the wrong piece grows exponentially. It is no longer an random glitch but a game-crippling bug. 9 times out of 10 you don't get the piece you grab, but some other close by or below it. When doing the edge pieces of a 300+ piece jigsaw, I ended piling all the wrong pieces to the board, then stored the edge pieces to another area of board and dumped the centre pieces back to the stream. There must be something wrong with the selection algorithm, didn't bother to test if the screen resolution effects it.
My old review below still holds, it would be a nice game without the effing bug! At it's current state it is only playable with low piece counts.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Pretty good small puzzle game. I was a bit wary about the "floating pieces in koi pond"-thing, but as the pieces are not rotatable and puzzle sizes are small, it is works quite well - it is easy enough to spot the pieces  and there is no need for extra temp storage trays. A couple of negatives: you can't build separate sections of the puzzle (the pieces do not bind unless they are in their correct final position), and picking the pieces from koi pond is not always wysiwyg - you sometimes get the wrong piece even though your mouse cursor is pointing for the correct one. Jigsaw puzzles are supposed to be relaxing and enjoyable.  This game is neither.  It's like someone tried to implement every poor design decision they could come up with, to see how much frustration they could stir up.
- Can't save a puzzle, have to complete the entire puzzle in one sitting.
- For some reason, the pieces float around the border of the puzzle, and when there are hundreds..........
- Mouse detection is horrible, if you actually pick up a piece you were aiming for it's a small miracle.
- Pieces ONLY snap together when put in their proper place.  No way to connect a few pieces and find their home later.
This is one of the most frustrating games I've ever played, it's almost like some psychological test to see the boundaries of sanity.

A nice diversion, but really not anything special. It's just jigsaw puzzles. And a few of the pictures don't really make for good jigsaw puzzles either, images being too homogenous. There's also no save feature which is... yeah, not great. And it's a bit of a pain to pull out the piece you want, especially on later puzzles where there are a lot of pieces. It's not really an authetic jigsaw experience either since pieces snap into place when they're close to where they need to be, but you can't put pieces together if you find, say, two center pieces that aren't connected to any edge pieces. It's easy to cheat the system and it forces a specific progression otherwise, which is a bit of a problem when you can't actually pull out the edge pieces you need because it keeps pulling up the wrong piece. There's not anything else to it except jigsaw puzzles, despite what the game's page says about interactivity. I got this free in a bundle, and yeah, that's about what it's worth. A good time-killer and mildly enjoyable but you could prooobably do better.

The question has to be asked, How much does this game cost? 15 dollars? For 5.4 Hrs? But it must be said that I played every English Ace Attorney game. So the game might not have been able to trick my already programed brain.
Speaking about Ace Attorney, how much does this game steal from that? Well the very basics but it also does a few things from the Ace Attorney Alpha. The Alpha of the famous Game Boy Advance game turned Game Boy DS was that the entire court case would be performed live. Every choice you made and every moment you saw, if done incorrectly could lead to your loss.
This is a game where you can lose. Not from life lost or quick bad end choice but from other reasons.
Now with that spoler out of the way....
Aviary Attorney does not have much animashion. Again it uses the basic drawings of Mr  J. J. Grandville, The mouth movement of characters are well enough. But outside of jumping about and false turning there is not much animashion around. Of course the game will do it's best with this limit and some of the jokes are funny. The music is good enough and sets a a basic tone. The backgrounds are again of Mr. J J so they are very nice to look at. And the options of getting around in the game are very nicely done. It makes sure you will have track of what you need and who every character is.
Overall I will have to say that the story is very nice for an Ace Attorney player. It will have some major diffrences and will feel fresh. To people that have never played that game this should be enough of a experince into the limited "lawyer logic" games out there. Speaking of that I would look into a free Konergate game called Socrates Jones: Pro Philosopher. Get past the very first character and ask you self. "Was this fun?" "Was this wasteful?" "Do I want to keep going?"
If that game bore you to tears, well then Aviary Attorney would have more plot and a much serious case on its hands. Overall thought if you did enjoy it, your likely to enjoy Aviary Attorney. I mean that. People that enjoy games that you need to read a lot and go with logic will enjoy this. The game is also slightly harder.
But now I'll finish with this. Since 2016 the group behind this game have gone quiet. Apparently some side game or other story was to be released. So...You might want to also look into what Kickstarter project offered and what they delivered.
Thats all. It gets my thumbs up.

Aviary Attorney is a visual novel that follows the adventures of defense lawyer Jayjay Falcon and his cheeky assistant Sparrowson. The player investigates crime scenes and collects evidence, which eventually must be presented in court.
What makes this game so adorable are its unusual but inspired design choices: The setting - Paris mere days before the revolution of 1848 - makes use of contemporary caricatures by J. J. Grandville. The illustrations are perfectly complemented by the  classic compositions of Camille Saint-Saens' Carnival of the Animals. The dialog is often tongue-in-cheek or just plain silly, the characters likeable.
The game only lasts 6-10 hours. But the plot is smarter than it seems at first, positively sucker-punching the player a few times. It's absolutely possible to miss out on vital pieces of evidence or make the wrong conclusions, and thus losing a case. I liked that a lot!

I hated Daylight at first until I understood what it was than then chillaxed and for the £5 I paid for it on ebay, it wasn't bad.
Basically this is a souped up chase/light puzzle game like slenderman, with some procedural aspects in the way the world is generated.
Very little storytelling and the tutorial elements are lacking, so here's what you have to do. Hidden around each level are "remnants", sheets of paper which glow read in the dark. You can see how many you have next to an icon in the bottom right corner of the screen.
When you have them all you have to find a key item which then allows you to exit the level. All the time you are being chased by shades which you can dispell with flares, which you will find dotted around each level.
You will also find glowsticks which, as well as illuminating your surroundings, show you objects which can be manipulated: climbable blocks; searchable boxes etc. Environments in the playthrough I did include an old hospital, catacombs, a beach, and forest.
At the end there is a reveal of sorts but it is brief and confusing but interesting nontheless.
If you stream the game on twitch, it responds to things people type in chat, producing 'scary' sounds and events in response to various keywords people type. Apparently, I was never quite sure if it worked.

Make no mistake, this game will scare the bejeesus out of you, and if it doesn't, then mister - you're a better man than I.
But is that enough?
Because, basically, that's all you get. If you're a fan of the horror genre in general, be it movies, books or games then you'll probably be able to predict what happens next. This game unashamedly trots out all the horror tropes - almost by the book - for better or worse, and for veterans of the genre, this might make it seem a little tired.
But for some, the fact that it plays from the Horror Cliches 101 textbook can work in its favour. You will be deliciously on edge as you pass by that wheelchair, because you just know it's going to suddenly move its squeaky wheels in your direction. If I look through this window, is a ghastly face going to appear on the other side, looking back?
It's moments like these that make this game so intense and frightening at times, to say nothing of the supernatural denizens that reside in the asylum that you may or may not come face to face with.
But if you're expecting deep gameplay and open ended exploration you will be sorely disappointed. Although this game does what it promises - scares the crap out of you - there's nothing much else really to it. You wander around hunting for Remnants, in game lore items, while waiting for the next supernatural event to occur. And, well, that's pretty much all she wrote.
It becomes somewhat tedious after awhile trudging through the same recycled corridors. And let me tell you, there are a LOT of corridors. For a game that was hyped as much as it was for using the Unreal 4 engine, the graphics and textures look somewhat muddy and washed out, at least they did on my rig. They definitely have a previous-gen look about them. And this is baffling, considering the fairly hefty system requirements. Though the sound design is excellent, and perfectly complements what's going on onscreen.
For the price though, give it a shot if you're a fan of survival horror games or horror stuff in general - you'll enjoy it, at least for a while - for this game is best enjoyed in short chunks, rather than extended play sessions.
In summary, it's horror-by-the-numbers fare that will absolutely have you browning trou, but apart from the scares, there is little on offer here in the way of gameplay and with surprisingly meaty running requirements at odds with the ordinary graphics you'll want to be a survival horror fan to appreciate this. If you want something you can savour, and enjoy being scared then, for the price especially, you can't go wrong here.

Don't get me wrong, I love AC like no other series, but good lord this game is a poor man's version of the Witcher 3. The world feels lifeless and dead, and I have no investment in the people or characters. The sidequests were repeatative and the parkcore and stealth gameplay atributes took a step back in my opinion. I actually liked the combat of AC: Syndicate and Unity (one of the few things I liked) but they changed it. The main story was interesting but meh, revenge based AC games have gotten...old. The sad thing is the wasted potential of this game. It could have been alot better.
There is a silver lining however. After the 2 AC titles horrifically failed, this one at least tried to copy an amazing game [Witcher 3] and improve itself. Ubisoft still needs to work on its world development [a lot] and refine the gameplay mechanics, but I think they took a step towards reviving the franchies.
So final verdict-
if its your first Assassin's Creed game, play it. It'll be an enjoyable 50 hours or so especially without the knowledge of better past AC games.
if your a longtime fan... play it to discover the origins of the Assassin order, but don't expect anything too special.

DeadCore is a fantastic FPS parkour puzzle speedrunner game. The objective is to reach the top of a mysterious tower by running, jumping, and using your trusty Switch Gun to activate and/or deactivate switches, enemies, moving walls, and gravity fields, while trying not to get disintegrated by lasers or fall to your death (which is by lasers most of the time anyway because a floor of lasers follows you upwards whenever you reach a new checkpoint). Most of the enemies don't actually kill you, but the turrets and troopers launch you away (often into lasers) and the mosquitoes slow you down (so you can be killed by moving lasers).
The whole game can be speedrun in less than an hour, but it takes several hours to finish the first time, familiarise yourself with the levels, learn some speedrun strats, and find the hidden Sparks to unlock the game's true ending.
+ The controls are simple and responsive: WASD to move, E to boost, M1 to shoot, M2 to aim (personally didn't find much point in aiming), and M3 to blast.
+ The feeling of speed is very nicely communicated (did I describe that right?)
+ The graphics are very nice and sleek-looking, even on very low (;_; my computer)
+ The levels are well designed, with some tough challenges, often with multiple paths, and encourage a bit of exploration to find the collectables
+ Speedrun mode! Leaderboards! Beat the devs!
+ Beating the dev times, completing a paticularly difficult section of a level, finding short cuts, finding hidden collectables, and just being launched high into the air and boosting around, gives a lot of satisfaction.
+/- The difficulty ramps up quite a bit, and in the later levels you will die many times to the challenges. This is a personal thing, I enjoyed the difficulty but some people won't.
- Story doesn't really make sense. Or maybe I'm too literal-minded.
- You have no body and it's a bit hard to know what your hitbox is going to do
Overall a great game, I highly recommend it to fans of first person parkour or speedrun games, and people who like a challenge.

Knightfall is a cheap copy of Final Fantasy 8's card game. It is a 2 player game where you fight to have the most control of a 3x3 grid. You alternate turns, placing cards with stats on the board, trying to convert your enemy's cards to your colour and taking board control. When all 9 slots are filled up and your opponent passes, you count the number of cards you own versus your enemy. The victor is the one with the most cards. There is no drawing in this game.
The cards are divided into 4 types, Red, Yellow, Grey and Purple. Red is when you compate adjacent stats. Yellow is for the enemy's opposite stat. Grey compares the weakest number in the enemy's card to your adjacent stat, and Purple skips 1 card to shoot over it. There are also a whole bunch of abilities such as swapping card positions, buffing card stats, transforming cards into other cards, placing down invisible cards (petit) and items which allow your cards to attack again with a small buff or poison your enemies.
Conclusion, the idea is a pretty interesting one but sadly execution is blundered by the Pay To Win business model and Power Creep. In this current state, I would not recommend this for long term gaming. If they revamp it and improve it, it's possible.

Do you like Danganronpa?  How about Zero Escape?  Ever wonder what would result if a developer took a stab at combining them both while including their own elements?  If you answered "yes" to all of the above, you have a pretty good idea of what to expect from
.
One of the strongest parts of the package is the visuals, as the in-game images and trailer on the store page suggest.  At this price point, I was more than willing to give leeway on the graphical side of the equation.  However, I was pleasantly surprised to find that not only do the character art, locations, and other visual assets hold up, they represent a level of quality typically seen in VN-based games costing an upwards of 8-10 times as much.  They are certainly comparable (if not at times superior) to those found in the aforementioned games that this one is most certainly patterned after.
As for the audio, while simple and mostly subdued, it remains adequate and fits the games locales and events quite nicely.  The music is mostly derivative, but still adds ambience to the environment laid out by the games often impressive visuals.  Unfortunately, the characters do not appear to be voice acted, with only the occasional sigh, grunt, groan, or surprised reaction being heard.
Another fairly solid and engaging part of the game can be found in its setting and thematic elements.  12 "sinners" are gathered together to play the Arbitration game... a series of five events where the winner can receive atonement for their crimes, with the losers suffering the penalty of a horrific death.  Scoring is kept track via a collection of coins the player possesses at any given time.  While additional coins are added to a players total for winning events within the Arbitration game, they are subtracted accordingly for losing, failing to meet objectives, etc.  If a players coin total is reduced below zero, they are effectively ejected from the game and subject to a grisly demise.  Time limits are also put into place, heightening the tension and adding to the dark mood the game is trying to convey.
The characters, along with their personalities and interactions, also assist in setting the stage for the events that play out.  The player character, He Chuyan, is written as the typical "golly gee, I'm not sure why I'm here, but I'm going to do my best anyway" stereotype found in entries of the Danganronpa series.  Likewise, most of the other characters consist of high-level archetypes made popular in other visual novels.  Still, they are serviceable and fit well into the thematic elements of the game.  Just don't be surprised if this game fails to tread any new ground in its character personalities or overall designs.
The weakest part of the package, and the one that unfortunately holds the game back quite a bit, is in it's English translation.  For the Visual Novel portions, this is less of a deal breaker and a fairly fluent English speaker can likely piece together not only the story at large, but the individual character emotions without too much concern or rereading.  However, the events that take place during the Arbitration game suffer quite a bit in their far less than optimal translation.  This is particularly true when the rules of each game are explained and the character dialogs during those events are concerned.  I found myself having to play through each game several times before I was successful... not really due to any lack of skill or reasoning, but because the details were incredibly unclear regarding what I was supposed to be doing at any specific time.
A better English translation is certainly possible as I was able to rearrange and reword things in my head to provide something closer to what the developers likely intended.  Perhaps a future update, via developer DLC or fan made, will become available and the game would be far better for it.  Also, native controller support would be a nice update as some of us enjoy these games from the comfort of our couches.  Until that day (maybe?) comes, controller support can effectively be had via the various mouse emulation programs available.
Overall,
is certainly worth the extremely low price of admission, particularly if you've played and enjoyed Danganronpa, Zero Escape, or both.  You won't find much that strays too far away from those well-worn franchises, but it's a clone that is both serviceable and even impressive at times as it attempts to stand on it's own.  Unfortunately, the less than stellar English translation represents somewhat of a stumbling block throughout.

The entire first level and most of the second level are completely void of any danger and just try to creep you out with such scary tactics as a chair sitting up by itself or drawers flying open or a wheelchair wheel spinning by itself.  The only times when I was GENUINELY scared were the times when you're not allowed to carry a protective flare and you have to take the Macguffin back to the gate while being chased by a ghost; and those moments were only scary because it's easy to get lost in the samey-looking levels and the "spooky" ghosts making a loud noise whenever you look at them.  And the thing is that because of the formula (find six letters that let you unlock the Macguffin that opens the next level and run away from ghost) these moments don't stay scary for long as you know EXACTLY what to expect by the third time around.  And it's a shame because the game actually has a quite nice athmosphere with dark, claustrophobic hallways of a rundown insane asylum and a dark forest. With the rising popularity of YouTube let's plays and Twitch streaming, horror games have enjoyed a bit of a resurgence. This resurgence is, oddly enough, not due to people's desires to play these games themselves, but rather to watch others play them on the internet. I digress, whatever the reason, developers are back to delivering scars and suspense to those who have the steely nerves required to complete these games. Daylight attempts to elbow it's way to the front of the crowd, nudging past fan favorites like Slender: The Eight Pages, Outlast and Amnesia: The Dark Decent. With it's procedurally generated mazes and visuals bolstered by Epic's Unreal 4 engine, Daylight has the goods to garner the interest of fans but does it deliver the tension and scares of it's contemporaries?

Daylight wastes no time with any kind of lead-in or build up. Immediately, you take control of Sarah, a girl stranded in a dilapidated hospital who... Well, you aren't really told anything about Sarah...You don't see her face, aren't clued into her age or her background and why she's in the middle of this hospital is a mystery. The most intriguing aspect of Sarah is the bizzare maze-like network of lines that appear on her arm. With only her cell phone and a mysterious male voice to guide her, Sarah must wander around in search of documents called remnants and collecting all of the documents in an area allows her to obtain a sigil which unlocks a magically sealed door to the next area. If this sounds vaguely familiar, that's because it's pretty much the same set up as the Slender games. Along the way, pictures will fall off of walls unexpectedly, drawers from filing cabinets with shoot across the room and wheelchairs and IV drip racks will squeak across the floor in this veritable digital funhouse.

Nestled between each area that hosts a remnant hunt are areas that require some light puzzle solving and collecting more documents that attempt to build a narrative. The puzzles are inconsequential, requiring some switch flipping and crate pushing. Sarah can also use glowsticks to illuminate objects of interest since apparently the magical elements she encounters respond to chemiluminescence... Lockers, supply boxes and crates can all be opened for flares, glowsticks and documents. The problem is that all of this can be made frustrating as a result of clunky controls. Opening a locker can involve and awkward tango while trying to prompt the contextual command to pop up and grant Sarah access to it's contents. Pushable crates can only be moved from one side so players must circle them like a shark in order to find the side they can interact with. Sarah also moves at a ponderous pace by default meaning the patience of a zen master is required to navigate the environment. While she can sprint, the exaggerated head bob can make some players sick and is at the very least disorienting, making exploration difficult. The witches that want to tear Sarah limb from limb appear at random, often behind players and can be warded off with flares. Flares and glowsticks are not exactly in short supply but the real challenge is making it to the magically sealed doors with the sigil in hand since your trusty flares cannot be used. It can get frustrating when you find yourself cornered by a spawning witch with no recourse.

While players can get the same type of gameplay from several other games on the market, one would at least expect the narrative to differentiate Daylight from other titles. This would be a mistake however, since Daylight is on a strict diet of cliches and hackery. By dropping it's protagonist into a scenario without any introduction it drives a large wedge between players and the characters involved. Where the protagonists of other horror games reflect on their growing unease or decaying sanity, Sarah does nothing to reflect on her predicament aside from calling out into the dark, announcing that she is aware of some unseen presence. All of this culminates in an inane plot twist that has little consequence given the abysmal character development. There is nothing for players to be invested in and the mysteries surrounding the hospital, it's patients and Sarah merely come off as set dressing.

Given that Daylight is running on the shiny new Unreal 4 engine, one would at least expect it to look great but the procedural level generation betrays this expectation by requiring environments to be modular making it reminiscent of being trapped in one of Skyrim's dungeons. One room offers few details to distinguish itself from another and, were it not for the fact that there is an ever present map on Sarah's phone, getting lost would be a frequent occurrence. Props are generic and as a result many areas don't feel like they have a purpose and the decaying buildings that players have to navigate look sparse, with even simple details like windows being few and far between. Lighting is also rather generic as a result of this design so don't expect to see any of the extraordinary expressionist surroundings offered by a game like Outlast. Continuing the trend of treading well worn ground, Daylight also suffers from it's choice of environments by featuring horror game staples like a hospital, prison, sewers and a forest. Ultimately, Daylight lacks the all important atmosphere that allows a horror game to truly get under your skin in a way that jump scares cannot. Despite looking like a student project, the frame rate has a tendency to chug in some areas and I did experience a crash during my two hour playthrough. Sound design keeps the tension up but does little to stand out from similar games.

Daylight is truly embarrassing as it gormandizes on cliches and tropes, digests and squeezes them out of it's sphincter for Twitch streamers and let's play hosts to gobble up. There is absolutely no reason to endure Daylight, even with it's short play time. The decision to make Daylight a procedurally generated experience cuts it's nose off to spite it's face. Randomizing the design of levels does so much to negatively impact an already lackluster experience by stripping the atmosphere from the experience. The hubris required to commit such an atrocious design blunder in order to add replayability to a title that isn't even worth seeing through once is staggering. Everything you can find in Daylight is available in other, more enjoyable games. The uninspired gameplay and fan fiction grade narrative have no place in a world where titles like Amnesia and Outlast exist. If only this game never saw the light of day...

NOTE: Playtime is inaccurate, I played for six hours in offline mode.
Aviary Attorney is an animal themed take on Phoenix Wright with a French Revolution era twist.
Pros:
+Iconic art style is both detailed and full of charm
+Many unique animal characters, each one a clever use of their respective animal
+Revised Phoenix Wright formula that makes investigation sequences, examining rooms, and cross examining more streamlined and less frustrating overall
+A creative storyline with surprisingly deep themes
+Multiple endings
+The game will not hold your hand; you CAN LOSE TRIALS and the game WILL progress. Your client's life is truly in your hands more than ever before.
+The ability to select an investigation day and load it from the start menu cuts makes it easy to backtrack should you fail a trial
Cons:
-Some of the mysteries are too simple, far easier to figure out than the ones in the earlier Phoenix Wright games.
-Relatively short at six hours to get one ending (add another hour or two for the others)
Aviary Attorney, despite being clearly inspired by another game series, is a truly unique gem of a game bursting with charming characters and visuals, not to mention an intriging plot filled with political turmoil. Anyone, Phoenix Wright fan or no, will get a kick out of this game.

Charming and picturesque,
is a very well written text adventure game following the style of the 'Ace Attorney' games.
I'm gonna start by saying that the illustrations the game has are absolutely fantastic. There's an wonderful amount of detail and love made in each and every one of them and they provide a great way to convey the theme of 19th century France in which the story takes place. You might be thinking that lack of graphics would make the game feel dull and empty,but in all honestly the great works of French caricaturist J. J. Grandville, while seeming like a relic of bygone era when the artists had very few options and mediums to express their craft, manage to build a perfectly fitting atmosphere for the player to experience the story. The background illustrations are an accurate historic depiction of 19th century Paris based on public domain lithographs. It's really some amazing work that the developers have put into creating this gem of a game and it shows from the very first moments.
Music and soundtrack is by legendary romantic-era composer Camille Saint-Saëns and it creates a suitable audio experience that ties greatly with the game. Many of the classical compositions you will listen during your playthrough are familiar via other works of art but they never feel like out of place for the game.
The characters despite not uttering a single line of audio dialogue, excel by the phenomenal writing of the game. They are very colorful and have their own quirks which will you pleasantly discover during the playthrough. They can be funny, ruthless, conniving, innocent or just pure evil. They come to life even as anthropomorphic caricatures and that's a sign of brilliant writing.
The dialogue is the main strength of the game and is superbly written for the most part. There are great lines, lots of humor and tongue-in-cheek moments, horrible/amazing puns and it gets serious when needed.
Gameplay consists of gathering evidence and interviewing suspects and witness. Should you gather enough information regarding your case, you'll need to present in during the trial on court day by cross-examining the witlessness. Presenting the proper evidence at the proper time will sway the jury in your favor. Truth be told the gameplay mechanics are incredibly simple but I do believe that any further amount of complexity would deviate too much from the theme of the game. While it might appear fairly straightforward there are a few situation where you could fail a case so it's important to be thorough with your investigation.
There's a total of 4 acts to experience with the 4th having 3 possible endings depending on your actions on the 3rd. Acts are self-contained in their stories but also there are several recurring characters who will appear throughout the whole game.
I do however have a few minor complaints about the game. A personal pet peeve of mine was the lack of a 'on-the-spot' saving system. Instead the game saves after the end of a day. Not a huge gripe but a minor inconvenience in my book. I would also mention that if you skip a piece of dialogue by accident there's no way of going back to read since the game has no chat log so I would advice caution.
All in all, Aviary Attorney was a very pleasant experience for around 4 hours. The dialogue and characters are masterfully done and each moment of written dialogue with the anthropomorphic characters was pure delight. The gameplay elements might be simple but the game excels in creating an engaging story for the player. If you want a twist of the 'Ace Attorney' games, then Aviary Attorney is guaranteed to you keep you entertained.

Boss 101:
~~~~~~~
Here we go again, your brother Chris is back in hospital. You’re always been extremely supportive of him and his love for extreme games. The downside is . . . he seems to get hurt most of the time he enters them. On this occasion, the length of his stay will be at least two weeks, with several broken bones. Despite this set-back he is in good spirits, mainly because you have given him a camera for his birthday which can be mounted on his helmet. Finally, Chris will be able to film his future exploits at the upcoming extreme games. Still, it’s hard to lay down in bed for that long without watching thrilling homemade movies. Then, he sits up straight on his bed with his eyes fix on yours, his finger pointed towards you, saying with a loud voice “You’re the one who’s going to eliminate the Robotic Union from our Galaxy and face the ultimate Robot Boss 101! Come on, brother, can you film your exploits for me!” Your response, without a spot of hesitation, was: “Sure bro, I’ll film it all for you. Especially when I get to beat Boss 101!”
Boss 101 is an arcade / shoot’em up / adventure game where you play Max, who is located in a command centre deep in space, and whose mission is to free thirty-one cities by eliminating the Gigantic Robotic bosses and their minions who guard them.
Before you start the game, I would suggest going through the short and very well done tutorial.
The game has a few different aspects to it. First, the command centre, where Max and his talkative jetpack S.T.E.V.E are stationed. The command centre consists of five levels. The first level is the operative room where you’ll receive a call from Tanya Goodson, from Earth, via a small red telephone (part of the story), the endless boss room to catch more money, a pet storage, and arcade game and a very good Wikipedia of the game.
Levels two and three are where you can upgrade your abilities and buy guns. To be honest with you when I first browsed around and saw how much most of the items cost (in millions), I thought to myself, how am I going to be able to afford them? Especially after a few goes against the first Boss.
The forth level is where you can customize Max; how he looks and what additional abilities he will carry with him into battle. All I have to say is to look at the costumes that give you the unlimited time ability first! The rest you’ll have to discover by yourself. The last one is the Debug level; unfortunately for you, you’ll have to unlock it, but when you do, you’ll be able to buy the good stuff.
Next you’ll have to launch the game (battle phase). First, you’ll see a screen with thirsty-one Warp Gate and of course the first one will be unlock. After entering the gate, a new menu will appear where you’ll have to press a button with the description - Make a Boss -. A boss will be regenerated semi-randomly for you. Check out his vital information to see which weapons will inflict most damage and which ones won’t give him a scratch. This is going to be your last chance to give Max the right equipment to successfully win the battle.
The gameplay is fabulous; so much fun! The bosses usually have several weapons at their disposal and will fire them at will, while minions will pass through from right to left. Some of them will also fire a few projectiles towards you to make your life slightly more hectic. Another thing I really enjoy is the variety of enemy minions. To be honest, I haven’t count them, but there are plenty. Every time you shut down a minion or hit a boss, your coins gauge will increase bit by bit. The big dough comes in if you manage to destroy the boss. On top of that you’ll see small characters in flying saucers. You must grab them as there are Gopher scientists (a race) and you must collect all of them. If you do so, you’ll be rewarded with a secret project which only the Gophers can finish. In some fights, you’ll be given a mission to escort citizens too. To succeed, you must keep their transportation in the air and destroy the boss too.
I really like the retro graphics. You can play this game with your keyboard or gamepad. Personally I had a better experience with the gamepad. I try to surf every point of each game I review and I must admit that I really appreciate discovering a well written game Wikipedia.  When you start to buy the good stuff, it become easier.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great retro graphics
-	Thirty-one levels with randomly regenerated bosses
-	In-depth game Wikipedia
-	Stacks of hats, pets & weapons
-	Fun little story with cut-scenes between levels
-	Plenty of re-playability
-	Achievements and trading card
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Buy better equipment and the game seems to become a bit easier
-	A bit repetitive
Boos 101 is plenty of fun with lots of content. Definitely a game to check out!

In all honestly, I walked into this game pretty blind as to what it was.
I knew it had a bullet hell type combat system and that there was something to do with hats. I had also heard from Toborprime's stream how beautiful, fun, and awesome this game was. So I gave it a shot.
Well, 10hrs and a couple cups of coffee later... I'm addicted through and through (to the game that is, the coffee addiction was pre-existing)
I loved everything from the unique type of hats you can wear (most are references to pop culture both old and new), to the dialogue you have with each boss. I mean... I killed one of the level bosses and he went down in a blaze of glory lamenting that now he'll never get to see Pitch Perfect 3. Awesome.
Just imagine flying through the air, shooting lethal smiley faces at enemies with a "friendship" gun, while wearing a garbage bin costume....and winning! Not to mention that the boss is literally an amalgamation of what is probably Dr.Robotnik's spare robot building parts.
However, there are some things that did initially affect my opinion of the game.
When you first start the game, you're given a tutorial on what each menu does, how it affects you and etc.
The problem is, once those menu tutorials are over, you're left to your own devices in the command center. With no direction on how to proceed, what you're "1st mission is" or etc. I was completely overwhelmed till I started just clicking on things and figuring it all out. In a way, this isn't so bad because it forces the player to learn what everything does, but it also serves as a point of frustration that may turn some away.
Once you find the groove, that overwhelming feeling never really comes back, cause you understand the signal and the noise (signal being the main campaign levels and progression with the noise being the kite flying, pet gathering, endless levels mode, arcade machine and varioius other things).
Not really sure how that could be lessened unless the player is given their first fight before being plunged into the command center full of options, or something to that tune.
All in all, it's a really minor frustration that didn't lessen my experience of the game as I moved forward. I loved exploring everything it had to offer. I even got all the achievements, which I almost never do for any game!
You can easily see the passion and skill the team poured into this game with every art asset, menu screen, secret achievement, music, and dialogues. It's definitely worth everyone's time.

This is a tough call. All in all the game is lovely and you can tell right away that the devs care about it deeply. However, gameplaywise it falls short. Why is that? And why do I recommend it anyway? First a list of the pros and cons:
The first three items on the list are closely tied together.
let me give you an example that is fairly objective in my eyes:
I play Endless Ironbot Mode which lets you play boss after boss. Usually such modes are designed to test your skill and/or for practice to prepare for the boss fights later in the story mode. By now I'm pretty much maxed out in upgrades even though I'm only 2/3 in the story and have barely replayed any of the levels. Not only do I beat every boss without getting close to dying, I also get the achievement after beating the 20th boss (which was my goal in the first place) and 50.000.000$. Only from this run, which took 15-20 minutes, I could buy ~75% of all the unlockables in the game (if I hadn't bought them already). This alone would be already pretty bad.
But now comes my real concern. Although I'm eager to quit the mode I decide to play boss Nr. 21 and see how far I get by only jiggling the control stick up and down and holding fire of the default weapon. Guess what? I beat the boss and lose only a third of my health! Without dodging any shot! It's fair to say that at this point Boss 101 is more of an interactive screensaver rather than a video game. [To be fair I started playing the game when there haven't been different difficulty levels yet. They got patched in after release. My game could be still set to easy by default, no way to tell.]
This isn't simply easy though, it virtually takes away the option of dying. I figure this is why the mode is called "Endless": you will quite literally never die nor reach the end. Now if someone tells me "only wait until you fight Boss 82!" I'd wonder why I'd even play the mode until then: There are no leaderboards and the earned cash is meaningless. It would be nothing but a challenge of patience. Also just ramping up enemy dmg and health won't do the trick. The game suffers from being too simple in the first place.
In general, Boss 101 requires no strategy, skill or thinking. When the bosses are made up of different parts that have each their own abilities and special shots etc. why can't I blast them off separately, allowing me to prioritize targets and going for a basic strategy? For God's sake, this game cries for such a feature, it's almost self-evident! Instead you click a button, the boss gets generated and the game tells you: knifes do more dmg, pistols do less. Very well then, game, I guess I'm going to equip the knife then, won't I? That's it. Press the button, look at the boss, equip a weapon that makes sense. You'll do this over and over again. In the fight it doesn't matter where you hit the boss, it's all the same.
And why can I select from countless of outfits, one crazier than the other, and it's only me who ever sees my pick? Why not making a player profile that shows my character and pet to others, connected to the leaderboards? Another obvious feature!
You might wonder by now why I am so harsh with a game that I end up giving a thumbs up. Two reasons: First, I can't give a neutral or so-so-rating and I can't bring myself to vote it down. Second, it has so much more potential! On some parts Boss 101 looks polished to a point where the player can't ask for anything else, on other parts it's evident that the devs didn't see the forest for the trees. Quite typically you get that with games that had no real QA process to go through. It's a shame. The meta game is just so very well presented to us with a nice pace on the story and characters you want to listen to. Yet the gameplay, as it is right now, really doesn't work. Random generators are fun and all but will mess up your balancing completely, this here is a case study. All the succesful Shoot 'em ups (the ones I can think of, that is) have carefully crafted level design and thoughtfully planned boss phases for good reasons.
I will, however, recommend this game without any hesitation to lovers of casual games and new gamers up to the age of 12. Core gamers and especially Shmup veterans should either stay away or wait for a sale. – Go ahead and gift this game to your younger brother!

FULL DISCLOSURE: I am good friends with the developers and have been watching the progress of this project for quite some time. They also used some music of mine I had lying around - was very happy to contribute! Other than that, I had nothing to do with the development - just a fan and friend.
Boss 101 feels like something Nintendo might have cooked up. The feeling you get when you play it is like taking a trip to Disneyland while playing Earthbound on the lookout for packets of Z-Bots (remember those?), Monster-In-My-Pocket, and M.U.S.C.L.E - lots of love and TONS of effort went into creating an adventure (and SERIOUS unlock-a-thon) that has no right to be as damned charming as it is.
The hat store alone will leave you in tears (the "holy crap I'm in the bestest toy store ever" kind).
It looks like a shooter, sure, but it PLAYS more like a hilarious adventure/RPG beneath the surface. The shooting bits are still tons of fun (especially when you get to see what insane assortment of boss parts are glued together to create some of the most imaginative and hysterical giant killer robos ever), and can be pretty brutal late-game if you aren't equipping the right sort of gear going into the battle (poison resist, health buffs, using a gun that the boss is weak to).
And the dialogue. THE DIALOGUE. The dialogue, one-liners and character interactions caught me off guard so many times I was afraid to drink anything while playing.
Yeah I got it for free. Yeah I want my friends to do well. And yeah, that might skew my perception going into the thing (especially since I am not a big shooter guy) -- but that doesn't change the fact that I enjoyed the hell out of this adventure, nor does it change the game's wit, charm and heaps of originality. I wish I could play it all over again, not knowing a thing about it. At 9.99, this thing is a steal.
Oh yeah, and there's an arcade. HAVE AT THEE!

Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams is a platforming game where you play as a pair of characters that can switch on the fly, changing the environment, the enemies, and in a lot of parts, the available collectible crystals. Crystal collecting and switching are at the core of this game, and not much else.
Don't expect much of a story. I'll be honest, I found none myself, so this is really just pure game. The problem is that the game it is isn't very good.
Navigate levels by jumping and either spinning, which turns the character into a kind of cannon ball that can break walls or attack enemies; or twisting, which allows the character to descend slowly and with more control after a jump.
The levels are long and boring. These are not especially challenging, though a few will be tougher and longer. The switching mechanic adds to the challenge, but ultimately, like a lot of this game, can get tedious pretty quickly.
The challenge can also come from ropey controls. The controller support is good, I think that the problem is in the design. The directional pad or analogue sticks give the same responsiveness. The characters have a loose feeling to how they move, so things can feel a little imprecise. For a game that depends on tight controls and quick action it can become very frustrating very fast.
The camera tracking isn't great either, in spots showing little enough to navigate a jump or see an enemy you might unintentionally run into. Panning and tracking can be too iffy, and some of the deaths I encountered came from camera mischief.
Dying in this game isn't strictly punished, though the scoring system is affected. The Scoring in this game is very strange, and in order to unlock further levels you will need to score stars. Stars are scored by finishing levels with a lot of crystals and few deaths. There are a LOT of crystals, and the more deaths you have the lower your stars will be by the end of the stage.
This is where the game shows its greatest weakness. As a platformer it is mediocre, tedious, and the pace is grueling. Finishing a stage takes patience, not only with the camera and controls, but with the boredom.
Visually the graphics are okay, but not great. Colors really pop, but the overall aesthetic is pretty ho-hum. Music tracks loop and after a while became pretty annoying. It isn't bad, but in a level that runs for over 7 minutes, and a lot of gem collecting, it can get really old.
Save your money, there's better out there.
