Hi,
I guess you're wondering whether this installement of AC series is worth your dime. And noone can blame you, knowing how Ubisoft has, patheticly, turned such a great franchise into a year-to-year money grabbing business. This is no longer the case with AC: Origins (hopefully for the foreseeable future as well). I'll share my opinion as to why.
Pros
Graphics - this game looks stunning no matter what kind of a "I don't play Minecraft because it's squared" creep you are. Ubisoft has taken a step further with ACO and the result is an environment where you simply want to stop and take a picture as if you're actually there. The characters are very detailed, the physics work fine most of the time, the saturation is perfect. Dungeons are a big hit too, they're both creepy and inviting. The sand being carried by the wind in the desert, the distortion effect of heat, the faraway mountains, it all looks stunning. The animations are done mostly right too.
Sound - The sound greatly enchances the graphics, especially in ACO. The sound of wind dashing through the trees and grass along with some sounds of wildlife is something nearly every game has, yet not many make you feel as if the nature is truly alive. The hallucinations in the desert sound like they're in your head, which adds to the creepy atmosphere. Sound of crumbling rocks, falling debree and birds as you scale the mountains is real cool. The characters are voiced with emotion and some story behind them, which made me listen to all the conversations instead of skipping. It didn't seem like only a few voice actors worked on this, but a whole army.
Gameplay - swithcing to an RPG system was definitely a great idea. The combat is not fluid and responsive, the loot system is real good. The dash works as intended, if you manage to dodge the attack and it does not reach you, then you're safe. It all transitions well from combat to parkour and riding, with the help of well made animations.
Cons
Parkour - Bayek does not have grappling hooks or ropes like his counterparts, but scaling rather impossible to scale places never felt so easy. It makes it look so easy your kids could do it. It looks cool, but lacks depth and dfficulity and, n turn, realism. It is still enjoyable though.
Story - it is bland.. I mean, the sidequests are better written than the main storyline. On that note, throughout the game Bayek is trying to balance his deeds so that Gods would send him to the field of reeds when he dies, and yet many of the quest objectives are to kill, kill, kill. I understand that they needed to promote the new combat system, but this is a bit over the top. I will not go any further to avoid spoilers, but if I had to compare the quality of the story with another game it would be Crysis 3, where it's trying to make you feel like you're in a some grand scheme, but it fails to do so and you're left with nothing but gameplay to fill that missing spot and make the best out of it.
Overall
I recommend this game. The freedom given to you to explore an intimidatingly huge world full of detail, by any means you like, is awesome. I have completed nearly everything this game has to offer just to see what lies beyond and  don't regret a minute of it.

At times i really disliked the game because of unfair sections and annoying checkpoints but at other times i just loved every moment. I played through the campaign which according to steam took me around 3.5 hours which some people might think is a little bit short. I'm gonna get this out of the way first 'cause this game has HUGE problems that make it, actually, a pretty bad speedrunning game. I do like it, though.
1. For whatever reason, you cannot shoot anything at point-blank range. This includes switches as well as enemies that are about to knock you off the edge of a platform. This kind of gets in the way of things. A lot.
2. The boost pads are horridly inconsistent. Often not propelling me with enough height or distance to get to the next platform, resulting in either a death or at best a bit of wasted time.
Neither of these can be intentional at all and they really destroy any consistency in running levels, two glitches that really need fixing. That being said I did 100% this game, so.
A few other problems I had:
Overuse of enemies, especially cases of enemies awkwardly crammed into otherwise fine level segments. Some of them feel like cheap shots.
The sparks vary in quality a lot more than the rest of the game. Three of them had really strict time limits compared to everything else in the game and a good number of them didn't bring much if anything new to the table, it feels like the devs ran out of ideas making them. I do like having them, though, adds a lot of length to the game and it's not like they're awful levels in general.
I feel like instead of giving these massive goliath levels, the main levels could have been split up a bit more. Levels 4 and 5 are both big enough to be two, even three levels. Though they're really not that terribly long when you know them well enough (and have the spark paths down).
Checkpointing could use some work, sometimes it's fine and other times there's a bit too much between checkpoints.
This is a minor gripe, but for a game with branching level paths and an emphasis on speedrunning, it's really strange that there are definitive "best paths" in the form of sparks; there's literally no arguing with any of them, they are always faster and most of the time actually easier too, due to being shorter.
I have no clue what any of the story is. I read the logs and saw the true ending and I don't get it.
Now onto the good:
The controls. They're stellar. Really. The jump feels great, the dash feels great, rocket jumping is intuitive enough, the basic move speed is really good for this kind of game. The dash meter is a bit short at first but it gets better with upgrades, so, EHH.
The level design. There's a lot of creative ideas in the main level and the game never really repeats itself (aside from a few instances of VERTICAL LASER TUNNEL and DASH THROUGH LASER TUNNEL moments, the former of which generally comprise most of the worst sections of the game, the latter always being fun enough to not get on my nerves). Each level introduces a new mechanic (well, save for the second level, though you could argue that the branching paths count as a new mechanic, the first level is pretty linear aside from the shortcut paths).
The difficulty curve is pretty smooth too. It starts out pretty simple and ramps up fast but not dauntingly so, each new section gets a bit harder than the previous section and you suddenly realize that "super hard" section two levels ago is a piece of cake compared to the "super hard" section you're facing now, which will probably be a piece of cake by the time you hit the next level's "super hard" sections. But really, it's all manageable. As long as you actually learn from mistakes, at least.
The game's also gorgeous to look at, though admittedly it gets kind of samey after playing for 20 hours or so, but the scale of the levels is still pretty breathtaking, admittedly.
I like this game. I don't love this game. But I think it's worth playing. It's leagues better than Cloudbuilt, at the very least, though the parkour mechanics would've been great to have here too but eehh it doesn't really need them when the rest of the mechanics are good enough.
So yeah, that's me rambling for a while about a thing.

My 4 hours of gametime taught me the following about this game :
Terrible combat
Terrible voice acting
Terrible dialogues
Terrible quests
Terrible camera
That may seem a bit simplistic, but let me say a thing about each of those points to underline my stunning opinion.
Terrible combat = I actually like the concept of how it probably was supposed to play out, with guard breaks, countering, blocking and all, but the actual execution is just bad. Best example would be you fighting 2 guys while your party member gets stunlocked by 2 other guys (My party member died in every fight btw...I am not sure what I was doing wrong, but they already have major troubles with a single opponent, let alone fighting 2 guys at once, while I battle 3 or 4 at the same time ).
If one of the 2 guys blocks, you get thrown back and the other guy won't get hit, even if he didn't block. In return his attack goes through and hits you, since you can't block or evade. Another problem is that your character is staggering like a drunk hobo after each hit, which makes you exceptionally vulnerable to other enemies stunlocking you into death. You have an evade, but that still lets you receive damage, even if you roll through an attack. Enemies have way less trouble, after all you're just one guy and can't abuse the mechanics like they do. My combat was mostly me hitting guys and then running in a circle while my health slowly recovered and repeat :l
11 hr edit : Companions are still useless, but I realized that you have to set them to "defend" for them to survive 30-45 seconds and hold off a few enemies while you quickly try to dispose of the others. You also get Technomancer skills after chapter 1, which allow you to use a few magical things, which (other than the shield) never really did much for me. I will praise the game for making you feel an effect on levelling up your skills though. That really makes your character feel more powerful in combat, even though sometimes it still ends in a 50/50 win/lose luck draw.
Terrible voice acting/dialogue = &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; seems a very popular word in France and it shows in this game. Sure, it's prison but do you really need a &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; in every second sentence you hear  and sometimes even 3 times in one sentence ? The game also opens with a fat guy wanting to♥♥♥♥♥♥a new prisoner called "Innocence" (you couldn't make that up..) and the hero stopping him, by standing in the entrance and staring, while occasionally clanging his bracers (or whatever the hell he was clanging). What follows is one of the most insanely scripted monologues I've ever witnessed, which gently dismisses you into the magical world of Mars : War Logs. It doesn't get better from then on as you'll just slowly die while listening to all the other guys sharing their colourful expressions with you.
11 hr edit : Same thing.. Less horrible than chapter 1, but the dreadful voice acting remains and the way people say things just does not sound natural at all.
Terrible quests : Alright, sure, I haven't done that many, but the fact that annoyed me the most was, that you always had to double and triple check locations you've already been at, just because you got a new quest and now you can look at that box which wasn't interactive before. The game even does that multiple times. Some guy will give you a quest to find 5 pieces of whatever and you'll have to run all around the camp again to check which barrel or metal heap is made interactive now. After that another guy will want 3 whatevers and you'll run all over the camp AGAIN looking for WHATEVER IS GLOWING NOW.
I can not say how much that ticked me off and how much time it's wasting, especially since the locations aren't even marked on the map. Yep, sure, just let me run around the starting area for another 15 minutes, after I've already fully explored it twice...Even the quest to get samples from sick dogs requires you to run all over the camp again and search for the dogs who now conveniently spawned GOD KNOWS WHERE. You even had to kill 2 or 3 dogs before that quest, which are still dead by that time, but you can't loot those...hah...why would you...haha...nah...
11 hr edit : Thank God that was exclusive to Chapter 1. The other chapters offer your normal fetch/kill/deliver quests, but no more random running around to try to find Waldo. Acceptable.
Terrible camera = That's mostly a problem in combat, since it's hard to keep enemy groups of 4 or 5 guys in focus during a fight and you're also often fighting in enclosed spaces. At times I couldn't even see where to dodge and who to hit, just because the camera basically looked down on the ground while I was frantically trying to avoid getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to death again. Joy joy..
11 hr edit : Still the same..The camera in combat can be your worst enemy at times, They should have pulled it further back for a better overview to allow their "tactical" (cough cough) combat to play out better.
Anyways..You might be asking yourself "Hey, you're telling me so much about how you're bad at this game, but what exactly IS THIS GAME ? I WANNA KNOW WHAT IT'S ABOUT, THE GAMEPLAY, CAN YOU CRAFT ? IS THERE ROMANCE ?"
It's basically an action rpg on Mars, you being some guy called Roy, fighting evil with a steel pipe or a similar weapon (or, if you're lucky and have enough ammo, a nailgun). Gamepad controls are alright, graphics are rather...meh..You will get xp to put into skills, you can upgrade your weapons and armor and so on and so forth..pretty standard fare and I was trying to give it a shot after reading a few reviews, but in the end I can't recommend it at all, unless you can stomach all the problems or are just a  better player than me. It has a distinct B-Movie charm, but you also need to accept the B-Movie gameplay and I can not :p
11 hr edit : If you manage to somehow slog through Chapter 1, which is one of the most dreadful and terrible experiences in any rpg I've ever played, you should be okay with the rest of the game. The other chapters offer the things which you can expect from any action rpg and doesn't do them neither terribly well nor bad. I wish the loot was a bit more varied and the currency seems rather useless, seeing as how I haven't bought a single item from a shop during the whole game. You will also only encounter 5 different weapons (all of them being pipes or bars) and maybe 6 different clothes. Enemy variety is also pretty sparse (dogs, moles, soldiers, soldiers with shields, technomancers), but by now you certainly know what to expect anyways..

An assembly programming game.  Very comparable to TIS-100, and prettier, but simpler.
Puzzles start out trivial (just copy input to output), and get comparatively harder (factor this number into primes) as the game goes on.
The instructions available are, if anything, even /less/ complete than TIS-100 -- copying data from one spot on the floor to the very next spot takes 4 steps at minimum -- but is ignorable except when trying to go for the size or speed challenge ratings.
If you're a low level coder, C or similar, this game will be easy, although some of the size/speed optimizations can still be challenging.  If you like logical puzzle games (like Spacechem), you'll also enjoy this game.
It is not a "learn to program" game, though; it is a "think logically" game.
Some things are weird, and point at a tablet base for the game -- comments are drawn, not typed. You can only copy entire programs, you can't copy a selection.  Things like that.  It can still be annoying at times, especially when you want to write a long comment.
At first, it made me feel smart. Then in just a few levels in, it started to make me feel like the dumbest organism on the face of the earth.

From the developers of World of Goo and Little Inferno, here comes Human Resource Machine. In this game, we play as an employee of Tomorrow Corporation, the strange company that also showed up in their previous two games. Our role is quite simple: we'll receive a series of inputs, and we must write a program to obtain the desired outposts. It sounds (and is) simple at first, but as you progress through the game, you'll get more and more challenging puzzles to solve, including some optional ones that are really difficult.
I must admit, I had great difficulty with some of the latter puzzles. After all, programming has never been something I'm good at, but even then, this game is good to learn some basic skills. It's also interesting to see the logic behind some of the "programs" you build, how a series of simple commands can perform complex operations, like building a Fibonacci sequence up to the number you receive, or being able to take a number and output the digits that form it.
As far as the story goes, it's quite minimalistic in this game, even more so than in their previous games. There's a few cutscenes, plus dialogue from your "bosses" on each level that give you some insight into their lives, but nothing really elaborate. Not that it's a bad thing; even though the story in Tomorrow Corporation's games is fun and thought-provoking at times, it's always played a secondary role to the gameplay. The artstyle is the same we've seen in their previous games, and the soundtracks feels similar as well; again, that's not a bad thing, as their style always feels unique and quirky.
To conclude, I'd say that this is a fairly enjoyable game, one that I recommend to everyone who wishes to learn some basic programming, or who enjoys Tomorrow Corporation's quirky games.

This is my first CCG so take this with a grain of salt. I like this game. It's not really meant to be a time-sucking game, but with the latest update right before official release (I played an early access version) it can have a slightly faster pace too.
You play by collecting cards to build a deck. 15 cards makes a deck. You can select a ranked or a "casual" mode for each individual match you choose to play. When in a match, you and you opponent take turns placing a card on a 3x3 grid. When either player can't play a card or, with a full grid, ends their turn with fewer cards on the grid than their opponent, the match is over. If you win, you a granted one of 3 different kinds of chests - a normal, advanced, and elite chest (I believe it's random.) You can only have 4 of these chests in your inventory at a time, and they require a timer to unlock and open. In these chests, you can gain additional cards and in-game currency. Cards that you gain from chests are automatically added to your collection. Duplicate cards can be upgraded with in-game currency once you have enough of them. You can buy this in-game currency - as well as other more advanced chests and more - with real money, but if you're like me and only play for free, then don't upgrade your cards past level 4 (it's really cheap to do so up to level 4) unless they are very good cards you want to keep in your deck (there are at least 100 different cards in the game right now.) That's the basics right there.
I reccommend this game because it's a fun use of time, and it's easy to play in "reasonable" blocks of time (you aren't really going to gain anything by playing more than 4 or 5 matches at a time.) The matches themselves are relatively quick (2-5 minutes?) And it has more than just a couple different strategies to have fun with.
If you don't like waiting for rewards to unlock, you might not want to play this game for long. The wait isn't very long though - only an hour to unlock a normal chest. I also don't like that you can't have a timer running on more than one chest at a time - but if you're patient, it just means it will take you a little bit longer to get more rewards. In all, it's definitely worth at least a try because - here's the best part ....
IT'S FREE!

If you have played some Artifex Mundi / Spark CE engine HOGs, this one is quite a bit different and I like that. Many of the puzzles are fresh. The technical side is also different, I think it runs on a different engine, all of the character animation is in actual realtime 3D (60 fps or however fast your display and GPU can handle it). Many locations are in 360 degree graphics, CGI instead of handdrawn as far as I can tell. You can turn in the 4 different directions, and the consistency of the locations between different view positions is high (something that many other HOGs lack). All of this means that I think the production values are pretty high and this game must have cost more to make than most other HOGs. (The Artifex Mundi games seem to have changed to a cheaper production in the more recent games, with the prerendered cutscenes not even having 3D CGI characters but handdrawn 2D ones with crude animation, which I find also visually cheap)
Unfortunately, the engine and visual production values doesn't automatically translate into better gameplay. The hint button is more necessary than in other HOGs, and the HO scenes are not as satisfying. The list of items you need to find is not fully displayed, only 8 or so at a time.
The voice acting and the story were ok, nothing exceptionally bad or good imho.
I would like to see some more HOGs of this kind, with evolved gameplay they could really freshen up the HOG market. But since this game was made some time ago (2014 or earlier) and I haven't come across any other game of this kind yet, I'm not sure if there is going to be another one. If you happen to know a HOG with a similar technical side as this one, leave me a comment.

This was the first "hidden-object game" I ever played. I hadn't even known that the genre existed beforehand; I was expecting a point-and-click adventure like, say,
only set in Prague and with no nekkid ladies. So I guess it speaks to the strengths of
that it not only eased me into the genre in a way I could understand, but also impressed me enough that I've gone on to purchase (and enjoy) other "HOGs" as well.
Briefly, for those that don't know, a HOG is similar to an adventure game except that the emphasis is on
objects rather than using them. You're mostly presented with static images rather than 3-D worlds (though usually with ambient effects like flickering lights or running water), and you have to pick out semi-obscured objects with the mouse cursor. Occasional puzzles and cutscenes are often interspersed between the object-hunting sections. Production values are typically high, they usually tell stories involving magic or light horror elements (we're talking ghosts, not gore), and interestingly many of them seem to have female protagonists.
fits this description to a tee.
To be honest, though I genuinely enjoyed
while I was playing it, I don't really have much to say about it now that it's over. It was perfectly charming and well-made, neither too easy nor too hard... and I hardly remember anything about it a month after I played it. Like some other HOGs I've played since then, it felt a bit like a Sunday crossword puzzle: relaxing, enjoyable, and utterly disposable at the end of the day. I seem to recall a golem turning up at some point, which was kinda cool, as well as a kindly old shopkeeper, and also some hunky but non-threatening dude that I probably hooked up with in a PG-rated kind of way at the end. It was perfectly enjoyable, if not entirely memorable.
I hope I'm not damning this game with faint-sounding praise. It
good. Buy it if you like HOGs, or are curious about the genre. Your two bucks will get you about five hours of chilled-out, well-crafted fun.

Alchemy Mysteries: Praugue Legends is a Hidden Object Puzzle game which I am hesitant to recommend. The game starts out fun, with simple clicking mechanics and easy to see objects, but as the story rolls on the game gets much harder, and almost impossible to pass without the use of the hint button down in the bottom-left corner. I am recommending this game because of a few fun puzzles that are very well made and very challenging and a story that isn't great, but isn't lame either.
So what's the problem with this game? Why is the game nearly impossible without that precious hint button? Well, there is an "open world" kind of style to this game. Sometimes you have to find an item somewhere in the world and you wouldn't have a clue where it would be... I found a box of matches under a window leaning on a pole, quite a distance from the objective and there are plenty more examples of that. So your go to option is the hint button. Mindlessly pressing the hint button and then waiting a few seconds for it to load back up again isn't very fun, but that's the only thing you can do to complete the story. This makes it very time consuming and boring traveling around the "map"...
The puzzles, or "minigames" are fun though. They offer a great challenge, but it's obvious they aren't impossible. Some of the puzzles took a good 10-15 minutes for me to complete, and most of them are random so you can't look up a guide to complete them. This is the feature that really makes the game fun, and the reason I'm going to recommend this game,  even if it's only just. If I had to give it a rating, I'd give it a 5.1/10

If a horror game is valued on how scary it is, then Daylight is scary good. When I was a little kid, I always thought that horror stuff is just some comedy thing for me.
Daylight made me stop thinking that way.
I jumped 3 times within one hour of gameplay, and was subconsciously thinking "oh please no more of those Shadows". I even felt relieved after I stop playing it.
The gameplay was simple. Find Remnants, get the Sigil and unlock the lock. However, as you search desperately for those Remnants, you will be bombarded by noises that makes me search for the source of the noise, just so I can breathe easier. Things gets worse, however, when your smartphone, which is your source of light that doubles as your map, gets distorted. It is a sign that means you have to prepare to be terrorized. And yes, it is what caused me jump 3 times.
Daylight doesn't put much into its storytelling, however. Remnants have a little bit of text that might explain some things, but it wasn't made very clear what was all of this mess about. It means that the only source of suspense in Daylight is its horror factor, not story. It was somewhat disappointing, but a game whose experience-between-games are never the same are ill suited to receive a story.
Graphics-wise, it was fine. The Unreal Engine 4 draws shadows and textures finely, but user interface can be improved to give a better ambience. However, objects may fall somewhat awkwardly, to which I question about the ragdoll physics. It's still good, nevertheless.
The audio for Daylight is pretty solid. The SFX for falling objects, disturbances and when the Shadows are attacking you is fairly good. VO isn't bad either; the main character speaks lines at pretty much random intervals, but it was made clear that she was scared and tried to put up a front at times, just so she can stay alive. There is no music in-game, but the menu music was describing the ambience fairly well.
Simply put, Daylight is good. If you're thinking that horror games don't scare you, try Daylight.

Daylight is a game that both dissapointed me, and suprised me at the same time, which makes it difficult to recommend to a larger crowd, but will appeal to horror fans in need of a fix.
In Daylight, you play as Sarah, as she wakes up in a hospital with, get this, no memory whatsoever about how she got there or why she is there. This is basically an excuse to go wandering in dark halls while getting all spookied and whatnot. But is Daylight scary? Most of the time, yes, yes it is. I will admit to getting startled a few times, and being genuinely creeped out by the atmosphere. On the other hand, sometimes when the game wants to be scary, it falls flat on it's face, often coming off as if it's trying too hard to be scary.
The gameplay is certaily a flaw for this game. Daylight follows the standard "Slender" formula, as you walk around finding pages that give insight on the story while you get chased by a witch that will appear and dissapear throughout the level. Often times, the witch would spawn in front of me, which got annoying. But sadly, I was never really threatened, as I could pull out a flare to, quite comically, set the witch ablaze, which took a lot away from her, considering I was never in short supply of flares. Also, much like Slender, I often found myself walking around in circles looking for the last page.
To close this review, for 15$, I don't believe that the 60 minute running time will be enough for most players, and the lack of any challenging gameplay, plus hit or miss scares, make this a hard one to sell. For those of those who need a quick fix for a horror game, feel free to drop the cash, otherwise Daylight is better left alone.

A solid platformer that loses steam in the final third or so. Unlike some other reviewers, I think the game controls well. The jumping feels tight and the spin allows for precise air control. The art style is vivid an engaging, particularly with the way the environments change depending on which color character you are. There are lots of hidden areas you'll need to find if you want to collect every gem in every level, which theoretically means lots of replay value. The game also has several side modes (time trial, "hardcore," "ultra hardcore") that could add playtime for the direhard Giana Sisters fan.
My main complaint is that the levels become far too long as the game goes on. The frequent checkpoints mean you don't have to replay segments over and over or anything. But even with those checkpoints, each level in the last world takes 15-25 minutes to complete. There are no mid-level saves, so either finish a level in one go or lose all your progress.
The game also is kind of a one-trick pony, and that one trick gets a bit tired by the end. There are too many "float with the yellow girl and then slowly dodge spikes while falling down" sections. The Balloon-Fight-esque bubblegum mechanic is downright terrible and used over and over in the last ~10 levels. The combo of very long levels and repetitive level design means that all those side modes aren't particularly appealing. They don't change any of the problem areas; in fact, they mostly just amplify them.
I enjoyed the first two worlds (out of three) quite a bit, and I think the game is worth the asking price for those levels alone. It just loses steam toward the end.

Mars Logs Review
B-Budget Mad Max/Mass Effect Weird Baby
TL;DR at bottom.
Interesting beginning, follows another character rather than the MC. Tells a realistic, dirty life of a foot solider that can be related to in our world.
Story/Dialogue: Story started out strong. Dialogue is can be a bit wonky, but its wonkiness can be refreshing compared to AAA by the book dialogue we are used to. One negative though is that some dialogue was written, yet not voice overed, makes the game look more budgety than it should. There is character relationship development lite. Mass Effect kind, but a very lite version of it. So yes you can sex your companions. Overall the storyline was average, the world created was somewhat unique. Plot twists were somewhat weak and predictable.
Combat/Gameplay: Combat at first felt very fluid. That continued to the end. New combat elements were introduced but overall combat still was not complicated. Slight RNG in combat made it more interesting. I believe this combat system for an melee action RPG is one of the best I've played yet. The system of 'wounding' and 'stunning and the RNG makes for less scripted combat and more reactionary one.
RPG Elements: Quests interweave with one another, if you help one character it might unlock a dialogue option for another. There are multiple ways to complete quests, some locked by other quests. In example there is a character that you can convince to help escape in different ways, with different outcomes for each. The tricky part is you do not know which is the best way, and some of the ways they might not survive at all. Makes for a deeper and more unknown decision making process that you won't know the consequences of your actions until later, very good system. Talent tree focuses on three different fighting styles, ala warrior/rogue/mage. But any good playthrough a player will dabble in all trees to get the strongest talents, which are a must, otherwise combat can be quite challenging as some other newbies on the reviews cry about the combat difficulty.
Audio/Graphics: Audio was pretty standard, graphics  were suprising decently done for a BBB
budget game.  Enviornments were reptitive though.The enemy models and combat effects looked nice. Animations were fluid.
Overall/End: A decent B-Budget game. Really an unknown game at the bottom of RPG barrel. Beat it in 20 somethin hours. Looking forward to playing Sequel. (The Technomancer) Graphics and some models were repetitive. Combat was the best aspect. Storyline was alright. I would reccomend it if you plan on The Technomancer.
Verdict:
7/10

I liked this game a lot. I heard it was compared to Mass Effect but it's absolutely nothing like that game, beyond the "Renegade" and paragon choices. To be clear, though, in this game, Renegade choice is made exclusively by choosing to level up anything in the Renegade skill tree. It doesn't matter in the least what your actions and dialogue choices are. If you level up even one thing in the Renegade skill tree, you get the bad reputation and there's nothing you can do to fix it. I didn't like that. Point in fact, the Renegade skill tree had useful things--more health upgrades, ways of fine-tuning your use of the nail gun. But, beyond that, it was focused on stealth abilities. In this game, stealth doesn't matter a whit. So there's little if no reason reason to level up the Renegade skill tree at all, or at least wait to do anything with it until after the first chapter of the game, maybe somewhere in the middle of the second chapter, where the choice is made once and for all whether you're going to be Renegade or Paragon. This game was more like the Fallout series, set in a world that's ravaged by war and everyone lives like a refuge. I missed fast travel, since hiking back and forth between headquarters in the second and third chapters became somewhat tedious. I played the game on the easiest difficulty because I prefer to experience games with little combat challenge and mostly social interaction and questing. There wasn't a single challenge in the game on that difficulty. In the future, I might play at another level just to get the achievements. Also, the game is stingy for the most part through the first part. You get what you need and little else. The upgrades on weapons and armor you can get in the second or third chapter are all you need to take you through the rest of the game. I relied a lot on my handmade, upgraded weapon. Second to that, I used the nail gun. I would have used explosives more often but you're only allowed three slots to bring up a skill fast. I chose the health one, nail one, and, later in the game, one of the electricity "spells" to go into my quick access slots. I didn't use the Technomancer skills all that much but I suppose if I had I would have found them powerful. Maybe next time. The romances were beyond disappointed. I played on the side of the General the first time, then the Resistance, romancing the ladies in those arenas each in turn. It was how do you do I'm Roy, I love you let's get it on, and that's all she wrote in each relationship. I didn't romance Mary because she was little more than a mindless, airhead robot. It would have been cruel to romance someone who'd been so abused and brainwashed all her life. But I may do it that way next time I play just to see how it plays out compared to the other two options. I played out all the endings but I preferred the ending when Innocence lived. Otherwise there seemed little point to having played. All-in-all, I found this a good game that can be played over just a few days.

I've seen other reviews for this game stating that the creators of Mars: War Logs wanted it to be Mass Effect-like and then continue reviewing it on based this comparison. I don't find it to be entirely justified and seeing Mass Effect elements in it seems to me like more of wishful thinking than actual intent of the creators, and I don't find it's fair comparing it to ME anyway. It's important to note that some M:WL-s faults can be written off as results of budgetary constraints, however, some of them do stem from flat out bad writing, design and editing. Once you get over the fact that you want to give the small studio an A for effort and look at it for what it is, the game has a couple of highlights, but in general it's less-than-half-way there, I'm sad to say.
Pros:
+ Combat. The combat system is the sole shining gem in this game. My small complaint would be that I found that the difficulty varies weirdly in between combat sequences, being very easy at one point and maddeningly challenging the next. There was far more of the latter than the former, however, so I'll chalk it up as a plus.
+ Story and the overall idea. This is a weird one, I know, considering that it was half-way there (the other half will be in the 'cons'), but the half that was there I found enjoyable and I liked where the creators were going with the idea. IGN picked on the naming of the characters, but I found it to be a rather original bit, I just wish it was explained a little more thoroughly.
+ Skill tree. It's not as expansive as some of the bigger RPGs' (obviously), but it holds its own and is decently thought-out.
Cons that I can forgive, because they can be explained by the small budget:
- Voice acting. Not even average. It's actually laughably horrible.
- Facial animation. It just falls flat.
- UI. Very clumsy, making the crafting system a bit awkward.
Cons that I can't necessarily write off as resulting from budgetary issues:
- Cutscenes. They're sometimes framed and edited really badly, cutting out half of characters' faces. I'll take it back if I somehow find out that it was intentional, but it didn't feel like it.
- Backstories. This is the other half that I didn't like as much. The game did a poor job explaining the background of the setting, the missions and the characters, leading to quite a bit of confusion and overall feelings of "meeh."
- Unnecessary combat. Tying in with the previous point, the game just kept throwing in gangs of some sort in the streets for you to fight for absolutely no apparent reason. I feel like there should have been either an explanation or less such generated gangs.
- Unnecessary doors, walls, hatches. Considering that there weren't any loading screens between the smaller sections of the maps, I fail to see the point in having to climb walls and open doors for each tiny section of the map. And I seriously mean tiny. It's like the studio thought that letting you walk 10 uninterrupted meters is boring, so they put a wall in the middle of it for you to climb, because **** you, that's why.
I understand the impulse of wanting to give this game a break, because it's a small studio and for the tiny budget they had, they did a fairly good job. However - as I mentioned earlier - once you get over the feelings of pity and wanting to give it an A for effort, it's really not that good of a game. From what I've seen, most positive reviews for this game come from grading it on the budgetary curve, but there are some people out there who seem to legitimately enjoy this game. I would still mark it "recommended" for the purposes of trying it out yourself and making up your own mind. But under no circumstances should you buy this at full price.

The game is mostly ok with a few above average moments and a few awful ones. Give the game a spanking when it goes too far and enjoy the rest. Visually the game looks like what you'd expect to find in a post-apocalyptic, ramshackle colony on Mars. Technically nice even if what you're looking at is rusted and filthy.
Combat is what i really like because it's challenging. Very difficult to just rush and crush and very rarely are you swarmed by hordes of weak enemies. Take a little bit of time to try and fight tactically and it may work, and be pleasent. Or it may suck. It's not a perfect game. But Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines *was* a perfect game and it had it's share of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ combat.
I like Mars WL enough that i'm not bored or disgusted by it, but i can't say that it's really very good. The game doesn't understand the difference between swearing to acentuate context or verbiage, and swearing just because reasons. It comes across as crass and pathetic rather than fitting. Sure guys in prison camps swear and occasionally explore sodomy, but Mars WL just tacks it on with almost no impact. Portraying emotion is very rarely done well.
It's a game that fluctuates a bit. Reaching occasionally lofty heights and on other occasions slamming it's face into the sewer grate. You will probably facepalm a few times and wonder how some bits made it into the game without anyone asking "Why are we putting such♥♥♥♥♥♥in our game?" But i found it easy to forgive because it's really kinda petty and small and nothing is terribly insulting.
The Martian setting is a-ok. Well presented and fits the gameplay. Combat is good if you want to be engaged. If you want to plow through mooks you might get some satisfaction later in the game when AoE attacks become available but more likely you'll hate it right off the bat. You're frequently outnumbered and your teammates are worth their weight in♥♥♥♥♥♥offensively. If they focus on some D, they can keep a few enemies off you long enough to make a difference.
And that is why i like combat. Because smashing my face into a brick wall fails and i'm left with a headache but also ideas on how to defeat opponents without headbutting myself to death. There's explosives; grenades and mines can create a temporary opportunity or flatten a squad if you're lucky. There's also blinding attacks which work on enemies with unportected eyes. Dodge rolling is sometimes better than running away, and other times it can lead to some backstabbing. You can block, swing and miss, or guard-break enemies, and they can do the same to you. RPG leveling up can give you advantages including wounding enemies or leaving them stunned, etc. etc.
Oh you can also show the enemy what a fancy faux-steampunk pistol you have. Maybe you can even fire a shot before they interrupt and beat you sensless. Envy, you see?
I would not play Mars WL if combat was a cluster♥♥♥♥ or a clickfest and tactical combat basically meant "spam attack as quickly as you can!". I get why some hate the combat but that may be because they had different expectations. I was told before playing that combat was solid and was not dissapointed. It's good.
What isn't so good is stealth or exploration. There is no exploration except in the KOTOR vein. Explore all areas before you leave if you want to find all the scraps, but you're mostly confined by the story or area. Some areas are devoted solely to combat, others are mostly talky/questy/looty hubs. Stealth is a mixed bag. Since combat awards a pittance of XP and loot most of the time it's perfectly acceptable to avoid it. However combat is occasionally unavoidable and most of your leveling up goes straight into making you better at combat or having the ability to craft better equipment that makes you better at combat.
Oh, there's also crafting. It's fine. Not mind-blowing but not blown out of proportion either.
Stealth is best used to scout the enemy location and position yourself well for a usefull sneak attack. But a stealth RPG this is not. It's mostly hand to hand combat with RPG elements, so stealth isn't as useful or fun as it was in Deus Ex. A "swing a pipe in the direction of the enemies skull ... ON MARS" -RPG. Yes gimmicky, but not bad.
There's also a bit of morality though fortunately being a good guy isn't sickenning and being a prick isn't that advantageous. Kinda reminds me of the ways of the Open Palm and Closed Fist from Jade Empire, if it actually meant a thing. In JE that is.
You can also have conversations with your companions from time to time and their attitudes may cha... you know what? Go play the game! I've written a book here and you've stuck with it to nearly the end so obviously you're at least a little bit intrigued.
Like cold pizza and cheap beer, a good game is still good. Even if it could be a lot better.

Extra/Replayability: The extra challenge comes in the form of optimizing your solutions, which isn't really as satisfying as completing them for the first time. The cutscenes are... well. I don't think anyone was going to play this for the cutscenes anyways.

[Summary/TLDR at the bottom.]
Human Resource Machine is a graphically cutified,
-simulating and thus educational logic puzzle game. You are given the task of formulating solutions to problems based on transforming a sequence of digits and/or letters to another one using very basic instructions like copy from here to there, add, subtract and more. Your avatar will then act as a processor in human form and execute your orders stubbornly as given, either leading you to the expected result or total mayhem.
If this sounded weird or complicated to you – well, it is getting more complicated the further you get into the game, but don't worry: Human Resource Machine does a great job of introducing players to instructions and their combinations step by step without the need for any experience in programming (read the additional information at the bottom of this review concerning this rating). This also happens in a humorous and casual way with lots of irony and social criticism.
At the end of the game you might have an idea of the typical workday the little fingernail-sized chip that is hidden somewhere in your computer has to go through.

Pixel Puzzles lets you put pieces on a board until they form a picture, but fails to deliver a worthwhile jigsaw experience. Why? Well, two reasons, mostly.
Firstly, the game doesn't care if you find two connecting pieces and put them together, which is how I (and most people) usually go about completing a jigsaw. Instead, it only cares if you put a piece in it's correct position on the picture, because yes, I absolutely knew that random piece went in that exact spot when it's closest neighbours are 6 pieces away.
Secondly, while I actually like the little pond with pieces floating around, constantly shuffling, the fact that 9 times out of 10, I can't just click on the piece I want and actually get it, rather than another piece floating in the area, is extremely frustrating.
Due to these two glaring design flaws, I cannot recommend this game. I'm sure there are some people who will be satisfied with it, but I'm also sure there are far better alternatives out there.

While I enjoyed this game, and played it to completion, one particular flaw was simply to big for me to recommend it.
First, the Good:
1. It's jigsaw puzzle game on Steam!
2. Plenty of pictures gives you plenty of jigsawing to do
3. Different puzzles have the pieces "cut up" very differently, adding to the variety
4. As you'd expect, it's pretty relaxing just slowly taking your time to work on the puzzle, and then it feels really good when the puzzle is almost completed and you can just plop the remaining free pieces in the remaining holes without any searching :)
The Bad:
1. The worst issue with the game - picking the puzzle piece you want out of a group of other pieces is an exercise in frustration, especially in the latter puzzles when so many pieces are floating in the river.  You can click directly on a puzzle piece, and the game then hands the piece that was hiding underneath it - over and over again.  I sometimes took me literally a dozen tries to pick up a single puzzle piece!  This one flaw by itself is what had me click the "No" for this review.
The final puzzle is by far the largest, and has 350 piece.  As soon as I started it and saw the river absolutely full of overlapping pieces, I despaired - only to find out, to my amazement, that I was flawlessly picking up every single piece that I was intentionally clicking on! 30 pieces in a row, with no mistakes - what sorcery is this???  It's as if the QA testers complained to the programmers that this puzzle was unplayable, and they fixed the issue
.  Yes, it seems ridiculous, but I honestly cannot think of any other explanation.
2. No way to save progress in the middle of a puzzle.  Some puzzles take hours to do, and if you exit the game, you gotta start them all over!
3. The music, while pleasant enough in the beginning, just loops over and over and over, and it's the same song for every single puzzle.  Thankfully you can mute it, though that also mutes the few sound effects.
4. The colors in a most of the pictures seem washed out, though maybe that's a style thing.
The Differences From Physical Jigsaw Puzzles Which May Be Good or Bad Depending On Your Point Of View:
1. The puzzle pieces are always oriented in the proper direction, so there is never any need (or ability) to rotate them.
2. When dropped on the board close to their correct spot in the picture, the puzzle pieces automatically shift and stick there.  There have been many times where I'd accidentally plop a piece down in the right spot.  This also allows you to "hunt" for the right spot by just moving a piece around the board in small increments.
3. There is no way to stick two puzzle pieces together when you know they match each other, but do not know where exactly in the picture they belong.
4. The only way to view the full picture of the puzzle you're solving (without taking a screenshot of the level-select screen) is with a hint-style button, which slowly lights up as you place pieces in their proper spots.  When you do use the button, it turns the board you're solving into the complete picture for a few seconds during which you can still move and place the puzzle pieces.
So yes, I mostly enjoyed the game when it was not frustrating me with the puzzle piece selection issue.  If the devs fix that, I'll switch the recommendation to Yes.
All you need is strong fingers.

This current review might sound a bit harsh, non the less, I do like this game as you might see based on the playtime.
Over all this game already is pretty well balanced, even though there still are a few bugs popping up here and there. Still, for an ea game status this one is pretty well made so far.
In terms of pay to win.... I don't really think so. It takes time to collect the cards... way longer as it would, if you buy them, but just the fact, that you can buy stuff, doesn't make this game pay to win. Every card has its pro and con and even the strongest card is powerless, if you transform it or take it over due a sacrifice. Depending on the way you play, you can even win against an opponent that could have spent several hundred bugs, with just some basic cards. So pay to win is not really that much of a problem here.
The game itself contains two currency's silver and gold. Silver is the ingame currency and gold the one you have to pay for. Still, you can obtain gold ingame as well, but it sure takes its time. Silver is used to buy single cards, which are obtainable in the daily changing store. Other than that you will spend the most silver on upgrading you already obtained cards adding for more attack and sometimes some additional effects. You will get silver with every chest you open.
Cards are obtained from chests instead of booster packs. Over all there are three types of chest each containing a different amount of cards and each with the chance of getting legendary cards. Every 7 hours you will get a low chest without playing a single game - these stock up to 2 chests to redeem. The 2nd chest will replenish itself every 24 hours and needs 5 games to be won to open it. This is the 2nd best chest in game, offering a good amount of cards, silver and even some "gold". So playing this game from time to time and opening this chest will let you progress. Still, you can buy gold for real cash and buy silver for gold... non the less, both is not required to be able to play this game, at all.
The difference to the usual trading card games would be the way you have to work with your cards. Upgrading requires to own a single card several times to be able to upgrade. The main problem will be getting the right amount of cards to upgrade and the silver to upgrade them.... let's call it an endurance test.
Endurance test would be the right description for the entire game. All it currently offers is a duel mode, which either is ranked or not. Besides the 5 wins you need to open the 24h free chest... there is nothing special about or to obtain - after 5 battles a day you are pretty much done.
You will win a random free chest to open in addition to the free ones you always retrieve, but those either cost gold to open or take 3 / 12 / 18 hours to open them. Since you can only open a single chest at a time you have pretty much nothing to do once you played your 5 games, as you can only hold up to 5 chests. Other than the 5 chests you will receive nothing from battling others. You can increase your rank, but this doesn't do anything besides having a rank or a higher rank.
So in short.. you will spend about 25-30 min to do your daily routine, getting the chests and have done your dailies... you can open the small chests... so 5 min play every 3 hours or... well every 12 / 18h. Other than that you might only be interested in increasing your rank (after reaching lvl 10).
Actually the developers are pretty generous, if you look at the ways to obtain cards and progress, still the time in between could be used way better and if it's just some random KI events popping up or "some" non pointless stuff to do. Even winning some silver in a game would add more motivation into playing more than the minimum amount of games needed. The only difference between this and a Facebook game would be the naming "chests" instead of "energy" to play it.
Still, I like to come back to this game and play it. The strategy part about it really is fun. Not playing lets progress you as well and if you do put a little bit thought into your deck and try out some different strategies, you can really have a lot of fun with this game. Sometimes even more than 5 games ;)
With cards increased you gain XP, as well as finishing some quests. With raised levels you get more characters to play with and different abilities to go with. So every few levels you can put some more thought into different playing options.
Figuring out the best set of cards to go with and how many cards of which type might be needed to win.

I loved the Ace Attorney series. It's a shame they aren't on Steam. Now that I've gotten that out of the way I bought this game looking for a familiar vibe. This game is all that and more. Even though the comparison is clear this game has it's own unique style and a couple of different mechanics that make it more evolved than it's lovable aforementioned cousin.
Everything from the visual style and music all the way to some time management mechanics make Aviary Attorney a game all it's own. The setting and graphics remind me of a Piranesi painting. If you don't know who that is don't worry, just know the art is extremely detailed and works with the setting being 1840s France. The fact that the main cast are two well dressed dapper birds are characters that aren't quite endearing but at the same time are well animated through their dialogue and actions. There's definitely a lot of light hearted humor mixed in with all the evidence gathering and hard work that befalls an attorney.
The real guts of this game is the time management before a trial. This is where things  can get a little tough. While most games of this kind tend to have a straightforward path in this game it's entirely possible for you to miss some evidence or lose a case. You have to manage your time before the trial wisely and make sure you're properly prepared for court. Losing sucks but life goes on and so does the game. You can also get penalized in court for wasting time with red herring questioning. I feel like that level of challenge makes you think a bit more strategically because if you only have 6 days before a case then you have to choose what is relevant to pursue. It really makes you think, but not too much.
I've only played through the first 2 cases and so far I like what I see. It's a fresh take on the genre and adds some things that make it a different kind of animal. Definitely pick it up if you're into the Ace Attorney series. It's fresh, entertaining, and the writing's solid.

I had a great time with this game. It is clearly influenced by the Ace Attorney series of games, and I feel like it has accomplished its own little place in the library of puzzling law games. It has its own unique quirks and style, with interesting characters and cases to play through. There's a lot I like about this game, and a few things I feel could be improved upon.
The theme and art style are really charming. It is set in 19th century France and you play as a falcon lawyer named Jayjay Falcon who is accompanied by his assistant, Sparrowson. Both characters are very fun to follow and see their dialogue and banter they have together. All of the characters being animals is a neat twist and gave everyone their own added flair of unique personalities. The hand-drawn art style was also very pleasant.
The game is witty and well-written, and the cases themselves are interesting. You spend the days before the trial doing your investigations and it is less linear than in Ace Attorney. You can unfold the case in different ways depending on where you investigate first and what choices you make. The game is unique in that each case can actually have a different outcome depending on what pieces of evidence you do and don't find, resulting in different endings for each case and different endings for the game. This is hindered slightly by the non-functioning save system. There is an option in the menu for saving & quitting, but the game doesn't save. The game only saves at the end of each day. The game still works well without this function, but it shouldn't be there if it does not work. Also, considering the cases have different outcomes, it would be nice to not only save whenever you'd like, but to have different save files to easily go back to try and go for a different outcome of a case. Especially since events in the third case affect the ending you receive. Although, this game does have replay value, so I don't think many people would have a problem going back and starting the cases from the beginning to see what other sorts of things they can do that they missed from their first play-through.
Another thing that's a bit of a negative is that there is no option to read through previously read dialogue. So if you accidentally skip through some, you cannot go back to read it. Other than the few nitpicky thing here and there, this game is a lot of fun for any Ace Attorney fan or mystery/puzzle fan in general. I really hope a sequel is in the works for Aviary Attorney.

It is Slender.  You trudge through some corridors, find sheets of paper and walk away from a ghost lady.  Sometimes you get to watch canned animations when climbing over objects, and very rarely you pull a switch or two to open up a new part of the level.
The default field of view is atrocious, and there is no menu to change the control scheme, although the FOV can be changed in configuration files, and likely so can the controls.  The lack of accessible menus for these things, however, shows such immense negligence on the part of the developers.
There's some controversy over getting that Jessica Chobot fellow to write the story for the game.  Except she didn't really write it.  There are a bunch of tiny blurbs scattered everywhere on small sheets of paper that are undoubtedly as original as tiny blurbs can get, but the dialogue can't possibly be attributed to an actual author.  Every single line of dialogue is a platitude that the writer got from somewhere else and thought sounded cool.
Being a graphical apologist on many levels, I understand that the visuals are fine to look at, but it's rather humorous that this is the first Unreal Engine 4 game to be released.  It looks overall like something you'd find released early in the last console generation, with lots of shortcuts taken, like stacks of books being little more than blurrily textured rectangular prisms, or wood grain textures with the sharpness of cheap plastic.  Little bits like the cloth physics and lighting are much more contemporary, but they don't warrant such steep system requirements, especially since most of the game is set in very tiny corridors.  It's all the baggage of a cutting edge game engine without any of the cutting edge.
What a wonderful time to be alive.

From the get-go we are tossed onto our asses into an asylum with only a cell phone and a cheap Malcolm McDowell imitator barking nonsense over the speaker. He just spouts out grade-school philosophy such as “Life is but a butterfly’s dream,” and “Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned… and you’ve scorned them all.” With @John_Henry_Eden_ebooks as our good company, we stumble around in the dark hallways (using useless glowsticks and flares) of which you will see the same of many times. One of Daylight’s big selling points is that it is randomly generated as you play so you can never have the same play experience twice. Well that doesn’t help when every single room is the same non-memorable one over and over again, does it?
The goal of every area you visit is to collect 6 “remnants”, which is an absurdly vague way of saying “Find 6 pieces of paper with a red rune on them, some of which will be hidden in boxes on the walls and in desks”. Once you’ve stuffed enough Macguffins into your jacket, Ol’ Phoney pipes up mentioning that the “Sigil” has been revealed. While that sounds like something deep and meaningful, all it really turns out to be is a pair of surgical scissors or a porcelain doll floating in a room covered in glowing writing that you most likely already found before you had all six remnants. In taking the Sigil, you become defenseless as you are no longer able to whip out any flares or glowsticks to protect yourself.
…oh, right. I forgot something. The ghost. From the outset you’re being pursued by an apparition that appears out of the blue with little rhyme or reason. My first encounter with it was as follows: I heard a banshee cry out from behind me as I was in mid-turn. My cell phone minimap was beginning to distort with random artifacts and glyphs. I stopped moving and waited for a moment, noticing that I could see what appeared to be the leg of the creature standing there just to my right. I contemplated for a moment what may happen should I continue to turn. All the while it persisted on making weird hissy noises. And then, almost as quickly as it came, the creature disappeared. It felt like one of those hilariously bad special effects sequences in old low budget films where they paused recording while the person or object was moved off camera while everyone else held still before continuing to record to give the illusion that they had vanished in an instant.
You see, Daylight has a lot of problems. It fails to be truly engaging to the player at any point. All plot exposition is taken care of via the notes and remnants (there are two colors of seal on the paper to designate the difference!) which you can skip most of and most likely will because it is all drivel. Any tension is completely ruined by the fact that none of the game’s systems work to support each other. Sarah can sprint indefinitely, which makes the ghost a trivial occurrence in the event that it manages to even spawn. Resource management is merely an afterthought thanks to being given free flares and glowsticks in almost every other room. And if you manage to fill up too much on either, finding one in a container causes you to just completely discard it. I’m pretty sure no human alive is going to just throw out a precious glowstick before finding at least one extra pocket to cram it into.
The game does not look nearly as demanding as it claims to be and none of the setpieces are visually interesting or even memorable. Between the campy dialog, shoddy notes and head-shake inducing comments in the UI message area claiming “They will come to haunt you”, every bit of the writing is downright amateurish and is something to be ashamed of. The in-game Twitch streaming support tells me more about what was on the developers’ minds than anything else in the game. They were banking on the braindead simple stream avenue to perpetuate the game with its enticing look and promise of replayability via randomization.
What they forgot to do was make a game worth playing, watching or thinking about.

I supported the game during its initial campaign on Kickstarter and I'm very happy about the outcome, even though I hardly have time to game these days. I've played the original Giana Sisters for hours, days and weeks back in the past and Twisted Dreams is absolutely stunning in details.

I'm no game historian so don't expect me to get into the details of this one. It's not really relevant anyway, because there's more than enough daylight between the modern Giana Sisters and other platformers to have them stand on their own. For one thing, you might be hard-pressed to find another platformer this busy and colorful outside of the Trine series. And for another, you might be hard-pressed to get through all of this one's long and winding and occasionally cruel levels. Still, for as long as you can hang with it, you'll be treated to some solid action.
All you're getting for story here is that the titular sisters get whisked away to some dream realm, one ends up nabbed by a bigass dragon, and the other's got to get her back. That's going to involve a LOT of platforming through strange and threatening lands, collecting a LOT of multicolored gems, and dodging a LOT of traps. Your lone sister actually has the power to flip between versions of herself, the cutesy blonde one with a floaty Mario twirl move and the punky redhead with a Sonic-style spin attack. Flipping versions also flips the world, opening or closing some paths, phasing in or out hazards, and causing all sorts of other chaos.
The theme of Giana Sisters, really, is a LOT of everything. Maybe more than you would want, too, because these levels are huge and sprawling and feel like they take forever to finish. All you need to do to get through a level is reach the end but there might be a dozen or more checkpoints between you and there, each one marking a brief respite between devious traps. You'll face long sequences of jumps over spike pits, rides on perilous platforms, precarious bounces off enemies, and so on. These are all standard fare for platformers but get taken to almost comical extremes in how far they get stretched out.
The element that keeps the formula fresh is the flipping mechanic, which is used to great effect throughout the game. You'll soon be expected to flip worlds to open new paths, make platforms solid, phase out spikes, and more, all in the midst of these platforming challenges. You can flip worlds with a button press but your special movement powers flip things as well; if you're the twirly girl and you use the spin attack, that flips you to the other form and flips the world as well. As you might imagine this adds to the complexity as you have to keep track of which world you want to be in when you use your key movement powers, but I found it quite a bit of fun once I adjusted my thinking to it.
Levels are still going to take forever to finish, and that's without hunting for the hundreds of gems and other collectibles scattered throughout them. The average level has around 300-400 gems to collect, and the final stage of each world (which is significantly longer than the usual lengthy levels) can have well over 700. You'll actually need a fair number of these to earn stars that unlock later levels, and gems also come in different colors that can only be collected when flipped to the right form. On top of that are giant crystals hidden away in the most secret of areas which unlock concept art and other bonuses, and those will require significant exploration and puzzling to score.
If you're down for marathon levels and collectathons, Giana Sisters will more than fit the bill. The base game is plenty challenging (especially the bosses, since you can only take two hits), and there's half a dozen even harder modes to unlock from there. It's a game with a lot of technical appeal but honestly not much depth or heart to it, so don't go in expecting characters to get attached to or any sort of satisfying story. This is a solid game for the hardcore or speedrunning crowds, but even your average platform fans will find a few hours of enjoyment here.

Let's start with the good things about this game: It's pretty (although it's not Trine), it's difficult in a challenging way, the repetitive music isn't irritating, some of the bits of levels are really well designed and make you feel great when getting through them and the twisting/changing world mechanic is well used.
The bad? Everything else. The first two bosses are easy, the last one too hard (over an hour to beat ffs). Too many parts of the games' levels are badly made and rely on knowing what's coming next; there's just no way of seeing what's going to kill you just off screen until you hit it. The levels themselves are very samey and generally forgettable. Dying doesn't feel like a new opportunity but rather a frustration and a test in patience. That thing that looks like a platform? It's not. That platform that you can jump on? It's slightly transparent in this world and you'll fall through it. Those purple spikes against a purple background? You'll see them when you walk into them...Lastly, you need a certain about of stars to unlock a boss. For a lot of people that will mean back tracking through levels and replaying them soley for the sake of getting those last few stars. Great way to elongate a game and a great way to annoy people that just want to do the next bit.
There are other modes including time trial and I can go over levels again and again trying to get more stars but I'm just fed up with it and have no desire to ever go back to this. It's a shame, I like difficult games. VVVVVV and Super Meat Boy frustrated me but I'll always love them. This is just going into the virtual bin along with an empty box of headache pills.

DEADCORE REVIEW- COVERING THE GAME AS A WHOLE! (Tried to make this as complete as I could- sorry it's long).
After watching the trailers, I thought this looked like a pretty fun game... and boy did it deliver! When I dived into it, I was more than just in awe! Deadcore is definately on my list of top games in 2014! I highly recommend Deadcore to anyone who wants a challenge, or likes speed runs, fps puzzle, or platformers in general.
The gameplay is fast paced, extremely satisfying and the mechanics are brilliant. The general idea of the switch gun is simply genius, and adds a unique element to the game. The other abilities are also great- dash, g-mod and blast are unlocked further in and add more challenges and allow you to go back and explore previously unaccessible areas. Please note that the BLAST EXPLOIT HAS BEEN FIXED- so you can't use blast to climp up easily. You will have to play the legit way like I did! :p
The world itself is dangerous, mysterious and intriguing. It is quite an adventure through this game and it keeps you interested and curious. There are lots of different secrets to unlock- new pathways, and hidden collectibles- logs, music tracks, sparks, and more powerups- like ammo or dash boosts. The logs you find develop a small, story like explination that really adds to the feel of the game. Sparks unlock areas that are a faster route, but also more challenging. Exploring the world is unexpectedly fun- by that I mean that a first glance at the game would not suggest there is the exploration element. The soundtrack is perfect for the game- with a mix of fast paced, awesome tracks. The design is kinda Tron like, and suites the game perfectly.
It has a very good learning curve and a very high skill cap. You gain more abilities, experience and knowledge the further you get. Sometimes, you will get stuck on a particular part and it will be EXTREMELY RAGE INDUCING. My advice is to NOT RUSH and to analyse the challenge so you know where you're going wrong. Timing can be a very key factor to success. The enemies are cool but can be very frustrating, especially as I found the hit boxes on them are very small- one issue I had was that sometimes you hit the cubes and they don't deactivate- the shot needs to be too central for my liking. Wasps can be infuriating, and turrets are considerably rapid fire. The "bosses" are pretty awesome. Another issue I had was that you don't get a good feel of your size- meaning lazers can often hit you when you think you're clear. Some of the lazers I thought were a little too punishing- particularly ones that rotate. Also, I hate the laser tunnels you have to dash through. Sometimes the game offers little to no room for error- and the slightest wrong move can kill you.
This adds to the overall challenge though, and when you do get past that one bit you were stuck on, it is SO REWARDING! Each level gives new challenges that increase your skill. I myself am not very accurate and my reflexes aren't too sharp, but I feel they have improved because of this game- so what I'm saying is even the less skilled players can pick this game up and improve.
Lvl 1 is simple and pleasant- a good eye opener that leaves you jaw dropped in awe as you look up at the massive tower ahead. Lvl 2 is still quite easy, with some more tricky challenges. You are getting tested a bit more. Lvl 3, the difficulty starts to pick up a lot! Lvl 4, for me, was my least favourite lvl. It is the most demanding in terms of your pc- as you're in a storm of effects. The difficulty is extremely high and quite frustrating- mostly on the 1st time. Lvl 5 as a whole is shorter and a bit more rewarding than lvl 4. As a whole is it less difficult, but it has the hardest specific challenges. The end to lvl 5 is extremely rewarding- with a really epic challenge at the end. I won't spoil what you find at the end.
Conclusion: Deadcore is a genius game that I definately recommend. It is extremely challenging but equally rewarding. A FEW minor issues, but nothing you can't overcome eventually. AWESOME AND UNIQUE GAME- Want to thank the people behind this awesome game- Deadcore needs more recognition! I am a little sad that I have finished it! XD I would definately be up for a sequel! (That would need lots of thought though). DEADCORE IS AWESOME- BUY IT!  9/10

The control scheme translated from a controller to a keyboard scheme is done in the cheapest, laziest way possible and makes no sense on a qwerty layout. To simply map every button on a controller to a different keyboard button when a mouse could easily speak for 95% of them is just lazy. To not be able to reconfigure said buttons is even more lazy.
As for the actual game; the combat system is solid and a nice callback to the ATB system. They also went through a lot of effort to get the proper voice actors for all the characters that show up along the way - except for the squealing, flying pi- I mean squealing, flying fox whose high pitched tone gives me a headache.
And for the story, which is a main selling point for any game with 'Final Fantasy' in the name: It's on par with a Sanic fanfic. The character portraits are frustrating and the story is even worse. The game will go out of its' way to drive home a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ joke to the point where breaking a character portrait OR EVEN THE STORY is fine in order to crack a pun. When you manage to alienate the player to such an extreme that even during the -supposedly- deepest, most tragic events of the story all you want to do is punch your own player characters' faces in - you've failed as a writer. Which is especially poor for an FF game.
Final Fantasy 9 exist on Steam now. It's cheaper, it is bigger and better in every way. It's in a completely different class to this title and even though it is nearly two decades old - still prettier to look at.
(Also, the minigames are♥♥♥♥♥♥ but at least the developers seem to have acknowledged that, because they are skippable.)

I'm not recommending this game solely based on the combat system.
And it's quite possibly the worst combat I've seen in any game. It's extremely simplistic with very basic attacks, blocks and dodging.  However, none if these work very well. Your primary weapon is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ pipe, and sometimes you have a nail gun or grenades. You can't even use power attacks with melee weapon, and you barely do damage to even the weakest enemy. In a lot of places, you are facing up to 8-10 enemies. Your companion Innocence is just trash, who can barely deal damage. That means that you'll be fighting all of these enemies alone, in addition to doing close to zero damage. In other words, fighting these crowds is extremely difficult unless you have grenades or mines, but these are rare to find.
The blocking is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ because a lot of the time, you can't tell whether the enemy is attacking you, or breaking your block (which deals damage). This means that blocking is useless in many fights. If you wanna avoid blocking you can always dodge. Then again dodging is also useless, because you'll either crash into your enemy, or the enemy's range will surpass your dodging ability, thus hitting you.
Killing even one enemy takes forever, and imagine what killing a bunch of them is like, when you don't have any attacks that can deal damage to many enemies around you (except for grenades that will hurt you if close). The stealth system doesn't really work that well either, because you move very slowly, and when you approach and hit from behind, you don't do a lot more damage than you normally do. Combat is basically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
If we look away from the terrible combat, there's not a whole lot positive about the game. The graphics are very sub-par, especially when considering that the game was released in 2013, because it actually looks and feels like it's from 2006/07 (except close up faces). The dialogue along with voice acting is also pretty lame. A plus in my book is that the setting is pretty unique.
If the studio have had more money on their hands, this could've turned out a lot better, because quite frankly, the graphics are outrageously bad for its time. And obviously the dev team must've been on heroin when they designed the combat system.
