Okay, so let's get this out of the way: This is the B movie of RPGs, at best. The dialog is stilted, the character animations are stiff, the character development is shallow at best. There are stale tropes everywhere, both of the game sort (Pointless crafting system that has you spend a third of your time rummaging through crates and piles of trash? Camera that spins around in combat? Binary branching plotlines? All check) and of the narrative sort. The protagonist is incredibly bland, pretty much all the female characters are given stereotypical roles, obesity is used as a visual marker for sexual predation, and the threat of sexual violence hangs heavy over the miserable denizens of Mars (though interestingly, it hangs over men as well as women). There's a seedy bar that you can find by following the street signs helpfully advertising "Seedy bar". It's not a great story, nor a great game.
That said, I always try to look for the positives, and Mars: War Logs has some qualities if you're willing to tough out all the issues. Mercifully, it's very stable - I didn't encounter any bugs or obviously broken systems. Beyond that low bar, though, combat is surprisingly streamlined and fluid. It's simple, understandable, and actually fun - and to my shock, most of the enemies you defeat aren't actually killed, but rather just left writhing on the floor (you can choose to kill them for extra cash, but I never needed to). It might actually be one of the most bloodless RPGs I've ever played, and it's done in such a simple, obvious way that it makes me feel a bit gross about all the other RPGs where I play as the good guy but slaughter hundreds or thousands.
The art style (minus the animation) is actually pretty good, creating a rusty-feeling world and some strategically-placed sci-fi aesthetics, such as with the Technomancers. The story also has a few genuinely unexpected twists. At least three times I found myself surprised or even shocked that things weren't going the way I had expected them to, and that's rare. I don't know how the developers managed to craft a game that was 90% shallow tropes and 10% really surprising and interesting turns, but they did it.
The world itself is also really interesting. Mars often shows up in fiction either as a harsh wilderness to be tamed (in early colonization settings) or a rebellious, oppressed colony struggling against greedy Earth overlords (in late colonization settings). Mars: War Logs does something different entirely - Earth or even spaceflight barely get any mention at all, and instead Mars feels like it's been abandoned, with people fighting over scraps of water and fertile soil. There's also a fantasy-esque vibe to the setting that is really interesting, and it's enough to make me put the sequel (The Technomancer) firmly on my wishlist.
So in short: this is, at best, a bargain bin, shoestring budget version of Mass Effect, written by people who mostly uncritically repeat tropes from other media. But it takes place in an interesting world and has hints of intelligent and surprising writing, and the gameplay is entirely welcoming. Give it a shot if you can appreciate or tolerate the videogame equivalent of eyerolling B-movie cheese, and you may just find yourself enjoying it and wanting more.
(And better. Please, please let The Technomancer have better writing.)

In a nutshell, Human Resource Machine is an introduction to programming logic. You are tasked with creating autonomous instructions for your corporate slave/minion to follow such that he/she can complete various mundane tasks. These instructions come in the form of copy and paste commands, loops (called jumps), addition and subtraction operations, and more. There is no prior programmer experience required, as the game does a great job of slowing introducing its various concepts and gives the player tons of feedback along the way.
For those who are a little more familiar with programming, each stage has optimization challenges that ask you to find solutions with either the fewest commands or the shortest number of steps. On top of that, there are optional challenge stages that are much more advanced than their main-game counterparts.
I had a very mild exposure to programming prior to this game, so I fall more into the "new person interested in programming" category. For someone like that, I believe that Human Resource Machine is a great, fun and intuitive introduction. While starting out very basic, HRM's puzzles become extremely challenging and encourage you to think creatively to solve a variety of problems. This game actually gave me a new appreciation for programming, as even the simplest of tasks can require a ton of steps. Defintely not a game for everyone, but if you're at all interested in getting into programming, this is a great start!

In this game you are trying to get from one side of a map to the other by almost any means necessary (sneak, kill, or distract). Along the way you pick up coins to restock equipment or upgrade your bag/quiver. Additionally, you want to collect rubies that a crow/raven has dropped (This will add to your end of level score). Your end of level score will be judged to determine what medal you earned for that level. The medal earned determines how much xp you get. This xp can be used to slightly increase character traits (there is a max for each stat).
PROS
=> Puzzle like game play
=> easy controls
=> decent combat system
CONS:
=> short game
=> some levels force a kill or two to prevent a full pacifism play through
=> sometimes feels a little too easy
Explanation of combat system:
there are 3 modes while you are travelling  in a level; there is undetected, curious/timewarp, and detected.
UNDETECTED:
=> you are free to move about however you please
=> enemies move at set intervals (some are pathed, some are not)
=> any action can be completed at this time
CURIOUS/TIMEWARP:
=> during this phase you start combat/interactions
=> You have 3 actions (choices between movement, kill, shoot) before it becomes the enemies turn (you can use water/timewarp to refill the action gauge)
=> during this time if you walk into a red zone or do certain actions (breaking pots, shooting an enemy) you will attrack the intrigue of enemies. when your turn stops they have 3 turns to find you and will use that last spot as last known point.
this turn will go back and forth until either A) they reach the spot and get no further clues to your location or B) they are dead. After this the game will reset back to undetected
DETECTED:
=> you were spotted in a red zone (vision zone) of an enemy
=> THEY start combat phase (this plays out identically to Curious/timewarp. they just start instead of you).
A very well crafted, fun casual/puzzle game. Highly recommended!!!

I’ve never seen the TV series “Lost,” but from what I’ve heard about it, if I had randomly just picked it up in the fifth season – that’s about how I’d feel when starting out in Boss 101.  It’s not necessarily that the story is elaborate or that the game is complex, it’s just that so much is thrown at you so quickly that it is thoroughly overwhelming.  But once you get your bearings and navigate through all of the vibrant colors, it starts to be a bit more approachable.

At its core, Boss 101 is a boss rush shoot ‘em up styled game that has you taking control of a kid who befriends a robotic jetpack and uses it along with a variety of weapons to smash the robotic overlords that have taken over the planet and broken the moon in half for some reason.  That’s about as straightforward as I can make it.  Before Cuphead, I may have turned away from boss rush games like this, but that game proved to me that there’s some merit in their design.  Much like Cuphead, it does allow the player to drop in and out of the game with short notice and without any problems.  It can also be similarly rewarding as beating bosses is ingrained in any gamer as a triumphant moment.  The thing that makes this so much different from other boss rush games, however, is that this seems like it’s only a portion of the game rather than the main focus.
The first moments in the game put you on a path with an informative tutorial that feels somewhat longer than it actually is. You’re bombarded with views of the main base and all of its quirky little features that include many dialogue options, mini games, and other things that I have a hard time classifying like pet selection and just plain flying a kite.  Boss 101 seems work hard to establish a narrative in all of the chaos that is presented to you up front, and what it does convey is a very light hearted affair that is full of funny lines and movie references at every turn.  It puts this in front of you from the onset and doesn’t seem to trail off at any point.  It keeps the game endearing while it melts your brain with sensory overload.
There are many things that can overwhelm you in Boss 101.  One of the most obvious things is the full palette of colors and movement that fills nearly every screen.  At any given moment, there could be dozens of things moving around the screen, exploding, shooting, or just whizzing by.  After some time it becomes a bit easier to focus on the foreground and the important parts, but it’s truly a visual spectacle.  Continuing in the realm of excess, you have a wide collection of weapons to buy and upgrade, a half dozen or so skills to be upgraded such as health and main machine gun damage, and nearly 300 ‘hats’ (costumes) that can be purchased and worn.  These hats are both cosmetic and provide stat bonuses of various sorts like lessening certain types of damage or increasing your damage.  It’s also possible to separate your cosmetic appearance from the one represented by the stats of a hat, resolving something that often frustrates more fashion-focused RPG players.   If that wasn’t enough to get your head spinning, when it comes to the actual boss fights, you’re required to smack a randomize button that puts together a twisted collection of parts into a ‘boss’ that has a long list of stats that make it easier or more difficult.  It may be weak or strong to a certain type of weapon, or use a particular weapon/damage type.  All of these things are meant to be matched up with your loadout in a way that is beneficial to you and of course gives you the largest reward.  Yet here is where I found my biggest issue with the game.
Being so thoroughly overwhelmed by everything in front of me, I eventually stumbled in to the boss fights figuring I’d get my butt kicked a few times, but to my surprise I just sort of breezed through.   I got stuck for a little bit, but once I got my upgrades in front of the difficulty curve, I sort of zoned out and breezed through a bunch of levels without even trying to randomize myself an advantageous boss fight.  I just used the base machine gun and blasted away dodging as much as I could.   I didn't expect this to be the entire game though, as I had already maxed out the majority of my skills fairly early on, but it seemed as long as I didn't go up against a boss that had a resistance to machine guns, it stayed relatively easy.  That is, until the final boss battle where I finally had to equip myself properly to win.  However, it is odd to me in any game when the difficulty level seems to be something that the players have to establish dynamically for themselves.  Not that I am against selecting a difficulty level, but I’m one of those people that 90% of the time just goes for the suggested difficulty and hopes that the game is balanced for that.  It just seemed like after a while I was on cruise control to get the next little bits of the story handed to me rather than being challenged by the gameplay.
You’re probably reading all of this and wondering why I still recommend this game.  It’s actually pretty easy for me to get a sense for quality in Boss 101.  There’s so much going on but as you dig through it and set it out in its respective pieces - nothing is really bad on its own.  It just feels so muddled with everything in one game that I question how it is going to appeal to new players not committed to enjoying a mellow story with plenty of wholesome moments.  I actually spent a fair bit of time starting out just playing the in game arcade minigames, which is odd because they’re so functional despite only being a minor sidenote compared to everything else.  At the end of the day though, you’re going to have to be a fan of a more casual game than you’d expect from a shoot ‘em up and one that you’re going to have to get used to before it really appeals to you.  I just hope that the developers try to focus on making the whole experience more cohesive and make it more worthwhile to face off against the walls of stats both for the player and the bosses.  If the the gameplay centered more around dynamically equipping yourself to beat bosses, it might make the central gameplay loop more enticing and make the game a longer run.

I don’t write a whole lot of reviews, and usually it’s for strategy or roguelike type games. Schmups, well… I’m actually quite terrible at that kind of games. Too fast. I’m getting old, I guess. But this… this is rare fun. Fun enough to pull me out of my comfort zone and have me play something that I usually stay away from.
Boss 101 is one of the most addictive game that I’ve played in recent memory. It’s lovingly crafted and brimming with content. It’s a game that rewards you for playing it, every chance it gets: with unlocks, and weapons, and pets, and hats, and mini-games, and a gameplay that just feels right. The humor is spot on, well-done and unpresumptuous – it doesn’t hit you on the head while screaming in you ears "Aint’t I funny?". The graphics are nice, detailed, but still very crisp – you’re never going to wonder at what exactly you’re looking at.
It’s just an enjoyable, ingenious, well-crafted game. Boss 101 makes me happy, as simplistic as this may sound. It does its own thing, in its own way, and it succeeds at it very well.

I admit I haven't played the game for long but i've done a dozens n dozens of matches and the game itself is quite fun and interesting.
You mainly have a deck consisting of 15 max cards and as you play a match with your deck, you hold 5 cards max in your hand, placing cards by turn on a 3x3 grid.
Your deck can be tweaked and changed before every match, checking what cards you want to include or use. The beauty of these cards is that they are upgradeable, being able to make them more powerful as you continue playing. The cards have 4 values, one per side [left, top, right, bottom]. They also have a specific role that defines which other cards or values they can attack. Some have skills like swapping, boosting and such aswell. All this offers a high variety of options making the deck building and gaming quite interesting and strategic.
You can also find new cards from loot boxes after you finish a match. So far i've seen three kinds of lootboxes; common, uncommon and rare.
[Cons] The main downside I found with this game were infact the loot boxes. After every match you get a lootbox and that is quite interesting. The problem is to open the lootbox, according to the rarity, there is a cooldown. The most common lootbox has a 3 hr cool down. Uncommon has a 12 hour cooldown and the rare lootbox has an 18 hour cooldown.
What made it feel even worse was that you can't have multiple boxes on cooldown and even more worse, you can only hold 4 lootboxes at the same time.
So after 4 won matches, which wouldn't take that much time to win, you can't win more lootboxes until you open one that you have. Personally when i tried to open the first lootbox and continued to fill all 4 spots, by the time i was done, the first lootbox still had a 2 hr 40 min cooldown, and that was to open only one box. I won other matches to confirm that you can't get any more than 4 lootboxes or one thing that saddened me was that you can't swap lootboxes. So if you have 4 common lootboxes, you're stuck with them and can't win other matches to get better boxes.
There are also 2 other types of loot boxes given for "free" by the game. One is free to open after an 8 hr cooldown; most time it contains normal loot. The other one becomes available to open every 24 hrs and even then, to be able to open it, you need to get 5 new wins; this one usually has much better loot.
With all this said, I have to say that the "loot" restriction is mostly felt only in the beginning as you're trying to learn the game. In the beginning it was a bit disappointing to me cause i couldnt open them immediately for new cards to tweak my deck. I believe something in regards to this should be done as it makes a player easily shy away from the game, probably explaining why so far the game has so many mixed reviews. This is eventually not felt anymore as you start to balance when to open loot boxes and such. Definitely should give the game a couple of tries before dropping it.
I don't know if devs read this but as suggestion,
> Cooldowns should be a bit reduced as they are heavily felt in the beginning.
> Allowing multiple cooldowns would be more optimal. I feel like this should still be restricted on some levels so maybe include limited cooldowns according to the type of lootbox you decide to open [common, uncommon, rare]
> Adding more lootboxes slots would be better too as 4 feels a bit too few.
> Add more "condition" lootboxes like the 24 hour one. That 5-wins condition to open that loot box made it feel like an actual reward to work for.

Deadcore is a very unique game, but if i had to compare it to something, it would most likely be Portal franchise.
In essence, it is a very, very difficult and demanding first-person platformer based on combinations of few monumental platforming skills - double jump and dash. You also use a weapon, but game involves very little combat, as your enemies are just mechanical traps which the weapon disables for a brief moment. Game also features some mind-bending gravity shifting & jump-pad mechanics, which only add to the overall flavor of super tough experience.
You have to keep in mind - this game was designed with speed-running in mind. Given, i beat the game in 8 hours and my actual run time not taking into account all trial-and-error was 4:11 hours, you can see how much repetition can the game require from someone with not that decent hand-eye coordination. However, with perserverance you can definitely beat it and the pay-off, while confusing, in the end is worth it. Despite all the frustration, i do see it as a great, unique gaming experience and i do recommend it you try it.
+ Graphics - very, very cool and in places (especially epilogue level) breathtaking.
+ Level design - though some checkpoints are too scarcely placed it is manageable.
+ Sound design - very good, all actions you perform give adequate feedback and add to the mysterious sci-fi atmosphere.
+ Performance - first i thought it wasn't that great, but it was, turns out my integrated and dedicated GPUs were fighting about this game. However there are few notable locations in game where the overwhelming amount of enemy-trap thingies and visual filters murder the fps. That does not hinder game progress however.
+- Story - depends on how you look at it, there are logs scattered across the levels that tell the lore, but i did not find the story to be a significant part of the game. I will, however, look up all the possible endings cause i don't believe i can achieve them myself.
- Music - i personally didn't like that drum & bass here at all and found it a little unfitting, but perhaps my slow pace had something to do with that.
Overall score - 9/10. A great purchase, definitely not only on sale price. For a completionist there's more than enough collectible hunting and time trials.

Great return to form. Probably my favourite Assassin's Creed since II.
Definitly the best world they have built to date. It is amazing what they could do with a desert. It is really facinating seeing ancient Egypt in almost all its glory. The time frame is also a great choice, seeing the worlds of Egypt, Greece and Rome coming together. I really wish they added the codex that they had in previous games to this world, as it just lead me to hours of wikipedia articles. Having that in game as you discover locations would have been great. Truely a facinating time.
That does bring me to the first gripe I have with the game: it does not make full use of this world they have created. They have this amazing transitional period. Remember that more time has past between the establishment of the Pyramids and Cleopatra's reign, than between her time and modern time. The Pyramids were more ancient to them than they (Jesus included) are to us. However, it doesn't form much more than a back drop. Very little of it is explored in the story and the characters. You also have all these facinating people, like Cleopatra and Caesar who are really generic and by-the-numbers in the way they are written into the story. They just brush over all this history for a very cliche revenge/romance plot.
The story is not bad. There are some great moments, a few which are quite emotional, but it could have been so much better.
Moving over to the side quest storylines, they are not much better. Most are just your standard fetch quests and bandit camps. They tried to create small unique stories for each one, but they just felt like a poor man's Witcher. They even tried creating a world of grey, but they were not very well executed. However, this is where much of the world building takes place. Some missions are short and fun, but many can be a slog.
Speaking of the side quests, they highlight one of the weekest points in the game, some of the voice acting. The VO in the main story as well as with the established characters are great. Some of the NPC's and minor side characters are pretty atrocious, however. They have these very poor Egyptian and Greek accents and the delievery is sometimes way out of place. There is one old female actress that plays a few characters. She speaks so slowly and her cadence is incredibly staggered that it is actually painful to listen to her. However, this is just a minor gripe. Given the scale of the game, most of the characters are perfectly fine.
Combat is much improved over previous games. It a lot more flushed out and no longer the QTE dodging sequence of ther previus games. It is nothing spectacular, again something similar to what the Witcher is like.
Otherwise, everything is really great. I hate grinding through large open world games doing the same thing over and over again, but there is something about this world that keeps me coming backl

This game is the first I've played that feels like a real life escape room. I considered the puzzles 40% cakewalk and 60% "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ how the ♥♥♥♥ do I get out of here? I'm so screwed." Great puzzles!
This game is a legitimate challenge. I was able to figure out most of the puzzles on my own, but I needed assistance on a few, and honestly, I still don't know some of the answers (the process of elimination got me through a couple of them).
The final puzzle is a bit of a letdown, but it may be due to the language barrier. The English translation is a bit misleading, but I was able to determine the correct answer regardless - I just didn't feel confident in my answer.
Overall, this game is outstanding, despite some of its noted flaws. If you love escape rooms, get a group of people (2-4, I'd say), buy this game, and spend an evening playing through it together. If I could erase my memory and go back to play it again, that's what I would have done.
If anything, add in a hint system to give the player a nudge in the right direction. That would make it a little bit more like many escape rooms (in America, at least), where limited hints are provided. Then again, the discussion boards on Steam should be enough to provide the helpful push to complete each challenge, so that isn't really a necessity.

I'll just put the bottom line good and bad out there from what i've seen so far.

As always with these types of games it is best experienced with headphones in the dark.
The good.
Dark creepy atmosphere that is easy to get drawn into.
Excellent lighting effects.
Jump scares abound.
Easy to learn and use controls that remind you of amnesia.
Interesting story that is told through random flashbacks newspaper articles and some weird old dude talking over the phone.
Ghosts and shadows will definately make you jump out of your skin.
Pretty good quality graphics.
Reasonably priced game at 15$ Though I was smart and preordered. Try to get it for less than 10$ if you can.
The bad.
Persistant choppy lag that didn't go away even after I lowered the graphics setting to damn near mid 2000s era quality. This hindered me greatly and caused me no end of doom and frustration, Others are having the same issues as well I may add, this problem MUST be fixed as it is causing some poor souls' games to crash in bad cases.
Recycled enviroments that while randomly generated just don't fit together properly. One second I was in an insane asylum then a morgue then a prison cell block then back to an asylum. They could fix this by having certain areas only spawn around other areas that match them, Then we wouldn't have the confusing unrealistic layouts and everything would flow together seamlessly and make this feel like a true full on retail game.
Jump scares abound. Hey, This crap has been done to death if you like it more power to you but most people are tired of this recycled predictable scare tactic. "Penumbra 1-2&3, amnesia 1&2,Outlast, and a whole slew of other games not to mention a few more that are STILL being developed all have already done it." (PS buy penumbra and amnesia if you haven't already. Totally worth it.) and while the ambiance IS creepy the jumpscare to ambiance ratio is a bit uneven leading to you just being annoyed by damn ghosts trying to kill you constantly.
Shadows that chase you endlessly. It is KINDA difficult to get♥♥♥♥♥♥done and find all the clues you need to get through the game when the same freaking ghost appears every single time your freaking flare goes out causing you to lose health or die almost instantly. It makes exploring and finding what you MUST have to progress through the game nearly impossible and makes you not want to play it again. This must be fixed as well, I actually had to quit my game because I couldn't advance.
Repetitive linear gameplay dispite the randomly generated maps. Do NOT let their talk of randomly generated maps fool you into think that this game will constantly be a new adventure, You will STILL be hunting for the SAME objects in the SAME areas and the only thing that will be different is the layout. Nothing else changes and you still have to find 6 objects to make an object appear that allows you to proceed to the next area where you do the same exact thing. It is the very definition of Tedious.
IN CONCLUSION.
The game would function PERFECTLY if it were not for the lag as that was the only technical issue I personally have had and it seems to be the big issue with the game itself as many others have the same problem. While pretty to look at the quality of the graphics don't mean anything if the game is so full of lag that everything is constantly fading in and out of focus or glitching out! The game flow is obstructed by random out of place enviroments that just don't fit in which makes the game feel unrealistic which can make it hard to put yourself into the game if you are a fan of attention to detail. There are too many jump scares and not enough buildup to get to those scares which makes most of them in turn, cheap, repetitive, and predictable.
The game at it's core is tedious at best and a never ending array of poorly placed areas won't change that and if the developers thought it would distract people from their lazy game design they are dead wrong. As you play this game you will notice that it is nothing more than a mere knockoff of other better indie games, This one will not be worth your time until it is patched and hopefully updated and offered at a reduced price. get it for less than 9$ if you can as it may not even work at all for you. I give this game an A for effort but a D for execution, With a little more polishing this game will be a buyable and enjoyable game but until then I say steer clear and force the developers to put a little more effort into the game to encourage others to buy it. I give it a 2.5 out of 5.

Having just finished Daylight a couple minutes ago, it's still fresh in my mind. I beat it in one sitting in the span of about 80-ish minutes. I can't exactly say it was what I expected, but I don't exactly know what I expected.
First off, the game is quiet repetitive. Each area of the game requires you to collect about six "Remnants" which if you've played Slender you can just call "Pages" Once you've gotten all of the Remnants you then must go find a "Sigil" which is a haunted item that unlocks the next area. Each area begins with a small transition stage where a lot of story related notes are. This formula persists throughout the entire game and can get dull after a while.
The game's backstory is told mostly by notes and the Remnants you collect around the level, it isn't too much. Mainly just exposition about the hospital, what happened there, and how it was shut down. While the main storyline in the game is almost invisible. The game doesn't tell you why you're there and the only reason I know why is from a developer interview with TotalBiscuit where it was mentioned. But other than that you pretty much walk through the hospital and listen to the voices of two people. Yourself, who's only comments usually consists of "Is someone in there?" Or "Oh god! Make it stop!", and the... Other person, who talks to the main character (Sarah) throughout her quest. I don't believe the game ever tells you who he is or how the hell he's talking to you in the first place. I'm assuming it's through the phone but I'm not sure. The ending is... Okay. Don't expect it to wow you in any way and expect to get a little whiplash from it's sudden climax. It felt like they were rushing to clear things up, explain it all, and end the game right then and there.
The horror aspect isn't anything special, but it's well done. I jumped out of my seat quite a few times upon encountering the ghost. Named "Shadows" by the game. You're only way to fight them off are using the flares, which don't look as good in-game as they did in the demos with the incredibly violent, dark shadows. In the actual game their shadows aren't as defined and it's pretty much just a brighter glowstick that burns ghosts. The glowsticks act as the game's "Help me" button. Using a glowstick reveals key items such as containers that might contain items and key items. (Mainly containers though.) As well as providing a decent amount of light. The ghosts are scary enough, but there is something I wanted to mention down below.
Okay, so this game is VERY inconstant with some of it's gameplay demos before release, mainly in the aspect of the enemy's appearance. Some show them as a floating green monster with a big gaping mouth and long limbs, but in reality the game's enemy is... Well, there isn't really much to spoil. If you've seen a creepy ghost lady in a horror movie, then you've seen the Daylight monster. It's rather unoriginal. It looks cool, don't get me wrong, but it's unoriginal. While the green monster didn't look too scary, if they gave it a better design it would have been really cool to see. As I also mentioned before, the flare's don't look like they advertised in some gameplay demos, casting large, jagged dynamic shadows across the area? No, not really. It just creates a large, bright red glow. I wouldn't label it as false advertising, as later trailers showed the scary woman ghost. It's just confusing.
My rating of Daylight would be about in the 6/10 for you people who like that sort of rating. It's a fun game to play while it lasts, and the procedural generation gives it some replay value, but it's rather slow and repetitive with a story which isn't too interesting. Collectibles may be another reason to replay it, however for some reason you can't reread collected notes unless they were Remnants. It's got it's scary moments, and for the price it isn't too bad. I happened to get it for free from a giveaway from a Youtube channel. InstinctiveHDGaming. Go check him out, he's pretty interesting.
But enough advertisements, I'm going to go and see if I can rack up enough money for the new Outlast DLC, hopefully that can satisfy my horror cravings.

Wow...I can't even. I started playing Dune 2 with my mom. I remember when Command and Conquer was new - and I was so upset! As upset as a 4-5 year old can get, anyway. I wanted more Dune. I got C&C
I opened up the first GDI mission to an actual guy, video of an actual dude talking to me, telling me about the mission. It was the first time I'd ever heard actual sound effects and music, the first time I'd seen video in the game. The videos were memorable, the characters were brilliantly cheesy. I absolutely loved the series. Then EA killed it off brutally, ending any hope of a continuation of a series my parents, my brother, and I all played and loved.
I saw Petroglyph form years ago, and I'd been hoping for a reboot of that same zany spark that made the C&C series so great. When a friend pointed this game out to me mid-semester I was strapped for cash. I saw the Petroglyph name on it and bought it at the cost of skipping several meals. I didn't play it until recently.
I got my younger brother to buy it, we opened it up. The title screen came on. It was definitely Frank Klepacki's style - we both got psyched. We opened up the coop campaign screen. I saw that there was a brief mission description on each map - and that they were all unlocked - but I thought nothing of it. We hit the 'start button' and...
Nothing. No video briefing.
Okay. So we decide to play. We'd selected 'normal' because we're both RTS veterans. We built our harvesters and noticed something else...resources are limited and non-regenerating.
I clicked around several times. Why weren't my infantry acknowledging me? No "Yes sir!" or even distinct sound effects, no 'buzz' like the Scrin nor even a beeping classic Dune 2 style.
About 5 minutes in, we get rushed by the AI, who brings a continuous stream of vehicles and multiple different types of infantry into the first mission. We get destroyed - we have no vehicles ourselves and we were told not to build rocket infantry for the first 'bonus objective', which I interpretted to mean something like bonus units - Emperor: Battle For Dune style - or something of the like.
Wow. So we go again. The AI shifts strategies. They're silent for most of the first part of the mission and then BAM a massive amount of them hit all at once. Okay. We restart one more time.
This time we decide to rush the AI. I decide to try an old RA2-era style economic choke hold and sneak my troops down a route the AI is loathe to use. I get my army sitting around waiting for their harvesters and boom. Erase their harvester from existence.
Then another one comes within half a minute. And another. Then another. Endlessly. This wouldn't be a problem except for the harvesters knocking down infantry en masse and the infantry tending to chase the harvesters, putting them directly in their path. Fantastic. So I send enough infantry down to just zap the harvesters from existence for a bit.
The AI doesn't respond to that. They let me sit there and run them completely out of resources. They run a massive army back and forth between a pre-set rally point in the first map (for player 2, check the NW corner) and leave me to my own devices.
In the next several missions we noticed a pattern: We lost the ability to produce certain units crucial to countering the AI. For example, one mission gives us infantry and transport helicopters. The AI comes in with artillery, anti-air and anti-ground helicopters.
It ends up being one of the most obnoxious, boring, bland RTSes we've ever played.
Also, for the co-op campaign, it's all one faction. The AI have the exact same roster you do - they just get much more of it.
TL;DR:
-This game has less storyline than Dune 2 from the early 90s/MS-DOS era.
-This game has less unit variety among factions than Dune 2.
-This game has less map variety than Dune 2.
-This game has less engaging music than Dune 2.
-This game has no video briefings, no real briefings, no dynamic events in map ("Commander, NOD forces are bringing in the pain from the northeast. Battlefield expanded"), no regenerative resources. It's like if Tiberian Dawn was stripped of its personality and made into an e-sport.
Verdict:
-You might be better served by playing C&C 4 for a co-op RTS campaign than this.
-You'll definitely enjoy Dawn of War 2's co-op campaigns better than this.
-The DoW series is MUCH more enjoyable than this, now that I mention it.
-Skip this. Petroglyph's made up of a team that can do and has done FAR better than this.
Fun game but not enough people play it. 8-bit hordes may resolve that problem.

Well, it is a jigsaw game and it is actually pretty good at what it stands.
It does have some problems, though. The music can be pretty repetitive and instead of relaxing it can actually make you pretty sick of it after some time playing the game (You can turn it off, of course, so it's not that great of a problem). It is also pretty hard to see the pieces when they're flowing along the river (where all the to-play pieces are at), since it is smaller and they get one over the other.
Also, when you pick a piece, it usually picks not the piece that you're aiming at, but instead another random piece (after some thoughts, I think it actually picks the piece that goes closer at the top of the puzzle, although it actually changed with some puzzles).
But if you like jigsaw puzzles it can be fun for a while. Also, you can leave the game open and return to it from time to time, like a real jigsaw.

There are some minor technical issues (like volume control bugging and piece fishing being annoying at times).
But other than that the game is fun, beautiful and relaxing.
(I only wish you'd be able to turn off the music but keep the sound effects on).
Absolutely recommended.

In the immortal words of IGN "Like Skyrim with puzzles".
But seriously now, it's freaking awesome. I mean who doesn't like a good jigsaw puzzle? This is just it, only in digital edition. As the title says, this is about Japan so you get pictures of various motives and places from Japan to puzzle out. On one side this is somewhat easier than normal jigsaw since you can get lucky and randomly hit the right place for your piece which is then locked there. On the other, this adds another dimension to normal game by having you pick floating pieces of the puzzle from the water. With that we get to the only real problem the game has. Said picking of the floating pieces flat-out sucks in the latter puzzles. You will see the piece you want, you will click on it, and you'll get another, seemingly random, piece. It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I got around it by moving some of the pieces to the table, that reduces the number of them in the water which then pretty much solves the problem. Of course it's not perfect since you'll then have a mess on the table but it worked for me. That said i was afraid when i got to the last picture, which is a behemoth of the 350 pieces, that i will never solve it due to the picking shenanigans but for some reason it worked perfectly there. How that is even possible is beyond me.
All in all i had a great 10 hours with it, even if it was frustrating at times, and i will gladly recommend it to anyone.  Especially if you can get in on a discount for a buck or two.

The game starts out with big, simple pieces so you can solve the puzzles easily, as well as help you get started with how the game is played. As you move on to the next level, the pieces get smaller as well as having to deal with more pieces at one time.
My only real complaint is that you can't put pieces together to make a whole piece and then try to place that whole piece in the spot it belongs. You have to "know" where each piece goes on the board. So the point is you have to find where the piece goes on the board without being able to make clusters of pieces.
Overall a very good idea for people who are into "puzzle" games. Think about it, when you buy this, you get  40 puzzle boards to complete. Each board you pass gets harder to solve because the pieces get smaller. Versus getting a "REAL" puzzle, you can't lose pieces, and you can't lose the game.

It's like "What if Phoenix Wright had GOOD writing?"
Really excellent visual novel game with a charming woodcut art style and multiple endings.  Would definitely recommend, especially if you're a fan of Phoenix Wright.

Positives:
Great music, great art, great story. The sense of humor is on point, as is the sense of drama. It's technically possible to miss key evidence for each case, but in practice you're likely to get the important things and do well enough anyway.
Negatives:
It's pretty short for the price tag, even after grabbing all the endings. It also lacks a few of the convenience features most VNs have(particularly skipping through previously-seen dialogue & being able to scroll back through recent dialogue).
On the whole I'd say it's worth it, especially if you can pick it up on sale.

First off, I want to say I had an absolute blast with this game. I loved playing with my friends and voicing all the characters with them. It was funny, tense, and unexpectedly sweet at times. It truly is one of the most fun games I've played in a long while.
I also like that you could fail a case, but still continue on with the story. And that bomb at the end of the first case? DAMN!
Unfortunately, the endings did not do the rest of the game justice. Don't get me wrong Act 4s A-C were also great, in their own way, but they all just... end. It feels like the writers just wanted to wrap up the game they had. So they cut off right after the climax with:
The lovely side characters you meet? Depending on what route you are on, you never meet them again. Wanna know the motives and backstories of the killer Inspector Volerti has been referencing this whole time? Too bad! Wham. Bam. Reveal.
Act 4 has great build up, which could've lent itself to great, dramatic moments but it feels like as soon as that point is reached the game ends.
Also, the game gives you a feel of having a much more complex mechanic than it actually does.
The only case that really matters is at the end of Act 3.
All in all, I love the game but it deserved better endings.

As someone who has spent $10 on a game where you date birds as a Japanese school girl whilst battling a world ending cult, I was expecting the same tone from Aviary Attorney. At first during the first case's investigation, it seemed like it but with more mystery and drama rather than nonstop bird antics.
Immediately, I knew I was getting myself into something much more in-depth and emotional and so far I am extremely satisfied with the game.
Overall, I enjoyed the game with its memorable cast, witty humor, and well-crafted story. I can see myself playing it again and again just to read any text and watch any scenes i potentially missed.

A wonderful visual novel with delightful visuals and music. Likeable characters and amusing dialogue bring together the several acts, keeping me engaged from start to finish. If you enjoy light hearted humour and puns then there will be no shortage of chuckles for you in Aviary Attorney.
I do have a few gripes. Namely: that you cannot go back to view previously read dialogue; that the third act hinges heavily upon a preset path of strict conditions to achieve the best ending; and that the fourth act ends up being extremely linear regardless of which path you end up in after the third act. The fourth act is less about the cases than the narrative, which is fine; but it felt me leaving a little deflated hoping for a real test of the attorney's lawyering skills and instead receiving a large amount of non-interactive character drama.
There is also one particular scene in the third act where the background art takes a horrible nosedive in quality during one of the most dramatic moments in the game. I understand there is only so much of Grandville's art to use for the narrative, but it clearly stands out amongst the masterpieces throughout the rest of the game.
With that said, the story was engaging regardless and though the game closes itself off in the latter half it was an enjoyable experience nonetheless. Maybe wait for a sale if you don't think 5-7 hours of lawyer drama is worth the asking price.

Aviary Attourney is a witty game heavily inspired by the Phoenix Wright series. Now gameplay wise, it's little more than a visual novel, lifting a lot of the "deductive" option choices from Phoenix Wright and leaving out much of the DS gimmick gameplay such as speaking into the console's microphone or blowing on the senser. Despite that, Aviary Attourney really holds up as an indie game of the genre because of its cleverly written plot that balances Phoenix-y humor with some surprisingly grounded themes of morality backed by some heavy outcomes based on your choices. The plot takes place in a semi-parodic version of 1848 France (so if the "touty, prissy Frenchy" setting is not your cup of tea, this game is not going to change anything) where everyone is some form of anthropomorphic Frenchman/woman. You lead a (Phoenix-y familiar) defense attourney trying to make a buck during a time when revolution is but a bulletshot away from erupting. Your decisions will determine the course of history in ths world and this is one of those few games where you decisions REALLY matter. It's perhaps the only game I've ever played that I felt absolutely compelled to play through every single ending and felt thoroughly rewarded for doing so. The devs have really gone through and made sure every single ending contributes heavily to the world building and subplot mysteries of this game. And for that, I found this game absolutely charming.
That being said...there are some technical issues. As of writing, the devs are working hard to fix a number of bugs for DRM free release. But when I played through the game, I had the game black-screen-crash on me about 5 times trying to get through a chapter. And there are few things to really dampen the experience of a mystery based visual novel type game than playing through the exact same plot drop five times. So bugs do exist and I don't know when they'll be fixed, but they definitely hurt the experience.
But...soon as those are fixed I thoroughly recommend this game for people who want a light-hearted game of animals in a pompous France trying to make a living even if it means the violent death of those who stand in your way. Or maybe not? That's up to you!

Are you looking for exciting gameplay? Deep narrative? A deeply rewarding experience?
Then look elsewhere.
Timberman is a cheap arcade title, that while good, is meant for short bursts of playtime.
Gameplay is simple; use the left and right arrow keys to cut down the tree on either its left or right side. As the tree comes down, so do branches and you must move to avoid getting hit by them as you chop. A stamina bar that constantly drains means you can't do this slowly either. The fun is trying to keep up a good pace without knocking yourself out.
This is supported by a nifty looping 8-big track, and a wide variety of unlockable characters to keep things fresh. Don't like the lumberjack? Unlock a mummy, a jack o'lantern, or versions of the Hulk, Bruce Lee or Freddy Krueger (under different names of course).
Oh, and there is also online multiplayer were you compete to see who can cut the most wood or last the longest in a set of rounds.
The game is worth the cost just to have a little game when you need to kill a few minutes or just want to goof off and not play anything serious. Super solid wood cutting recommendation.

FF8's Triple Triad, but much expanded and with some twists.

No game modes, no diversity.
No single player/PvE.
No rewards for losing.
Reward for winning are locked behind a timer, with limited "inventory slots", barring your progress in prolonged sessions.

World of Final Fantasy is an JRPG that blends a collection mechanic like Pokemon with a more depth combat system like Final Fantasy X. Additionally, the art style creates a unique chibi-like blend into the mix while retainingd serious tones throughout the whole experience.
While on paper it seems like a solid idea, the execution is far from perfect.
I haven't played the original PS4 version, but there are some major things that can be backtracked to the fact that this is a ported game.
This is an category by itself because of how different the Japanese and the English Dubs are and how different the animation is.
Unlike most Final Fantasy games, this game has a big emphasis on trial and error, which is equally satisfying and atrocious.
The combat system has one major flaw which stems from the collection mechanic. As you can only have your 2 main characters + 4 monsters in your party, you are very limited in your choice of skills to actually use. This leads to a certain default party which can deal with most threads. Only after roughly 20 hours in the game I had to use a different setup because of a boss. Before that I could simply beat everything without changing anything. After changing my team to certain elemental resistances I could beat the boss and progress.
Many people would probably dislike this trial and error method, but I wished for more of those (some of them come later in the story, too). The satisfaction of beating the bosses with the adjusted setup is far stronger than the distress of the failure of the default setup.
Other than that flaw, the combat system (I played on Wait-Mode) is very similar to Final Fantasy X with a round based combat, based on your Agility Attribute. But WOFF has less depth in the execution aspect. Almost every single boss is simply beaten by preparation or default tactics. But this doesn't mean that the combat system is not enganging. It's far the opposite. The execution of a prepared plan is what makes this system work and here lies its strength.
Other Final Fantasy games (and JRPGs to that extend) rely on the power of adaption within the combat to create different scenarios to which the player has to adapt. You can rarely make changes in your group or ability setup to accommodate for different bosses. But here shines WOFF. With a strong roster of monsters with very different abilitiy-collections, almost any monsters can be used effectively somewhere somehow in the correct setup. Sadly, there are some monster (like the Black Chocochick) which simply outshine other monster in their size category by far.
In short: the story is well rounded with a good amount of fan-service and sidestories to follow. While there are some loose ends and beginnings, it is a complete story with some unexpected twists and turns.
My biggest issue with the whole game lies in the aspect of the dynamic between the three main characters.
To sum it up: We have the male main character,... I can't believe I hit max.

This game was fun, but very short. Only 17 levels... actually 15 since "The End" can't honestly count as a level and the first one is technically a tutorial.
There are plenty of ways the levels can be completed and played, which explains the abundance of achievements for this small game. But for someone who isn't necessarily interested in getting achievements and would rather just play the game (like myself), I was able to complete the game fairly quickly and without having to use too many of the items in-game.
That doesn't necessarily mean that the game was easy, however. It definitely has its challenges when it comes to fighting certain enemies, figuring out how to open different gates, and finding ways to sneak around safely. But, what takes all of that difficulty away is the fact that if/when you do die, the game just restarts you in that same room. I personally think it would be more challenging if you were put back at the beginning of the level to start all over again when you die. It would make you take your character's health more seriously.
Also, not sure if this was a problem that only I was experiencing, but anytime I exited the game it would just freeze right there at the main menu. I could not alt+tab back to my desktop and the game wouldn't do what it normally should do (just close and return me to whatever window I was on previously). I had to open task manager just to get back to my desktop. It was just a minor annoyance.
I recommend this game because despite the couple of cons it has, it was still an enjoyable short game, but I also think you should only buy it when it's on sale.

Not too sure what to write here so here's a recipe for Pancakes instead:
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it:
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

For the most part, "PIxel Puzzles:  Japan" is a really nice game.  The pictures are nice, the puzzles are fun to do, and the interface is fairly good (the flowing stream of pieces is pretty good at letting you see all the pieces over time and you don't have to rotate pieces to fit them in).  There are some problems with it, though:
- The big problem is that you can't save your game mid-puzzle.  For the smaller puzzles, that's not an issue.  But, for the later ones, you're spending several hours doing the puzzles and can't quit the game without losing your progress on that puzzle.
- The next biggest problem is that as you advance to the higher-piece puzzles, it gets harder and harder to actually pick up the pieces you're pointing at (oddly, in the puzzle with the greatest number of pieces, that problem went away -- I have no idea why).  I'd like to see the algorithm they use since it must do something like pick up every piece except the one that's being clicked on).
- Again, as you move up to the higher-piece puzzles (starting at the 153 piece ones), it starts to get difficult to see the pieces -- they're too small.
- There needs to be a pond or something where you can place pieces you've pulled from the stream.  It would also be nice if we could place pieces together in that pond and have them stick together for later placement as a unit.
- There's a "reset puzzle" stone right in the middle of the bottom margin.  It doesn't confirm that you want to reset the puzzle.  It just does it.  I lost a couple of hours of play with that once.  Also, I fail to see the use of such a button.  Why would I ever want to reset the puzzle?
- In the options, the sound level doesn't stick across sessions.  That means you have to reset it every time you fire up the game.
But, even with those problems, the game is worth it.  Recommended.

First of all i should begin by saying that I enjoy story-driven games that present you with a movie-like experience.
I have played my fair shair of Telltale games, respectively.
Aviary Attorney shares some of the principles - you explore the world, collect clues and then are able to weave them into your dialogue options.
Unlike the Telltale games however, in Aviary Attorney, your choices actually do matter. I am not saying that you'd have a myriad of options, but if for example you investigate a crime scene and miss something, that particular clue will cause a line of reasoning in court go amiss.
You start as a defense Attorney and you are thrown into pre-revolutionary Paris where you go about and question witnesses, collect clues and then try to coherently present them in court.
The story is quite enjoyable, the humour is great and the art style is rather marvellous.
If you, like me, enjoy immersion into strange worlds and stories but you can't afford the time to play through, let's say a Witcher, and you are ok with limited gameplay (in terms of player skill) then this game is definitely for you.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game - but make sure you check how much time the average player spends in this, as this is rather short (which I personally found quite pleasing).

If you like Ace Attorney, this is a good alternate take on the court system. This game takes good advantage of its setting in revolutionary France for the overarching plot and theme. The investigation portions use a time system to visit locations. During my first run of the game, it never felt like I had enough time to visit every location and collect evidence. Combined with a save system that only lets you restart at the beginning of the day, that led to a frantic tension during the quick courtroom scenes where my case wasn't strong enough to always save my client. It's a nice difference to Ace Attorney's perfect cases that always go in your favor once deus ex machina hits. As you play through Aviary Attorney, you can revisit days to make better decisions and hopefully get a better ending for you clients...and yourself.
The only cons I had with the game was that the "Save & Quit" system didnt' always work, there were no control schemes for controllers, and during repeat plays, there was no easy way to skip through text quickly. These are petty annoyances, and I still enjoyed Aviary Attorney very much. The characters, setting, plot, and mechanics are all interesting.

I really loved this game. It's great for Ace Attorney fans, and I think should be great for non-Ace Attorney fans as well. Obviously, it's a visual novel, so don't expect much gameplay.
While this game is clearly a love letter to Ace Attorney, it attempts to stand out on its own too, and I believe it does that really well. The art style is really interesting, and really nice. The music is appropriate to the art style as well and gives the whole game a really nice atmosphere.
The dialogue is mostly what you'd expect from Ace Attorney. Doesn't take itself too seriously most of the time, but from time to time it'll get there. It's mostly silly stuff that you can expect. There's a couple references I don't totally like (Most are references to Ace Attorney, but I find that's acceptable considering the whole game is meant to be a love-letter to it.) but the references are very very few and mostly harmless.
Where as Modern Ace Attorney games are absolutely filled to the brim with horrible filler and unskippable flashbacks, I actually wish this game had a bit more. I think this game was desperately in need of a third case before the final one to really get a sense of the game and the characters in it, and honestly, I just wanted more stuff in general.
The first two cases are probably the best, as they're a lot shorter and a lot more focused. The last case isn't bad by any means, but it can get a bit off track at times, and due to there being multiple endings, it might have caused some other endings to feel less fleshed out and finished. It's still a great time, however. Like I said, the only real con with this game, I just wish there was more.
One last very slight issue, there's not exactly a fast forward button. towards the end, you'll be wanting to see the different endings, because they are quite different and a bit lengthy, but there's no fast forward button. It's easy enough to click through everything rapidly, BUT it woulda been nice to just have a fast forward button either way. Like I said, very slight issue.
Anyway, for 15 bucks, I'd say it's very worth it for a nice cozy visual novel. I got about 9 hours of it, and got all the endings, so I'd say that's pretty decent. I believe this game only goes on sale about once a year and its only 5 dollars off, so its up to you if you want to wait for it or not, but I think 15 is a great price.
I'm really hoping for a sequel. We could certainly do with more lawyer/mystery games that isn't filled to the brim with useless filler like the new Ace Attorney games are these days.

To be blunt, this game was very, very annoying. There was very little for me to like about this game. Unline the various hidden object games from companies like Artifex Mindi, I found this game to be very tedious and difficult to follow.
The inappropriate voice acting left a great deal to be desired. Although the lead wasn't horrible, the majority of the characters were completely out of place. Since when do all people (and ghosts) in Prague speak with vague Brooklyn and generic American accents?
Just about all of the hidden object sequences required interaction with your inventory, which completely breaks the flow. More often than not, you have to leave the hidden object game to find whatever it is that you don't have in your inventory.
There were several times where I was given no indication of where I needed to go to continue with the game. Even on the easy level, you will find yourself relying on the Help/Hint button to tell you where to go because the map shows no indication.
THe game also has a serious bug where hitting the Hint button or changing to the area just left or right results in the background disappearing and going completely to black. The only way to get the background back was to go to the map and use it to enter that same room.
Additionally, there are multiple instances with a green exclamation point in an area on the map, meaning that there was something to do there; but when you press the Hint button, it tells you to LEAVE THE ROOM!!! Then, why are you telling me that there's something to do in that room?! This happens CONSTANTLY throughout the game!
The game also has no tolerance for switching to another app while it's running. I had it crash and exit multiple times when daring to briefly switch to another application.
Finally, the story is disjointed and uninteresting. Don't misunderstand me. Hidden object games rarely have deep plots and story lines that I find intriguing; however, this storyline was very difficult to follow. The voice acting and reliance on the Hint button to progress through the game did not help.
I don't understand why this game, as I write this, has a "very positive" review. It's so badly done compared to games from Aritfex Mundi and others, frustrating to navigate, hard to listen to, and has such a disjointed storyline that I ended up finishing it only to get it finished. If you must have this because you want the achievements or the trading cards, do youself a favor and wait until you can find it on a deep discount.

Tepid casual gameplay, a few frustrating bugs, crashes, and gameplay decisions (what do the jump scares near the start add??), and fanfiction level writing.  Though I think they did a surprising amount of story research, because it comes across like historical fiction rather than monster-movie fare.
Everyone has "guilty pleasure" movies, things that they only like because of the actors involved, or maybe the corny dialogue is just right, or it explores your favorite trope that few other things do.  Movies where you sit down, turn off your brain, and grab the popcorn for an hour.  This is that kind of game.
Play only if you like : Golems, Alchemical Symbology, everything containing John Dee or Emperor Rudolf II of the holy roman empire, Stories vaguely reminiscent of the tale of Anastasia, Stories where the badguys are into human sacrifice.
... Starting this review, I was going to give it a thumbs down because of the gameplay.  I guess I can't though, because I like most of those things, and stories that deal with /all of them/ are rare.  Thumbs sideways.
[edit] :  On reflection, this game does have one amazingly good gameplay mechanic, that helps you figure out what to do if you run out of steam or get confused.  The map screen has on it every room you can currently or hypothetically access, and surrounding each room are a series of nodes : one for each sub-screen where you can look at something up close.  Every one of these rooms and nodes is color coded; grey question marks for places you haven't been, yellow and red ! for places you've been and have completed or can't /currently/ do anything at, and green ! for places that you need to do something at.  You can travel around without the use of this map, and the areas you can access are small and reasonably tight so fast travel is never necessary, which means it only gives you hints if you choose to use it.  All games of this type should have that, I think; it's spoiled me terribly.

Graphics are somewhat better than average in the genre, but some meta puzzles reminds of moon logic from old adventures, kinaesthetics are unpleasant for some reason and it's easier to use fast-travel all the time, small puzzles are often randomized which is not very good idea for casual play.
It's not that bad, but steam is flooded with superior artifex mundi games, which sometimes not look as good (for my taste, i can tolerate low-poly on 2d easier than deformative animation) but always offer more cohesive though not ideal natrrative.
Great game for the price. I would highly recommend it for any hidden object adventure fan. 8/10.

Man... Giana Sisters is like half of a good game, and half a bad game.  That doesn't make it bad.  But It also doesn't make it good or great.
To start with the game is competent, It's sad how many times I have to say that on Steam, but it's true, this actually is well polished, and quite beautiful.  The loading screens are great, the interface is great.  The only negative is the setup is outside of the game, but you know what?  Minor complaint compared to others.
The game itself is quite beautiful and the game play is solid.  Not perfect but the first few levels of the game are good.  The problem I have with it is those first few levels never really feel different.
The core of the game is there's two sisters stuck in different worlds.  A light and a dark world.  In the light world things are happy, and beautiful, with the press of a button the player switches to the dark world, which is kind of a Tim Burton look at the world.  Not "evil" but "darkish".   The game relies on switching between the two worlds.  In each world the sister that's in it gets a different attack, there's a dash move that can be done in any direction, and a twirling attack in the other world.
There's different music (similar but one has an awesome electric guitar in them and other has a different melody.  The music blends perfectly when switching.  In fact all the switching mechanics are well done, and surprisingly tight.  I like the theory of the game.
There's gems in each world, as well as gems that appear in both worlds and the players can collect them with time.  I mean every mechanic is sound and everything works together for the most part.
There's however one issue I want to bring up.  Certain enemies appear to be invincible.  Ok that's what happens, but they don't look that different, so the player doesn't have a way to know they're always invincible.   Even when you switch worlds they appear differently so it looks like someone can attack them in their world while the other is invincible.  Nope for those enemies they're always invincible.  Which is annoying.
There's one other big problem with this set up.  The levels are LONG.  Not just a little a long, but it feels like at least the length of four super mario brothers levels from the original game.  It's VERY long.  This isn't the worst thing but there's 21 levels, including boss levels (Which aren't shorter).    Honestly I get bored after two or three levels, and the reason for this is that the levels are the SAME, I mean the backgrounds are similar, the enemies rarely change, and the mechanics really don't change.
Overall it's a acceptable game, but that's all it is.  It's not a great game, and it's a shame, because the setup works, if the controls were a touch tighter for a few jumps, it's be good, but the problem is there's no variety, for 10 hours you're looking at the same levels.    T

Setting sail for uncharted waters! Destination: Giana Sisters – Twisted Dreams. Full and well done controller support in a game of jumps, twirls and dashes. It also comes with a twist. OWLS! DREAMS! GET THOSE CRYSTALS GIRLS!

Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams is a jump and run platformer game. It also is in a sense an old school game. But not the old and ugly kind. Here is why:
The above thrown together gives you a very challenging (although not at first, don´t let yourself be fooled ^.^) platformer with complex and tight, precise controls. Beyond the games nod to its older sister (The original “The Great Giana Sisters” Game came out for C64 and Amiga 500 in 1987) it does a lot of new things. And it does all of it in a good, solid, cute and punky way!
Giana Sisters sounds awesome. That is because it had its new soundtrack being done by the same guy that created the original score: Chris Hülsbeck. And that Soundtrack carries the game, it is that good! The controls feel perfectly precise and smooth at the same time. They are not easy to perfect though! Challenge accepted  In general the game feels very responsive and solid. Well done!
Every Speedrunner and platforming enthusiast can find his or her heaven here. The game offers 4 different difficulties and two additional game modes: time attack and score attack.  The casual gamer, like I am one in terms of jump and runs at least, may have to resort to easy or normal difficulty to be able to beat the game. But it does feel rewarding to finally make that bossfight or reach that certain hidden Crystal you saw back there on your first run before you horribly died of spikes in the ground you overlooked. (right?!, that’s the fun in it!)

For fans of the genre it may very well be a treasure. For me, being more of a casual not so skilled platform grandpa (I played Superfrog when it was new and hot, I dabbled with the original pitfall! When I was 8 years old …so you know, my reflexes have been better back then) it is a game I will play again, sometime in the foreseeable future. Because it is fun! (with a tiny bit of “painfully hard” for me).

Great music and visuals. However, for a platform that often relies on precision to complete a puzzle it has very floaty controls. You'll often falling off ledges or running into enemies when your character doesn't stop moving like you'd expect her to.
Quite a generic plataform game... But nice art and fun to play for a while.

This game borrows a -ton- of elements from classic games.
It has the asthetics and gameplay from Donkey Kong Country 2's jungle levels while emphasizing collecting all the little macguffin gemstones like an old Rare N64 game. Your player can descend slowly like Dixie Kong or lunge forward with a lockon spinning air attack like recent Sonic games. Also you actively switch between light and dark verisons of every level with slight alterations between the two like Link to the Past. You actively change dimensions to open gates and reverse the motion of platforms while juggilng your two movement options. The atmosphere and even the music changes completely as you alternate between worlds. Pity they reuse the same song in every level. Frequent checkpoints and infinite lives reduces the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to pure challenge without wasting your time.
That said it's only slightly above mediocre. I didn't feel any connection to the characters and the levels felt really samey. My zeal to collect every gemstone hovers below zero and I feel bad for the people who went out of their way spending dozens of hours backtracking every path to find them.
No powerups other than the base sheild, no animals to ride, no projectiles, only jumping on heads.
This game is decent but there are dozens of others that outclass it.

While Mars: War Logs is not a AAA game I still enjoyed it a lot.  Enough so to go back and replay it to see the other ending.  Almost all aspects of the game scream indie meaning things like Voice acting, character animations, character customization/skills, etc., are done failry well, but not quite as polished and deep as you see in other major titles like Mass Effect  In one respect, you could almost consider it a rudimentary version of Mass Effect.  Playing through the game you'll notice these shortcomings or lack of depth in each aspect of the game, but if you can look past theses definitely enjoy the game.
To be honost I am a bit of a snob and won't touch games unless they're of AAA caliber.  Mainly because I don't have a lot of time to play games so I want to spend what time I have on worth while games.  By chance I decided to give this game a try and the first couple hours of gameplay were enough to pull me in.  The environment and setting of the game look absolutely amazing.  The devs did a great job of creating a dystopian city on mars.  I found the story quite interesting and kept me intrigued throughout most of the game.  There are some pacing issues towards the middle, but if you stick to the main quest line, you can power through through these slow points fairly quickly.
The other thing this game did well was the combat system.  I thought it was done quite well feeling very smooth and polished.  It never felt awkward or clumsy where my character was slow or didnt attack when I wanted him to.  The one thing I found to be a bit irritating was its very easy to be swarmed by a group of enemies and die.  But to be honest this serves to make it more challenging.
All in all regardless of the shortcoming I still very much enjoyed this game.  A solid 7/10
TL;DR
Great story and combat system but lacks depth in all other aspects of the game.  They are still done well so if you can look past this shortcoming you'll definitely enjoy this game

Roleplaying- The game gives you the choices of how to build your character how you want, I play a combat oriented character but you can spec your char out for stealth but most encounters in the game do require you to engage in combat. Combat- Lots of gamers dont like the combat in the game but I find enjoyable, its not flashy like something you would get in the Batman Arkham games. Mars: War Logs is a great little RPG if you get past some quirks.
Many reviewers have commented on the slightly wonky voice acting but I actually find most of the character voices pretty convincing. Roy (our hero) is acted well enough throughout and most of the main cast are emotionally engaging. Some of the NPC dialogue is a little off but having grown up playing Gothic and Shenmue I find a little wonky VA only adds to the charm.
Graphically the game is not very demanding which is great for mid-range rigs because you can run it easily at 4K 60FPS. The texture work is very strong and the overall art style does a great job of representing an apocalyptic Mars. The environments are a claustrophobic maze of rusty metal work and red dust scattered with enough extra detail to hint at a much wider world outside of the cramped settlements.
Overall the level design walks a nice line between immersive detail and easy to identify game-play elements. Traversing the corridors and open spaces of the cities of Mars manages to maintain player interest by providing some stealth alternatives to the hack and slash routes while carefully concealing containers of loot to encourage exploration.
You will want to loot as many crates, opponents and rubbish heaps as you can in order to craft add-ons for your weapons and armour. The crafting system is not exactly deep, basically allowing you to buff your equipment to suit your playstyle while providing nice rewards for exploring every nook and cranny in the hunt for materials.
Character animation is mostly OK, with some unfortunately jarring animation resets, inhuman movements and the occasional amusing glitchy facial expression. Despite these shortcomings the game presents a very compelling story within an engaging world.
The game allows the player to influence the world with the inclusion of a moral compass (just like many popular Bioware franchises) allowing you to be a white knight or a badass, complete with associated charm / intimidation perks. Your behaviour has some influence on other characters and the out come of the story but not to a huge extent.
My one and only major problem with this game is combat. While some may consider this to be a deal breaker, I personally feel combat is secondary to everything else that makes a good RPG. This game often feels overly punishing, and getting stuck on some invisible ledge while enemies smack you from left and right can lead to some roars of frustration. It also has a habit of suddenly ramping up the combat difficulty just as you are starting to enjoy yourself. Overall though combat reminded me of KOTOR with the pause-able action queuing system and  little of Jade Empire in that I had to hammer space a ton to dodge around while healing and restoring mana.
I completed this game on Medium, if you are not up for a fair few deaths and re-loads I would suggest playing on Easy. The achievements are the same for both difficulties, with the game only awarding you extra achievements for playing on Hard or Extreme (neither of which I will ever do.)
As a final word of warning I will point out that some side quests are permanently miss-able depending on decisions you make. This makes getting the "Completionist" achievement impossible to get if you miss something early on (as I did). Saying this however I am more than happy to play again, try out the alternative ending and mop up what I missed.
The game took me around 15 hours to beat first time and definitely has re-play value with the final chapter changing dramatically depending on your choice of ally. I will be replaying on Easy though, one play through on Medium was tough enough for me!
