This was an impulse buy. I dont usually do that ever...but I've been following this game for awhile.  It seems promising. Procedurally generated levels every time you play = differant game every time.  Scary setting with nothing but a phone light and glow sticks to protect you. Seemed pretty interesting.  I played it for about an hour wasn't terribly impressed.  I was a bit scared at times sure, but not terrified as I wandered the hospital looking for items.
Gameplay revolves around going from floor to floor finding notes. Once you've found 6 notes on for each level or "board" you go to a certain room that has an item of one of the insane people. You pick it up and carry it to a special locked door that allows you to progress to the next "board".
That in a nutshell is the gameplay. Along the way you find glowsticks that show hints if you really need that.  All you do is click on everything, desks, cabinets, cupboards, whatever.  It gets very tedious very quickly.  There are some jump scares but  those are all that will get you the least bit frightened.  I only paid 10 bucks for it so its not terrible for a game like this. I just doubt i'll get 10 hours of enjoyment.  More like 2.  That equals 5 bucks per hour of entertainment. I guess for a video game thats not terrible, I just would've wanted more gameplay variety.
For a game like this it works, it really does. Its not annoying like outlast, where your camera light runs out of batteries after 5-6 minutes. You dont have to worry about battery power. You don't worry really about much at all.  Just click on all the doors, explore the hospital and pick up all the notes.
In conclusion I think its not a terrible buy.  Get it now while its on sale. Its not worth more than 10 bucks.

I REALLY wanted to like Daylight. I really did. It had alot of cool things going for it, like randomly generated levels, showing off the 4th version of the Unreal Engine, and Actually being a horror game with ghosts in it (count the amount of horror games with ghosts in them. I can only count them on one hand.) but it turned out to be another disappointment. Why??? Well, ill attempt to explain why.
THE GOOD
One of the good things going for Daylight is the lighting. Daylight has some great lighting, and it shows it off with the use of the different items in the game like the flares.  Another cool thing is most of the environments. From a sewer, to the outside, alot of the areas look pretty good and creepy. The only areas that aren't very good are the first two but besides that, they are very well made environments. One last thing is the sound. Not all of the sound is good and the way most of the sound is used is rather crappy, but many other SFXs are great, and are fitting with the setting. The sound that tells you a ghost is nearby and most of the old, worn out doors are very creepy, and set the mood perfectly.
Also, the way Twitch (Livestreaming) is integrated is neat as well.
THE BAD
Here's where it all goes downhill. one thing to make your game scary is be crafty and paced well. Daylight fails at this. Here are daylights "regular" scares.
- cheap jumps scares
-doors opening by themselves (SPOOOOOKY)
-Objects getting flung around
-and loud screams that get old about the third time they are used
Sure, most people will find this scary, but I don't. Jump scares can be scary if done right, but ones that are thrown out of nowhere with no buildup are not scary. Daylight does that so many times its not even funny. As for doors and objects magicly opening or get thrown, its such a done to death cliche I roll my eyes instead of being scared. And the loud screams are pretty self explanatory. The worst part is the gameplay. Here is the entirety of daylights gameplay. 1. Enter level. 2.collect 6 pages. 3.go to the key. 4. Go to exit. 5.rinse and repeat. Sound familiar, doesn't it? Yes, this is pretty much a rip-off of the smash hit horror game, Slender: The Eight Pages (which I don't like either). Not only that, but it gets extremely repetitive later in the game. Another thing that is bad is the lack of enemy variety. The entire game, you're being chased by ONE ghost the whole game, and its design is very bland. Because of this, it adds on to the repetition and bore-factor of the game. One last thing is the story and characters. The story is told through notes and slight (and I mean slight) exposition between levels. I would have been fine with this if not for the fact that it is very bland and uninteresting from start to finish. Most of the notes are either ZOMG I SAW SOMEONE RUN AROUND WHERE I WAS AND IVE NEVER SEEN HIM IN MY LIFE! To ZOMG SOMEONE DIED! It got to the point where reading them felt like a chore. Another thing is that the protagonist is SOOO annoying. I give props for not using the "silent character" approach, but id rather prefer that then this. The entire game Sarah will say "Is anyone there" to "What was that?" And it gets annoying real fast because of how many voice clips are used over and over again.
THE VERDICT
What a disappointment. It had alot of potential, but wound up being boring and uninspired. 3/10.

I wish that there were more options on Steam for ratings. I do recommend this game, but it's not without a few issues that are kind of frustrating to me. I'll get the bad out of the way and say that it is locked to 30 FPS. Many people claim this doesn't matter, but to me it does matter. My PC far exceeds the recommended settings (Ryzen 7 1700x, GTX 1080, 16GB RAM), but still in some places it affects the visuals and makes it look like the game is dropping frames even though it isn't.
Second, it cannot be played in full screen mode if you intend to use your computer for other tasks here and there while playing. The reason being that the Alt+Tab function does not work in full screen. If you run full screen you will have to exit the game from the pause menu and then close it from the start screen in order to exit out, just like you are on a console, before you will be able to access the other functions on your computer. I set mine to Windowed, but there is still an issue with the border not quite lining up, so I can see parts of the icons in my task bar, and a small section of the white border at the top. So far as I can tell, there is no way to correct this as of now, so you are either stuck in the game until you save and exit, or have to deal with a border that doesn't properly line up and can't be changed.
The game does not have the visual settings option that you would expect from a PC game. All the other ports I have still offer most visual options that normal PC games offer, but WoFF gives you a separate tool bar for that which has to be accessed in your steam library outside of the game. You cannot change the display options from the in game settings menu.
The configuration tool bar in your library only has Windowed and Fullscreen options, for display mode, and other than that you can only change the resolution, shadow resolution, and enable or disable Post-Processing. To me the settings are severely lacking and need to be updated asap. It's nothing game breaking or worthy of demanding a refund, but they definitely are issues worth noting. If you have a PS 4 and your PC is below the recommended settings, I would just buy it on PS4, since it's not possible to turn down most settings on the game like a normal PC game (or even most ports for that matter).
As far at the game itself goes, it's beautiful. The game runs well for the most part and has some really astonishing visuals. Playing it makes me feel like they took all the best things from Final Fantasy, Pokémon, and Kingdom hearts and rolled them into one. The combat flows well, tutorial system is geared to help you learn the deeper intricacies of how the game functions, and the characters are likeable and fun. There is monster capturing, stacking, and  leveling to add a great deal of customization to your party.
Also, there are lots of gameplay options available so that you can customize the game to function more like your personal favorite FF, from the turn based or active battle time choices, to the battle menu options there is a lot of room for movement within your personal preferences. If I had to rate this game in stars (which I'd much rather do than giving it a yes or no) I would say it's a solid 8.5 as a game and 7.5 as a PC port. May update that later as I progress into the game, but that's where I'm sitting after about an hour of frustration, trying to customize the functionality of the port to little avail, and about 4 hours of actual gameplay.
Finally, it should be noted that there are lots of cheat options that can be turned on and off, which were not offered in the console versions. These can make the game easier for you after you finish it on normal (or if you just don't care for the challenge at all your first time). There are also options to customize the in-game sound track and voice languages. I haven't tried it yet, but it appears to have an option to turn the voice acting off altogether (if you don't want to listen to the English or Japanese options) and read the game like it's pre FFX!

To start off, this is a simplistic RTS game with simple graphics and 2 (four if you include the fantasy factions from 8-bit Hordes) factions to date. Each faction has unique units and campaigns (but only the renegade campaign is free).
The campaign for the renegades is quite straight forward. You get your units and either hold out for a set time, get cash or you destroy certain targets. No convoluted objectives. The campaign for the renegades is quite long at 25 levels and can be difficult at times depending on the difficulty and mission you're playing. Each mission also grants bonus' for the start of each mission you play from that point forward. While this does introduce a nice twist, it can sometimes actually be a detriment, especially when it gives you buildings and turrets but no power plants. Overall though, it's a positive thing and is very helpful at times. As mentioned above the second campaign is paid DLC.
On to the units. Before, the small selection of units meant that you ended up either spamming tanks or aircraft. However, with some changes and balancing this is not the case anymore. The infantry used to be rather ineffective and pointless, but since the renegades infantry is now the only way to detect the guardians' stealth units, you'll find yourself useing them to avoid ambushes from the guardians' snipers and spectres. While the guardians lack anti-air and have little anti-tank, their aircraft more than make up for this if you can get heavy drones, which balance out the fights when paired with their infantry. The renegdes can bring a heavy (mammoth) tank to the fight however, which is always fun. Overall, you'll end up building a mixed army if you want to win.
The super weapons. The guardians satalite laser seems effective at dealing with the armies deployed by your enemies, but I've seem limited effectivness against buildings. The renegades nuke being quite the opposite. It's rather easy to dodge, but does incredible damage, even against buildings.
The tech trees. The tech trees are easy to learn, and quite simplistic. Simple enough that games are quick and fair for both sides. Not much more I can say.
Other notes: The game does have transport units, which is quite helpful for certain maps and strategies, in addition to each unit having a decent transport capacity. This game does not however, contain any neutral tech buildings or infantry garrisoning such as in other RTS games.
No unit cap, take that as you please. There is a few glitches and errors, but not enough to completly ruin gameplay for me (Too few and far between). Do get your friends to buy it too if you wanna play online, Much easier to find matches that way. Font too small on laptop? Why are you reading, Get out there and shoot some people!
As a final verdict, I would recommend this game for those RTS fans (or those who just want a quick, fun online match) who have a little (8) bit of cash laying in your wallet and want a new game.
(note: As I have not yet played 8-Bit Hordes, I've yet to be able to comment on the intergration and unit balancing)

Designed as an introduction to the world of RTS games, 8 Bit Armies is the same formulae as Red Alert 1 and 2, even toting ex-Westwood devs on their team. It pushes accessibility and an ease of use that even someone who had never played an RTS game before could pick up and play.
8 Bit Armies features a cell-phone game style progression system for its singleplayer campaign, having players go back and get higher scores on previous levels to unlock advantages to start the next level with. There is also a separate Co-Op campaign. While these modes are enjoyable, you begin to see the problems of 8 Bit Armies. The game has 2 factions, both of which are fairly similar. You'll soon notice that the accessibility and simplicity that 8BA pushes tends to overpower the depth.
8BA is incredibly shallow. You don't have much room at all for 'gimmicks' or specializations. The winner of the game is whoever has more units on the field. There isn't really much strategy at all. The game first appeared on Steam as an Early Access title, and even after all this time, it doesn't feel much different. I suggested a few of my friends buy the game, which they did, but we ended up wanting to wait until there's more to it. After all, there are (and always will be) more people playing Red Alert 2 etc online than 8BA.
It's no lie that the RTS genre is struggling, but skin-deep attempts like this isn't going to bring it back anytime soon. Progress is far too slow (especially for a title no longer in Early Access). Unless they make some real changes, you're better off playing one of the 16 fully featured Command and Conquer games.

As a long-time fan of WestWood studios, who had all of their games on hard disk, and now thusly have all their games on Origin, I shall say that while I do enjoy this game, I find myself floating to other games in the genre instead. But in the few cases I jump on it's a lot of fun to experiment with countering the current strategies.
However, with that said I'd also like to mention the fact that the A.I using a single, brutal-against-newer-players strategy, which involves constant steamrolling and steamrolling, throwing a few units at a time at the enemy base to occupy them, and then when you build an army up they mass together a big ball ofaircraft, anti infantry, and anti ground and steamroll your army, then steamroll your base, I've seen it happen.  It's even happened to me, and I haven't been able to counter it.  Which brings me onto another point:  There needs to be a better way of expanding.  I find myself stuck on 1 base and then long distance mining because it's so expensive to expand, I really don't think building a daisy chain of buildings to the next oil derrick is a good idea.  I'm not going to say make it so that you can build anywhere without limit, since that can turn into a whole lot of balancing issues.  No, what I'm saying is simpler.  Give us back the Surveyor. (and nod/scrin's equivilant.) Surveyor should be unlocked either with the motor pool, barracks, or the tech lab.  The Surveyor should have the ability to unpack into a mini HQ, which you can build near, simple right?  Makes expanding cheaper and more avaliable.  That's pretty much my only gripe with the game, but it's a bigg'un.
In conclusion, yes this is a fun game, but no, it's not fully fleshed out.  I hope you take my suggestion into consideration, Petroglyph, I've been a fan since I was four.  All the best you guys!

Pros:
- Fun C&C style base building and resource management
- Easy to learn, not so easy to master, combat
- Voxel based graphics that suit the game in a charming way
- Good soundtrack
- Workshop support for community made maps (including remakes of classic C&C maps)
- Competetive multiplayer that seems to be (at the moment) populated by a reasonable amount of people as to not have to wait that long for a game
Cons:
- Lack of singleplayer content
- Only 2 factions (but credit to the dev(s), they update regularly, and I'm sure factions will eventually be added to)
- Perhaps a slight lack of diversity in terms of units and playstyles

You actively change dimensions to open gates and reverse the motion of platforms while juggilng your two movement options. The atmosphere and even the music changes completely as you alternate between worlds. Pity they reuse the same song in every level. Frequent checkpoints and infinite lives reduces the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to pure challenge without wasting your time.
That said it's only slightly above mediocre. I didn't feel any connection to the characters and the levels felt really samey. My zeal to collect every gemstone hovers below zero and I feel bad for the people who went out of their way spending dozens of hours backtracking every path to find them.

This game is decent but there are dozens of others that outclass it.

I installed this game having just finished The Technomancer! I came across it on an accident and was excited to discover another game set in the same universe that takes place alongside the other game's events!
Instead of playing as the techomancer, Zarchariah "dull-as-drying-glue" mancer, We step into the shoes of Roy "Temperance", a grizzled prisoner in camp 19  who has decided he's going to break out with the help of a starry-eyed simpleton named Innocence, fresh from the front in the war between Aurora and Abundance!
Like its successor, Mars: War Logs bares a striking resemblance to KOTOR, only on a much smaller scale. This can be both a good and a bad thing. Bad, because a lot of the areas felt samey and it didn't feel as if I was going on a grand adventure with my rag tag warrior posse. Good, because even with the tremendous about of backtracking (to complete quests) that these games seem to love, the areas were so compact that it didn't take too long to get from one place to another!
I'm kind of sad to say that while I did enjoy the game from start to finish, I wasn't always invested in the story and the characters. A lot of developments felt rushed and several moments you were clearly supposed to "feel something", Like when a companion inevitably dies, I found myself feeling nothing.
On the subject of characters, the only one I really cared about throughout was my guy Roy, sure he was as bland a cheese sandwich, but I found myself never getting tired of hearing him talk, so that's a plus! I WISH I could say the same for everyone else! This game is a complete reverse of The Technomancer in terms of voice acting. In Technomancer, everyone but your character was very well voiced! But here, the only one I cared to listen to was Roy, It also didn't help that besides the main group, there was only about 3 face models shared among the regular NPCs.
Companions are...useless. I think that was part of the reason I paid no heed to them or their backstories. I nicknamed Innocence, "hopeless" because he would just stand there and take the hits half the time, that is if he hadn't gotten stuck on a corner somewhere. I was disappointed to learn that not only could you only have one companion follow you around, but you couldn't even upgrade them with better weapons and armor, what you see is what you get. The only good that comes from having other characters follow you, is as meat shields to divide enemy attention.
So, all sounds pretty bad so far right? Sure, it's not super polished and a lot of it isn't that engaging, but regardless I enjoyed myself and scoured every single bit of each area for salvage, upgrades and side quests! Despite being flawed, it's still pretty charming, besides, the combat and upgrading is where the fun is.
Unlike The Technomancer, when you get into a brawl, you feel mortal and a lot less untouchable. You have to analyze a situation and decide how best to deal with each fight. Between you smashing people with blunt objects, throwing sand in people's faces, casting lightning, creating energy shields and rolling about to evade all kinds of oncoming death, there was never a dull moment in combat! There are companion commands (although they're rather simple) and you can have your follow assume a particular battle stance, or focus their attention on a particular kind of enemy.
I do wish there had been a little more variety in enemies, throughout the game I think perhaps there were 5 tops.
Upgrading your abilities and crafting upgrades for your weapons and armor always felt like it really made a difference, and the visual upgrades were always appealing and made you feel all the more badarse!
There are three trees in which you can upgrade roy, one focuses on his technomancer abilites (lightning, shield, force blast), another focuses on combat, and the third focuses on "renegade", never knew exactly what was meant by that, it just let you upgrade your more underhand tactics like throwing sand, sneaking about, giving you more health, etc.
All in all, the game was average but I had a lot of fun! Even if it was frighteningly short in comparison to it's successor, I completed it in just over 10 hours, but like I said, I contribute most of my 30 hour play time in The Techomancer to backtracking all over the place.
Not as good as Technomancer, probably because part of that game's purpose was improving on the ideas shown in Mars: War Logs. But I still liked it regardless! For anyone wanting more of the series, this is a must buy, just don't expect to get mass effect!
I give Mars: War Logs a 6/10~

Maybe I don't play hidden object games that much, but Alchemy Mysteries consistently disappointed me at every turn. Invariable backtracking, outrageously tedious puzzle games, and a storyline that's plagued with plotholes. The only thing this game has going for it are the animations for characters and ghosts, most of which are ruined by the absolutely awful voice acting.
Backtracking is really the focal issue in this game. It's almost as if they couldn't design enough levels to fit all their useless hidden object minigames. Get the items from the briefcase, use them in another room, go back to the briefcase, get an item, use them in another room. It drones on and on until they breach your monotony with another boring cutscene of someone NPC talking with peanut butter in their mouth.
Also, I couldn't help but ask my self, "Why the heck do I need all these items?" Maybe I'm just not into hidden object games as much as the next person, but why would I need to get a duster to wipe away some cobwebs, when the main character consistently picks up handfuls of spiders in hidden object minigames? Why do I need a god damn rapier to open up a wall cover when I had a hammer/crowbar in my inventory?
I digress.
I could put all of that aside. The horrible voice-acting, the trainwreck minigames, and the awful storyline. I could give Alchemy Mysteries the benefit of the doubt on everything above, but the one thing I will not are the puzzles. I literally spent an hour on a single puzzle because of how comically difficult it was. Allow me to give you an example of the puzzle because these things pop up like weeds in games like this.
You backtrack through the game and find two clock hands. Great, you can finally put them on the clock and fix it so you can progress the story. Once you put them on, you're looking at a clockface with three different-styled hands. You have to match all three hands with their respective shadows, but you only have three buttons and each button moves two hands at the same time. That's not fun; that's actually really god damn boring.
Maybe I'm not masochistic enough, but I was struggling really hard to continue this game after an hour of that puzzle. I just kept pressing buttons until I finished the game because there's no strategy, structure, or style to a minigame like that. It's all random and good luck figuring that out quickly. These puzzles, though.. They're littered throughout the game and I kept dreading the time I'd have to do one again.
I cannot recommend this game at this time.
Boring story, horrible voice-acting, bad puzzles, and backtracking that doesn't make any sense. The jumpscares and animations are the only thing going for this game and, even then, it's ruined by the lack of depth and (clearly) money that the developers didn't have to hire someone competent enough to read their lines off realistically. Alchemy Mysteries is not even worth the price on a discount.

Adorable little game.  From the very pretty stained-glass style artwork to the almost chibi-like character design.  I was very surprised to see this was designed by a russian studio as there was a pervasive albeit subtle Japanese influence throughout, everything from the mumbled voice-effects of certain characters to the overall wonkiness and illogicality of some plot points and character actions.  But it was not ever enough to put me off, as I generally steer a mile-clear of anything in gaming that is pure anime.
The gameplay is overall very minimal and on the casual end of the spectrum, but fun in its own right and is integrated in the story well.  Tasks generally include point'n'click object finds, dragging items/characters around, completing non-standard jigsaws, choosing answers to both sides of a conversation, and there's even a few "battles" but they are twisted on their head in a very pleasing way.  In one, you try and "adorable" your way through someone's anger, and in another you defeat your own laziness!  Quite short altogether, I probably only played less than half my shown runtime, and it certainly doesn't outstay it's welcome, but I did feel it wrapped up awful quick, no doubt setting the stage for sequels.
There was a couple of spelling/grammatical issues and once there was the wrong face used in a dialogue tree which confused the whole conversation flow but nothing that was too immersion breaking.  If you want an hour or so diversion you could definitely spend your money on a lot worse!

And it delivered in spades: it's beautiful and extremely fun to explore, it has memorable and relatable characters, the combat system is a bit better than past games but it definitely needs more kill animation variety, loot variety is great... love the visual design of everything, and best of all: the ubisoft open world bloat has been reduced dramatically and replaced with a million side quests with stories so now I have a legit reason to want to go everywhere.
Of course, it's not perfect: back to the loot... it has great visual variety, sure, but it lacks a lot in attributes and elemental affixes to make it actually rewarding, a lot of characters and (side)quests are memorable and a lot feel like they had a great idea but then forgot what they were writing about and promptly dropped them before they could get any real resolution... comes with the territory of having so many quests(and obviously not having the level of skill that TW3 writers have) I suppose, and the post-release content, aside from the generally great patches, leave a lot to be desired... it feels like they half baked everything so far; outfits miss physics interaction or effects that you'd think they would have... same thing with the mounts, or the fact that the FF15 event is just so amazingly LAZY(quest length and the 4 legged chocobo camel mutant what the hell) compared to the Square counter-part, the trials of the gods all basically being copied and pasted, and the packs are ridiculously over priced.
Overall though, it was a lot better than I expected and I can forgive the faults based on the ambition of the game alone.
I'm just a little wary about the expansions they'll be releasing if their current offerings are any indication of quality control.

Aviary Attorney is like Ace Attorney, except with animals. In Aviary Attorney you play as a bird named Falcon with your assistant Sparrowson solving murder cases.
Pros
- Pretty good story
- Loveable chracters, Sparrowson in particular is really charming to listen to
- All of the endings are pretty good and satisfying
- Neat presentation that perfectly captures the time period the game is based on
- Well done music that, again fits with the game's time period
- Most realistic cross-examination I've seen in a lawyer game that Im aware of and is quite fun
- Interesting day mechanic, although kind of frustrating at points
Cons
- Pretty short, it took 7 hours to beat the game and the game costs $16.99
- I guess this point is based entirely on varying mileages but, the game overall was pretty easy, I only struggled on case 3
- The day mechanic makes no sense to me, you can spend an entire day at one location having a conversation and spend a day there, but you can go there again and have a slightly shorter conversation and not waste a day, it's not that I hate the mechanic it's just that it makes no sense to me
- There was some static with loading screens that lagged, but that's just a nitpick
- Can't skip entire events instead you have to keep on clicking, which becomes very tedious when replaying the game
Overall, I really liked Aviary Attorney. However, I'd recommend getting the game on sale because $16.99 is pretty pricey considering the length of the game. Regardless, it was fun, charming and a delight. I'd give it a 7/10. Kudos to Otter Guy for gifting this to me. :3

The code structure itself reminds me of the Basic coding language, though the commands aren't the same names (GOTO is called JUMP, and there is an arrow you use to indicate where).
Other than the coding stuff (which is completely taught to you in-game, so you don't have to already know it), it is also just a really good puzzle game, with "optimization" challenges that push you to not just solve the puzzle, but to have the best possible solution. Even if you are familiar with programming, the challenges and puzzles can sometimes get the best of you, and I poured 8 hours into this game my first weekend with it (this weekend).
Absolutely love this game, and recommend it to programmers and non-programmers alike.

I had programming experience coming into this game, but I imagine that those who are not experienced will take longer on the first half of the game and learn the concepts. The game has a very well formed difficulty curve, and eases you into the levels nicely.
By far the best part of this game are the optional levels. Be sure to play those.

However, I don't think the game is worth $10. I would wait for a sale.

8 bit armies is a game that attempts to cater to people who are interested in getting into the RTS genre as well as the competitive side in a more friendlier way than most other RTS titles. Unfortunately, it is let down by a number of different issues. I can't really give this game a thumbs up or thumbs down from my perspective and that comes down to the fact that game has a lot of cool things going for it while being hurt through too much simplicity.
Youtube Review: (8 minutes)
Pros:
1. There are a good amount of units. There was only one faction on launch but they have added a free faction (for multiplayer and skirmishes) to the game which has helped make it more interesting. For a 15 dollar game it's pretty surprising how many units there are.
2. Aesthetically it's great. Animation quality is great with good music and decent sound design (the bleeps and bloops constantly going off can be a bit irritating but it's still well done).
3, Content heavy. With co-op, multiplayer and a single player campaign as well as steak workshop and a level editor there is plenty of content here if you enjoy the game.
Cons:
1. UI is too simplistic. This is a huge problem. While there is information about each unit on the side bar it doesn't give me information like total health, armor, damage or anything like that during a game. This can hurt people who want to get their foot in the door for playing competitivly.
2. Hotkeys are dumb because of minimal UI. Hotkeys for each unit are displayed next to said unit. I have not been able to get a total unit count on my screen. This is a problem. It's entirely possible that when you play a game you have to go through each hot key and try to find which units are apart of which hotkey but you won't find how many are to the hotkey. I might need to know how many tanks I have bound to key one. I could have enough to attack and win the game but if I don't I could lose which is why I would want to retreat but I won't know the answer because my soldiers might be too spread out to count them.
3. No hook. While the game has plenty of content there is nothing to keep me playing. Having tons of units are great but if they all look tiny and similar then it's hard to get excited when creating them. Without any interesting mechanics or even individual unit abilities and upgrades, troops don't feel distinct. The campaign is essentialy skirmish matches without any interesting objectives or scripted scenarios. How about taking control away from the player and give them only a few units to win a mission to get them to think outside the box on how to effectivly use each unit to their maximum potential? It doesn't have this.
Overall. I felt 8-bit armies to be lacking mechanically but it has the groundwork to be a strong RTS. If you are a fan of the genre you might want to pick it up on sale. if you are new this might not be a bad place to start without having to delve into older games (like warcraft 3 or starcraft 1) but don't let this paint your picture of every RTS game. There are better ones then this and some do what this game does but better in terms of teaching the player (starcraft 2).

This game has a lot going for it.  However, the "twitch" factor is very high.  To make a pun that current owners of the game will get … it’s “Sky High.”  It is my sincere hope that enough reviewers will echo my sentiments & that the developers will eventually enable a control panel & permit a “God Mode” so that talentless old folks like myself can at least observe the level design & artwork, which is quite good.
I've unlocked a gravity ability, & I have given up on level 4.  I've seen You-Tube posts of nerds with superhuman gaming powers (& obviously way too much time on their hands) hurtling through the levels like a hot knife through butter, yet I apparently do not have the patience to die as much as I have...anymore.
Don't get me wrong: it's a gorgeous game.  The movement is good.  The levels are well designed (despite their difficulty & oftentimes confusing mechanics.)  The colors are nice & the textures are good enough.  The game loads quickly & respawning is mercifully instantaneous.  It simply is too “twitchy” & it lacks a compelling story line to keep me intrigued.  The level I gave up on is particularly dark & chaotic.  Keeping track of which way is up became ridiculously impossible.
I would recommend this to someone young with very good hand eye coordination & a LOT of spare time on their hands.  I would NOT recommend this to anyone who has ever experienced a seizure.  Even some folks with no history of seizures might experience one while playing “DeadCore.”  I feel very fortunate to have purchased “DeadCore” for only $3.99 during a holiday sale; I can honestly say that the levels I DID get through were worth exactly that but not one penny more.
One last thing: folks who compare this game to “Portal” or “Portal 2” are vastly overstating this game.  There’s a gun.  It’s an FPS.  There’s apparently some sort of AI that’s taken over things & made a mess of the world.  Beyond that, there is no comparison.

and you progress only via checkpoints after a big puzzle or a small set of shorter sequences. There isn' a lot of story or anything that would immerse you deeply. You can find some logs on the way to uncover a few flavor texts adding to the experience but in the end it's always about getting up and wondering what's up there. Besides the hidden logs you can find a few upgrades for your abilities
and some music tracks.
For me, as someone who can be an aweful jump-precision dyslexic, the game took almost five hours in total for one playthrough with not nearly all upgrades and logs. Later playthroughs will be faster since you already got a bunch of upgrades and more experience. Also, once found, you will keep all your abilities even if you replay some levels which opens up new pathways to progress. Other than that there's not a whole lot of replay value unless you want to do speed runs and fight for a spot on the leaderboards.
The level design is cool and futuristic. It's super open and you can always see past levels below you which gives the game sometimes a continuing fun-house experience (interestingly enough my fear of heights never kicked in while looking down). The sound blends in nicely into the graphics and the setting overall. You don't have super loud stepping sounds, all rocket jumps from platforms basically blend into the surrounding ambient humming and there's nothing that will really♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. The only sounds that stand out are the different kinds of drones that will be in your way; they all have very distinct sounds that will make you go 'uh-oh' by the end of the game.
Speaking of the drones: What I like about them is that there's only a single kind of drone that can actually kill you in the end. All the other kinds of drones are just there to poke you and♥♥♥♥♥♥you off: One lets you see your perception of some colours so you won't see deadly laser barriers anymore, one just bumps into you and shoots you off a cliff, etc. They are highly annoying but you usually get a chance to safe yourself if you react fast enough.
The level design is mostly very good and there are enough ways to build a huge amount of interesting tasks with varying degree of puzzle factor and agility requirements. In a lot of cases you get to choose a super fast reaction route that can be very unforgiving or a path that makes you train a certain rhythm of actions to reach your goal. But most of all levels focus very much on a certain kind of agility training, so there is not a lot of real puzzles left (although I still had to stop and think at times on how the devs thought this will be possible to do at all).
I was a bit disappointed by the lack of background music. Most of the time you don't hear a lot (which might've been a good sign because the music blends in but in the end it was just nothing noteworthy there to listen to) and when you hear it you want more than just the two minutes of it. Also, the music is kind of hit and miss. Given that I totally despise most of drum & bass I still found some very nice parts in some songs in the game but a lot of times I was kind of bored or annoyed.
The other thing is how hugely disappointing the mystery of the summit is. I mean, there could've been something but in the end
The logs are just so horribly written that I didn't bother to read most of them really carefully since it was either some weird monologue about some of the tasks you are going through (and some of the drones/abilites) or a dialogue that mostly just talks some sensei-stuff that is utterly boring.
Finally, there is this whole
thing a lot of people are complaining about and I kind of get it. It can be super annoying when the drone you just disabled wakes up just half a second to early or you fall down from that one doulbe-jump 'n dash sequence for the tenth time. Also, at some parts it's completely unclear how you should be progressing there without going for some healthy
action. Also, sometimes checkpoints are coming in at a ridiculously high frequency where you just think "where was the problem here, I was just walking in a straight line?" At other times you will find yourself playing for 2-3 minutes going through an insane adrenaline rush inducing sequence that's really hard (and can let you die a couple of times) and then you respawn back at the beginnig. Some better ordering of the checkpoints might've helped here.
The main problem with most people playing the game is probably that they think you can play it like a
game. What
actually is is a side-scrolling jump and run that is played from a first-person perspective. For about 50% of the game I didn't know that myself and was at times♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about how some sequences are laid out. But in the end I understood that it's not about puzzles and thinking, it's very often just about running into something and figuring out the rhythm. Then you will get adrenaline rushing in your blood and after a longer sequence you land on a checkpoint, turn around, look at what you just crossed and think "Wow, how did that happen, exactly?"
Those are a lot of moments where the game shines and is super fun. At the other hand some sequences are so hard to manage or way too long that it makes you freak out and punch something Borderlands-Brick-style. But those are not most moments. It's a game with a high sense of urgency that is very real once you find a bunch of timers running inside your head on when to jump next. It's fast and keeps up a nice pace with only few moments to catch a breath. Oddly enough I found it very relaxing to play after work because of all those immense jumps, combined with the your abilities which give you a real nice sense of free movement in three dimensions.

Incredible.  The gameplay behond Deadcore is essentially a first person platform game which just so happens to have a gun to activate things. The game challanges you to climb a large mechanical tower made of levitating blocks higher and higher with checkpoints along the way. Sometimes it seems incredible how high one level can go.
The way you get around in Deadcore is by jumping platform to platform, using jump pads, stragetically whilst activating markings on some of the surrounding blocks, whilst dodging red lazers, autoturrets and floating security droids shaped as blocks or orbs which try to knock you off or into lazers in various ways. timing is important.
Throughout the early levels you get introduced to different abilities to climb this monstrous tower of jumping puzzles, turrets and lazers. A double jump at first, a boost which you can use twice before recharging, or hold down for a powerful boost forward and finally a kind of boost orb which when used properly can help propel you in the air after a double jump. However the gun you carry around is more like a tool and you can only fire 30 times, until you get a checkpoint where the gun refils with shots. This can be specially annoying when defending yourself from drones as you try to figure something out, only to reach where you wanted to go and find a marking to activate, with no point but to kill yourself and try again and learn through trial and error.
Just as you get used to the rhythm of shooting markings to activate jump pads at the exact moment, barely fit through lazers like the Japanese game show concept 'Hole in the Wall', then the game literally turns itself upside down with transparent markings on to of blocks which temporaliy affect your gravity in that purple highlighted area and that's where it gets a bit like Portal, getting completely misco-ordinated whilst climbing a tower upwards, suddenly realising what direction you are facing in mid air and quickly making a landing whilst some floating drones are trying to send a pulse wave so you can get incinerated by a nearby patch of red lazer.
Utterly brilliant and taxing, like my earlier reviewed 'A Story About My Uncle' but instead relies on perfectly timed jumps and a repetition and rhythm as you jump pad to pad and activate marking by marking. It's more like a physical training course and the reward of getting to a checkpoint where you can auto save your progress (and go back to the real world) is so satisfying, but it's so easy to fall into a trance doing each action at the right time and each move at the right measurement and you will swear a lot.

A very solid platformer with a mysterious and interesting backstory and speedrunning support? For only ten bucks?! Well kinda...
Deadcore's gameplay mainly revolves around you navigating through six levels of a massive tower called the Ziggurat. Along the way, you'll find powerups like a rifle that allows you to stun enemies and activate switches, a dash move, the ability to alter gravity in certain areas, and a radial blast that can act as a rocket jump. This, mixed with very solid level design (for the most part) and very nice graphics make this game worth the ten dollar price tag.
HOWEVER, while the game has a nice and smooth difficulty curve for the first three levels, as soon as you reach the fourth level there's a rather large, and even a bit cheap at times, difficulty spike.
The game begins throwing everything it has at you and expects you to keep track of pretty much every aspect of the area around you. Your timing has to be spot on, along with your aim, which can be a bit clumsy at times.
But, I don't feel that this ruins the game's overall experience. It's fun, it's challenging, and I definitely recommend you to pick it up if you like platformers and a good challenge.

This is a good-looking 2.5D platformer that reminds me a bit of the Trine series (a partial reason behind me purchasing the game in the first place).  It's pretty simple to pick up and learn, with the primary gameplay mechanic being a "swap" between the two sisters at the push of a button, and each sister has their own ability to assist with the platforming and problem solving in the game.  Giana Sisters provides some challenging areas that don't get too frustrating thanks to some pretty flexible checkpoints.  There is definitely replay incentive for those who want to collect 100% crystals on each level, as there were a ton of hidden areas I missed, even after doing what I thought was a pretty exploratory approach to the game.
There are two somewhat minor areas of criticism I have for this game, although these may not be as big of a concern to others for various reasons:
First, there is virtually no story here at all.  There's a brief cutscene of sorts in the beginning, and after that, it's pretty much 100% gameplay throughout the rest.  Obviously if you're looking for a large narrative-driven aspect in your video games, you're better off looking elsewhere, but I don't mind it here so much because the gameplay held up well enough to keep me interested through the end.
Second, the length - there are three worlds in total containing six, seven, and ten levels respectively.  While I do like the game's style/art design, I didn't really notice a huge amount of variance from one world to the next, but new gameplay elements are added frequently enough to where this wasn't a deterrent for me.  Nonetheless, I ended up completing all three worlds in under 10 hours, which I spread out over the course of about two weeks.  I do find that fairly short, although considering the game's asking price (I didn't kickstart it; bought it in a Steam sale), this is honestly a pretty fair offering.  Plus, the stand-alone Owlverlord DLC adds another world's worth of content if you like what you get here.
Overall, I was pleased with my experience with the game.  There's a somewhat interesting history with this franchise, and I'm glad I got to experience what I'd say amounts to a successfully kickstarted project.

Message Quest is a quick, cute little game in which you help a reluctant herald find the hero needed to save the world! It's easily under 2 hours long to complete, even if you're going for 100% completion, which can be good if you're a person like me with little free time nowadays or terrible if you're looking for a meatier game.
Message Quest's gameplay is essentially a series of basic puzzles that are each partially explored without ever focusing in on a single defining mechanic. There's not really anything innovative to the puzzles' design, but they get the job done. If you're playing this game, you're doing it for the story, not the challenge.
As for the story...it's got some hiccups. The main character is a lazy herald that the player literally needs to drag through the adventure. There's a clear story arc with the character, and I get what the writers were going for, but that doesn't make our cowardly hero-seeker any less irritating throughout the early chunks of the game.
A pet peeve of mine: there are some misspelled words that stem from it being translated into English. Those really should have been caught before the final launch, and certainly by the time I played the game. It's frustrating to see such basic mistakes in a game that IS so narrative driven.
That said, even with all the above issues, I did feel I got my $2 worth. There's something charming about the art design, and the developer's passion is clear in every aspect of its design. You can tell they were providing a toolbox of basic puzzles to tell the story they wanted. When it shines, it feels like a modern fairy tale, and there's a real heart to it. Oh, and it's pretty awesome to see a pregnant woman actually get to be a central character in a game; character diversity in storytelling is always nice to see.
Is it going to blow your mind? Probably not. In fact, I'd say this game is better suited for younger children, since the storybook feel, lack of failure states, and unrestricted help button make it easy to progress. I could see playing this with my future kids one day, and I think they'd love it for the same reasons we all love fairy tales growing up. That's why it gets the thumbs up from me, even with all of my reservations. Just know what you're getting yourself into before you buy.

Or was that intentional, revenge is never enough. I don't know only Bayek could answer that one.
Graphics are what you would expect from the likes of Ubisoft and don't disappoint.

To me, the main character Bayek is one of the more aggressive combative assassin and less of a silent stealthy killer. Also worth noting he's one of the few assassins that doesn't get his hands burned when sliding down ropes. Truly a badass.
I also enjoyed they attempted to add a bit of the naval ship battles like in black flag. To me that one of the most enjoyable part of black flag and it's nice to see it incorporated again however brief.
All in all a great game in the genre I would definitely recommend it.

Its not fair to write a review with so few minutes of gameplay such as mine, but im here to inform those who might run into similar issues. I want to make it clear that this review is based off the large impression it slapped into my face.
Got an obvious error message in corner of screen that i can't close telling me how my graphics need to be updated... They don't and I'm running a top of the line laptop. Trust me for what im running I shouldnt have any issues with this game, but instead even after changing options to run smoothly it remains laggy.
Immediate issue starting campaign, for a new user just coming back to Assassins Creed (I played the original and the 2 after it), it throws you into a story thats already progressed. The game literally kills an important figure for you without 1 second of game play. Thats just bad story telling imo.
Combat didnt feel smooth at all. I like the idea their going with, something unique you dont typically see, very similar to For Honor with motion. With that being said terrible idea for a player vs computer, would work really well player vs player.
Here was the biggest turnoff for me though. Before purchasing I always do a decent study of their addons/passes/ additional purchases offered. First thing I see for this game thrown in my face are the micro transactions. Normally not a big deal for me, i love buying additional content that adds so much more to the game. These transactions however, were more focused on selling gear that offers little value overall rather than quality content that adds more to the story. An example is: 4 pieces of gear, and one mission. In other words your buying the gear rather than the mission itself.
You know its bad when addons/expansions are offered after only a couple months of the orginal release of a game. Even official reviews said the story is worth 30hrs of gameplay. Like wtf, im paying $60 for 30hrs? I'm sure others are different but in my personal opinion for every $1 i spend on a game, I should be able to get at least 1hr of story gameplay. Thats my golden rule. Moving back to the original issue though, I even read reviews claiming that buying a season pass doesnt guarantee all the extra content their offering.
Honestly I am flabbergasted by how many good reviews there are for this game when comparing it to Shadow of War, which had received the most hate I've ever seen about "micro transactions". All based off of crates which had no influence on the gameplay of the game, very similar to the items offered by this game which are half cosmetic like mounts and the other half being weapon/gear. Which leads me to believe that companies or marketers are still paying people to create reviews to influence the sales of the game, similar to the scandal steam announced before. Hence why im creating this review, to leave a heavily honest first impression.
Put simply it's just not the Assassins Creed that I had fallen in love with. Its more of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ company, Ubisoft, thats known for killing great ideas/games. Dont believe me? Check out why For Honor died within months after release, heres a hint: It had nothing to do with the game but rather multiple large issues related to Ubisofts poor decisions.

Aviary Attorney is a wonderfully put together detective game which combines a beautiful old-fashioned picture book art style with a fun branching plot and witty animal characters.

All in all, if you enjoy the detective gaming genre (E.g. Ace Attorney or the banter from Frogware's Sherlock Holmes series) and/or interacting with birds from Hatoful Boyfriend - then this might be a game for you.

WARNING: Some slight Spoilers are written in the Review!
NOTE: This Game takes as Inspiration the Ace Attorney Series, hence I will compare it furthermore in my Review with said Series
Aviary Attorney puts you into the Role of Private Defense Attorney "JayJay Falcon" with his Assistant "Sparrowson".
The Setting is set in France 1848.
The World itself is depicted like the Reality, so all past/present Events (and to some Degree also Persons) are real in this Game.
Like the Ace Attorney Series, the Acts begins with a Request to defend/meet someone. From there starts the Investigation for Clues/Evidences before the Trial Day comes.
You carry a Wallet with some Money for buying/bribing Persons for Info/Evidences. If you solve Cases, you get Payment. Otherwise you can earn Money by playing a Card Game in the Student Tavern.
When the Investigation begins, there are 2 major differences:
1) Visiting Places costs Time (1 Day) and sometimes you cannot visit all places for a Search. Choosing wrong Places or simply waste Time will end with not enough Evidence for the Trial. This can result in a GUILTY Verdict for the defending Client. In the Ace Attorney Series, the Game will only let you proceed if you have collected everything possible.
2) Throughout the Game you will be faced with many Decisions to be made. Most of the Decisions will alter the Story and influence where you will end in the last Act. In the Ace Attorney Series, the Outcome is always the same, so you cannot influence the Story at how it proceeds.
Unlike the Ace Attorney Games you can lose the Game for not having enough Evidences before Trial or/and choosing wrong Answers/Decisions. You can always reload an Act and even pick the desired Day, so no skipping endless Texts until you reach a Decision Point.
The Courtroom Part is nearly identical. Witness will state a Testimony -> Cross Examination -> find the Objection hidden in the Testimony -> rinse and repeat until final Verdict from Judge and Jury.
Here are some of my + / o / - Points:
Positive:
-Fantastic Artwork and Designs, which gives off a "Classy" Atmosphere
-Good Orchestral Soundtrack which fully supports the Art Design
-Serious Story with dark Undertones
-Funny Sidekick which assists the Protagonist in many different Ways
-Most Animals have Jobs or Personality which supports/contradicts their Character (Example: A Donkey as an arrogant all-knowing Librarian, A Fox who works as a cunning Private Investigator, etc.)
-Decisions during In-game can alter the Story and its End (3 different Endings)
-Finding Errors in Witnesses Testimony through Evidence are logically built
-Many Possibilities to gather Evidence/Infos through Gifts, Bribing, etc.
-Visiting Places costs Time, therefore making it crucial to decide where to go next
-It's possible to lose Cases if not enough Evidences are gathered
-Possibility to load previous Acts and all of its Days!
-Card Game for earning more Money
Neutral:
-No Possibility to access Inventory, etc. while on the City Map
-You can earn more Money through playing a Game at the Student Tavern to avoid Shortage, but it's not that difficult if you keep winning the Cases
-Casual Cinematics which can be accessed from the City Map (only on specific Points and optional), can sometimes contain Spoiler
-French Words/Places/Persons can sometimes be confusing
-No Steam Overlay
Negative:
-Only 4 Acts
-Short Duration of the Game (5-8 Hours)
-Memory Leak Bug during my Play (Fullscreen)
-No Skip Button during Texts if you want to reach certain Points
-Some Decisions (Example: Tell Truth/Lie) aren't really Decisions, since Sparrowson will interrupt if choosed wrong and decide the "right" Course
Fazit:
What caught me primarily, was the Artdesign. I love it and the Characters inhabiting this alternate World.
Ace Attorney Fans will get a familiar but very different Experience.
My real Negative Point, was the short Duration for this Game. Could have been longer, but just take it as it is.
For those who like also Visual Novels with Decisions, can't make a bad "Decision" with this Game ;)

This always kept me on edge and hoping i'd get another flare soon.
On the negative side of things, I don't think this game does Unreal Engine 4 justice. Everything from the textures to some of the lighting just looks very mediocre. Instead of the in-game objects looking sharp and clear on max settings, they seem to just look fuzzy. I don't know if they just directly ported the PS4 version of the game with minimal changes or what.
The other thing is the player character's commentary about the area around you. Alot of it seemed out of place and even annoying at times. Watch some gameplay on youtube before you decide to buy. Otherwise, avoid.

-Locked to 30 FPS

But the most annoying thing for me were the random crashes every 15-20 minutes. Just when I start enjoying the story, the game crashes. And just that, no error messages, nothing, it just randomly crashes and you have to start again from your last save. No change of settings, no mods, nothing helped to fix them.
This is the first time I got so frustrated that I applied for a refund.
I know people are suggesting mods, or disabling some services in Windows, but I think that making a user do this just to properly enjoy the game is unacceptable. Besides, disabling services affects OS functionality (e.g. you can't type in Modern Win10 apps if you disable Touch Keyboard and Handwriting Panel Service, etc.). A game should work without the user having to do all this stuff.
It's such a shame that a really good and charming game like this gets such a bad treatment on the PC. For now, I'd avoid the PC port and get a PS4 or Vita version, at least until this one gets fixed (if it ever gets fixed, that is).

If not for the ammount of stages. this game would be a 10/10.
Sneaky Sneaky is a stealth game with a cartoon-ish art style. In the game, you have to get back a sack of gems that is taken away from you on the start, There are 17 Stages, and Three "Scenarios", Respectively, The Woods, The Canyon (Desert) and The City, each one presents different enemies and different mechanics.
The main character (Your character) has 4 Different "Skills":
- Health : Ammount of hearts (Most enemies deal 1 Heart of damage, Some deal 0.5, some deal 1.5 and some deal more.)
- Melee Damage : Damage with the sword (You have to be on the tile next to the enemy to meele him)
- Ranged Damage : Bow (You have to manually aim)
- Walking Distance : Ammount of tiles you can walk using one (Of three) "Charges" while in "Combat Mode".
Each time you level up you can add one point to each of them (12 levels total), Health has 5 Possible upgrades, Melee has 2, Ranged has 2 and Walking has 2.
There is a shop where you can buy, Health potions, Ham (bait), Mana potion (Fills your "Charges" while in combat mode), Hammer (lets you break rocks), Sleepy potion (You add them to arrows and you can make your enemies sleep instead of killing/harming them) and The barrel (You "wear" a barrel and you are completely sneaky for one stage.)
Cons of the game :
- Short - 17 Stages, While they are all "Easy" if you dont care about maxing out the points.
- The game doesnt force you to use all mechanics. - I personally only used The bow, sword, health potion and ham. If you are very good (And full of patience) you can finish all stages flawlessly with only a bow and sword.
Pros:
- Its fun to try and beat all stages 100%. - + Achievments
- The gameplay can get intense if youre almost getting caugh.
- Lots of different paths to get to the ending.
- Lots of different enemies and mechanics
- The art is fun, which makes you be able to play the game for an indefinite ammount of time without tiring of it.
- Some posters have some fun jokes - "The right to brag." , "20 Mins of backrub", etc
- Variety of enemies
- Price
- I only stumbled across 1 bug
Conclusion:
I recommend the game to people who like to 100% everything, as it is fun and due to the art style, you can play it for a long time. It is cheap and provides you with at least 3 Hours of fun! I'd say that even peolpe who dont like puzzle games should buy it, to be honest.
Sound/Music : 9/10 - Funky and matches the game. Creates a mood.
Art : 10/10 - The art style matches the game perfectly, Everything is colorful so it doesnt tire your eyes.
Enjoyability : 8.5 / 10 - If there were more stages, this game would be flawless.
Overall : 9/10
Suggestions:
- Add scoreboards so we can compare our scores for each stage to other people! Would incentivate lots of people to buy due to the competitivity!
- Add Bonus points due to time (The less time, the more extra points)
- Release more stages!
- Add map editors, so we can create our own stages and share with people on an in-game hub!
Props to the devs. Very fun game!

Easy and boring game. Not challenging at all. Finished it in 2 hours. If it wasn't on sale (2$), I would have never bought it,
.
.
.
But seriously...
I have finished the game and completed almost every achivement. It took me aproximatly only 3.5 hours. And that's one of the cons. The game is really short. It isn't really hard of a puzzle game, but it will take you some retries to complete some levels and if you are going for the "gold star" on everything it will take even more retries, but that is the meaning.
Gameplay:
The game is very simple. You move your character around/hide and try to avoid getting "Detected". You will need to kill the enemies before they kill you or if you think everything out and "time" perfectly you will kill everyone without getting damaged. It is possible to avoid every enemy and complete the level (but that is very boring!). After completing a level you will get a certain amount of exp (determines on how good you completed the level). You use the exp to level up you character. There are not many possibilities to level up your character, only 4 things you can level up and it is kind off boring. But since the game is short it is okay, you wont need many charcter upgrades.
Levels are not so long. It will take you aproximatly 5-8 min to complete a level (it depends on how far you are in the game). One level is build up of many (5-12) "scenes" and the design of the scenes in 1 level are the same. Levels vary a little from each other, but it's only when you enter a new region that they change design the most. There are 3 regions, Impwood (6 levels), Cursed Canyon (5 levels) and Summer Canyon (5 levels). Impwood got the forest design, with a lot of trees and bushes, Cursed Canyon got sand and skeletons, while Summer Canyon is in a kingdom/city.
Game design:
It is simple, just as the game. It is not as pretty as games like "Bastion" or "Braid". But since the game was so cheap, the design is "okay".
Conclusion:
Simple game, not a hard puzzle game, it will take you some retries to complete the levels. The game is short (3-5 hours, depends on how fast you do it). All computers can run it.
-If it is on sale and you like wasting your time on simple puzzle-games, you should totally buy it!

There’s a little something charming about the robopocalypse but it doesn’t really matter. Solve the programs
The entire point of the game is to code basically. You have a limited instruction set where you can add, subtract, jump, jump conditionally, and combinations of those. You use these primitive instructions to solve problems ranging from dividing to sorting. Overall, the game is a lot easier to get into compared to something like TIS-100. A drag and drop system with an easy system to get help really goes to making this really friendly for people not familiar with programming. For people that are, it’s similar to a programming in a SUPER basic assembly and the challenge comes from making the programs run as efficiently as possible with the fewest instructions. If you’ve done any programming in the past, you’ll probably be able to solve the problems without many issues and the efficiency is the difficulty. If you’re into low level stuff, great but I was kind of hoping for functions or the ability to put a number in a register but sadly those aren’t there. However, I can understanding wanting to stick to a limited instruction set.

Cartoonish visuals and it ran great. No issues

Overall, it’s a good way to get familiarized with programming and is pretty new programmer friendly.

If you can handle a lot of dedication go for it this game will take up days of your life figuring things out on your own. For me however it was incredibly frustrating because I really needed hints on how to go about things but all i got was an answer sheet, like if you're doing level 20's multiplicaiton you'll get your answer is 63 since it's 9 x 7 but how do you go about getting to that step is what I was desperately looking for.
TL:DR this game is just requiring more dedication than I could give it because it is just asking for way too much with little help at a difficulty scaling that jumps too high after a point

This is an absolute cracker.
The simplest way to describe Human Resource Machine is as a game that "gamifies" writing computer code. Each level is essentially a particular computational task that you need to complete. Easy to begin but gets VERY tricky. Many of the hard achievements, which comprise of among other things requests to optimise your code, were certainly beyond me!
It has the same surreal, Tim Burton-esque feel of the developers earlier title, World of Goo (which is a classic) but it's a totally different game. It has great music, whacky graphical style, and being set in a large corporation, takes potshots at modern office life in a most amusing way.
Recommended to anyone who loves great puzzle games (and anyone tempted to minimise the skill required to optimise computer code).

I grew up and actively participated in the skill jump scene seen throughout various quake/halflife/unreal based games. I enjoyed the skill based challenge of these, they were rudimentary but there was something about the use of the game mechanics in such a unique way that captivated me. It never felt unfair, it was my own lack of skill. It didn't hurt there was an active community as well to be part of.
So along comes a game designed to capitalise on this as so few games have got FPS platforming right. Great looking and with some relatively tight mechanics.
However, where I rarely felt cheated before, past the half way mark deadcore constantly has sections of rote memorisation. There are long and un-checkpointed parts that force you to replay countless times to learn them. Even a half-decent FPS player would find it hard to impossible to judge many of the jumps on reaction. This is especially evident in the gravity sections, with no easy indication of orientation, its very easy to get lost before being summarily thrown into the abyss.
There are enemies whose only purpose seems to be to frustrate and foil jumping runs, you can only delay and cannot kill them. Your gun has limited ammo between checkpoints, that are again put further and further apart. This gun is required to activate switches yet can be depleted to stop aforementioned enemies, I cannot see how this was a sensible design choice.
Overall, an interesting concept with fantastic graphics, but layering on artificial difficulty with too many frustrating and confusing gameplay elements to remain as fun as it starts.

This game will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ it's best played in short bursts to avoid frustration until you get the level layout down and can attempt speedruns. However with this difficulty comes a very high skill ceiling, meaning that people who have a knack for it or put in the time to get good will get REALLY good, good enough to show off to friends and impress Youtube subscribers.
People have complained that this game only appeals to speedrunners and streamers and that it's a game designed to be watched rather than played, which I have to agree with, if you're not up to the challenge.
This game won't hold your hand, if you can't think fast enough and react quickly enough to solve puzzles on the fly while being knocked around by loathsome little death cubes and shot at by turrets, you won't be able to master this game. Maybe you'll be able to beat it through trial and error, but this is a game that rewards the player enormously for mastering it.
Playing this game goes something like this:
"I can't do it!"
"This is impossible!"
"Ok I see how it's supposed to be done."
"@!#& I almost had it!"
"I did it!"
The trailer says all you need to know about the gameplay, solve increasingly confusing puzzles as fast as you can, gameplay is very tight, there is absolutely zero chance of you making a wrong move or missing a jump. The game is too simple to have any real flaws, and I can't in good conscience call it's fair but punishing difficulty a negative point.
In short, this is Portal on crack, please do not feed the cubes, keep your hands and feet inside the gravity field at all times.

This is technically a competant platformer game, and the visuals are absolutely stunning. The game is capable of making you think outside the box a little to beat certain puzzles, which is really cool.
So why don't I recommend this game? Well, this may be a personal thing, but I felt that this game fell into the pitfall that a lot of these type of games do: Just because you have trouble on the last in a series of puzzles, you will need to replay the previous ones over and over and over and over and over and over and over again, to the point where, to me, it genuinely stopped being fun or interesting. It quickly went from a game of thinking to a game of repeating stuff I've done a dozen times just to get yet another shot at the one part that was actually giving me trouble.
I didn't hate this game, since when it played fair, it was genuinely very good. But it got far too frustrating for me since I simply hate having to repeat things I've already completed. I'd gladly play a sequel that doesn't do this.

This is purely a matter of taste.
Do you like those simple, almost pedantically hard platformers of yesteryear? If yes, then you will probably like this game.
But if, like me, you're not really a of fan of those and were hoping that this was one of those modern puzzle platformers with stories you can be invested in and/or more cerebral gameplay mechanics (such as Braid, Thomas Was Alone, or FEZ), then you should be aware that that's not what this game is.
The game's main charms are the quite wonderful art style and the neat gimmick of being able to shift between worlds... But if you're not enjoying the gameplay much, these charms will wear thin pretty quick. This game has no real story and its gameplay really doesn't consist of much more than a series of well-timed jumps and collecting gems. Even the world-shifting gimmick ultimately does not seem to do much beyond making certain platforms appear or disappear. Checkpoints seem sparse, and after having to go back and redo half the level many times due to missing some unforgiving jumps (and being unable to save during a level), I realized that this game was just not for me.
There's no doubt that this is a well-made game. But it just isn't for everyone. Get this game if you feel a lot of nostalgia towards the late '80s or early '90s when platformers were hard but simple. Otherwise, give it a pass.

PROS
+ Decent story with surprising choice-driven consequences,
+ the story was memorable,
+ Music is good,
+ Excellent skill tree,
+ Nice weapon and armor update system,
+ Combat system is very much like Batman Arkham Asylum and Mad Max,
+ Value priced @ $15; even better if on sale,
+ there's a sequel out now if you enjoyed this adventure and wanted to continue it,
CONS
- The ending felt a little rushed,
- The Epilogue could've been better,
- Voice acting is occasionally bad,
- Too many loading screens
- As you can see from my playtime, it is short, likely between 7 - 15 hours
FINAL THOUGHTS: I like this game. It reminded me of the low expectations I had when I played Gothic 1 and Witcher 1. I ended up buying The Technomancer. only because I liked how the Mars' story felt at the end. Overall it is a good RPG with many of the RPG elements you come to expect including unexpected choice consequences. Plus the combat system and skill tree makes the game fun. Also, there's are several points where you can replay to make a different choice to see a different outcome.
FINAL VERDICT: 7/10

Alchemy Mysteries acts as one of those games that deserve the much wanted middle thumb, or neutral rating. I emntion this fact for various reasons. First, it's a HOG game, meaning there's not much playtime, there's lots of hidden object scenes, and there's mini games, and various puzzles. Okay, so the positive aspects of Alchemy Mysteries can be considered as not many in this context. Reasonably well structured hidden object scenes, in which point&clicking all over the screen will do the trick. A soundtrack that is not memorable, but suits the game's atmosphere nonetheless. And a story that, a few of the times, can be considered as "good".
But, thing is, this title's negative aspects are too many, in contrast with the positive ones. I mean, the ending is cheesy, rushed, and not really adequate to what the main story was aiming for. The voice acting is bad, sometimes even terrible. There are two puzzles that, in my opinion, are not well made and even though I managed to complete them without help, I found them not rewarding in any way. And, finally, the constant backtracking to different scenes, and the existence of numerous items that will probably not even be used because someone will take them from you at a certain point in the game.
I mean, it's really up to you as a gamer to decide whether or not to purchase this game, because it's price point is really, really low. But, in my opinion, I would pass. It all comes down as being a game that, besides "teaching" some alchemy story, has no point and no interesting story to it. It's up to you.

If you enjoyed Ace Attorney, GET THIS GAME.
This game is certainly niche.  I doubt anyone was clamoring for a furry procedural game set in revolutionary France based off of a charicaturist's sketches and period classical music.  And yet..!
It's definitely made in the vein of Ace Attorney, but it also goes out of its way to turn the genre on its head at times, and even gives a bit of a branching plot depending on whether you win or lose the cases (and yes, you can lose a case and continue the story!)  But I truly admire the story Sketchy Logic has put together with the elements they chose.  The art, music, setting, and gameplay all manage to tie into each other for the story, which has surprising depth for its brevity.
My only complaint about the game is that there is not more of it, which is a happy complaint to have.  And even then, I felt very satisfied by the game as a whole as I watched the credits.  Anyone who enjoys the time period, Ace Attorney-styled games, or even examples as games as an artistic medium should give this one a go.  I loved it.
